formation.text: A one-stroke numeral graph for the abstract number one. It is classified as indicative, but the concrete route is unresolved: the line may have marked one directly or may have developed through counting with fingers or rods. This is a whole-graph analysis, not a compound of smaller parts.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogram (指事): a horizontal stroke, indicating the number “one”.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ʔit. Descendants from the *ʔit etymon account for the majority of the dialectal forms for “one” in Chinese (Mandarin, Jin, Gan, Hakka, Hui, Xiang, Yue, Wu groups, etc.).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology Database, CUHK)
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 一 entry
evidence.text: The entry says oracle-bone and bronze forms represent the concept of one with an abstract horizontal stroke, and that these forms and the small-seal form use one horizontal stroke for the number one. It cites oracle-bone 《合集》21575「一牛」 as a numeral use. The page also discusses 弌 as a more complex form: it reports the received Shuowen label 古文一, then gives a later proposal deriving the shape through 戈 and 一, and marks the suggested 戌-based precursor as unattested and tentative. This is a source account, not independent verification of every proposed graphic transition.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 一

evidence.source: 古代漢字研究 — 漢数字の起源
evidence.field: 第一章「一から四の起源」, section 1, paragraphs 154–180
evidence.text: This scholarly discussion presents several accounts for 一 through 四: a count of extended fingers, counting rods, or an abstract indicative mark for the imagined number. It describes the one-line indicative account as drawing quantity one with a single line, but concludes that the exact route (direct mark versus mediation by fingers or rods) cannot be decided on the evidence discussed. Its author favors 指事 as a general precursor, while acknowledging uncertainty about the concrete graphic process. This is a modern study's analysis, not direct proof of a specific depicted object.
evidence.title: 古代漢字研究 ―漢数字の起源―

formation.text: The formation is disputed. One proposal interprets the crossed graph as depicting a cut across a line, then suggests the sign was borrowed for the numeral because the words may have sounded alike. The competing account documents 七 for “seven” in oracle-bone writing onward; the original referent, spoken name, and proposed sound connection are not established.

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Research on Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study reports that 七 has recorded the numeral from oracle-bone writing through early Western Han clerical forms. It describes the early graph as crossed horizontal and vertical strokes, and says a bent lower vertical stroke appears after the Eastern Han. Its proposed explanation for the graphic change is avoidance of confusion with 十. The article cites specific examples, including oracle-bone 合集10650, Western Zhou 小盂鼎 inscription 集成2839, Qin Shuihudi slips, and Eastern Han-period Wuwei medical slips. It also discusses alternate spellings 桼、漆、柒 and copy or printing errors in those forms; these are numeral spellings, not necessarily stages in 七’s graphic development.
evidence.title: 数词{七}的用字研究（一）

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The database says interpretations of 七’s shape are numerous and unresolved. It favors the analysis that 七 is an early form of 切: 一 and 丨 represent cutting across a line, and after 七 was borrowed for the numeral, 刀 was added to form 切. It also records a different proposal that the shape originated in a hand gesture. This supports reporting the cut analysis as a proposal rather than established graphic fact.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Oxford University Press, William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart
evidence.field: Old Chinese reconstruction system and scope
evidence.text: The book description identifies this as a reconstruction of Old Chinese phonology, morphology, and lexicon based on several kinds of comparative evidence. The locally supplied Baxter–Sagart row for 七 gives MC tshit and OC *[tsʰ]i[t], gloss ‘seven’ (local file `sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv`, 七 row). That local table row was checked as requested, but it is local data, not an independently inspected external character record. No 切 row was supplied, and the accessible external pages inspected here do not establish a matched reconstruction pair for 七 and 切; therefore sound similarity is not treated as proof that 七 originally named cutting.
evidence.title: Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Research on Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study identifies 七 as the long-standing graph for the numeral. It reports crossed horizontal and vertical strokes from oracle-bone writing through early Western Han clerical forms, citing oracle-bone 合集10650 and Western Zhou bronze 小盂鼎 (集成2839). It describes later differentiation from 十, with a rightward bend in the lower vertical becoming established after the Eastern Han. This account treats the history as numeral writing and graphic differentiation; it does not establish an earlier ‘cut’ meaning.
evidence.title: 数词{七}的用字研究（一）

evidence.source: Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica, 漢字「七」：字形演變
evidence.text: The page proposes that 七 originally meant ‘cut,’ that bronze forms added a short stroke across the horizontal, and that the seal form bent the vertical to distinguish 七 from 十. It further says the numeral use was a loan and 刀 was added to make 切. These are the page’s assertions; they conflict with the Zhengzhou study’s account of 七 as numeral from oracle-bone writing onward, so the cut origin and borrowing sequence remain disputed.
evidence.title: 漢字「七」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The database favors an analysis of 七 as an early form of 切: 一 and 丨 are interpreted as a line cut across, after which 七 was borrowed for the numeral and 刀 added in 切. It also describes interpretations as numerous and unresolved and records an alternative hand-gesture proposal. The parsing of the strokes and their semantic role are thus part of a disputed account, not independently established component meanings.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

formation.text: The graph’s construction is disputed. A paleographic account interprets its three equal strokes as counting rods representing three; a later lexicographic account associates them with Heaven, Earth, and humanity. The evidence does not establish that the earliest graph copied rods or settle these accounts as its original formation.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Institute of History and Philology, Xiaoxuetang
evidence.field: 字形演變; 金文 record 集成04261; explanation
evidence.text: The entry lists a bronze-script record identified as 集成04261, Chu manuscript forms and a Small Seal form. It explains the three equal horizontal strokes as three counting rods used to record the number three. The page does not textually describe each early glyph image, and this explanation does not by itself establish that the earliest graph was directly devised by copying physical rods.
evidence.title: 漢字「三」：字形演變

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcription of Shuowen Jiezi with Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.field: 三 entry; 許慎 account and 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen account defines 三 as “the way of Heaven, Earth, and humanity” and says it is formed “from the number three”; it also records 弎 as an ancient form written with 弋. Duan Yucai distinguishes the definition from the graphic explanation and comments that the three strokes embody the three powers. This is a later lexicographic account, not an independent Shang attestation. No semantic extension chronology follows from this gloss.
evidence.title: 說文解字「三」

formation.text: 上 is an indicative graph, not a compound of semantic or phonetic components. Its early construction is interpreted as a short mark above a reference line to indicate the upper position; sources differ on whether some early lines were curved or horizontal. This historical analysis describes the earlier construction, not a decomposition of the present strokes. The received Shuowen text also classifies 上 as indicative, a Han-era analysis rather than independent confirmation of the earlier history.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析 / 上 / 字形與用例
evidence.text: The database describes the oracle-bone graph as a short stroke above a baseline, which could be curved in early forms and was often straightened in later forms because straight horizontal lines were easier to carve. It reports that early oracle-bone and bronze forms were similar to 二, with a vertical stroke added in late Spring-and-Autumn bronze forms to distinguish 上 from 下 and 二. It gives the original meaning as 'above/upper side.' Its examples include oracle-bone 上帝 (Heji 16703), 上甲 (Heji 6384), and a paired 上/下 passage (Heji 6204); Zhou bronze examples include 上 meaning 'above,' as in 㝬鐘, and 'on/at the side of,' as in 啟尊. These are source-reported readings and examples, not direct inspection of the inscribed artifacts here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 香港教育局 字源考釋
evidence.field: 字形流變 / 字形解說
evidence.text: This character-specific account presents oracle-bone 上 as two horizontal strokes, the longer lower stroke representing a horizon and the shorter upper stroke marking 'above.' It says later bronze and small-seal forms changed the upper stroke to a vertical stroke to avoid confusion with 二, and the modern standard graph adds a dot. This differs in detail from the CUHK account's curved-baseline description, though both identify a positional marker above a reference line and later graphic differentiation.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 — 上

evidence.source: 許慎《說文解字》 text as presented by Shuowen.cn
evidence.field: 小篆字頭 丄 / entry text
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry reads: '丄，高也。此古文上，指事也。凡丄之屬皆从丄。上，篆文丄。' It treats 丄 as an ancient form for 'high/above' and labels it 指事; it identifies 上 as the seal-script form. This is evidence for the Han lexicographic analysis, not independent confirmation of the earlier graphic history.
evidence.title: 说文解字在线字典查询

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology)
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 上 as an indicative graph: a short mark above a longer reference line indicates the upper side. It describes some oracle-bone examples with a curved baseline, later often straightened because carving a horizontal line was easier. It reports that early oracle-bone and bronze forms could resemble 二, with a vertical stroke added in many late Spring-and-Autumn forms to distinguish the graph. Its examples include Shang-inscription 上帝 and 上甲, Zhou-bronze spatial uses, and a Chu-script form with 辵 added as a semantic element for upward movement. These are the dictionary's reports, not independent inspection of each inscription.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》；白于藍撰「上」條
evidence.field: 上部 / 上 / 字形與用例；PDF p.14, printed p.2
evidence.text: The entry calls 上 an indicative graph. Its oracle-bone forms place a short horizontal mark above a longer reference line; the bronze form continues this pattern. Spring-and-Autumn forms add a vertical stroke, which the entry identifies as the basis of the clerical form. Warring States forms vary: some add decorative strokes or omit the upper short mark, while others add 是 or 止 as meaning determinatives, yielding forms analyzed as 从是或止、上声. The entry gives the original meaning as spatial, opposite 下, and reports extensions to high places, heaven, and ruler. Checked the 上 headword, numbered glyph sequence and labels, prose through the end of the entry, and the transition to 帝 against the attached original-resolution scan. PDF page 15 begins 帝, not a continuation of 上. The diagrams cite 《甲文编》 p.3, 《金文编》 p.5, 《类编》 p.2, 《楚系简帛》 p.17, 《古文典》 p.656, 《汉语字形表》 p.3, 《说文》 p.7, and 《篆隶表》 p.3; those cited pages were not separately inspected.
evidence.title: 字源, 李學勤主編, 天津古籍出版社 / 遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692; WorldCat lookup inaccessible

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》；白于藍撰「上」條
evidence.field: 上部 / 上 / 字形與用例；PDF p.14, printed p.2
evidence.text: The scanned entry identifies 上 as an indicative graph: oracle forms place a short horizontal mark above a longer line to indicate the upper position. It describes Spring-and-Autumn forms with an added vertical stroke, varied Warring States forms, and the original spatial sense contrasted with 下. I inspected the supplied scan pixels: the 上 headword, glyph sequence and labels, and the prose through the entry’s end; page 15 begins 帝, so this is not a continuation. The listed underlying glyph dictionaries were not separately consulted. No OCR error was found.
evidence.title: 字源, 李學勤主編, 天津古籍出版社 / 遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692; PDF p.14, printed p.2

formation.text: An indicative graph (指事): the short mark’s position below the longer line signals “below.” One account identifies the upper line as the horizon; another describes it as a reference line. The graph is analyzed as a whole, not as a compound of separate sound and meaning parts.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 下 as an indicative graph: the Shang oracle-bone form places a short stroke below a longer reference stroke, expressing the lower position. It reports that the curved reference line was later commonly written as a horizontal line; early oracle-bone and bronze forms are identified as 𠄟. The entry says a vertical stroke was added in late Spring and Autumn forms to distinguish it from 上 and 二, and that Warring States regional forms no longer used 𠄟. Chu forms may add a short decorative stroke above. This conflicts in detail with the Academia Sinica account, which describes the reference as a horizon and puts the distinguishing change in small seal writing.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 下

evidence.source: 中央研究院文字學資料庫 / Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The graph-history note says the oracle-bone form has two horizontal strokes: the longer upper stroke represents the horizon and the shorter lower stroke is an indicative mark for ‘below’. It says a different 下 form arose in small seal script to avoid confusion with 二, changing the lower horizontal stroke to a vertical stroke. The page lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu bamboo-and-silk, small-seal, and Shuowen-seal sections, but its machine-readable text does not identify a dated specimen for each stage.
evidence.title: 漢字「下」：字形演變

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes the oracle-bone form as two horizontal strokes: the upper, longer line represents the horizon and the lower, shorter line is an indicative mark for ‘below’. It says a small-seal form changed the lower horizontal to a vertical stroke to avoid confusion with 二. This account is not fully aligned with CUHK’s placement of the added vertical stroke in late Spring and Autumn forms.
evidence.title: 漢字「下」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.field: 《說文》 entry and 形義通解
evidence.text: The entry quotes the received Shuowen explanation: 「丅，底也。指事。下，篆文丅。」 It interprets the oracle graph as a short stroke placed below a curved line, later often made horizontal; it says late Spring and Autumn forms commonly added a vertical stroke to avoid confusion with 上 and 二. It cites oracle-bone uses 《合集》7428 and 《屯南》1115, bronze uses including 番生𣪕蓋, and later extensions to humility, ‘descend’, and ‘capture/take’ (《戰國策·齊策六》). These examples show uses, but the entry does not provide a complete dated semantic sequence.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 下

formation.text: 不 is treated as a whole pictograph, but its depicted subject is disputed. Proposals include plant roots or a germ, a flower calyx, Shuowen’s bird flying upward toward the sky, and a tassel at the rear of a 戈-related graph. The last proposal’s abstract has incomplete glyphs, so the graph identity and proposed sound link remain unresolved; no separate phonetic component is established.

components.text: Treat 不 as one whole picture, not as established separate parts. Proposed subjects include roots or a germ, a calyx, a bird rising toward the sky, and a tassel on a 戈-related graph; the last proposal’s graph identity is unclear.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 形義源流通解 / 甲骨金文字形、用法
evidence.text: The database reports two competing analyses of the oracle-bone and bronze graph: a ground line with root-like strokes, interpreted by some scholars as a plant root and linked by Chen Shihui to 茇; or a flower receptacle/calyx, identified by other scholars as the original graph for 柎. It also records 不 as a negative adverb in oracle-bone inscriptions, with an example glossed as a question about whether it will rain, and gives bronze-inscription uses for negation, ‘great’ (read 丕), a state name (邳), and personal or clan names. These are source-reported analyses and examples, not a settled derivation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析：不

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The database labels 不 the original form of 胚 and interprets the horizontal stroke as ground and the lower strokes as roots of a germinating seed. It separately notes the flower-calyx interpretation and says the graph was later borrowed for negation, leaving the original sense lost. The page lists oracle, bronze, Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen stages, but its text does not give dated attestations for each stage.
evidence.title: 漢字「不」：字形演變

evidence.source: 周堯 (Shan Zhouyao)
evidence.text: The article reviews the bird account in Shuowen and the flower-receptacle/calyx account advanced by earlier scholars, then questions whether the oracle-bone forms fit the flower interpretation. It also considers a root-related interpretation and concludes that the graph appears connected with plants or roots, while explicitly leaving its original sense unresolved for want of sufficient lexical evidence. The article records variant oracle and bronze forms and discusses forms whose lower strokes do not fit a calyx analysis.
evidence.title: 「不」字本義為花梢說質疑

evidence.source: Xu Shen, as quoted in the CUHK Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The quoted Shuowen explanation says 不 depicts a bird flying upward and not returning downward, with 一 representing the sky. This is a historical lexicographic explanation, not confirmation of the graph’s original referent; the modern database presents it alongside competing root and calyx analyses.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析：不

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The page supplies no defensible decomposition into an independent semantic component plus a phonetic component. The database’s listed historical stages concern the graph 不 itself; the separate root and calyx proposals interpret the entire graph. The horizontal stroke and lower strokes are parts of those proposed depictions, not established sound components. There is therefore no supported component-to-character pronunciation comparison for a phonetic component.
evidence.title: 漢字「不」：字形演變

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》
evidence.field: 不 entry; PDF p. 1050, printed p. 1035; scan /home/catalin/hanzi-etymology-books/research-ocr/ziyuan-full/page-1050/source.png (source scan SHA-256 daf01258755f33f165f0cf5d38e795da205fcbfdf0993ed76a145cde698ad629)
evidence.text: The printed 不 entry calls 不 a pictograph and reports the calyx/stalk analysis: it cites 《甲骨文字典》 for 不 as an original graph for 柎, glossed as the base of a flower receptacle, and quotes the 《詩·小雅·棠棣》 gloss with Zheng Xuan’s note that 不 should be 柎 and that 不 and 柎 were homophonous in ancient pronunciation. It then characterizes the Shuowen explanation as inaccurate and describes borrowing 不 for negation before verbs and adjectives. The scan shows printed headword 不 and the cited quotation; I directly inspected the pixels for the entry and the continuation on the next page.
evidence.title: 字源 — 中华文史学术论著库 (bibliographic record for 李學勤主編《字源》)

evidence.source: 周堯, 「『不』字本義為花梢說質疑」
evidence.text: Zhou reviews the flower-calyx account and challenges it against oracle-bone shapes, noting forms that the account does not explain. He entertains a plant-root possibility from graphic comparison, but says that ancient texts do not use 不 with a root meaning and leaves the original sense unresolved. This cautions against presenting the calyx account or the proposed root link as settled.
evidence.title: 「『不』字本義為花梢說質疑」

evidence.source: Park Hyun Joo (박현주), ‘不’字의 원형과 선진시기 의미 변화 고찰
evidence.text: The accessible abstract proposes a distinct account: 不 imitates the tassel at the rear of a particular graph for 戈, with a sound relationship to a tassel word. The abstract supplies incomplete glyph characters for the proposed weapon variant, so its precise identity and full argument cannot be confirmed from this record. This is an attributed proposal, not corroboration for the calyx or root explanations.
evidence.title: ‘不’字의 원형과 선진시기 의미 변화 고찰

formation.text: Derived: 东 is a cursive-derived form of 東. For the older graph, a significant but disputed analysis sees a tied bag and proposes that its sign was reused for “east” because the object’s name may have sounded like the direction word. The object’s ancient name and pronunciation are not known, so this sound-based explanation remains a proposal. Shuowen preserves another historical interpretation, reading 東 through 木 and 日 within 木; that account does not establish the graph’s early origin.

components.text: 东 is one whole graph derived from cursive 東, not a combination of independent 日 and 木 parts. In a disputed analysis of the older graph, 東 depicts a tied bag; this reading is not settled.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Pictograph of a basket or a bag. The current meaning "east" is a phonetic loan. The simplified character 东 was adapted from the cursive form of the traditional character 東.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text: From cursive script of 東 /东 (dōng); compare 車 → 车.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 東字甲骨部件分析
evidence.text: Database analysis says oracle-bone and bronze forms depict a sack containing material, tied at both ends, and gives “bag” as the original graphic sense. It says 東 was used by borrowing for the direction east in both oracle-bone and bronze material, citing the oracle-bone inscription 合集9735「東土受年」 and the poem 詩·召南·小星「三五在東」. It relates 東, 橐, 㯱, and 束 graphically and says 東 and 束 differentiated from one character. This is the database's analysis, not direct proof of the pictured item's spoken name.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析（東）

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 說文 comparison in 形義源流通解
evidence.text: The database quotes the Eastern Han 說文解字 entry:「東，動也。从木。官溥說：从日在木中。」It rejects the analysis of 東 as sun within a tree as an explanation of the graph. This is a historical account preserved by 說文, not confirmation of the early graphic origin.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析（東）

evidence.source: 陳雅雯, 成大中文學報 27, article “說「東」”
evidence.field: discussion of competing paleographic and loan analyses, pp. 158–160
evidence.text: The author disputes treating every early 東-shaped graph as a sack: she notes that many oracle-bone occurrences appear in personal, palace, place, and ritual names rather than an attested sack sense, and argues that assigning the original sense 橐囊 remains debatable. She also objects that a sound-only loan from 橐 to 東 is insufficiently demonstrated without explaining the graphic image's role; she treats the Shuowen and Dong-Fusang cultural reading as a possible substantive tradition and cites Allan's analysis of forms containing elements interpreted as 日 and 木. Thus the bag account is a well-supported database analysis but not an uncontested conclusion.
evidence.title: 說「東」

evidence.source: Outlier Linguistics
evidence.field: 東西南北, part 1, sections 東 and 束/橐
evidence.text: The article proposes bag-like origins for 東, 束, and 橐, reports 東 and 束 used interchangeably in bronze inscriptions, and analyzes east as a sound loan. It compares Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese forms 東 *tˤoŋ and 束 *s-tʰok, describing shared initial/root material despite differing codas. It also explains simplified 东 as derived from a cursive shorthand of 東. This is a modern specialist account; the specific name and pronunciation of the pictured sack are not independently recovered, so the phonetic pathway from the object's name to the word for east remains a proposal.
evidence.title: Explaining the Directions 東西南北, part 1: 東西

evidence.source: Outlier Linguistics, citing Baxter and Sagart
evidence.text: Outlier gives a simplified Baxter–Sagart 1.1 Old Chinese comparison: 東 *tˤoŋ and 束 *s-tʰok; it gives 橐 *tʰˤak and 石 *dAk for a separate sound-component discussion. These are reconstructions, not recorded pronunciations. The piece discusses 橐 and 石 as an internal phonetic relation, distinct from the claim that the whole graph 東 was borrowed to write “east.” No object-name pronunciation for the pictured bag is provided.
evidence.title: Explaining the Directions 東西南北, part 1: 東西

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The source analyzes 东/東 only as the traditional character 東's cursive-derived simplified form; 东 itself is not analyzed as containing independent 日 and 木 semantic components. This supports no component-origin claim for modern 东 beyond graphic derivation.
evidence.title: Explaining the Directions 東西南北, part 1: 東西

evidence.source: 陳雅雯, 成大中文學報 27
evidence.text: The article argues that a sack as the original referent is debatable because many early 東 contexts are names or ritual terms rather than attested sack uses. It also questions whether sound resemblance alone explains borrowing and discusses the possibility that early graph forms relate to 日 and 木 and that the Shuowen account preserves cultural tradition. This is a counteranalysis, not a settled alternative proof.
evidence.title: 說「東」

evidence.source: Outlier Linguistics
evidence.field: 東, 束 and 橐 graph and sound analyses
evidence.text: The article treats 東 and 束 forms as closely related and reports them interchangeable in bronze inscriptions; it proposes the 東 bag image was borrowed by sound to write “east.” It gives Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese 東 *tˤoŋ and 束 *s-tʰok, while describing 橐 *tʰˤak in its separate discussion of 石 as a sound component in 橐. These reconstructed forms do not independently establish the spoken name of the depicted bag, so the whole-graph loan’s source-name match remains unverified.
evidence.title: Explaining the Directions 東西南北, part 1: 東西

evidence.source: 說文解字 online
evidence.field: 東 entry and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The entry gives the Eastern Han dictionary’s account「東，動也。从木。官溥說：从日在木中」. The online transcription also gives Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary linking 木 to 榑木 and comparing 東 with 杲 and 杳. This is a historical graphic interpretation, not direct evidence of the oracle-bone graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「東」

formation.text: The traditional graph’s formation is disputed. Shuowen analyzes 兩 as 一 plus 㒳, with 㒳 meaning ‘divide evenly’ and also supplying sound; this is a lexicographic account, not confirmation of the graph’s original construction. Other proposals read the form as a chariot front or as a modified chariot part marking a pair of horses, but neither depiction is established. A proposed analysis as two 丙 forms is also unverified. The modern shape 两 does not resolve these questions.

evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi online transcription, entry 兩
evidence.field: text lines 6–8; Duan Yucai note lines 15–35
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry defines 兩 as a weight of twenty-four zhu and analyzes it as 从一、㒳, with 㒳 meaning ‘divide evenly’ and also supplying sound. Duan Yucai likewise explains the weight as twice the weight of a Huangzhong measure, while treating 从一㒳 as associative; this is an early lexicographic analysis, not independent paleographic confirmation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「兩」 — Shuowen.org

evidence.source: 李運富, “兩字職用演變研究（一）,” 河南大學漢字文明研究中心
evidence.text: The study reports 㒳 as the initial form, attested in early Western Zhou bronze inscriptions such as 盝驹尊 and 卫盉; an upper stroke form 兩 appears by the Spring and Autumn period and gradually replaces 㒳, with 兩 dominant after the Han. It distinguishes the Shuowen/Duan account (㒳 for ‘two’, 兩 for the weight unit) from scholars who consider 㒳 and 兩 one graph. It reviews the yoke/chariot hypothesis and raises objections: the forms and early uses do not securely establish a noun meaning ‘vehicle’. It proposes, cautiously, a modified chariot-front form used as a dedicated measure for a pair of horses. This proposal remains a hypothesis, not a demonstrated original depiction.
evidence.title: “两”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, “Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1”
evidence.field: data table search result and methodology note
evidence.text: The reconstructed 丙 *praŋʔ and the dossier’s 兩 *p.raŋʔ are similar in the Old Chinese transcription reported in the dossier and search-indexed official source, but a primary entry for 兩 could not be independently opened and compared. Thus the proposed 丙 phonetic analysis is plausible in sound terms but not verified here from the exact paired entries, and the graphic interpretation of the two forms remains a separate question. Do not treat this reconstructed comparison as evidence for the meaning or name of a depicted chariot part.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (20 September 2014)

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, received 說文解字 entry for 兩
evidence.field: entry text and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The entry defines 兩 as 24 zhu, the weight unit, and analyzes it as 从一、㒳, glossing 㒳 as ‘divide evenly’ and saying it also supplies sound. Duan Yucai treats the analysis as associative. This is a traditional lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the graph’s original pictorial basis.
evidence.title: 說文解字「兩」 — Shuowen.org

evidence.source: 李運富、何余華, “两”字职用演变研究（一）
evidence.field: discussion of disputed 車 and 丙 analyses
evidence.text: The authors recount analyses connecting 兩 and 丙 to parts of a chariot, then question whether the shapes fit the vehicle evidence and whether early uses show a noun meaning ‘vehicle’. They note that a supposed oracle-bone example for 丙 is uncertain and could instead show a measure word. Their alternative paired-horse measure account is explicitly conjectural. The source does not establish the original name or pronunciation of any depicted tool or vehicle part, so no borrowing based on such a name is supported here.
evidence.title: “两”字职用演变研究（一）

formation.text: Treat 个 as a whole graph. The transmitted analysis of related 箇 has 竹 for the bamboo category and 固 as a sound element. A commentary reports 个 as an alternate form meaning half a bamboo, but this does not establish that the modern classifier was borrowed from the spoken name of a bamboo object.

components.text: Read 个 here as a whole graph. A proposed breakdown into a tally and a person is not established as its historical construction.

In the related graph 箇, the transmitted analysis assigns 竹 the bamboo category. The curated seal-script-style image shows 竹 above 固; it illustrates this analysis, not a dated stage in 个’s graphic history.

In 箇, the transmitted analysis identifies 固 as the sound element. The cited Old Chinese forms for 固 and 箇 are similar but not identical; this comparison does not establish the spoken name of a bamboo object.

sound_limitation.text: The cited comparison gives a Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese form for 箇 and a reported form for 固, but no directly verified same-system reading for 固. The comparison supports reported similarity, not independent proof of the analysis or a bamboo object’s name.

sound.text: The reported Old Chinese forms are similar but not identical; the comparison is compatible with a sound relationship but does not independently verify the component analysis.

evidence.source: makemeahanzi
evidence.text: A tally 丨 of people 人

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcription of Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry says 箇 is a bamboo measure/stalk (竹枚) and is made from 竹 with 固 as phonetic. Duan’s commentary says the text also has 个 as an alternative form meaning half a bamboo; he attributes this report to a Tang edition quoted in 六書故 and discusses later uses of 个 for an individual piece. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of every proposed graphic or semantic link.
evidence.title: 說文解字「箇」

evidence.source: CUHK 漢語多功能字庫, 個 entry
evidence.text: The entry maps traditional 個 to simplified 个; gives 個 the Guangyun fanqie 古賀 and the Guangyun category 見母、歌/箇韻、去聲、開口一等; and analyzes 個 as semantic 人 plus phonetic 固. It cites Zheng Xuan’s explanation at 儀禮·士虞禮 that 个 is like 枚 and the vernacular 个/個 name is similar in sound. It also lists modern single/individual senses. The entry supports the traditional phonosemantic analysis of 個, but does not make 个 itself a person-plus-固 compound.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「個」

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction table, version 1.1 (2014)
evidence.field: pronunciation comparison: 箇, 個, 个; methodology note
evidence.text: The table lists 箇, 個, and 个 with Mandarin gè, Middle Chinese kaH, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *kˤa[r]-s, glossed piece/item or tally/piece/item. It explains that the Middle Chinese notation represents information from rhyme-book sources and is not itself a reconstruction. In this same system the three listed graph entries have matching readings, which supports phonetic compatibility of the written forms. It does not establish the original spoken name of bamboo or prove a historical loan from an independently recoverable bamboo-object name.
evidence.title: BaxterSagartOCbyMandarinMC2014-09-20

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 固 entry (reconstruction data attributed there to Zhengzhang 2003 and Baxter–Sagart 2014)
evidence.text: The entry gives 固 Mandarin gù, Middle Chinese Baxter kuH, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *[k]ˤa-s, and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *kaːs. It lists 箇 and 個 in 固’s phonetic series under Zhengzhang with *kaːls. Comparison within Baxter–Sagart therefore gives 固 *[k]ˤa-s versus 箇/個/个 *kˤa[r]-s: related but not identical reconstructed forms, consistent with a phonetic relationship rather than a claim of exact identity. Modern readings also differ in tone: 固 gù versus 個/个 gè.
evidence.title: 固 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart reconstruction table
evidence.field: scope of the cited reconstruction system
evidence.text: The authors specify that their table is a Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction list (version 1.1, 2014), sorted using Mandarin and Middle Chinese information, and that the symbols mark uncertainty where evidence does not decide presence or identity. Duan Yucai’s commentary reports 个 as an alternate form meaning half a bamboo, citing a Tang edition as quoted in 六書故. This records a historical lexicographic explanation; it does not independently establish a dated graphic chain from that form to modern 个.

evidence.text: The table lists 箇 with Mandarin gè, Middle Chinese kaH, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *kˤa[r]-s, glossed ‘piece, item’. This is one reconstruction system’s entry for 箇; it is not evidence for the original spoken name of a bamboo object or, by itself, proof of a whole-graph loan.

The file page describes a public-domain release for the drawing. This is a modern redraw of a historical script form, not a photograph or direct image of an ancient artifact. formation.text: Treat 中 as a pictographic whole: reported early forms show a long shaft crossing a central feature, sometimes with streamers. Proposals identify it as a flag or marker, drum, or ritual pole, but the referent remains unsettled. The reviewed analysis rejects the arrow-and-target account. The later Shuowen analysis instead parses an enclosure crossed by a vertical line; it does not establish the early design.

components.text: The early graph is described as a shaft crossing a circular or square feature, sometimes with streamers. Since the feature’s referent is disputed, this records the proposed pictorial whole rather than identified modern parts.
In the received Shuowen analysis, 口 is an enclosure in a later parsing of the graph. This interpretation is not an established breakdown of the earliest forms.
In that Shuowen analysis, 丨 is the line passing through the enclosure from top to bottom. This later interpretation does not establish the line’s role in the earliest graph.

evidence.source: CASE 報科學（國立臺灣大學）
evidence.field: 最早的「中」字及其造字初義、用法
evidence.text: Reports late-Shang oracle-bone and bronze forms with a long vertical shaft and sometimes attached streamers, plus a central circular or square feature; it also notes forms without streamers. It cites oracle-bone examples of 立中 in military, weather-related, and ancestral-ritual contexts. The author reviews competing interpretations of the center feature (including drum, central marker, sundial-related feature, and attachment) and says the evidence does not settle its referent. The article rejects the arrow-and-target account as unsupported by the graph and describes several other functional reconstructions as partly conjectural. Thus the dossier's flag-and-drum story is one proposal, not a secure component analysis.
evidence.title: 甲骨文、金文裡的「中」、「或」及何尊銘文裡最早的「中國」（上）

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 text and Duan Yucai commentary, reproduced by 說文解字 online
evidence.field: 《说文解字（附检字）》; 段玉裁《说文解字注》
evidence.text: The received Shuowen gloss is 内也 and parses 中 as 从口、丨，上下通. Duan's commentary discusses textual variants and interprets the line as entering the enclosure from above or below; this is a historical lexicographic analysis, not independent confirmation of the Shang form's original referent.
evidence.title: 中字说文解字在线查询_中字字形演变_中字篆体字形_中字说文解字注

evidence.source: CASE 報科學（國立臺灣大學）
evidence.field: 最早的「中」字及其造字初義、用法
evidence.text: The article describes late Shang oracle-bone and bronze forms with a long shaft, sometimes with streamer strokes, and a circular or square feature at the center. It reports variants without streamers; Western Zhou bronze forms continue both types, and some omit the central feature. The article reviews flag, marker, wind instrument, gnomon, arrow-and-target, drum, and ritual-pole interpretations. It rejects the arrow account for lack of an arrow shape and describes several other functional explanations as conjectural. The article ultimately favors a ritual pole bearing an ancestral inscription, but that is its conclusion, not a settled referent.
evidence.title: 甲骨文、金文裡的「中」、「或」及何尊銘文裡最早的「中國」（上）

evidence.text: The received Shuowen gloss is 內也, with the analysis 从口、丨，上下通. Duan Yucai discusses textual variants and reads the line as extending into the enclosure from above or below. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent evidence of the Shang graph's original referent.
evidence.title: 中字说文解字在线查询_中字字形演变_中字篆体字形_中字说文解字注

formation.text: This character has two documented relationships: an older lexicographic association with 幺 and its standardization as the simplified counterpart of 麽 in 1956. The available evidence does not establish how the 么 and 幺 shapes are graphically related, so no internal component analysis is warranted.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Variant form of 幺. In simplified Chinese 么 is also used to mean "[particle]", while in traditional Chinese this meaning is written with a separate character 麼.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text: Variant of 幺.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text: Simplified from 麽 (elimination of 麻). Officially adopted as the simplified form of 麽 in the Chinese Character Simplification Scheme (《漢字簡化方案》) in 1956.

evidence.source: 漢字簡化方案（1956）, reproduced at Wikisource
evidence.field: 第一表; 国务院决议
evidence.text: The 1956 scheme’s first table explicitly pairs 么 with 麽 as the simplified character; the decision says the first-table forms were to be used from 1 February 1956. This supports 么 as 麽’s standardized simplified form, independently of its older use as a graph variant of 幺.
evidence.title: 汉字简化方案

evidence.source: 汉典
evidence.field: 國語辭典; 康熙字典
evidence.text: The entry gives a citation from 列子·汤问 using 么 in 么虫 with a gloss of small/fine, and quotes the Kangxi dictionary saying 么 is俗幺字 while warning that its use for 麼 is俗作么、誤. These attest distinct traditional lexicographic treatments: 么 as a vulgar/variant 幺 and a separate use written 么 for 麼. The page also cites a Tang poem by Li Zhong using final 么 in a question; dating that poem’s composition to Tang does not establish the date of its surviving manuscript spelling.
evidence.title: 麼 mó、me、ma、má - 汉典

evidence.source: 国务院; 1956 漢字簡化方案 transcription
evidence.field: 国务院关于公布汉字简化方案的决议; 第一表
evidence.text: The document says first-table forms were to be used from 1 February 1956 and pairs 么（麽）. This establishes 么 as a standardized simplified counterpart of 麽 from that scheme; it does not negate the distinct older lexicographic association of 么 with 幺.
evidence.title: 汉字简化方案

formation.text: 九 is analyzed as a single pictograph of an arm associated with the elbow. A distinct historical account describes a bent shape reaching its end; a dragon-or-serpent interpretation is also recorded, but neither alternative establishes the graph’s origin.

components.text: The graph is treated as one whole picture, interpreted as an arm associated with the elbow; its exact referent is uncertain. It is not analyzed as a compound of smaller elements.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese Character Database: With Word-formations）
evidence.field: 甲骨部件分析 / 九 / 形義通解
evidence.text: The database reports that oracle-bone 九 depicts an arm and is the original graph for 肘; it says the same form continued in Shang–Zhou bronze and Warring States writing. It cites 《合集》13677正「疾九(肘)」 as an oracle-bone use for elbow, and 《合集》358「𤉲(燎)九牛」 and 《合集》8108「九月，才(在)鯀」 as numeral uses. It also cites a bronze vessel inscription recording the king’s nineteenth year. The database attributes the elbow analysis to 丁山、明義士、李孝定, and says the graph was later borrowed for the numeral.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 許慎《說文解字》, digitized text at 維基文庫
evidence.field: 卷九 / 九部 entry (entry is in the page; this web extraction did not expose its exact line)
evidence.text: The received Shuowen account says 九 is the transformation of yang and depicts a bent, reaching-its-end shape: 「九，陽之變也。象其屈曲究盡之形。凡九之屬皆从九。」 This is an early historical explanation, not confirmation of the oracle-bone analysis; Xu Shen did not have access to the oracle-bone corpus.
evidence.title: 說文解字/09

evidence.source: Kotobank, 普及版 字通 entry 九
evidence.text: 字通 offers a conflicting pictorial account, interpreting the graph as a dragon or serpent form (specifically a forked-head form), and repeats the Shuowen bent/ultimate-shape explanation. It says 九 is used for the number nine and gives other conventional extended or borrowed senses. This reference demonstrates competing accounts but does not establish the dragon interpretation as the graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 九(キュウ)とは？ 意味や使い方

evidence.source: 真柳誠研究室, 古代漢字研究―漢数字の起源―
evidence.text: The study records earlier scholarly proposals: 林義光 treated the original meaning as ‘bent/curved’; 丁山, 明義士 and 李孝定 proposed an elbow graph later borrowed as a numeral. Its summary of 李孝定 describes a graph based on 又 (hand) extended and bent to indicate the elbow. These are reported scholarly analyses, not direct evidence that the object depicted can be identified with certainty.
evidence.title: 古代漢字研究―漢数字の起源―

formation.text: The whole graph is treated as pictographic, but its referent is disputed and no internal component split is supported. The Shuowen account interprets it as female genitalia; another account interprets it as a snake. The Shuowen commentary and the snake account each propose that the graph was later borrowed for grammatical words: a sign for an object could be reused if the object’s name sounded like those words. Neither depicted object nor the proposed name-to-word sound match is established. A child crying, a vessel or funnel, and a mouth-related form are other reported proposals, not verified explanations.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Origin unclear. Variously explained as a pictograph of a snake, a vulva, a funnel, a crying child, or an ideograph depicting a pause in speech.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 女陰也。象形。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形) — A child (子) with their mouth (口) open crying. The original form of 嗁 (OC *l'eː, “to cry”) (Chi Hsu-Sheng, 2014). The child's arms were removed during bronze inscriptions and the two components fused together in the modern form.
Other various possible explanations include:
* The traditional glyph origin given in Shuowen explains the character to be a pictogram (象形) of female genitalia.
* It was once interchangeable with 它 and may have originated as a simplification. Hence, it could be the pictogram of a snake.
* It may have been created to represent the modal particle (語氣詞／语气词 (yǔqìcí)). In some bronze inscriptions, it appears to be a mouth (口) with a curved line descending from it to represent air coming out of the mouth.
* It is possibly a pictogram (象形) of an ancient funnel or wash basin. It may be an early form of 匜.
* It may have signified a big-headed scorpion with its legs flattened, signifying as something very "flat" or "stretched out".
; classical sentence-ending copulative particle, topic particle
Unclear. Possibly Sino-Tibetan, connectable to Tibetan ལ (la), which is often used as a marker (for oblique locative, dative, possessor in constructions with a copula verb, etc.) but also a topicalizer like ནི (ni, “as for”) (Schuessler, 2007).
On the other hand, Pulleyblank (1995) notes the similarity with anteclassical 唯 (OC *ɢʷi) as a copula and a topicalizer.
; also, too, as well

evidence.source: Xǔ Shèn, Shuōwén Jiězì (quoted in the dossier and independently summarized in Wiktionary)
evidence.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary gives 女陰也。象形 (“female genitalia; pictograph”). This is an ancient lexicographic interpretation, not independent confirmation of the depicted referent.
evidence.title: 也 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for Excavated Texts and Paleography, Liu Hongtao, “上古音‘也’字歸部簡論” (search result; page open failed)
evidence.field: paleographic analysis, as reported in search result
evidence.text: The result reports one scholarly analysis that 也 depicts a child with an open mouth crying, is the original graph for 啼 ‘cry’, and was clearly distinct from 它 in early scripts; it says the two began to be confused only after Emperor Wu of Han. This is a reported scholarly analysis, not independently verified from the article text in this session.
evidence.title: 劉洪濤：上古音“也”字歸部簡論

evidence.source: Wiktionary historical-form and etymology entry
evidence.text: The entry presents Spring and Autumn, Warring States, bronze, Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen forms, but says the form references are mostly derived from Richard Sears’ Chinese Etymology site and collections including Jinwen Bian and Yinxu Jiaguwen Bian. It lists the crying-child proposal and alternatives including the Shuowen genitalia account, possible confusion with snake graph 它, a mouth-and-air interpretation, and a vessel/funnel proposal related to 匜. These are competing hypotheses; this page does not settle the original referent. No glyph image was visually inspected for this report.
evidence.title: 也 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC), citing Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai’s commentary
evidence.text: Shuowen says 也 is a pictograph of female genitalia; Duan’s commentary treats that as the original sense and says the graph was borrowed for a grammatical particle. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the depicted referent or a dated record of when the borrowing occurred.
evidence.title: 也 yě - 漢典

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Chinese Character Knowledge Database
evidence.field: 字形演變 and 本義 explanation
evidence.text: The record lists a bronze inscription example, 集成10008, Chu manuscript forms and a small-seal form, and asserts that the original meaning was ‘snake’, depicted in the shape of a snake, later borrowed for function words. This conflicts with the Shuowen account; the page offers an interpretation, not decisive proof of the graph’s original referent.
evidence.title: 漢字「也」：字形演變

formation.text: 习 is a derived simplified graph rather than an independently analyzed ancient construction. The received Shuowen explanation analyzes 習 as 羽 plus 白 and glosses it as repeated flying. A competing analysis of oracle forms proposes 日 plus phonetic 彗, with a proposed original sense of drying in the sun. The graph’s original construction remains disputed.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Simplified form of 習.  Origin unclear. The traditional component 白 was removed for simplification.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text: Simplified from 習 (elimination of 白 and 羽 → 习) in the 1956 Chinese Character Simplification Scheme by the People's Republic of China. Not known to have existed prior to that.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database gives the Shuowen account ‘數飛也。从羽从白’ (‘repeated flying; from 羽 and 白’) and separately proposes an oracle graph 日 plus phonetic 彗, whose original sense was sun-drying. It cites oracle-bone ‘習一卜/二卜/三卜’ examples as repeated divinations, and Warring States Guodian slips as evidence for learning-related use: 性自命出 slips 60–61 and 語叢三 slip 10. It treats the bird-practice explanation as an account of later borrowed senses, not a settled account of the earliest graph.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 習

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database says the element resembling 羽 in the oracle graph is interpreted as 彗 rather than 羽, citing the absence of an oracle 羽 graph and comparison with the 彗 phonetic in the seal form of 雪. In this analysis 彗 supplies sound and 日 meaning; the graph’s original sense is sun-drying. It reports the later Shuowen analysis as 羽 plus 白 and describes those components as graphic confusions by small-seal script. The proposed referents and changes are source interpretations, not independently established merely by resemblance.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析: 羽

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi, as transcribed by the Chinese University of Hong Kong database
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry defines 習 as ‘數飛也’ and analyzes it as 从羽从白. This is an early lexicographic explanation of the received form, not independent proof of the oracle graph’s original components or meaning.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 習

evidence.source: Local repository data supplied in the research packet
evidence.text: The supplied Baxter–Sagart 2014 row for 習 has MC zip and OC *s-ɢʷəp (with root *ɢʷəp ‘wing’?). No 習 row was supplied for 彗, so a same-system comparison of the proposed phonetic element 彗 with host 習 cannot be reported from this input. The row does not itself establish that 彗 is phonetic in 習.

formation.text: 書 is traditionally analyzed as phonosemantic: 聿 contributes a writing-related meaning, and 者 is assigned a phonetic role. 书 is the standardized simplified counterpart, formed by regularizing a cursive shape of 書.

components.text: Within 書, 聿 is the semantic element associated with writing. The supplied historical comparison glosses it as a writing stylus or brush, but does not establish its original pictorial form.

Within 書, 者 is assigned the phonetic role in the traditional analysis. Baxter–Sagart gives readings for both graphs in the same system, but they do not by themselves explain the historical sound relation.

sound_limitation.text: Baxter–Sagart gives 書 as MC syo / OC *s-ta and 者 as MC tsyaeX / OC *tAʔ. Their Old Chinese initials differ, and these values alone do not explain or establish the historical phonetic relation assigned in the traditional analysis.

sound.text: In Modern Mandarin, 者 is zhě and 書 is shū. This present-day pair does not establish their historical phonetic relationship.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text: Simplified from 書 from cursive script with phonetic corrupted, now resembles a simpler hand holding a brush.

evidence.source: makemeahanzi

evidence.text: 箸也。从聿者聲。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *hlja): semantic 聿 (“writing brush”) + phonetic 者 (OC *tjaːʔ).
Unknown (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.source: Wiktionary (Chinese), entry 书
evidence.text: States that 书 is the simplification of 書 and describes the change as regularizing a cursive form into standard script. This supports the direction 書 → 书 and the classification simplified_form; the entry does not date the first use of the simplified shape.

The source says the sounds were more similar in older Chinese. This is a secondary account; it does not override the locally supplied Baxter–Sagart row for 書 or establish the corresponding 者 row.

The Old Chinese forms do not share the same initial: 書 has *s- and 者 has *t-. The supplied local Baxter–Sagart rows for both characters match these values. This is a same-system comparison; by itself it does not explain the historical phonetic relationship assigned to 者 in the traditional graph analysis.

The Old Chinese initials differ (*s- versus *t-), so the rows do not support the prior claim that both share *t-. They document the readings but do not, by themselves, explain why 說文 assigns 者 the phonetic role in 書.

formation.text: 買 has competing analyses. The early lexicographic account treats 网 and 貝 as a meaningful combination, while another proposal treats 貝 as semantic and abbreviated 羅 as phonetic. The latter sound role is not established by the available comparison. The traditional net-and-shell interpretation is plausible but does not by itself prove the graph’s original motivation. The modern simplified form 买 is linked to 買’s cursive shape, though that specific derivation is not established here.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Pictograph of money (貝) coming out of a netted bag (网). The simplified character 买 was adapted from the cursive form of the traditional character 買.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 市也。从网、貝。《孟子》曰：“登壟斷而网市利。”

evidence.source: 漢典 (Hàn典)
evidence.field: 說文解字 and 說文解字注
evidence.text: The Shuowen entry defines 買 as 市 and analyzes it as 从网貝 (net + cowrie/money shell), citing the Mencius phrase about using a raised position to monopolize market profit. The later Shuowen commentary explicitly calls the structure 會意. This is an early lexicographic analysis, not independent proof of the graph’s original motivation.
evidence.title: 買 mǎi - 汉典

evidence.source: 教育局中國語文教育研究及評估組資源：字源考釋
evidence.text: This source says the oracle, bronze and seal forms contain net and 貝 as semantic elements and interprets the graph as using a net to obtain cowries, which served as ancient currency; it gives the basic sense as exchanging money for goods. Its wording is a traditional graphic interpretation; its displayed paleographic forms were not visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 - 買

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Baxter and Sagart (2014)
evidence.text: The page reports the competing analysis that 買 is phonosemantic: abbreviated phonetic 羅 (*rˤaj) plus semantic 貝. This differs from Shuowen’s explicit net-plus-cowrie 会意 analysis. The accessible material does not provide Baxter and Sagart’s character-specific argument; therefore the phonetic analysis is recorded as an attributed proposal, not established fact.
evidence.title: 買 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Baxter and Sagart (2014)
evidence.text: For 買 the page gives Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *mˤrajʔ, Middle Chinese meaX, and modern Beijing Mandarin mǎi; it separately gives Zhengzhang Old Chinese *mreːʔ. These are system-specific reconstructions and must not be merged. The local Baxter–Sagart row for 買 agrees: meaX, *mˤrajʔ, GSR 1240c (sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv, row 2225). No matching local 羅 row was verified in this search, so the comparative pronunciation of the proposed phonetic component was not independently checked here.
evidence.title: 買 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

formation.text: The received account treats 了 as a whole pictograph related to 子 with its arms omitted. A separate commentary interprets the graph as crossed or entangled legs. These are competing readings of the graph, not confirmed depictions of an early inscription.

components.text: The graph as a whole is interpreted in the received account as 子 without arms. This is a disputed pictorial reading; the evidence does not confirm the referent of an early inscription.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 尦也。从子無臂。象形。凡了之屬皆从了。

evidence.source: 《说文解字》 text and Duan Yucai commentary, accessed through 汉典
evidence.field: 了字说文解字 / 说文解字注
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry says 尦也。从子無臂。象形 (“crossed legs; from 子 without arms; pictographic”). Duan Yucai glosses 尦 as legs crossing while walking and describes 了戾 as things twisted or knotted rather than straight; he says the character was borrowed for 憭悟, ‘understand/clear’. This is an historical analysis, not independent proof of the depicted referent.
evidence.title: 了 liǎo、le - 汉典

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese glyph origin and etymology sections
evidence.text: The page reports a Shuowen pictographic interpretation as a baby without arms and cites a commentary interpretation of entangled legs. It says the relation of ‘finish’ to the graph may be a phonetic loan, while ‘entangled legs → tie → finish’ is another proposed semantic path. It reports verb ‘finish/be completed’ developing into perfective 了 and subsequently a sentence-final change-of-state particle, with the perfective use common by Tang. The page says ancient-form data mainly derives from Richard Sears’ Chinese Etymology collections; no primary ancient inscription image was inspected here, so an original referent or paleographic sequence cannot be confirmed from this evidence.
evidence.title: 了 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: 汉典, quoting 《说文解字》 and Duan Yucai's commentary
evidence.text: The entry quotes 尦也。从子無臂。象形 and its account of a form derived from 子 without arms. Duan Yucai interprets 尦 as legs crossing in movement and explains 了戾 as twisted or knotted things that do not extend straight; he also reports borrowing for 憭悟. These are historical interpretations, not direct proof of the depicted referent or an inscriptional development sequence.
evidence.title: 了 liǎo、le - 汉典

evidence.source: Wiktionary, character entry
evidence.text: The entry reports the received Shuowen pictograph explanation as 子 without arms, alongside a commentary interpretation involving entangled legs. It says the relation to ‘finish’ may be a sound loan, while an entangled→tied→finished path is another proposal. It reports the verb ‘finish/be completed’ developing into a perfective particle, common by Tang, and later into a sentence-final change-of-state particle. These are secondary summaries; the page does not establish an early graph referent or dated intermediate semantic links.
evidence.title: 了 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

formation.text: Pictographic: the early graph depicts a hand holding something. Proposed identifications of the object include a flag, document container, brush, or implement, but none is established. A later dictionary analysis divides 事 into 史 and abbreviated 之 as a sound element; this does not establish the formation of the early graph.

components.text: The early graph is a whole picture of a hand holding an unidentified object. Competing proposals identify the object as a flag, document container, brush, or implement; it is not securely identified.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 職也。从史，之省聲。

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: Oracle-bone and bronze component analysis; forms and senses for 事
evidence.text: The database reports that 甲骨文 forms for 事/史/吏/使 were initially one graph, analyzed as a hand holding an object, and later differentiated. It records 事 in bronze inscriptions for duties/official work, events, an office, and in one cited inscription for a verb meaning to send/command; it also gives later transmitted-text examples for matters, undertaking, and serving. The object held is disputed: scholarship cited there proposes a flag, a container for bamboo records, a writing brush, or a hunting implement. These are competing interpretations, not established identifications. Examples include 麥鼎 and 克鼎 for office/duty, 琱生簋 for event, and 小臣守簋 for command/serve.
evidence.kind: secondary scholarly database reporting primary inscription evidence
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component analysis, 又

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: Graphic history and competing interpretations of 史 and related graphs
evidence.text: The database says 史、吏、事、使 were once a single graph, depicting a hand holding something, and became separate graphs. It attributes several rival identifications of the held object: a flag (吳其昌), a container for bamboo slips (王國維), a brush (馬敍倫), or a hunting tool (陳夢家); 徐中舒 proposed a forked hunting implement. It notes graphic differentiation in small-seal forms and cites a proposal that this differentiation occurred around Qin-Han. It also reports oracle-bone uses of 史 for an office/clan/person, matter, and ‘send’; bronze uses include office and uses interchangeable with 事 and 使. This does not establish the object's name or pronunciation, nor that 事 originated as a phonetic loan from a tool name.
evidence.kind: secondary scholarly database reporting primary inscription evidence and named scholarly analyses
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component analysis, 史

evidence.source: CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: Oracle component account for 事; graphic history and bronze examples
evidence.text: The database describes oracle forms as hand (手) plus an unidentified component, depicting a hand holding something. It says the graphs 史、吏、事、使 later differentiated; in bronze forms an unbranched upper stroke is commonly assigned to 史 and a branched form to 吏/事. Bronze examples use 事 for duty, events, an office, and a command/serve verb. The identification of the held object is disputed: proposals include a flag, a document container, a brush, and hunting implements. These are source-reported analyses, not an established object identification.
evidence.kind: secondary paleographic database reporting inscription examples
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析, 又

evidence.source: 漢典
evidence.field: Shuowen analysis reported by an accessible character-specific page
evidence.text: Search results and the consulted 事 page identify the Shuowen account as 職也 and 从史，之省聲: ‘office/duty’; from 史 with an abbreviated 之 as phonetic. This is Xu Shen's later lexicographic analysis and is not independent proof of how the earlier graph was formed. The accessible result also reports two Guangyun fanqie readings, 側吏切 and 鉏吏切; these are not Baxter–Sagart reconstructions.
evidence.kind: dictionary reference reporting historical lexicographic analysis
evidence.title: 事 shì — 汉典

formation.text: Indicative: two strokes mark the quantity two. An early lexicographic explanation describes the sign as paired instances of 一, later clarified as doubling that stroke; this account is not independent proof of the graph’s origin.

components.text: The whole graph consists of two horizontal strokes used together as a numeral sign. It has no meaningful internal components; the paired-ones explanation describes the strokes’ relation, not separate component roles.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Two horizontal strokes, representing the number two.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogram (指事) - two parallel strokes. Compare with 一, one stroke meaning one, 三, three strokes meaning three, and 亖 (sǐ), four strokes meaning four. Duplication of 一 (“one”).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *kV-ni-s. Cognate to Tibetan གཉིས (gnyis), Sikkimese ཉི (nyi), Tangut 𗍫 (*njɨ̱¹), Burmese နှစ် (hnac), and Nuosu ꑍ (nyip). See also: 次 (OC *sn̥ʰis, “second; next”), a cognate within Chinese languages.

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, Shuowen Jiezi entry 二
evidence.text: The Han-dynasty Shuowen entry reads “地之數也。从偶一。凡二之屬皆从二” (“the number associated with earth; formed from paired ones”). Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary corrects 偶 to 耦 and explains 耦一 as doubling the stroke 一. This is a historical account of two equal strokes, not independent proof of how the graph first arose.
evidence.title: 說文解字「二」 - 「說文解字」在線查詢

evidence.source: 漢典 (zdic.net), 二 entry
evidence.text: The dictionary characterizes 二 in ancient writing as two horizontal strokes used as a primitive counting sign, and lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu slip/silk, Shuowen, Qin slip, clerical and regular-script form categories. This supports a straightforward numeral-sign analysis; its simplified listing is not a dated inscriptional history.
evidence.title: 二 èr - 汉典

formation.text: 五 is treated as an independent graph, with no established internal semantic or phonetic components. Its original graphic motivation is disputed: proposals include a tally mark, an early form of 互, and a hand with visible palm lines. The cord-device proposal lacks an independently established object name and pronunciation.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 形義通解 / competing graphic-origin proposals
evidence.text: The entry records several proposals for the graph's original motivation: Yu Shengwu treated it as a tally mark; Ding Shan identified it as an early form of 互, a cord-collecting device; Zhang Bingquan proposed an outstretched hand with visible palm lines; and Ji Xusheng took a five-horizontal-stroke form to be four plus a decorative stroke. The database questions the last proposal, citing Ji Xusheng's view that the five-stroke graph is not 五. These are attributed scholarly analyses, not a settled consensus. The database does not establish the name or pronunciation of a depicted object behind the cord-device proposal.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Repository local structured reading data, checked against Unicode Consortium Unihan record
evidence.text: The supplied local row for 五 is kMandarin wǔ, matching the inspected official Unihan record for U+4E94. Local Baxter–Sagart row for 五 is py wǔ, MC nguX, OC *C.ŋˤaʔ, gloss five; it matches the authors' published table. These records concern 五 alone; this research identified no sound component in the graph requiring a component-versus-host reading comparison.
evidence.title: Unihan data for U+4E94

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 形義通解; competing graphic-origin analyses
evidence.text: The entry says oracle, bronze, and seal constructions are the same and that the original meaning is unknown. It records Xu Shen’s heaven-and-earth interpretation and Zhu Fangpu’s agreement, alongside proposals that the graph was a tally mark (Yu Shengwu), an early form of 互 depicting a cord-gathering device (Ding Shan), or an outstretched hand/palm lines (Zhang Bingquan). The entry reports Ji Xusheng’s objection that a five-horizontal-stroke form was 四 with a decorative stroke, not 五. These are attributed analyses; the page does not establish a pre-numeral sense or the name and pronunciation of the proposed cord device.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

formation.text: The received 說文 analysis divides 些 into 此 above 二, but does not establish either part’s function in the original formation. The formation type remains disputed: modern shape and later phonetic-series listings cannot prove an original sound or meaning contribution.

components.text: 此 is the upper element in the received analysis. Its role in the formation is unproven; later grouping with the 此 phonetic series does not establish that it supplied 些’s original sound.
二 is the lower element in the received analysis. The evidence does not establish that it contributes “two” or another meaning to 些.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 語辭也。見《楚辭》。从此从二。其義未詳。

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 些
evidence.text: The page lists the modern graph composition as 此 over 二 and groups 些 in the 此 phonetic series, giving Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese forms *saːls, *sjaːl, and *seːs. These are secondary compilations and do not by themselves prove either an original 此 phonetic role or 二 semantic role; the page’s historical-form images were not used to establish a developmental sequence.
evidence.title: 些 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 形體資料表; record of component analysis
evidence.text: The entry identifies the received Shuowen Daxu Xinfu form as composed from 此 and 二, and records variant forms including 㱔, 𡭟 and 呰. It reports no available oracle-bone, bronze, or several other early paleographic source records in its form table. This supports the received form description, not a demonstrated semantic role for 二 or phonetic role for 此 in the original formation.
evidence.title: [A00056] 些 - Ministry of Education《Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants》2024

formation.text: Treat 京 as a whole pictograph of a tall built structure or platform. A competing account describes a high man-made mound; neither interpretation establishes a dated route to “capital.”

components.text: 京 is treated as one pictorial graph, not divided into modern-looking parts. Descriptions of early forms interpret them as a roof, tower, and wall; the selected oracle-style glyph is a modern redraw, not an ancient artifact.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 人所爲絕高丘也。从高省，| 象高形。凡京之屬皆从京。

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database labels the graph forms as oracle-bone, bronze, and small-seal script. Its explanation identifies the oracle-bone and bronze forms as a tall building: roof above, tower in the middle, and wall below; it says the small-seal form simplified the tower element to 口. This supports a building interpretation, but the database does not provide dated individual attestations in the accessible text.
evidence.title: 漢字「京」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database reports a high platform / tall tower interpretation and quotes Shuowen’s high-mound analysis. It also gives a related-size interpretation (large) and reports 郭沫若’s comparisons linking 京 to large mounds, granaries, animals, and strength. These are dictionary interpretations, not a demonstrated dated chain from mound to capital.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 京

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry cites 詩經·小雅·甫田, “曾孫之庾，如坻如京,” with Mao’s Han-period gloss “京，高丘也” (‘京, a high mound’). It also cites 管子·輕重丁 for a granary sense, 左傳·莊公二十二年 for “equal/compare,” and 白居易·琵琶行 for capital-city use. The latter is a Tang poem; this is an attestation by cited work, not an exact manuscript date. The sources available here do not establish when capital use began or whether it arose through mound-to-settlement semantic extension, another path, or a distinct word sense.
evidence.title: [A00065] 京 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, International Computer Chinese Characters and Variant Forms Knowledge Base
evidence.text: The entry labels 京 forms as oracle-bone, bronze, and small-seal script. Its explanation reads the oracle-bone and bronze forms as a tall building, with roof, tower, and wall; it says the small-seal form simplifies the tower element to 口. This is a database interpretation of the graph, not a dated sequence of individual attestations.
evidence.title: 漢字「京」：字形演變

evidence.source: Wikimedia Commons
evidence.field: 京-oracle.svg description, source, license, image file
evidence.text: The file page identifies this as a vector depiction of 京 in Shang oracle script style, gives B08320 at hanziyuan.net as the image source, and states that the vector was created with Inkscape. Its page marks the representation public domain. The asset is a modern redraw, not an ancient artifact photograph.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph depicts a person in profile. Descriptions interpret its strokes as a head, body, arm and legs; this explains the figure, not a proven stroke-by-stroke sequence. Two early graphic variants are described as equivalent in meaning, with one underlying the Small Seal form and the other developing through clerical writing into regular 人.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry identifies the graph in oracle-bone inscriptions (合集6175), bronze inscriptions (集成00944), and the Small Seal script / Shuowen. Its account interprets the profile figure’s upper end as the head, middle as body, one extended stroke as arm, and lower part as legs. This supports a human-figure pictograph analysis; the stroke-by-stroke description is the database’s interpretation, not a separately demonstrated chronology.
evidence.title: 漢字「人」：字形演變

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry lists oracle-bone form 合集6175, bronze form 集成00944, and Small Seal / Shuowen material. Its account reads the graph as a person standing in profile: head, body, an extended stroke as arm, and legs. This is the database’s graphic interpretation; it does not date those specimens or establish a stroke-by-stroke chronology.
evidence.title: 漢字「人」：字形演變

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》
evidence.field: 人 entry; printed p. 698; PDF p. 711
evidence.text: The 人 entry identifies the graph as pictographic, resembling a person in side view, and gives its basic sense as ‘person.’ It describes two early graphic variants—one joining head-like and torso-like parts, another joining head-like and arm-like parts—as equivalent in meaning; it says the former underlies the Shuowen Small Seal form, while the latter was more common in clerical script and developed into regular 人. The attached scan visibly shows the 人 headword, the form sequence, and this explanation. The continuation on PDF p. 712 is the separate 仁 entry, not a continuation of 人.

formation.text: The early graph is commonly described by its visible parts: a mouth-like upper shape and a lower mark. Interpretations of the whole include a mouth-related sign and a wooden clapper; another proposal connects it with groaning or chanting and suggests the graph was reused for “now” because the words sounded alike. The object’s name and that proposed sound match are unknown, so this borrowing account remains unproven. In the later Shuowen analysis, 今 is divided into 亼 and 乁, with 乁 identified as an ancient form of 及; this dictionary analysis does not settle the early graph’s construction. Separately, 今 is documented as a phonetic element in 吟. That later sound role does not establish that groaning or chanting was the original word written by 今.

components.text: Early forms are described as a mouth-like upper shape above a lower mark, sometimes omitted. This is a proposed pictorial reading of the whole graph; the mark’s referent is disputed.
In the received dictionary analysis, 亼 is the first part of 今. This later division does not establish 亼’s role in the early graph.

The received analysis identifies the second part as 乁, an ancient form and variant of 及. This does not make 及 an ancestor of the shape in 今. Another transcription gives 绁; the intended shape and reason for the discrepancy remain unresolved.

formation.text: Early forms are described as a person with two or four flanking marks, a picture-based construction whose details remain disputed. The received 說文 analysis divides the graph into 八 and 人, but that later account does not prove the original construction.

components.text: Early-form descriptions identify a human figure corresponding to 人. In this proposed picture-based analysis, it depicts a person; whether it was a distinct component in the original graph remains uncertain. The received 說文 analysis later identifies 人 as one part.

Early forms are described with flanking dots, but their identity and role are disputed: they have been interpreted as marks for “between,” armor or covering, secondary status, or ritual sparks. Identifying them as modern 丶 is tentative.

evidence.text: The database describes oracle-bone forms as 人 with two or four dots flanking the figure, and reports an interpretation as “between” attributed to Yang Shuda and Shen Pei. It cites 左傳·襄公九年 and 左傳·襄公三十年 for 介居/介於 between two great states. It also records disputed readings: an armor/clothing interpretation (Luo Zhenyu, Wang Guowei, Ma Xulun), oracle-bone 介 meaning ‘junior/secondary’ (Rao Zongyi, Qiu Xigui, Wu Shichang), and Warring States slips using 介 for 個 (‘one item/person’). The database gives the Shuowen account 畫也。从八从人，人各有介, but this is an early lexicographic analysis, not independent confirmation of the graph’s origin.

evidence.text: Xu describes the oracle-bone shape as a person with dots at both sides (some variants have two dots on each side). This is the author’s argued hypothesis, not settled evidence: the article itself notes that the dot component’s meaning and the graph’s original semantic construction remain disputed.

formation.text: The construction of 他 is unresolved. A common account analyzes it as 亻, contributing the person category, plus 也 as a proposed sound element, but the supplied historical readings do not establish that phonetic role. A separate traditional account analyzes 佗 as 人 plus phonetic 它 and links 佗 with 他; it does not establish that construction for 他.

components.text: 亻 is the conventional side form of 人 and contributes the person category in the common analysis of 他. 人 is also assigned that role in the reported analysis of the separate graph 佗.

也 is commonly proposed as the phonetic element in 他, but that role remains disputed. The supplied historical readings differ, and their current Mandarin readings do not establish an ancient sound relationship.

sound_limitation.text: The historical comparison and current Mandarin readings do not establish that 也 functioned as 他’s historical phonetic element; the structural analysis remains disputed.

sound.text: In the supplied table, 也 is MC yaeX / OC *lAjʔ and 他 is MC tha / OC *l̥ˤaj; these readings differ and do not establish 也’s phonetic role.
