evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 亻 represents the meaning and 也 represents the sound.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *l̥ʰaːl): semantic 亻 (“man”) + phonetic 也 (OC *laːlʔ).
Corrupted form of 佗 (OC *l̥ʰaːl, *l'aːl), which is found in Zuozhuan.
Etymology not clear (Schuessler, 2007). Perhaps cognate with 誃 (OC *l'al, *l̥ʰjalʔ, “to separate”).
The modern sense of "he, she, it" only emerged after the Han period in colloquial passages, and displaced classical 其 (OC *ɡɯ) and 之 (OC *tjɯ) in Mandarin dialects (Pulleyblank, 1995).
The phonological development from Middle Chinese was irregular. The expected reflex is tuō, which is sometimes used in literary contexts for the classical "other" sense, but in most Mandarin dialects it is read like tā.

formation.text: The traditional graph 們 is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 亻 contributes a person-related category, while 門 supplies a sound cue. This construction describes the graph; it does not explain how the plural-marker meaning arose.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声): semantic 亻 (“person”) + phonetic 門 (OC *mɯːn).
First attested in the Song dynasty (Lü, 1940). Various other glyphs representing *mVn have been attested in Song dynasty texts, including 懣, 滿, 瞞, 門.
It is probably related to 弭 (MC mjieX) (in 我弭) and 偉 (MC hjw+jX) (in 兒郎偉 /儿郎伟 (érláng wěi)) attested in the Tang dynasty (Lü, 1940); it is related to 每 (měi), as in 我每 (wǒměi), common during the Jin (Jurchen), Yuan and early Ming dynasties (Lü, 1985).
Proposed etymologies:
* From the personal pronoun plural marker 輩 (OC *puːls) (Lü, 1985; Feng, 1997; Li, 2013).
* From 門 (MC mwon, “door; clan; family”) (Ota, 2003; Yu, 1989; Li and Shi, 2000).
* From 每人 (MC mwojX nyin, “everybody”) (Norman, 1988); compare Eastern Min 各儂／各侬 (“everybody”), used in 我各儂／我各侬 (“we; us”), 汝各儂／汝各侬 (“you (plural)”), 伊各儂／伊各侬 (“they”).
* From 物 (MC mjut, “thing”) (Jiang, 1995).
* From plural features in Dravidian languages, cf. Classical Tamil -m, -mar, -mār suffixes, Tamil நாம் (nām, “inclusive we”), via Indic languages by means of Buddhist transmission (Chen & Ye, 2020).
Also compare 您.

formation.text: 作 is conventionally analyzed as a phonosemantic graph: 人, written in its side form 亻, is treated as a semantic marker, and 乍 as a sound element. The received Shuowen text says 从人从乍 and glosses 作 as ‘rise, begin’; Duan Yucai’s commentary explicitly calls 乍 phonetic. Another analysis proposes 人 was added to distinguish the work/action graph 作 from uses of 乍 meaning ‘suddenly’ or ‘temporarily.’ That account does not establish whether 乍 supplied the sound at the graph’s formation.

乍 is conventionally treated as the sound element in 作. Analyses of its early graph disagree: one interprets it as clearing vegetation, another as a garment lapel. Neither establishes the depicted object’s name or pronunciation.

formation.text: One reported analysis is phonosemantic: 亻 supplies the person category and 尔 a sound cue. A competing, unverified proposal reads 人 and 尔 together as “person” and “you.” The formation remains disputed because the available historical accounts do not directly establish how 你 was formed.

components.text: In one reported phonosemantic analysis, 亻 represents a person and contributes the semantic category. A competing proposal treats 人 and 尔 together ideographically; the available evidence does not establish 亻’s historical role in 你.

The right-side 尔 is proposed as the phonetic element. It is the standardized simplified form of 爾, which was used for “you/your”; 尔 is also described as a shortened form of 爾. In Modern Mandarin, 尔 ěr and 你 nǐ differ, and this comparison alone does not establish an ancient sound relationship or 尔’s role in 你.

sound_limitation.text: The present-day Mandarin readings ěr and nǐ do not establish an ancient sound relationship or 尔’s phonetic role in 你. One supplied secondary account gives Old Chinese *njelʔ for 尔 and *nɯʔ for 你, but these are not an independently verified matched comparison here.

sound.text: In Modern Mandarin, 尔 is ěr and 你 is nǐ. This comparison alone does not demonstrate an ancient sound relationship or 尔’s role in 你.

formation.text: A whole-graph pictograph of a wheat plant, with no separate phonetic component. One account holds that the graph was borrowed for the movement word; a competing account reverses the direction of borrowing.

components.text: The whole graph pictures a plant: the central upright shape is interpreted as its ear, the side branches as drooping leaves, and the lower strokes as stem and roots. These are parts of the picture, not separate components.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Humanum)
evidence.field: 來: competing accounts of 來 and 麥
evidence.text: The entry presents wheat-to-movement borrowing as its main account: the wheat graph 來 was borrowed for movement, and 麥 came to write wheat. It also reports a competing reverse account: 來 originally represented movement, while 麥 was formed with a movement-related foot element and later became the wheat graph after 來 was commonly used for movement. These are source-reported analyses; early attestations of both uses do not settle the direction.

evidence.text: The entry analyzes the whole oracle-bone graph as a wheat plant: an upright central ear, drooping leaves, stem, and roots. It proposes no separate phonetic component within 來. Academia Sinica’s Xiao Xue Tang likewise describes the early graph as resembling mature wheat. These are source interpretations of the graph, not a claim that its spoken reading was ‘wheat’ in every early occurrence.

evidence.field: 來: Shang oracle-bone uses and disputed borrowing direction
evidence.text: The entry cites a rare oracle-bone wheat use, 乙亥卜，受來禾 (合集 33260), and more frequent movement-related uses, including 往來亡災 and 王來正人方, as well as return, tribute, and prospective-time uses. Its main account treats the wheat graph as borrowed for movement; it also reports a reverse account in which 麥 was the movement form and later came to write wheat. These early attestations establish that both wheat and movement uses existed in Shang oracle-bone material, but do not establish which lexical use came first. The cited examples are not assigned absolute dates individually.

formation.text: 候 is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 亻 contributes a person-related category, while 矦 is proposed as the sound component. 矦 is associated with 侯, whose graph has been interpreted as a target picture. Since the target’s early name and pronunciation are unknown, that interpretation does not explain the sound relationship.

components.text: 亻 contributes a person-related category in 候. It is the conventional side form corresponding to 人, not evidence of a separate historical change in this character.
矦 is the modified visible sound element in 候. It is associated with 侯, but their precise graphic relationship and the sequence between these spellings are unresolved.

sound_limitation.text: The proposed sound comparison does not independently establish 矦 as the component’s graphic identity or its independent reading.

sound.text: A secondary reconstruction proposes a historical sound relationship between 矦 and 候. This supports the proposed phonetic analysis, but does not settle the component’s precise graphic identity.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text: Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɡoːs): semantic 亻 + phonetic 矦 (OC *ɡoː), as 𠊱. The 矦 component (here in modified form where the first 丿 stroke is omitted and the second 丿 stroke is written as a 丨 stroke) is an ancient form of 侯 (hóu).

Its character page lists one small-seal and four bamboo/slip forms, but no oracle-bone or bronze forms for 候. These are source statements; the available page does not establish the date or manuscript witness of each slip form.

It says the seal form was written from 人 and 侯, and describes the later regular-script shape as having the human-side portion of 侯 reduced to a short vertical stroke. It dates no specific transition. Listed senses include reconnoitre, watchtower (通堠), visit, wait, serve, and divination; the entry supplies classical citations, including 《呂氏春秋》 for reconnoitring and Tao Yuanming’s 晋-period ‘僮僕歡迎，稚子候門’ for waiting.

formation.text: The traditional account analyzes 假 as phonosemantic: 亻 contributes a person-related meaning and 叚 a sound cue. A competing proposal says 人 was added to 叚 to distinguish the spelling for borrowing from that for lending in Qin-period documents. This graphic proposal does not settle how the two analyses relate.

components.text: 亻 is the side form of 人. In the traditional analysis it contributes a person-related meaning; a competing proposal treats 人 as a graphic addition distinguishing 假 from 叚.

叚 is conventionally analyzed as the phonetic component. A cited Old Chinese comparison matches it with 假’s “borrow; false” reading, while other readings of 假 have distinct reconstructions. Descriptions of bronze forms concern 叚 itself and do not establish a graphic sequence for 假.

sound_limitation.text: The historical sound comparison supports the proposed relation for 假’s “borrow; false” reading, but does not establish it for every reading of 假.

sound.text: The local reading data give both characters a Modern Mandarin reading jiǎ; this current match alone does not establish their ancient sound relationship.
In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese notation, 叚 and 假 in the “borrow; false” reading share the reconstruction *Cə.kˤraʔ. The same dataset gives another reading of 假 a different reconstruction.

evidence.source: 田炜, 复旦大学出土文献与古文字研究中心 article reprinted by Sohu
evidence.text: The author reports that pre-Qin excavated texts contain 叚 but not 假, and that 假 first appears in Qin-period documents. He discusses a dated Liye document from Qin Shihuang year 26 (221 BCE): in the author’s reading, 叚 marks lending/giving out while 假 marks borrowing/obtaining. He proposes 假 was formed by adding semantic 人 to 叚 to distinguish a use of the word, while noting that Shuowen and Duan Yucai explain the relationship differently and do not explicitly explain why 人 marks “false.” This is a scholarly proposal, not an uncontested account of character formation.

evidence.text: The article quotes Shuowen’s analysis of 假 as 从人叚声, “非真也,” and reports Duan Yucai’s view that 假 and 叚 are near-identical in meaning. The author disputes a simple account in which “false” is derived from “borrow,” proposing a graphic differentiation of the written forms instead. The article also notes that later texts no longer consistently maintain the Qin-period 叚/假 distinction; a Han silk manuscript uses 假 for both borrowing and lending. These points separate graphic differentiation from a proposed semantic history.

formation.text: The traditional graph 兒 is pictographic: a person-like lower form and an upper feature together depict a child. The upper feature is interpreted either as an infant’s unclosed fontanel or as paired hair buns. Modern 儿 is a reduced form of 兒.

formation.text: A proposed early construction combines two pictorial elements: a foot above a person, showing someone stepping ahead. Its connection to the modern graph is unresolved. formation.text: The graph 八 is traditionally explained as two strokes turning away from one another to express separation or distinction. One account classifies it as an indicator graph (指事字), with the diverging strokes expressing distinction. These are disputed interpretations: other proposals connect it with 分 or 別, or interpret it as a concrete gesture or object, and the original referent remains unresolved. Oracle-bone inscriptions already use 八 as the numeral “eight,” but this does not establish that separation came first.

components.text: The whole graph consists of two diverging strokes. In the traditional interpretation they suggest separation, but no particular object or gesture is established. 八 is not a compound of modern components.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Pictograph of two lines facing away from each other. The current meaning "eight" is a phonetic loan. The original meaning "separate" is now written as 别.

The entry questions whether an abstract idea of separation should be called pictographic. These are reported scholarly proposals, not a settled reconstruction.

formation.text: The formation remains disputed, and no component breakdown is established. The shelter-picture proposal would make the whole graph pictographic; other proposals treat it as a conventional counting mark or as a graph later distinguished from 入. Pictogram (象形) – perhaps a shed. Originally using the similar-sounding word 廬 (OC *ra, “shed, cabin”) to represent the concept “six” (Liu Xinglong). Alternatively, it may be an ancient counting symbol.

formation.text: A traditional analysis treats 關 as phonosemantic: 門 contributes the doorway category, and 𢇅 is assigned a sound role. Accounts of bronze forms differ over elements such as 卝 and 串 and their functions.

components.text: In 關, 門 contributes the doorway category; it is omitted in simplified 关.

formation.text: The traditional graph 興 is commonly analyzed as a semantic construction depicting several hands jointly lifting an object. The received account parses it as 舁 plus 同, explaining the action as people working together; this reading does not establish the object’s identity or the graph’s original design. A proposed analysis assigning 型 a phonetic role is not supported by the formation evidence. 兴 is the standardized simplified form of 興, described as adapted from its cursive form.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Depicts four hands (舁) working together (同) to raise something. The simplified character 兴 was adapted from the cursive form of the traditional character 興.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 起也。从舁从同。同力也。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *qʰɯŋ, *qʰɯŋs): semantic 舁 + phonetic 型 (OC *ɡeːŋ).
Compare perhaps Burmese ရွှင် (hrwang, “to rejoice, be abundant”) (Luce, 1981).

evidence.text: The entry gives “起也。从舁从同。同力也.” Duan Yucai labels the analysis 會意 and comments that the graph explains 同力. It also quotes Guangyun senses 盛、舉、善 and notes the Zhouli poetic category 興. This supports the received lexicographic account but is not independent proof of the graph’s original design.

formation.text: The formation remains disputed. One historical account treats the graph as 一 with an abbreviated 冓 and explains it as one act yielding two; other proposals see a fish-related graph or a cord-making tool. None establishes a definitive component analysis.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 一舉而二也。从冓省。

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨、金文及簡帛字形資料
evidence.text: The database says the graph’s original construction and meaning are unsettled. It records competing proposals: Xu Zhongshu interprets the bone form as a fish and 冓 as two fish meeting, but notes that the form differs from 魚 and remains uncertain; Shirakawa Shizuka sees a tool for weaving cord; Xu Shen interprets it as 一 with an abbreviated 冓, meaning one act yielding two. The database says the oracle-bone context is fragmentary and unclear. It reports bronze examples used for ‘second time/again’ and also ‘two,’ and Warring States forms sometimes add 二 or 口, with 二 possibly contributing meaning. These reports support neither the dossier’s confident ‘two fish caught on a line’ gloss nor a definitive component analysis.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 字頭「再」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: 形義通解; graphic analysis and historical usage
evidence.text: CUHK says 再’s oracle and bronze construction and original meaning are unsettled. It reports competing proposals: Xu Zhongshu’s fish interpretation, with 冓 as two fish meeting (but the graph differs from 魚 and the proposal remains unverified); Shirakawa Shizuka’s cord-making tool interpretation; and Xu Shen’s account of one act yielding two, hence two/repetition. Warring States forms may add 二 or 口 decoratively, with 二 possibly also contributing the meaning ‘two’. The oracle-bone context is fragmentary and unclear. CUHK reports bronze uses for ‘second time/again’ (陳璋方壺; 叔尸鐘) and ‘two’ (𠫑羌鐘, twenty-two), Warring States bamboo use 再三, and a possible whole-graph loan for 在 in a Guodian slip, marked as uncertain.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 字頭「再」

formation.text: The traditional analysis treats 寫 as a phonosemantic compound: 宀 contributes meaning and 舄 supplies sound. 宀’s specific contribution is unclear; the suggestion that it evokes writing indoors is conjectural. 写 is standardized as the simplified counterpart of 寫.

evidence.field: 寫 entry; form, gloss, component analysis, and historical notes
evidence.text: The entry says 寫 means 置物 and is formed 从宀舄聲 (宀 as semantic element, 舄 as sound element). Duan Yucai explains 置物 as transferring contents from one place to another, cites the *Liji* for pouring contents between vessels and the *Shijing* phrase 我心寫兮 for pouring out the heart, and says writing and drawing later also came to be called 寫. His claim that 宀 was included because 寫之則安矣 is a traditional explanation, not independent paleographic confirmation of the graph’s original semantic motivation.

formation.text: Historical accounts give two distinct constructions for 淨: the graph for a moat by Lu’s north gate combines 水, meaning water, with 爭 as a sound element; the graph for “without dirt” combines 水 with 靜 as a sound element. These accounts do not establish the original construction of 净 from its visible parts 冫 and 争.

evidence.source: 臺灣教育部《異體字字典》

It dates the cleanliness sense to Mozi, 節葬下, and cites Guangyun’s ‘無垢也’. This does not establish that 净’s visible 争 was part of the ancient graphic form, nor that the character originated with the cleanliness sense.

evidence.text: Separates 凈’s Kangxi gloss ‘冷貌’ (cold in appearance; fanqie 楚耕切) from the cleanliness sense. formation.text: 准 is a later form of 準, and the evidence does not establish a separate ancient construction for 准. The traditional analysis of 準 is phonosemantic: 水 contributes water meaning and 隼 is assigned a sound role. The historical sound correspondence is disputed: Zhengzhang groups the readings in a sound series, while Baxter–Sagart reconstructs substantially different forms.

components.text: Within 準, 水 contributes water meaning. The traditional account connects the graph’s sense ‘level’ or ‘flat’ with water’s level surface; 氵 is its conventional side form.

Within 準, 隼 is identified as the sound element. Its assigned role comes from the traditional analysis; the historical sound correspondence remains disputed. This component belongs to 準, not 准’s current structure.

sound_limitation.text: The modern and Middle Chinese reading pairs do not establish the historical phonetic relation. Baxter–Sagart reconstructs 準 as *turʔ and 隼 as *[s]urʔ; Zhengzhang proposes a different relationship.

sound.text: The Modern Mandarin readings differ in both initial and final; their resemblance does not prove a historical sound relation.

formation.text: The whole graph is traditionally analyzed as a pictograph of a small stool or table. Its interpretation has not been confirmed against an inspected early glyph image.

components.text: The whole graph 几 is interpreted as a picture of a small stool or table. It is not divided into smaller elements, and no phonetic component is supported.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 踞几也。象形。《周禮》五几：玉几、雕几、彤几、䰍几、素几。凡几之屬皆从几。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形) – a small stool viewed from the side. The original version was 𠀃, in which the horizontal stroke at the bottom represents the floor and/or the ground.
See also the bottom component of 其, 真, and 典, in which 八 is the stylization of the legs of a table.
Unrelated to 鉛, in which the top component is a stylization of 八, representing stagnant water. Also unrelated to 朵, 凡, and 殳.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *krəj (“foot, leg; stool”). Compare Tibetan ཁྲི (khri) and Burmese ခြေ (hkre).

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese entry for 几
evidence.text: For the independent stool character 几, this page reports Middle Chinese kjijX and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese /*C.kr[ə]jʔ/; Zhengzhang /*krilʔ/. These are competing reconstruction systems, not variants to merge. The stool graph's pronunciation and meaning do not make 几 a phonetic component in itself; the dossier's cited material does not offer evidence for a sound role within 几.

formation.text: Early forms are analyzed as the pictorial combination of a foot, 止, and an enclosure, 凵; some oracle-bone forms use 囗 for the enclosure. An older lexicographic account instead describes plants growing upward, a reading associated with the later, less recognizable form.

components.text: In early forms, 止 depicts the foot moving outward. Later forms made this element less recognizable.
凵 depicts the enclosure or hollow from which the foot moves. Some oracle-bone forms use 囗 in its place.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨文、金文、簡帛形體；《說文》及廣韻條目
evidence.text: The database analyzes 出 in oracle-bone and bronze forms as 止 (a foot) over 凵, with some oracle-bone forms using 囗. It interprets 凵/囗 as a cave or dwelling and the graph as a foot stepping outside, with the original sense ‘go out’. It cites oracle-bone examples 合集5063 王出 (‘the king goes out’), 合集33006 出日 (‘sunrise’), and 合集7205 勿出兵 (‘do not send out troops’); the first is an attested motion use, while the latter examples show contextual extensions. It also cites bronze inscriptions for going out, paying/issuing cloth, issuing commands, and transmitting commands. These examples support early use in multiple related contexts but do not by themselves establish the chronology of each sense. The entry records two Guangyun fanqie readings, 尺類 and 赤律, in departing and entering tone categories respectively. The source reproduces Shuowen’s ‘進也。象艸木益滋上出達也’, which is an early lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the graph’s earliest form.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「出」

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, 漢字字形演變資料庫
evidence.text: The database describes the upper part in oracle-bone and bronze forms as 止, representing a foot, and the lower part as a cave-like shape: together, a person stepping outward. This supports the foot-and-enclosure interpretation independently of the Shuowen plant explanation. The page lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript and small-seal categories; its bronze examples include inscription 集成05410. The accessible text does not date individual oracle-bone specimens or spell out a full dated sequence of graphic changes.
evidence.title: 漢字「出」：字形演變

evidence.source: 國學大師字形演變
evidence.text: This page describes oracle-bone and bronze 出 as 止 plus 凵, and reports an oracle-bone variant with 囗 instead of 凵, understood as an enclosure/dwelling. It proposes that the feet and enclosure later joined graphically, making the seal form less transparent; in clerical and regular scripts the 止 component became distorted toward a form read as 屮. The page indexes examples from oracle-bone inscriptions (including 合集217 and 合集33050), bronze inscriptions including Western Zhou vessels, Warring States texts, the Shuowen seal form, and the Qin Shuihudi manuscript 睡.效60. Its period labels establish source contexts but no exact first-use date; its account is a source’s analysis, not a direct visual inspection in this research.

This is a scholar’s interpretation of the graphic evidence.

formation.text: A semantic compound: 刀 depicts the knife and contributes the act of separation, while 八 is interpreted as depicting the separated things. A separate analysis proposes that 八 also cues the sound; that role remains disputed because the cited comparison is imperfect.

components.text: 八 is interpreted as depicting the two things separated by the knife. One analysis also proposes a phonetic role, but the comparison is imperfect and does not establish that role or its historical mechanism.

sound_limitation.text: A sound comparison is reported, but its imperfect match does not independently establish 八’s identity as a phonetic element in 分 or the historical mechanism.

sound.text: The proposed comparison is between 八 and 分 in the sense “divide.” Mandarin bā and fēn differ; in the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese system, 八 is *pˤret and 分 is *pə[n], also an imperfect match.

components.text: 刀 depicts the knife in the separation scene; the traditional analysis assigns it a role in expressing separation.

evidence.text: Depicts a knife ( 刀 ) being used to cut two things apart (八).

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 別也。从八从刀，刀以分別物也。

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The database reports that oracle-bone and bronze forms contain 刀 and 八; it analyzes 八 as both representing two separated things and serving as a phonetic element. It gives the resulting sense as splitting or cutting apart. It also records Xu Shen's later Shuowen analysis, which explains 分 as 別 and says it is composed of 八 and 刀. This is a modern scholarly database's account, not direct proof that the earliest users intended both functions.

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi, 八部; online transcription at ShuoWen.org
evidence.text: The entry reads “別也。从八从刀，刀以分別物也” (“to distinguish/separate; from 八 and 刀; the knife separates things”). Duan Yucai's Qing commentary labels this 會意 and explains that the knife accounts for its role. This is an ancient lexicographic analysis, preserved in a later online transcription, not independent confirmation of the original graphic motivation.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The database states that 八 depicts separated objects in this compound and also acts as a phonetic element; it notes that some scholars (including 高鴻縉, 戴家祥, and 林義光) have considered 八 and 分 originally one graph because of phonetic and semantic closeness. These are distinct claims: the proposed phonetic function in 分 does not by itself prove that the two graphs were once one character.

evidence.source: 韻典網, Guangyun and Old Chinese lookup
evidence.text: For 分, the database gives modern Mandarin fēn and fèn; Guangyun categories 府文切, labial unaspirated, level tone, and 扶問切, voiced labial, departing tone, with Baxter-style Middle Chinese pjun and bjunH. Its Old Chinese query lists Zhengzhang-style pɯn and bɯns. For 八, the Guangyun entry gives 博拔切, a labial initial, entering tone, and reconstructions including Zhengzhang pɣɛt and Baxter-style peat; the Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese list gives 八 *pˤret and 分 *pə[n] for the divide reading. This comparison supports a plausible sound relationship but shows it is not a close rhyme match in those reconstructions; phonetic classification remains the cited database's analysis, not a result proved solely by these forms.

evidence.source: William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart, Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction, version 1.1 (2014), hosted by University of Michigan
evidence.text: The reconstruction list gives fēn, Middle Chinese pjun, and Old Chinese *pə[n] for 分 ‘divide’; a separate entry gives fèn, Middle Chinese bjunH, and Old Chinese *[m]-pə[n]-s for ‘allotted duty’. These are Baxter-Sagart reconstructions, not directly observed ancient pronunciations.

evidence.source: Dong Chinese character dictionary
evidence.text: The page presents 分 as a knife cutting two things apart, but labels 八 an iconic component and notes the modern Mandarin sounds do not resemble each other. It lists oracle script circa 1250–1000 BCE, early Western Zhou bronze circa 1000 BCE, Shuowen seal script circa 100 CE, and Eastern Han clerical script circa 25–220 CE. formation.text: 別 is a semantic compound: the knife and bare-bone shape together depict cutting flesh from bone, suggesting separation. The bone shape is associated with 冎, though their precise graphic relationship is unresolved. The proposed 刂 + 另 analysis is not supported for the traditional graph.

components.text: The left element in traditional 別 is described as a bare-bone shape, contributing the bone in the cutting image. It is associated with 冎, but their exact graphic relationship is unresolved.
The right element in traditional 別 is 刂, the conventional side form of 刀, depicting a knife. The sources do not establish a complete sequence of graph shapes for 別.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese University of Hong Kong）
evidence.field: 形義源流通解；字形、甲骨文用例、廣韻反切
evidence.text: The database analyzes the early graph as 刀 plus a bone element, depicting a knife separating flesh and bone; it gives the basic meaning as divide/cut apart. It cites the oracle inscription 《合集》17230正, “至于賓別,” but says the graph there has been interpreted as either a place name or a sacrificial name. The database lists two Guangyun readings: 皮列切 and 方別切, with Middle Chinese 並 and 幫 initials respectively. Its account reports semantic use for cutting, distinguishing, and parting in later texts.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：別

evidence.source: 中央研究院漢字字形演變資料庫
evidence.text: The Academia Sinica database describes the oracle graph as a knife beside a bare-bone shape, interpreted as scraping flesh from bone, and says the small-seal form has roughly the same structure. This supports a bone-and-knife analysis, not a phonetic 另 analysis. The page’s displayed explanation does not establish whether the bone shape is graphically ancestral to 冎 or merely related in form.
evidence.title: 漢字「別」：字形演變

evidence.source: 《說文解字》, 大徐本 digital text, Wikisource
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry is “𠛰，分解也。从冎从刀,” glossing it as splitting/disassembling and analyzing it as 冎 plus 刀. In the same section, 冎 is described as removing flesh from a person and leaving the bone. This is an early dictionary analysis, not independent proof of every detail of the oracle graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字/04

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》
evidence.field: 說文釋形；字樣說明；釋義
evidence.text: The Taiwan Ministry of Education dictionary records the Shuowen form 𠛰 as “分解也。从冎，从刀,” and separately records 𠔁 as “分也。从重八.” It warns that the left part of standard 別 is a transformed 冎, distinct from 另. Its entries give senses including cutting apart, separation, distinction, other/another, and the later prohibition sense, with examples ranging from Huainanzi and Shiji to Honglou meng. This supports rejecting the dossier’s proposed 刂 + 另 component parse as an account of the traditional graph.
evidence.title: A00339 別 — Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

formation.text: The usual analysis is phonosemantic: 至 contributes the meaning “arrive/reach,” and 刀 supplies a sound cue. In Baxter–Sagart’s Old Chinese system, 刀 *C.tˤaw and 到 *tˤaw[k]-s have related syllable shapes, though their reconstructed morphology and tone categories differ. A competing account reads an older seal-script form as 人 + 至, with 人 reinterpreted as 刀; the graphic transition and its chronology remain unresolved.

formation.text: The formation of 前 is disputed. One traditional account treats 歬 as a semantic compound: 止 and 舟 depict a boat moving forward. formation.text: The received form 動 is phonosemantic: 力 contributes meaning associated with strength and action, while 重 provides a sound cue. This analysis applies to the received form; the reported bronze-script graph does not establish that these parts were already present there.

formation.text: The received form has two distinct analyses: Shuowen depicts a pregnant figure enclosing an unformed child, while 字源 reads 勹 as wrapping 巳, together conveying 胞衣, in a semantic construction. Other analyses propose 勹 as a sound component. A competing proposal derives 包 from a separate child-holding graph that first wrote 抱; no dated forms establish that descent. The earliest formation remains unresolved.

components.text: Shuowen depicts 巳 as an unborn child. 字源 instead treats it as the child in a semantic construction with 勹, together conveying 胞衣. These distinct received-form analyses do not settle the earliest graph.

字源’s 包 entry reads 勹 as wrapping 巳 in a semantic construction conveying 胞衣. Its separate 勹 entry says 勹 has an independent origin, rejecting derivations from 伏 or 旬; this concerns 勹’s own history and does not rule out a role in 包. Received-form analyses also propose 勹 as a sound component, while its role in the earliest formation remains unsettled.

sound_limitation.text: The modern Mandarin match does not establish 勹’s historical phonetic role in 包. The Zhengzhang comparison is reported through a reference compilation, not an inspected primary reconstruction publication.

sound.text: Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction assigns *pruː to both 勹 and 包, supporting the proposed sound link in that system. These are reconstructed values, not recorded ancient pronunciations.
The 勹 headword gives bāo on 字源 p. 814 (printed p. 801); the separate 包 headword gives bāo on p. 817 (printed p. 804). Matching modern readings do not establish a historical sound role.

formation.text: The whole graph is pictographic: it depicts two human figures turned away from each other. This picture does not itself mean “north.” The proposed earlier sense “turn against” or “turn one’s back” is inferred from the image and later uses, rather than securely attested in excavated writing.

components.text: 北 is treated as one indivisible picture of two people facing away from each other. Its paired forms are not analyzed here as separate modern components, and no sound element within the graph is established.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 𦮃也。从二人相背。凡北之屬皆从北。

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The author says the two-back-to-back-person conception remains clear from Shang writing through the Shuowen seal form, with changes in writing strokes rather than conception. Cited examples include oracle-bone inscriptions 合集6057 and 29401, Shang bronze 集成2710, Western Zhou bronzes 集成2804 and 2819, Chu slips, and Qin slips. The author proposes the graph’s original use was ‘turn against/back on’ or ‘defy’; this graphic interpretation does not by itself date or prove that word sense.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study says 北 was used as a phonetic loan for the direction ‘north’ from the Shang period, and that this use continued as its principal function. It explicitly says it cannot identify secure excavated examples of 北 writing the hypothesized original ‘turn against/back’ sense; that inference is based on the graphic account and related later uses. The study traces proposed extensions from turning against to back of the body, back side, facing with one’s back, concealment, betrayal, abandonment, military flight/defeat, and defeated troops. It gives Qin-Han manuscript examples for ‘back’ and ‘back side,’ and examples from transmitted texts and excavated manuscripts for betrayal, abandonment, and defeat. These are an author’s semantic analysis; the attestation order should not be read as a complete chronology of spoken senses.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study describes 北 from Shang oracle writing through the Shuowen seal form as two people turned back-to-back, with changes in stroke execution rather than a change in the proposed graphic conception. It cites oracle-bone examples 合集6057 and 29401, Shang bronze 集成2710, Western Zhou bronzes 集成2804 and 2819, Chu slips, and Qin slips. The author infers an original sense related to turning against or violating from this graphic conception, while acknowledging that secure excavated examples of that sense are lacking.
evidence.title: “北”字职用演变研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study reports 北 used as a loan graph for ‘north’ from the Shang period, and says this became its principal and continuing function. It distinguishes this borrowing from the hypothesized back/turning-against sense and its proposed extensions. evidence.text: Depicts the front of a house. In some regions of ancient China, houses were typically built to face the south.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形): a hanging percussion instrument (bell), originally identical to the left side of 㱿. Later phonetically borrowed to represent 南 (OC *nuːm, “south”).
Sagart (1988) instead proposes that it is a pictogram (象形) of the front of a house. Archaeological evidence confirms that in antiquity, at least in some regions, houses were built to face south.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *g-nam (“sky, sun”) (STEDT; Schuessler (2007); Benedict (1972)); the south is traditionally associated with the sun & light, compare 陽 (OC *laŋ, “light, sun-lit south-side of a hill”).
: If so, cognate with Tibetan གནམ (gnam, “sky”), ནམ (nam, “night”), Tshangla ngam (“sun, noon, day, sky”), Chepang न्याम् (nyam, “sun, sunlight, storm-cloud, weather”).
Alternatively, Sagart (2004) relates this word to Old Chinese *nɨm (revised to *nˤ[ə]m in 2014) "belly, front of the body", further "south" to Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-nam (“rib(s)”), as one term for one body-part often shifts its meaning to another body-part nearby.
: If so, 南 is cognate with 妊 (OC *njɯms, “to carry inside one's belly → to be pregnant”), 任 (OC *njɯm, *njɯms, “to carry a burden, especially in front of the body”), also 腩 (OC *nuːmʔ, “belly (of an ox)”), Southern Pumi nõ⁵⁵, Burmese နံရိုး (nam-rui:, “side of the body, rib”), and thus is a semantic counterpart to 北 (OC *pɯːɡ, “north”), which is related to 背 (OC *pɯːɡs, *bɯːɡs, “back of the body”).

formation.text: The early graph’s construction is disputed. One analysis sees a person above an opening and connects the scene with departure; another identifies a covered vessel associated with 盍. Shuowen parses it as 大 plus 凵, treating 凵 as a sound element, but the vessel-cover analysis contests that parsing. A proposed link to 呿, “open the mouth,” is unproven. The suggested path from covering to departure is an interpretation, not a documented sequence.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 人相違也。从大凵聲。凡去之屬皆从去。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 大 (“man”) + 口 (“mouth, object”). Top figure simplified to 土, unrelated to 士 (“scholar, gentleman”), while bottom simplified to 厶; a conservative variant is 厺.
There are various interpretations of the combination of “man” and “mouth, object”. One is that the ideograph represented a man with a hole marked in his crotch, with the idea of “anus” (i.e. getting rid of) (Schuessler, 2007). Another is that it represented a man departing from a cave or city.
Alternatively, it may be the original character of 呿 (OC *kʰal, *kʰas, *kʰab, “to open one's mouth”), the meaning given by the combination of 大 (“big”) and 口 (“mouth”). The meaning “to depart” would be an extension of the meaning “to open one's mouth”, as the lips depart from each other when one's mouth is open.
Shuowen Jiezi interprets the character as a phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *kʰaʔ, *kʰas): semantic 大 (“man”) + phonetic 𠙴 (qū).
In addition, 去 is also the original character of 盍 (OC *ɡaːb, “to cover”). The 大 could be a cover on top of an object 口.
The man on top is simplified as 土 as in 赤 and 走 (< 𧺆).
There were two pronunciations in Middle Chinese. The rising tone pronunciation originally meant “to put away, to eliminate” (causative of “to go away”), and the falling tone “to go away, to leave, to depart” (anticausative). The merger of the two pronunciations already happened in Old Chinese and most extant dialects do not observe this distinction now.
This word is of Sino-Tibetan origin with the basic meaning of "to get rid of". Compare Tibetan སྐྱག (skyag, “to spend, to lay out; dung, excrement”), རྐྱག (rkyag, “dirt, excrement”), Burmese ကျ (kya., “to fall, to become low”), ချ (hkya., “to put down, to bring down, to lower”).

evidence.field: sections 1, 3, 4; oracle-bone forms and meaning history
evidence.text: The authors review competing analyses of oracle-bone 去: one proposal reads a 大+口 form as the precursor of 呿, ‘open the mouth,’ and distinguishes a vessel-with-cover graph as 盍; their own analysis instead identifies oracle-bone 去 as the early form of 盍. They argue that the departure sense later differentiated from 盍, and that Shuowen’s analysis ‘从大凵聲’ misidentifies the graph’s elements. They report that departure is not securely established in oracle-bone inscriptions; earlier proposed readings of two inscriptions as ‘leave’ or ‘go to’ are challenged. Their proposed semantic link—removing a cover as a reversal of covering—is an analysis, not a directly documented transition.

evidence.text: The article reports an earlier proposal that the oracle graph from 大 and 口 means opening the mouth and is the source of 呿, and a competing vessel-cover analysis associated with 盍. It rejects the former as unsupported by its account of oracle-bone composition and advances the latter. It separately describes departure 去 as differentiated from 盍 rather than a straightforward graphic loan. It also surveys disagreement in the Old Chinese rhyme classification of 去-series words. The excerpt does not independently establish the original pronunciation or depicted referent of the vessel graph, nor does it establish an early attestation of the word 呿 as the source of the departure word.

formation.text: The graph is analyzed in competing ways. One reading sees 又 as a right hand and 口 as a ritual prayer vessel, forming a ritual scene associated with service and assistance. The evidence does not resolve these proposals or establish their graphic sequence.

evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɢʷɯʔ, *ɢʷɯs): phonetic 又 (OC *ɢʷɯs) + semantic 口. Originally written as 又 as a phonetic loan in the oracle bone script; in bronze inscriptions, a meaningless 口 component was added as a distinguishing mark.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *g-(j/r)a (“right (hand)”) (STEDT). Cognate with Tibetan གཡས (g.yas, “right”), Jingpho hkra (khʒa⁵⁵, “right”), Burmese ယာ (ya), ညာ (nya).
友 (OC *ɢʷɯʔ, “be friendly; friend”) is the endoactive derivation of 右 (OC *ɢʷɯʔ) (Schuessler, 2007).
佑 (OC *ɢʷɯs, “to aid”), 祐 (OC *ɢʷɯs, “(of divinity) to assist; to bless”), 宥 (OC *ɢʷɯs, “to pardon; magnanimous”) are exoactive derivations of 右 (OC *ɢʷɯʔ) (ibid.).

evidence.text: The text gives separate entries: 号 is “a sound of pain,” formed from 口 above 丂; 號 is “to call,” formed from 号 and 虎. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the pictured interpretation.

evidence.text: This entry proposes a tiger with a line for exhaled air as an early ideogram, says later forms added 口 or 言, and analyzes modern 號 as 号 phonetic plus 虎 semantic. formation.text: This is a phonosemantic compound: 口 supplies a speech-related meaning category, while the traditional analysis identifies 气 as the sound element. The modern right side is written like 乞, but its exact graphic path within 吃 is unresolved.

components.text: 口 means “mouth” and contributes a speech-related meaning category in 吃. Its pictographic history does not mean that it depicts a scene within this character.

The visible right side is written like 乞, but the traditional analysis identifies 气 as the sound element. 乞 and 气 share a graph history in other contexts; the exact graphic path within 吃 has not been traced.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang-style Old Chinese, 吃 is reconstructed as *kɯd and 乞 as *kʰɯd. Their similarity supports a sound-series relationship, though the forms differ; Mandarin chī and qǐ also differ.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 吃 entry: readings, senses and documentary examples
evidence.text: The dictionary gives the Shuowen definition and sound component 气, notes that the modern right side is written like 乞, and records jí for the speech-difficulty sense and chī for swallowing food or drink. It cites Shiji and Hanshu for the former and a Ming military manual for the latter; it treats eating as same as 喫. Those citations support differentiated sense histories, though they do not by themselves settle the graphic mechanism by which 吃 came to write the eating word.
evidence.title: [A00510] 吃 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Shuowen.cn, transcribing Shuowen and Duan Yucai
evidence.field: 口 entry: graphic and semantic characterization
evidence.text: 口 is explained as what a person uses to speak and eat, and classified as pictographic in Shuowen. The page supplies a progression of 口 examples from oracle-bone and late Shang bronze through Warring States, Qin/Han clerical, Eastern Han stele and regular script. This supports 口's independent meaning and history, not an inference about the whole 吃 compound's earliest form.

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcribing Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai’s annotation

evidence.text: This database describes 乞 and 气 as historically sharing a three-line graph associated with cloud/breath, later differentiated in shape and use. It displays oracle-bone, bronze and small-seal categories for 乞. This evidence concerns the component’s history; it does not prove an oracle-bone 吃 form or trace the exact shape used in 吃.

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003)

evidence.text: The entry gives Mandarin 吃 chī, a jí reading, Guangyun 居乙切, and Zhengzhang Old Chinese 吃 *kɯd versus 乞 *kʰɯds/*kʰɯd. In that reconstruction system, the forms are similar enough to be compatible with a phonetic-series relation, though they are not identical. formation.text: Early forms have an enclosure, sometimes with 口. One analysis tentatively interprets the enclosure as a picture of a tube- or bucket-like object; another reads the enclosure itself as 同 and treats 口 as optional. The object’s identity and name remain unconfirmed. A later received seal-script analysis parses the form as 𠔼, an enclosing or covering element, with 口, an inner mouth or opening. This later analysis does not settle the early disagreement.

components.text: One analysis tentatively interprets the early enclosure as a tube- or bucket-like picture; another reads it directly as 同. The object and its name are unconfirmed, so the proposed pictorial role is disputed.
In the received seal-script analysis, 𠔼 is the enclosing or covering element, including the upper horizontal stroke. This later parsing does not establish the enclosure’s role in the early graph.
In the received seal-script analysis, 口 is the inner mouth or opening within 𠔼. This later parsing does not establish whether it was part of the earliest form or its role there.

evidence.source: 《說文解字》在線查詢
evidence.field: 同：許慎釋義及段玉裁注
evidence.text: The entry gives 說文’s gloss 合會也 and analysis 从𠔼从口. This records the received Han dictionary analysis; it does not independently decide the earlier oracle-bone graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「同」

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart
evidence.text: The search result for the authors’ 2014 reconstruction lists 同 as Middle Chinese duwng and Old Chinese *lˤoŋ, glossed ‘together, join’; it also lists 筒 as duwng, *lˤoŋ, ‘tube’. The PDF itself failed to open in the browser, and the retrieved result does not establish that the ancient object represented by the enclosure was named 筒 or had this pronunciation.

evidence.text: The entry reports competing interpretations of the oracle-bone enclosure: Qiu Xigui tentatively reads it as a tube- or bucket-like pictograph, while Wang Ziyang reads it directly as 同 and treats 口 as optional. It distinguishes the symmetrical side strokes of 同 from 凡, reports enclosure-only early Western Zhou bronze forms and more common enclosure-plus-口 bronze forms, then says seal script was reinterpreted as 𠔼 plus 口 and continued into clerical and regular forms. The entry cites oracle-bone examples for meeting/along-with, bronze examples for meeting and making alike, and later examples for same, unify, together, and assent/follow. Its examples establish usages but not exact semantic chronology or the links between senses.

formation.text: The received analysis is semantic: 夕 sets an evening scene and 口 depicts speaking. A secondary proposal treats 夕 as a sound indicator, but the cited material does not establish that role; the graph’s original motivation remains uncertain.

components.text: 夕 is the upper element. Its basic sense is the time around sunset and moonrise, sometimes extending to night. In the received explanation of 名, it supplies the evening setting. 夕 and 月 once shared a moon-like form; later, a dot distinguished 月.

口 is the lower element. In the received explanation, it depicts the mouth used to speak one’s name. The cited accounts identify it in 名 but do not describe a separate graphic history for it within this character.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 自命也。从口从夕。夕者，冥也。冥不相見，故以口自名。

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: character evolution; graph structure and interpretation
evidence.text: The database lists 名 across oracle-bone, bronze (including inscription collection no. 04293), Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen stages. It describes the upper part as 夕 and lower as 口, and presents the traditional account that both are semantic: people unable to see one another at night speak their names to identify themselves. This supports the form sequence and records the received interpretation; it does not independently establish that interpretation as the original motivation.
evidence.title: 漢字「名」：字形演變

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database says 夕 and 月 originally both used a moon-like shape without a distinguishing dot; later graphic differentiation assigned the dotted shape to 月 and the undotted shape to 夕. It describes 夕’s basic sense as the time around sunset and moonrise, while noting that some usage extends to night. This makes the Shuowen explanation of 夕 as ‘darkness’ a historical gloss, not proof that night identification was the original formation mechanism of 名.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 夕

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese character entry; reconstruction fields attributed there to Baxter–Sagart 2014 and Zhengzhang
evidence.field: historical pronunciation comparison; reconstruction system and scope
evidence.text: The page gives modern Beijing Mandarin míng for 名, Middle Chinese mjieng, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *C.meŋ, and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *meŋ. The phonological similarity of reconstructed 名 and Mandarin míng is compatible with comparison of readings, but this evidence does not establish a phonetic role for 夕. The cited entry labels 名 itself as its Zhengzhang phonetic series; it does not provide a paired reconstruction showing 夕 as the phonetic in 名.
evidence.title: 名 — 维基词典

evidence.text: An alternative proposal reported by the entry says 口 may once have represented both 口 and 名, with 夕 (interpreted as standing for a graph later written 明) added as a phonetic indicator to distinguish them. The searched material did not yield a primary paleographic argument or direct attestation establishing this reconstruction. It conflicts with the usual semantic 夕 + 口 account, but the accessible primary-style character databases repeat that traditional account rather than adjudicating the proposed alternative.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: character evolution; stage labels and received component account
evidence.text: The entry lists oracle-bone, bronze (including inscription collection no. 04293), Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen forms. It describes 名 as upper 夕 and lower 口, and gives both a semantic role in the traditional story of calling out one’s name at night. This records a received interpretation; it does not independently establish the original motivation.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry reports that 夕 and 月 both used a moon-like form before graphic differentiation; it says a dot later distinguished 月 from 夕. It cites oracle-bone examples with 夕 meaning evening, including ‘今夕雨’ and ‘王夕出’. Its note identifies the evening/moonrise interval as the basic sense and says 夕 can sometimes extend to night.

formation.text: The graph’s early formation is disputed. An early lexicographic account describes a human issuing commands and analyzes the graph with 一 and 口. Other accounts connect early forms with 司 or 毓, but none establishes a secure decomposition of the received graph.

components.text: 口 appears in an early lexicographic analysis of a human issuing commands. This identifies it as a component in that account, but does not establish its independent role in the graph’s origin.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 繼體君也。象人之形。施令以告四方，故厂之。从一、口。發號者，君后也。凡后之屬皆从后。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Oracle bone inscriptions often wrote 后 as 毓, depicting a woman giving birth. Wang Guowei posits the meaning extended from childbirth to succession, then to empress. In the modern form, the birthing figure would be 𠂆 and the child figure 𠮛.
According to Kōjien and 学研漢和大字典, ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 人 (“person (variant form)”) + 口 (“hole”) — a depiction of a person's (人) anus, with the additional meaning of “behind”, “rear”, as well as coming to mean “emperor/empress”, who would live in a palace “behind” worldly troubles.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *mV-qow (“head”). Cognate with Tibetan གོ (go, “head; headman”), མགོ (mgo, “head, top, beginning”).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology)
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 甲骨、金文、說文、廣韻
evidence.text: The database reports 后 in bronze inscriptions from the late Spring and Autumn period, with the sense 'ruler'. It says bronze forms distinguish right-facing 后 from left-facing 司, while oracle forms do not distinguish orientation; it attributes to Tang Lan and Li Xiaoding the view that 后 and 司 were originally the same graph. It separately reports Wang Guowei's identification of oracle 后 written with 毓. The database reproduces the Shuowen account ('successor ruler', human figure, issuing commands) as an early lexicographic interpretation, and records the Guangyun fanqie 胡口 and 胡遘. This supports competing paleographic accounts, not a settled decomposition of modern 后 into 𠂆 plus 口.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：后

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology)
evidence.text: The source asserts that orientation distinctions for 后 and 司 appear only in bronze forms and that oracle graphs are directionally indistinct; it attributes the same-graph analysis to named scholars. Thus describing 司 merely as a 'mirror image' of 后 risks projecting a later distinction back onto oracle script. No component-by-component derivation or corruption process is demonstrated in the inspected text.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：后

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology)
evidence.text: The database reports that the graph 后 is first seen in late Spring and Autumn bronze inscriptions with the sense ‘ruler’. It says bronze forms distinguish right-facing 后 from left-facing 司, while oracle-bone forms show no such directional distinction; it attributes the view that the two were originally one graph to Tang Lan and Li Xiaoding. It separately reports Wang Guowei’s identification of oracle 后 written with 毓. These are competing scholarly accounts, not a settled component analysis of the received graph.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

formation.text: For the “scold” use of 嗎, 口 contributes a mouth-related meaning category and 馬 supplies the sound, making the graph phonosemantic. This analysis is documented for that use; whether it explains the question-particle spelling is unresolved.

components.text: In the ‘scold’ analysis of 嗎, 口 contributes the mouth-related meaning category and is not identified as a sound component.
In the ‘scold’ analysis of 嗎, 馬 is the sound component. Its independent graph depicts a horse, but that pictographic history does not establish the question particle’s origin.

sound_limitation.text: The current Mandarin readings provide a sound comparison, but do not establish a historical sound relation for the question-particle use. The documented phonetic analysis concerns the separate ‘scold’ use.

sound.text: In Modern Mandarin Pinyin, 馬 is mǎ and 嗎 is ma (neutral tone). This current comparison does not establish a historical sound relation in the question-particle use.

components.text: In current simplified 吗, 口 is the left component. Its role in the question-particle spelling is not established; the mouth-related category is documented for the traditional graph’s separate ‘scold’ use.
In current simplified 吗, 马 is the right component corresponding to 馬. The phonetic role is documented for traditional 嗎 meaning ‘scold’, not established for the question-particle spelling.

sound_limitation.text: The current simplified Mandarin readings provide a sound comparison, but do not establish a historical phonetic role for the question-particle spelling. The documented phonetic analysis concerns traditional 嗎 in the separate ‘scold’ use.

sound.text: In Modern Mandarin Pinyin, 马 is mǎ and 吗 is ma (neutral tone); this current comparison does not establish a historical phonetic role in the question-particle use.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声): semantic 口 (“mouth”) + phonetic 馬 (OC *mraːʔ).
From 無 (OC *ma, “not”) (Schuessler, 2007).
For Philippine Hokkien 嗎 /吗 (--ba), it is borrowed from Tagalog ba (interrogative particle).

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary records the older lexical analysis 嗎 as a俗 form of 罵, citing 字彙:「嗎，俗罵字」, 四聲篇海 and 龍龕手鑑. It explains the spelling as 口 semantic plus 馬 phonetic for the ‘revile/scold’ sense. The record separately recognizes 嗎 as a proper character with additional readings and uses, so this account does not by itself explain the question-particle word history.
evidence.title: [A03210-003] 嗎 (罵) - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, International Computer Chinese Character and Variant Database
evidence.text: The database describes 馬 as picturing the whole animal, emphasizing its large eye, mane, body and long tail. It lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu-slip, small-seal and Shuowen form categories. This supports the pictographic history of 馬 as an independent graph; it does not establish an original horse-name pronunciation through 嗎’s graphic history.
evidence.title: 漢字「馬」：字形演變

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, International Computer Chinese Character and Variant Database
evidence.text: The database explicitly identifies 马 as the simplified counterpart of 馬. This supports origin_relation simplified_form for 馬 → 马 when describing the 馬 component’s visible simplified shape in 吗.

evidence.text: The source gives 口 kǒu, Middle Chinese khuwX, Old Chinese *kʰˤ(r)oʔ, ‘mouth’. The matching repository row in sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv (row 1898) agrees. 口 is a semantic component in the dictionary’s 口＋馬 account; no evidence examined here assigns 口 a phonetic role in 嗎.

This account concerns the ‘scold’ use, not the history of the question particle.

evidence.text: Directly inspected the scan. The appendix lists 妈 mā, 麻 má, 马 mǎ, 骂 mà, and 吗 ma (轻声) as examples of the four tones and neutral tone. This is a modern pronunciation chart, not historical evidence for 吗’s formation or the particle’s origin.

formation.text: 吧 is a phono-semantic compound: 口 contributes a semantic category, while 巴 supplies a sound cue. The specific link between 口 and the particle’s meaning is not explained.

components.text: 口 is identified as the semantic component in 吧, but its precise contribution to the particle’s meaning is not explained.
巴 is the phonetic component in 吧. The sound relationship does not establish what 巴 originally depicted or what that object was called; its graphic referent is disputed.

sound_limitation.text: The modern Mandarin pair comes from local Unihan data and does not establish the historical phonetic relationship. The Old Chinese comparison is reconstructed evidence, not a recorded ancient pronunciation.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction, 巴 and one reading of 吧 are both *praː; the same table gives 吧 a second reading, *pʰraː. These are reconstructed forms, not recorded ancient pronunciations.

The local Unihan rows list 巴 bā and 吧 ba as a modern Mandarin comparison for the sentence-final particle. This does not explain 酒吧 (“bar”), a separate whole-character loan whose sound basis is not established.

evidence.source: CUHK 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The dictionary analyzes 吧 as 口 (semantic) + 巴 (phonetic), records two Guangyun entries with fanqie 普巴 and 伯加, and gives the modern particle’s uses as agreement, suggestion/imperative, conjecture/question, and pause or conditional. It also cites a passage in the Qing-period novel 兒女英雄傳 for an onomatopoeic use. This supports a component analysis and separately attests listed uses; it does not provide a dated early graphic sequence for 吧.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 字頭「吧」

evidence.source: Wiktionary
evidence.field: Chinese glyph origin and reconstructed phonetic series
evidence.text: The page classifies 吧 as a phono-semantic compound, semantic 口 and phonetic 巴. Its table labeled Zhengzhang (2003) lists 巴 *praː and 吧 *praː, *pʰraː, among other 巴-series graphs. These are scholarly Old Chinese reconstructions, not direct ancient pronunciations. Together with the distinct Guangyun entries on the CUHK page, this supports sound correspondence without implying that the depicted referent or name behind 巴 is recoverable.
evidence.title: 吧 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary
evidence.field: Modern and reconstructed readings of 吧
evidence.text: The page gives neutral-tone Mandarin particle ba (Pinyin ba, tone 5/0 in the page’s conventions) and Cantonese Jyutping baa6 for the particle. Its Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese table separately lists 吧 *praː and *pʰraː readings, with 巴 as phonetic component. These historical forms belong to the Zhengzhang reconstruction system and the page’s two readings; they should not be collapsed into one certain pronunciation history.
evidence.title: 吧 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, National Taiwan University hosted article
evidence.text: The dossier’s inspected article presents disagreement about 巴’s own origin: some forms once read as 巴 are argued to represent a seated person component, while Shuowen’s snake account and other snake interpretations are discussed as alternatives. formation.text: The formation is disputed. One proposal treats the whole graph as a pictorial form derived from 舌: its central stroke is extended upward to depict a tongue projecting from a mouth, associated with speaking or telling. The received Shuowen account analyzes 牛 plus 口 and explains an ox striking a person while a crossbar restrains its horns as a way of signaling people. A separate proposal analyzes 口 plus an abbreviated 壴; 壴 may be phonetic and possibly semantic, but its function is uncertain.

evidence.text: This database presents Zhang Yujin’s account that oracle-bone 告 is derived from 舌 by extending its central stroke upward, representing an open mouth with tongue and giving the sense ‘speak/tell’; it also records a 牛+口 sacrificial interpretation as an alternative. It cites oracle-bone 合集1166甲 for 告 used as a sacrificial term read 祰, 屯南997 for a report of a deer, Western Zhou bronze examples for reporting, admonishing, and accusing, and a Guodian Chu slip example for ‘tell’. These are source-reported examples, not a proven chronological sequence of semantic change.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.field: 古文字構形分析與異說
evidence.text: The abstract surveys competing explanations: the traditional Shuowen 牛+口 account; Zhang Yujin’s proposal that 告 derives from 舌; and the author’s proposal that oracle-bone 告 is 口 plus an abbreviated 壴, possibly a phonetic element and possibly also semantic. The author says this proposal better fits parallel variation between the upper part of 告 and 壴-type graphs, while acknowledging uncertainty about that component’s function. The full paper PDF appeared in search but opening it was rejected; this item reports only the inspected abstract.

formation.text: 唱 is a phonosemantic compound: 口 contributes the vocal meaning category, and 昌 serves as its phonetic component. A Small Seal form is reported, but the earliest surviving form and graphic sequence are unresolved.

components.text: 口 marks the vocal meaning category in 唱. No distinct earlier form for this component within 唱 is established.

昌 serves as the traditional phonetic component. Zhengzhang’s reconstruction gives it a similar initial and rhyme to 唱 but a different ending; another reported reconstruction of 唱 differs, leaving the detailed sound history unsettled.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s system, the reconstructed forms for 昌 and 唱 share an initial and rhyme but differ in their endings; these are reconstructions, not recorded ancient pronunciations.
Middle Chinese categories show related initials and rhyme categories but different tones, consistent with a sound relationship without directly recording pronunciation at formation.

formation.text: The earliest graph’s construction is disputed: proposals include a star-related rite, a vessel, and an ancestral ritual. In the received small-seal analysis, 㕯 contributes meaning and abbreviated 章 supplies sound; this account does not explain the earlier oracle forms.

components.text: In the received small-seal analysis, 㕯 contributes the idea of knowing what is inside from outside. Its role in the earlier oracle-bone graph is not established.
The received analysis identifies an abbreviated 章 as the sound element. Its visible correspondence to full 章 is unclear, and this analysis is not established for the oracle-bone graph.

sound_limitation.text: The cited readings provide sound comparisons but do not independently establish that abbreviated 章 was 商’s historical sound element. Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese form for 商, *hljaŋ, is separate from the Baxter–Sagart forms and is not paired with them here.

sound.text: Mandarin zhāng and shāng have similar finals but different initials. In Baxter–Sagart’s Old Chinese forms, 章 *taŋ and 商 *s-taŋ share the final while their initials differ, a comparison consistent with—but not proof of—the received sound analysis.

evidence.text: The database calls the original meaning uncertain. It reports Zhu Fangpu’s proposal that the graph combines 丙 as a raised platform and a shortened 辛 interpreted as 薪 (fuel), depicting fuel burned on a platform to sacrifice to the Fire Star; commerce would be a later borrowed use. It also reports a competing vessel interpretation and argues that forms with added star-like circles favor a star-related interpretation. The database’s own discussion is a scholarly account, not a settled decipherment.

evidence.source: Kwang-chih Chang, Early China 20 (1995), Cambridge University Press
evidence.field: competing interpretation of original meaning and semantic development
evidence.text: Chang summarizes the longstanding disagreement about 商’s oracle-bone meaning. He argues that it first named a place associated with ancestral sacrifice, and that the graph depicted a rite before an ancestral image; he proposes extension from ritual to ancestral temple, its city, and then the Shang dynasty. This is one scholar’s argued analysis, not consensus; Cambridge’s accessible abstract does not provide the full argument for independent evaluation.
evidence.title: On the Meaning of Shang In The Shang Dynasty

formation.text: A semantic compound in the traditional analysis: 壴 contributes a drum image, while 口 contributes the idea of singing. The resulting drum-and-singing or music-making scene is a proposed motivation for joy; another interpretation links the graph to hearing drum music or setting up a drum for a festive event. These interpretations do not establish a sequence of meanings.

components.text: 壴 is identified as an early picture of an upright drum, with a top ornament, face, and support. Here it contributes the drum image; the evidence does not establish a phonetic role in 喜.
口 is the mouth element in the traditional analysis. In the proposed drum-and-singing explanation, it contributes the idea of singing rather than depicting a mouth as part of a literal scene.

formation.text: The received analysis is phonosemantic: 口 marks a mouth-related category, while 曷 supplies a sound cue. This traditional account does not independently establish the graph’s original formation.

components.text: 口 marks the mouth-related category in the traditional analysis. No pictured scene or earlier graphic form for 喝 is established.
曷 is assigned the phonetic role; its question-word meanings do not explain 喝. The reported sound comparison is broad: 喝 has multiple reconstructed readings, not all matching 曷 in the same way.

sound_limitation.text: The comparison is reported through a secondary source, and no primary reconstruction table for 曷 was checked. Multiple readings of 喝 mean it cannot be treated as one uniform pronunciation history.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, 曷 is reported as *ɡaːd; 喝 is reported with *qʰaːd, *qraːds, and *qʰoːb. These reconstructions suggest broad sound-series context, not an identical match across readings.

evidence.text: The entry gives “㵣也。从口曷聲” (“[㵣] also; from 口, with 曷 as phonetic”). Duan Yucai comments that a pronunciation note may have been omitted and cites older literary uses of 喝 for hoarseness or a hoarse voice. This supports a traditional phonosemantic analysis, but Shuowen is a historical lexicographic account rather than independent proof of the character’s original formation.

evidence.text: The dictionary transcribes the Great Xu edition’s definition and Duan edition’s explicit “从口，曷聲,” and records Mandarin readings hē, hè, yè. It associates hē with drinking; hè with scolding, calling aloud, and an exclamatory use; and yè with a hoarse or constricted voice. It cites 《論衡·氣壽》 and 《後漢書·張酺傳》 for hoarseness and 《舊唐書·哥舒翰列傳》 for a scolding use. formation.text: In its present form, 四 has an enclosing 囗 shape around inner 儿-form strokes; this visible structure does not establish the ancient identities or roles of those parts. Its origin remains disputed. One interpretation reads four horizontal marks as counting rods representing four, while another describes 亖 as a direct numeral graph. A competing proposal treats 四 as a graph depicting breath, identified with 呬, later reused to write ‘four’ because the words may have sounded alike; the original name and pronunciation of the depicted referent are not established. A separate proposal treats 四 as the original graph of 泗, depicting nasal discharge, then borrowed for ‘four’; this account lacks textual attestation. Neither borrowing explanation is established.

components.text: In the present graph, 囗 is the enclosing outer shape. This visible identity does not establish its role in the ancient formation.
In the present graph, 儿 identifies the inner strokes. This visible identity does not establish their role in the ancient formation.

evidence.field: 形義通解; paleographic account and cited bronze inscription
evidence.text: The entry offers two explanations: following Xu Zhongshu, oracle forms with four horizontal strokes represent counting rods and already mean four; alternatively, it says early bronze forms follow oracle forms, while a later Spring and Autumn shape was identified by scholars as the original graph of 呬, depicting breath from mouth/nose, then borrowed for the numeral because of sound similarity. It cites the bronze inscription 無㠱簋, “王易(賜)無㠱馬亖(四)匹,” as a numeral use. These are competing analyses reported by the database, not a settled derivation. The page gives no object-specific date for this inscription.

evidence.field: 形義通解; Shuowen and bronze inscription notes
evidence.text: The entry attributes the four-counting-rods reading of oracle forms to Xu Zhongshu. It separately reports that later Spring and Autumn forms were identified by scholars as an earlier graph for 呬, depicting breath from mouth/nose, which was borrowed for ‘four’ because of sound similarity. It cites 無㠱簋:「王易(賜)無㠱馬亖(四)匹」as numeral usage, but supplies no exact artifact date. Shuowen’s received account calls 四 an image of division into four and lists 𠃢 and 亖 as old forms; this is historical lexicography, not independent proof of origin.

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》
evidence.field: 四 entry, graphic formation and history; PDF p. 1279, printed p. 1264; continuation PDF p. 1280, printed p. 1265
evidence.text: The actual headword is 四 in the 四部. The entry describes the Shang form as four accumulated strokes, normalized as 亖, directly representing the numeral. It says this form continued alongside 四 in Western Zhou through Han bronze inscriptions. It dates another form series to Spring and Autumn and reports competing readings, including Shuowen’s ‘image of dividing into four’ and Ma Xulun’s proposal that 四 was the original graph of 泗, depicting nasal discharge and borrowed for the numeral. On the continuation page the book says Ma’s proposal lacks textual attestation, despite seeming plausible from the shape. The visible text names 泗 (氵 + 四), not 呬. The simple form continued while elaborate Spring and Autumn forms proliferated through Warring States–Eastern Han and were later eliminated. I inspected the supplied full-page scan pixels for both pages; printed page numbers 1264–1265 and the page-spanning continuation are visible. I checked the cited passage and the headword against the scans; no OCR substitution is proposed for the material cited.

formation.text: The graph is best treated as a pictograph of a spiral or revolving form. One interpretation specifies water turning in a circle, but the depicted object and exact original meaning remain uncertain. A competing proposal treats 回 and 囘 as originally distinct graphs and words, with 回 meaning “around”; their relationship is unresolved. No separate semantic or phonetic parts within 回 are established.

components.text: 回 is represented as one whole picture associated with a spiral or circular motion. The traditional description of an outer 囗 and an inner revolving shape is an account of its appearance, not proof that these are independent components.

formation.text: The traditional graph 國 is phonosemantic: 囗 contributes the territory meaning, and 或 supplies a sound cue. The curated Western Zhou bronze-style image shows an angular inner element within an enclosure; it is a modern redraw illustrating the structure, not an artifact or a sequence of forms. The current graph 国 has 玉 in place of 或, but the reason and pathway for this graphic change are unclear.

components.text: In 國, 囗 marks a boundary or territory. Some Warring States forms are reported with 匚 or 𠃊 in the same boundary-marker role. This component belongs to 國, the traditional graph from which 国 is simplified.
In 國, 或 is the phonetic element, but its original depicted referent is not known. 国 has 玉 in the corresponding inner position; the history of this substitution is unclear.

sound_limitation.text: The reconstructions support a sound relationship between 或 and 國 but do not identify 或’s original depicted referent. Modern readings alone do not prove its role in 國.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstructions, 國 *kʷɯːɡ and 或 *ɡʷɯːɡ are similar but differ in their initial consonant. These are reconstructed forms, not direct records of ancient speech.

components.text: 玉 is the visible inner element in 国, occupying the position of 或 in 國. It is a graphic replacement; the evidence does not show when or why this substitution arose.

formation.text: For 圖, competing analyses treat 囗 and 啚 as a meaning-based compound: the Han dictionary explanation connects 啚 with difficulty, while another interpretation treats it as territory. sound_limitation.text: The current Mandarin readings bǐ and tú do not establish an ancient phonetic relationship. A secondary account reports a matching Zhengzhang reconstruction, but it does not independently verify 啚’s historical reading or role in 圖.

formation.text: The received form is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 土 contributes meaning and 才 supplies sound. Early forms have competing explanations: one analyzes 才 and 士 as sound elements, while other accounts describe 才 reused for 在 with 土 or 士 added later. These accounts do not establish a complete graphic sequence.

components.text: The historical dictionary parses the received graph with 土 as its meaning element. Accounts differ over whether early forms already contained 土 or instead contained 士.

In the received-form analysis, 才 supplies the sound. Accounts differ on whether it occurred alongside 士 or was first used to write 在 as a whole. 才’s own ancient referent is disputed between sprout and stake-or-pile interpretations.

sound.text: The Baxter–Sagart Middle Chinese forms are similar, though their ending notation differs; this is compatible with the proposed sound role.
The Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese forms share similar initial and rime material, though their ending notation differs; this is compatible with, but does not prove, the proposed sound role.
Mandarin 才 and 在 have similar finals but different initials and tones; this present-day comparison does not establish their ancient sound relation.

components.text: One account analyzes early forms as containing 士, a proposed second sound element, later confused with 土. This role is disputed; the cited Baxter–Sagart comparison does not independently support it.

sound_limitation.text: The reported Baxter–Sagart forms for 士 and 在 differ substantially, so they do not independently establish the proposed sound role.

evidence.text: The database analyzes early bronze and oracle-bone forms as 才 plus 士, treating both as phonetic indicators and glossing the word’s original sense as existence. It says 才 was borrowed for 在 in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions, and later records bronze uses for existence/location, including 康鼎「王才(在)康宮」 and a date phrase on a bronze vessel. It reports that 士 and 土 became confused after the Spring and Autumn/Warring States period and that the small-seal form consequently has 土. It also reports a separate bronze use of 在借作士 in the Zhongshan king square pot inscription.
