evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 不宜有也。《春秋傳》曰：“日月有食之。”从月又聲。凡有之屬皆从有。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɢʷɯʔ): phonetic 又 (OC *ɢʷɯs) + semantic 肉 (“meat”). The hand shape has been abstracted to 𠂇; compare 右, where 又 has also taken this shape. The 肉 in turn has taken the form of ⺼.
The character may have been the original form of 侑 (OC *ɢʷɯs, “to urge to eat”). Alternatively, it may be the original form of 醢 (OC *qʰɯːʔ, “minced pickled meat”), which also has the 又 (OC *ɢʷɯs) element as phonetic.
Folk etymology traditionally explains it as a hand holding meat, hence “in possession of”. However, the oracle bone script shows no meat.
Shuowen Jiezi and other ancient sources have erroneously analyzed the character as a phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɢʷɯʔ): phonetic 又 (OC *ɢʷɯs) + semantic 月 (“moon”). Shuowen Jiezi defines 有 as "不宜有也" ("[to have something that] not should be had"), citing the Spring and Autumn Annals (春秋傳): "日月有食之" ("There are solar and lunar eclipses"). As eclipses were not auspicious to the Chinese, they were "something that should not be happening". The 月 component alludes to the inauspicious lunar eclipse.
Possibly Sino-Tibetan. Compare Tibetan ཡོད (yod, “to be; to have”). Related to:
* 侑 (OC *ɢʷɯs, “to offer, to sacrifice”) [causative, i.e. “to cause to have”]
* 又 (OC *ɢʷɯs, “again”) [adverbial]
* 或 (OC *ɡʷɯːɡ, “some; or”) [indefinite]

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph is conventionally interpreted as paired strings of valuables, often shells. Its regular form resembles two adjacent 月 shapes, but that resemblance does not make them moon components. The exact count and grouping of the valuables are disputed.

components.text: Treat 朋 as one picture of valuables strung together, conventionally shells. In the regular form its parts look like two 月 shapes, but they are not separate moon components; their precise grouping is uncertain.

Pictogram (象形).
The oracle bone script form consisted of two strings of five cowries. Some forms of the oracle bone script contained an additional 人 which later evolved into 勹 (OC *pruː), which served as a phonetic component. The glyph was eventually corrupted to a duplication of 月 (“moon”).

formation.text: The leading analysis is phonosemantic: 𠬝 provides a sound cue, and an added element may contribute meaning. The proposed added element is variously identified as 凡, 舟, or a tray-like shape; a competing analysis sees a person presenting a tray. The compound analysis is probable, but the element’s identity and meaning are unsettled.

components.text: 𠬝 is analyzed as a graph combining 又, interpreted as a hand, and 卩, interpreted as a kneeling person, to depict subduing. In 服 it is proposed as the phonetic component; the cited Old Chinese reconstruction gives both graphs the same form. The proposed pictorial analysis concerns 𠬝 itself, not its role in 服.

sound_limitation.text: The sound match supports a phonetic role in this proposed compound, but does not independently establish that 𠬝 meant ‘subdue’ in every early occurrence.

sound.text: The Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction gives 𠬝 ‘subdue; submit’ and 服 ‘garment; wear’ and ‘subdue; submit’ the same form, supporting 𠬝 as a sound cue in this proposed compound.

components.text: The added shape is identified in competing accounts as 凡 ‘tray’, 舟, or a tray-like form. One account proposes a change from a 凡-like form to 舟 and later to the modern 月-like shape; the exact forms and sequence are disputed. Another analysis treats the whole graph as a person serving at a tray. The element’s semantic contribution is not settled.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *bɯɡ): semantic 凡 (“tray”) + phonetic 𠬝 (*[b]ək, “to subdue”) – to serve. 𠬝 is the original pictogram for this character; 凡 was added later.
凡 here has been corrupted into 舟 and subsequently 月.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The database analyzes 𠬝 as an early graph for 服: its oracle-bone and bronze forms combine 又, interpreted as a hand, with 卩, interpreted as a kneeling person, depicting a person being subdued. It reports oracle-bone use as a verb ‘conquer’ and as a noun for conquered people, including sacrificial victims. This is the database’s analysis, not an uncontested reading of every occurrence.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 𠬝 entry

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The database calls 服 a later phono-semantic form of 𠬝, with 凡 added; it says bronze forms of 凡 sometimes became 舟, and later clerical/regular forms account for the modern 月-like shape. It also reports oracle-bone 服 used as a place name and bronze 服 for office or duty, citing 班簋. This supports a proposed graph history, but the page does not resolve the competing tray/service interpretation.

formation.text: This is a pictograph: the graph represents a tree as a whole, without a separate sound component. An older account describes it as 屮 above roots, but a competing analysis treats the apparent resemblance to 屮 as insufficient to establish a separate component.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph is traditionally interpreted as a wheat plant, with a stem, paired leaves and an ear-like top. The upper mark may instead be a distinguishing or ornamental stroke, so its exact reference is uncertain.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形) of wheat – original character of 麥 (OC *mrɯːɡ, “wheat”) or 麳 (OC *rɯː, “wheat”). The line in the middle represents the ear, the two lines pointing upwards represent leaves, and the lines pointing downwards represent the stem and roots. An additional horizontal line was often added at the top end of the character, possibly used to emphasize the ear of the wheat. Compare 禾; both are unrelated to 釆.
This character has been borrowed for “to come” since the oracle bone script. During the Western Zhou and Warring States periods, additional semantic components, such as 止 (“foot”) or 辵 (“to walk”), were added to differentiate the original sense from the borrowed sense. However, these additions were not inherited in later scripts.
Some consider the derivative 麥 from the addition of 夊 (“to walk slowly”) to be the original form for the meaning “to come”. If so, their meanings have interchanged due to frequent use of 來 for “to come”.
Shuowen connects “wheat” and “to come” from a mythological standpoint: 天所來也 (“it comes from the heavens”). This may be supported by archaeological evidence, which suggests that wheat is not native to China, but originated in the Fertile Crescent.
來 and 麥 have both been reconstructed to begin with *mr- in Old Chinese. The former retains the liquid as /l/, while the latter retains the nasal /m/.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *la-j ~ ra (“to come”) (STEDT). Cognate with 迨 (OC *l'ɯːʔ, “to reach; until”), 賚 (OC *rɯːs, “to bestow”), Burmese လာ (la, “to come”). Also cognate with 蒞 (OC *rɯbs, “to arrive”) according to Schuessler (2007). Unclear if connected to Vietnamese lại (“come; again”).

evidence.source: Academia Sinica CASE Press
evidence.field: Article on 來 and 麥, graph description and oracle-bone usages
evidence.text: The article describes late Shang oracle-bone and bronze 來 as a plant-shaped graph, with a stem, paired slanting leaves, and an upper ear-like part; it notes the upper extra mark may be an ear detail or ornamental stroke. It reports oracle-bone contexts using 來 predominantly for ‘come/go’, tribute, future year, and a place name, and argues the added foot graph 麥 was intended to mark the wheat word. This modern scholarly account gives contextual examples but does not independently establish a dated earliest occurrence of the wheat sense.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「來」與「麥」和中國小麥的身世之謎

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)

evidence.text: The account describes 來 as a wheat-plant pictograph and discusses competing readings of an extra top stroke: it may distinguish meanings, be ornamental, or represent part of the ear. formation.text: 杯 is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 木 contributes meaning and 不 is proposed to cue the sound. The received analysis of related 桮 instead gives 木 plus 否 as its sound component. The Warring States analysis supports the 木 + 不 account for those forms, but the earliest form remains unresolved.

components.text: 木 is identified as the meaning component in analyses of 杯. Warring States forms are described as having 木 on the meaning side; the specific link between wood and the vessel meaning is not explained.

For the Warring States forms, one analysis identifies 不 as the sound element. A competing proposal treats it as a remnant of a felled tree in a hollowed-tree vessel; the evidence does not settle its role in the earliest form.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, 不 and 杯 share an initial and rhyme nucleus, but differ in the reconstructed lateral and vowel length.
In Modern Mandarin, 不 is bù and 杯 is bēi; this present-day pair does not establish their historical sound relationship.

components.text: In the received account of 桮, 否 is its sound component. This analysis applies to the related graph 桮, not necessarily to modern 杯.

sound_limitation.text: Modern Mandarin fǒu and bēi do not establish the historical sound relation. The cited sources provide no paired historical reconstruction for 否 and 桮 in one system.

sound.text: The modern Mandarin readings are fǒu for 否 and bēi for 桮; this pair does not identify which readings underlie the received historical analysis.

evidence.text:
Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意) and phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *rteːwɢ): phonetic 卓 (OC *rteːwɢ, “high”) + semantic 木 (“tree; wood”) – table. The bottom 十 of 卓 has merged with or been replaced by 木. An obsolete variant that distinguishes the two components is 棹.
From 卓 (OC *rteːwɢ, “high”), as tables are relatively tall (compared to other pieces of furniture like 几 (OC *krilʔ, “stool”)).
Similar descriptive derivations for pieces of furniture include:
* 登 (OC *tɯːŋ, “to climb”) > 凳 (OC *tɯːŋs, “stool”)
* 倚 (OC *qralʔ, *qrals, “to lean”) > 椅 (OC *qral, *qralʔ, “chair”).

formation.text: 歡 is a phonosemantic compound: 欠 contributes meaning, and 雚 supplies a sound cue. The basic sense is joy or happiness. 欢 is a simplified form of 歡.

components.text: In 歡, 欠 is the semantic component. Its traditional explanation depicts a person opening the mouth with breath rising above, associated with breathing or yawning. A specific association with laughter in 歡 is possible but interpretive.

In 歡, 雚 is the phonetic component. It also has a documented bird-related use, but the precise referent and spoken name are disputed. The sound comparison supports its phonetic role without showing that a bird name was borrowed for ‘joy’.

sound_limitation.text: The readings can be compared, but the evidence does not establish that the bird pronunciation was the particular pronunciation intended when 雚 served as the sound component in 歡.

sound.text: In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese, 雚 *C.qʷˤar-s and 歡 *qʷʰˤar have a close onset and rhyme, consistent with 雚 supplying the sound; their prefixes and suffixes differ.

evidence.text: The dictionary classifies 欢 as a variant of 歡 and says 歡 is written in Shuowen as 喜樂也、從欠，雚聲. It cites 宋元以來俗字譜 entries from 目連記 and 金瓶梅 for 欢, and 字學三正’s statement 歡，俗作欢. This supports a pre-modern variant history for 欢; it does not establish that its modern status as the standardized simplified form began in those texts.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants, 欠 entry
evidence.text: The entry cites Shuowen’s account of 欠 as a person opening the mouth and breathing/yawning, with the form depicting qi emerging above a person. Later listed meanings include raising or moving the body slightly and deficiency. Shuowen’s definition of 欠 does not itself say that it depicts laughter; assigning an additional laughter-related nuance in 歡 is an interpretation, not a directly attested explanation in this source.

evidence.source: Hanyuguoxue, Shuowen entry for 雚
evidence.field: 《說文解字》大徐本 and 段注本
evidence.text: Shuowen’s 雚 entry calls the referent 小爵 and analyzes the graph as 从雈、吅聲, citing 詩曰「雚鳴于垤」. Duan Yucai emends the received gloss 小爵 to 雚爵/雀 and identifies the bird with 鸛; he notes that the received text of the poem has 鸛 and that 雚 is another textual form. Thus the bird gloss and the precise referent are textually disputed; the character 雚 has documented bird-related use, but this evidence does not recover an exact spoken name that would independently prove any loan claim.

formation.text: The received form is phonosemantic: 欠 contributes a semantic category related to vocal action, while 哥 supplies the sound. Earlier reported structures differ, but their relationship to this form is unresolved.

components.text: 欠 is the semantic component in the received analysis. It is described as a person with an open mouth and rising breath, linking it to vocal action. This does not establish that it appeared in the earliest form.

哥 is the phonetic component in the received analysis. Its historical use as a spelling for 謌/歌 is a spelling association; it does not show that 哥 originally meant “sing” or that 歌 originated by borrowing the whole 哥 graph.

sound.text: The Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstruction gives both 歌 and 哥 as *kaːl, supporting a historical sound relationship. The current Mandarin readings also match as gē; that modern match alone does not establish the ancient relationship. Equivalent Baxter–Sagart data for 哥 is not provided here.
Both characters are listed with the same current Mandarin reading. This is a modern comparison, not proof of their ancient sound relationship.

formation.text: Early 正 has competing analyses: 止, a foot, moving toward a city or destination, or 止 combined with an upper form identified as 丁 and proposed as a sound cue. 丁 is also described as citylike, but whether the upper element had both pictorial and phonetic functions is unresolved. The Han-era analysis of 止 plus 一 is a later interpretation, not confirmation of the early structure.

components.text: In the destination analysis, the upper form represents a city or destination. Other analyses identify it as 丁 and propose a sound role; these accounts interpret the same early strokes differently.

sound_limitation.text: Old and Middle Chinese resemblances support a proposed sound association, but do not independently establish that the upper strokes are 丁 or functioned phonetically in 正. The modern Mandarin readings do not establish an ancient relation.

sound.text: 丁 *tˤeŋ resembles 正 *teŋ-s, the separate “correct” reading; the resemblance supports a proposed phonetic association, not the graphic parse by itself.
丁 *tˤeŋ resembles 正 *C.teŋ, the first-month reading. This is a proposed sound resemblance, separate from the comparison with 正’s “correct” reading.
丁 teng resembles 正 tsyeng in the first-month reading; this Middle Chinese comparison is distinct from the “correct” reading.
丁 teng resembles 正 tsyengH in the “correct” reading; this Middle Chinese comparison is distinct from the first-month reading.
In Modern Mandarin, 丁 is dīng and 正 is zhèng; this current-reading pair does not establish an ancient sound role.

components.text: 止 is identified as a foot or step. In the destination analysis, it depicts a foot moving toward the upper form; the competing sound analysis also retains it as the foot element.

It calls 正 an early graph for 征 and gives its original sense as travel or a journey, not necessarily warfare. It records oracle-bone examples for military campaign 《合集》6441, first-month dating 《合集》22723, place name 《合集》22246, and a sacrificial name 《合集》14315. It also cites later bronze and Warring States bamboo-slip uses, including 正月, administrative/governmental senses, and 正直. These are reported source interpretations and examples; they do not establish a simple dated semantic path from journey to correct.

evidence.field: component analysis, historical forms and reading comparison
evidence.text: Dong Chinese presents 丁 as a sound/iconic component and 止 as the foot component, gives 正 Old Chinese *C.teŋ and *teŋ-s, and gives 丁 *tˤeŋ (with additional forms). It dates displayed forms to oracle script about 1250–1000 BCE, late Shang bronze about 1100 BCE, Shuowen seal script about 100 CE and Eastern Han clerical script 25–220 CE. This account independently supports a phonetic proposal but also treats 丁 iconically as a city wall. The possible phonetic role does not settle the depicted referent, and no reliable original name for a depicted object is established or needed for the component-level phonetic proposal.

formation.text: 比’s early construction is disputed. One analysis treats it as two person-like figures placed side by side; another proposes two 匕 signs, each picturing a shallow, long-handled food ladle, whose juxtaposition suggests nearness. That account also assigns 匕 a sound-cue role, but reconstructed similarity alone does not establish the role or the signs’ identity. The Han dictionary instead explains 比 as two 人 forms reversed from 从.

components.text: The person-like analysis treats the two figures as people placed side by side, suggesting juxtaposition; the early signs’ identity remains disputed.

In this disputed analysis, each 匕 is a picture of a shallow, long-handled food ladle; placing two together suggests nearness. The account separately proposes 匕 as a sound cue, though the reconstructed resemblance does not establish that role or the signs’ identity.

sound_limitation.text: The reconstructed sound resemblance does not establish that 匕 is a component of 比, or identify the referent of the early signs.

sound.text: In the Baxter–Sagart system, 匕 and 比 have similar Old Chinese reconstructions; this comparison alone does not prove a phonetic role.
Both characters have the modern Mandarin reading bǐ; this current match does not establish an ancient sound relationship.

formation.text: The traditional account treats 气 as a whole-graph picture of cloud vapor. Specialist analyses instead propose a referential sign, a cutting-related graph, or uses linked to 迄 or 訖, so the earliest construction remains disputed. Separately, Shuowen analyzes 氣 in its grain-provision sense as 米 plus phonetic 气; the qì sound comparisons do not match 氣’s distinct provisions reading xì.

components.text: In the traditional graph 氣, 米 contributes the grain-provision meaning. This account concerns the provisions word, not the disputed earliest construction of 气.

Shuowen identifies 气 as the phonetic element in 氣’s provisions analysis. The supplied readings for 气 and 氣 match under qì, but 氣’s provisions reading is xì and has different historical forms; the qì comparison does not demonstrate a sound match for that xì reading.

formation.text: The graph depicts a current with droplets beside it; its parts form one picture rather than separate character elements. The Han-era account adds a cosmological explanation, which is a historical interpretation rather than the graphic construction.

components.text: The whole graph pictures flowing water: the central stroke represents the current, and the side marks represent droplets. Early forms vary in the number and arrangement of those marks.

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: Oracle-bone 水 uses a central stroke for flowing water and side dots for droplets, with varying dot counts. As a component it can be reduced to droplets. Bronze and Warring States forms continue the water picture.

The database gives 水本義 as water and reports later 水準 as a compound for a leveling instrument, then an extended sense of a standard or level. It does not provide dated attestations for these later stages.

evidence.text: The entry analyzes 水 as a picture of flowing water: oracle forms vary in detail, with a central stroke for the current and side dots for droplets; component forms may reduce the current to drops. Bronze forms retain the flowing-water picture, and the entry says Warring States forms continue the bronze tradition. It reports Shang oracle use for water/flooding in 合集 10150, “其㞢(有)大水,” and another oracle use as a sacrificial name in 合集 14407. It also reports a disputed verbal use in 合集 23532 (“今日王其水𡨦(寢)”), with interpretations involving leveling ground with water or washing a temple. Bronze 水 is reported borrowed for 乞 ‘request’ in 沈子簋. These are the database’s reported readings and analyses; the record does not establish the disputed verb’s semantic connection to the noun.

formation.text: The traditional graph 漢 is analyzed as phonosemantic: 水 marks the water category, while its right side is proposed to supply a sound cue. The received analysis calls that side an abbreviated 難; another suggests 堇, and other accounts associate early forms with 𦰩 or 熯. 汉 is the simplified form corresponding to 漢.

components.text: 氵 is the conventional side form of 水. In 漢 it marks the water category relevant to the river name; it does not depict the river itself.

The right side of 漢 is disputed: the received analysis calls it reduced 難, another suggests 堇, and other accounts associate early forms with 𦰩 or 熯. Zhengzhang’s reconstructed readings make 熯 a possible sound comparison, but do not establish that it names the element in the early graph.

sound_limitation.text: The comparison with 熯 does not establish that 熯 identifies the right-side element in the earliest graph, and no reading for 𦰩 itself is established here.

sound.text: A proposed analysis associates this right side with 熯. In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, one reading of 熯 is *hnaːns, matching 漢 *hnaːns; 熯 also has the reading *hnaːnʔ. This sound comparison does not prove that 熯 names the early graph’s element.

components.text: 又 is the visible right-side element in simplified 汉, corresponding graphically to material on the right of 漢. This does not show that the traditional element meant 又 or that 又 retains a former sound role.

formation.text: The construction of traditional 沒 is disputed. The received 說文 analyzes it as 水 plus 𠬸; later commentary assigns 𠬸 a sound role, while another account describes a hand reaching into water. No inspected early glyph witness resolves these accounts, and the proposed sound component’s reading and historical relation to 沒 are unverified.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Simplified form of 沒.  Pictograph of a hand reaching in the water to grab something. Later the meaning shifted to "drown". This meaning is only used when the character is pronouned "mò". When pronounced "méi" (which is much more common), it means "not have". This meaning is a phonetic loan, unrelated to the original meaning.

components.text: 氵 is the compressed, stylized side form of 水. 水 is pictorial in origin, representing flowing water; in 清, 氵 contributes the water category.
青 functions as the phonetic component in 清. Both are pronounced qīng in ordinary Mandarin today; 青 also has a separate reading jīng.

sound.text: In the Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese system, reconstructed 青 *sʰleːŋ and 清 *sʰleŋ closely correspond, supporting 青’s phonetic role. These are scholarly reconstructions, not recorded pronunciations.
In modern Mandarin, 青 and 清 are both read qīng. The shared reading is consistent with the sound relationship but does not establish their pronunciation when 清 was formed.

evidence.text: 溫也。从火埶聲。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ŋjed): phonetic 埶 (OC *ŋeds) + semantic 灬 (“fire”).
Schuessler (2024) considers this a *-t derivation of Proto-Sino-Tibetan *nwe (“warm”), whence also Burmese နွေး (nwe:, “warm; lukewarm”), နွှေး (hnwe:, “to warm something; to revise”).
Often considered to be related to 爇 (OC *ŋʷjed, “to burn; to toast”) and 焫 (OC *njod, “hot”).

formation.text: 爱 is the standardized simplified form of 愛. In current 爱, 爫 sits above 冖 and 友. One graphic-history proposal traces the 友-like lower shape to joined or abbreviated 心-and-夂 strokes in running script; this does not establish an ancient role for 友. In the received analysis of traditional 愛, the gloss is “appearance of walking,” with a walking-related element written 夂 in one account and 夊 in another, and 㤅 as the sound element. The evidence does not establish a chronological change from 夂 to 夊. Accounts differ separately on the upper element of early 㤅.

友 is the visible lower component in 爱’s current structure. Its resemblance does not establish an ancient meaning or sound role in 愛.
Early 㤅 uses 心 as a meaning element for benevolence or feeling; this component belongs to the historical graph, not modern 爱.

formation.text: The proposed formation is phonosemantic: 父 contributes meaning and 巴 a sound cue. In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, 巴 is reconstructed as *praː and 爸 as *praːs, supporting a sound comparison. The analysis remains qualified because 巴’s early identity and original referent are disputed.

components.text: 父 contributes the meaning “father.” A transmitted Shuowen account describes 父 as a family head holding a staff, but that does not make it a picture of a staff-bearing person within 爸. The selected oracle-style image is a modern redraw of 父 alone, not an early form of 爸.

巴 is proposed as the sound component. One account describes it as a large-mouthed snake and proposes 巴蛇 as its original meaning; another interprets early forms identified as 巴 as a kneeling person. Neither settles 巴’s original name or referent. The selected oracle-style image is a modern redraw of 巴 alone, with an uncertain period; it does not attest 爸.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, 巴 *praː is compared with 爸 *praːs. In Modern Mandarin, 巴 bā and 爸 bà are also a current reading pair; neither comparison identifies 巴’s original name or referent.
In Modern Mandarin, 巴 bā is compared with 爸 bà. This current reading pair does not by itself establish the historical sound relationship.

formation.text: The traditional construction is 玉 with 元 as its phonetic element. Although this sound analysis is explicitly transmitted, the available comparison is compatible with it rather than independent proof; the original referent remains uncertain.

components.text: 玉 is the visible left component. It contributes a jade-related semantic category, but that alone does not establish that the whole character meant a jade object.
元 is the visible right component, identified in the traditional analysis as the phonetic element. Baxter–Sagart forms are compatible with this role, though they do not independently prove it.

sound_limitation.text: The reconstructed comparison is compatible with the sound analysis but does not independently prove 元’s identity or role in 玩. The similar modern Mandarin readings do not establish an ancient sound relationship.

sound.text: In the Baxter–Sagart 2014 table, the forms share a nasal onset and similar rhyme material; 玩 has an added suffix. The comparison fits the transmitted analysis but is not independent proof.
The local Unihan rows give the current Mandarin readings. Their similarity is not evidence by itself for the ancient phonetic role.

formation.text: Traditional 現 is analyzed as a phono-semantic compound: 玉 contributes a jade association and 見 supplies a sound cue. The simplified graph 现 uses 见 in place of 見. No character-specific early forms are documented in the cited evidence.

components.text: 玉 is the left-side element in 現 and contributes a jade association. The sources do not specify how that association relates to the verb ‘appear.’

見 is the right-side element in 現 and is conventionally analyzed as phonetic. Zhengzhang gives a nonmatching alternative reading alongside the matching one; Baxter–Sagart gives an exact match specifically for 見 ‘appear’ and 現 ‘appear’, while 見 ‘see’ has a different reconstruction. These comparisons support, but do not prove, the phonetic analysis.

sound_limitation.text: The matching Baxter–Sagart readings and the Zhengzhang comparison are reported in the cited material, but neither comparison by itself establishes that the visible element was 見 or functioned phonologically when 現 was formed. The modern Mandarin pair jiàn and xiàn describes current readings, not their historical relationship.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s system, 現 is *ɡeːns, while one listed 見 form is *keːns; the same source also lists 見 *ɡeːns. This comparison is not an unambiguous match and does not independently establish the graphic or phonetic role.
In Baxter–Sagart 2014, the sense-specific entries for 見 ‘appear’ and 現 ‘appear’ are both *N-[k]ˤen-s. 見 ‘see’ has a distinct reading, *[k]ˤen-s.
In Modern Mandarin, 見 is jiàn and 現 is xiàn. Their present-day difference does not establish their earlier relationship.

Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɡeːns): semantic 玉 (“jade”) + phonetic 見 (OC *keːns, *ɡeːns) — to appear.
Stativized form of the transitive verb 見 (OC *keːns, “to see”), formed by a nasal prefix and expressing the sense "to be visible; to appear" (Mei, 2012).

It separately reports a proposal, attributed to Mei (2012), that the “be visible; appear” verb is a nasal-prefix stativized form of transitive 見 ‘see.’ The page also reports the competing account that 現 first wrote a word meaning ‘jade luster’ and was later borrowed for the word ‘appear.’ These are source-reported analyses; this page alone does not establish the relative chronology of those lexical uses.

formation.text: The traditional account treats 班 as an ideographic compound: a knife divides paired jade. This is a proposed interpretation; the cited early bronze name uses do not confirm the scene.

components.text: The current left and right shapes are 王. In the traditional paired-jade analysis, these outer forms represent jade together; the evidence does not identify either 王 individually as 玨.

The current middle shape is 刂, the positional form corresponding to the full character 刀. This graphic correspondence does not date the change or establish the traditional interpretation that a knife divides jade.

formation.text: 球 is a phonosemantic compound: 玉 contributes the jade category, while 求 supplies a sound cue. The modern Mandarin readings of both are qiú; in Baxter–Sagart’s reconstruction they share Middle Chinese gjuw, while their Old Chinese forms differ slightly. These comparisons fit the traditional analysis but do not independently prove the ancient sound relation. The curated seal-style drawing is a modern rendering, not an ancient witness.

components.text: 玉 is the left-hand component and contributes the jade category. Early forms of 玉 are described as jade pieces strung together, but this does not establish 球’s own ancient graphic development.
求 is the right-hand phonetic element. A separate account suggests a winding or rolling association, but does not establish that 求 contributes this meaning in 球.

sound_limitation.text: The historical dictionary identifies 求 as phonetic. Modern and reconstructed readings provide comparisons, but do not independently establish the precise ancient sound relation.

sound.text: 求 and 球 share the modern Mandarin reading qiú and the Middle Chinese form gjuw in Baxter–Sagart’s system. Their Old Chinese reconstructions are 求 *[g](r)u and 球 *[g](r)[u], a similar but not identical comparison compatible with the traditional phonetic analysis.

formation.text: A semantic compound with pictorial and indicative parts: 屮 depicts a sprout, while 一 marks the ground beneath it. Neither part is proposed as a sound cue. In later forms, a mark added beneath 屮 developed into a horizontal stroke, making the lower part resemble 土.

components.text: Within 生, 屮 depicts the sprout rising above ground. It contributes to the plant image; no phonetic role is proposed.

In the early graphic analysis, 一 marks the ground beneath the sprout. A later mark added below 屮 developed into a horizontal stroke, making the lower part resemble 土; 土 is not identified as the original component.

evidence.field: 形義通解: graphic formation and evolution
evidence.text: The entry analyzes oracle-bone 生 as 屮 (a sprout) above 一 representing ground, expressing a plant growing out of earth. It says early bronze forms continue the oracle-bone structure; a dot was later added beneath 屮 as a decorative stroke and then became a horizontal stroke, making it resemble 土. Seal script retains the sprout-emerging-from-ground idea. The entry treats Shuowen’s gloss 進也 as an extended sense, rather than the graphic core.

formation.text: The graph’s formation is disputed. One interpretation treats the whole graph as a container pictograph. The received 說文 account parses it as 卜 plus 中. Other accounts relate 用 and 同 as graphic variants or a divided graph; a separate proposal analyzes 用 as 同 with a handle added and assigns 同 a phonetic role. These accounts are unresolved, and an internal sound component is not established.

components.text: One interpretation sees the whole graph as a container, with its body on the left and handle on the right. It proposes that the graph was borrowed for “use” because the container’s name may have sounded similar, but that name is unknown and the sound match cannot be checked. Competing accounts parse or relate the graph differently.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 可施行也。从卜从中。衞宏說。凡用之屬皆从用。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声): Formed by adding a handle to 同 (OC *lˤoŋ), which also acts as the phonetic component.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *z(j)um ~ *zuŋ, provisionally set up by STEDT. Cognates to 傭 (OC loŋ) and 庸 (OC loŋ), outside Sinitic, Southern Bai zv³¹ (“to use”) Burmese သုံး (sum:, “to use”), Ersu zi⁵⁵ (“to use”), Nuosu ꌬ (ssi, “to use”), Pa'o Karen [script needed] (sūŋ, “to use”).
Sun (1999) and Schuessler (2007) consider this word a cognate to Tibetan ལོངས (longs, “use”)
Definition 10 comes sound-matching of the character 蓉 from the term 細蓉 / 细蓉.

formation.text: Traditional 電 combines 雨, a semantic marker for weather, with 申, interpreted as a lightning image and proposed as a phonetic component. The sound analysis is supported by a plausible historical comparison, but the date and original intention of the combination remain unsettled.

components.text: In 電, 雨 marks the weather category associated with lightning. Its role at the graph’s first formation is unresolved.
In 電, 申 is interpreted as depicting lightning and is also proposed as a sound component. These roles do not settle the original intention of the combination.

sound_limitation.text: The modern readings are attested, but this present-day comparison does not establish the historical sound relationship or original graphic intention.

sound.text: These Old Chinese reconstructions have a plausible shared sound relationship, though their details differ.
In Modern Standard Mandarin, 申 is shēn and 電 is diàn; this pair does not establish their historical sound relationship.

evidence.text: The database interprets early bronze and oracle forms of 申 as depicting lightning’s bent, flickering path, calls it the initial graph for 電, and says 雨 was added as a semantic marker because lightning commonly accompanies rain. formation.text: The formation is disputed. One analysis treats 百 as an indicative graph, with a mark above a 白-like base indicating one hundred. Another reads a combined 一-plus-白 spelling and proposes that 白 was borrowed for the numeral because the words sounded alike or similar; it suggests the spelling later reduced to 百. A separate account calls 百 a “special phonetic” graph: 白 first wrote the numeral and supplied sound, and a dedicated 百 was later differentiated. That account also reads the Shang form as 白 with an added indicator, then describes lower 自 as a later corruption or change of 白. These proposals do not establish whether they describe different forms or stages.

components.text: The top mark is read either as an indicator of one hundred or as 一, “one,” in a combined 一-plus-白 spelling; these are competing analyses.

In the combined-spelling analysis, 白 supplies a sound cue. A separate account proposes that 白 first wrote the numeral as a whole graph and also supplied sound in the later 百; it describes a later lower 自 as a change of 白. These claims do not settle the earliest lower form’s identity.

sound.text: The reconstructed rhymes are similar, but 百 has a voiceless initial and 白 a voiced one. This supports a plausible sound association without proving the component analysis.

formation.text: One analysis treats current 的 as phonosemantic: 白 contributes the meaning “white,” and 勺 supplies a sound cue. In Zhengzhang Old Chinese, 勺 *pljewɢ and 的 *pleːwɢ are similar, supporting a plausible phonetic role without fixing the precise historical pronunciation. The traditional account quoted for 旳(的) instead assigns 日 + 勺 to “bright”; the graphic relationship remains uncertain.

components.text: In the traditional analysis of 旳, 日 is the semantic component for “bright.” This account does not establish when or how the graph came to be written with 白 in 的.
In 旳, 勺 is identified as the sound component. 勺 also means “ladle,” but that separate meaning does not make 旳 a spelling for “ladle.”

sound_limitation.text: The cited Zhengzhang comparison is between 勺 and 的, not the scoped host 旳, so it does not establish the historical sound relation in the 旳 analysis.

sound.text: In Modern Mandarin, 勺 is read sháo and 旳 dì. These current readings do not establish an ancient sound relationship.

components.text: In one analysis of 的, 白 contributes the category “white.” Its graphic relationship to 日 in the traditional analysis of 旳 is unresolved.
In one analysis of 的, 勺 supplies a sound cue. Zhengzhang reconstructs 勺 as *pljewɢ and 的 as *pleːwɢ; their similarity supports a plausible role but does not settle the precise historical relation.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Old Chinese, one reading of 勺 is reconstructed as *pljewɢ and 的 as *pleːwɢ. Their similarity supports a plausible sound relationship; reconstructions from different systems should not be combined.
In Modern Mandarin, 勺 is read sháo and 的 de. This current comparison does not establish their historical sound relation.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 白 represents the meaning and 勺 represents the sound. The character is based on the original meaning "bright white", which is unrelated to the modern meaning.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *pleːwɢ): semantic 白 (“white”) + phonetic 勺 (OC *pljewɢ, *bljewɢ).
The original form was 旳 with the meaning of “bright”, hence the initial 日 semantic. See Etymology 1 below.
For the "bright" sense, probably related to 曜 (OC *lewɢs, “to shine; daylight”); see there for more (STEDT).
The sense of “mark in a target” may be secondary. Alternatively, it may be an independent root on its own. Compare Tibetan རྟགས (rtags, “mark, sign”).

evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi, online text and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.field: 旳 entry; graphic history and gloss
evidence.text: The Han Shuowen entry records 旳 as “bright,” formed from 日 with 勺 as phonetic, and cites the Yi phrase 爲旳顙. Duan Yucai says 旳 is the brightness of white, that the common form became 的, and that the graph’s sense extended to an archery target. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the original graph’s pre-Han history.
evidence.title: 說文解字「旳」— Shuowen.org

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry 的
evidence.text: The page describes 的 as phonosemantic, semantic 白 ‘white’ plus phonetic 勺, and says the earlier written form was 旳 with 日. It displays a small-seal entry for 旳 but no securely attested oracle-bone or bronze forms of 的. Therefore this research supports the received Shuowen distinction between 旳 and common 的, but cannot assert an unbroken paleographic sequence or identify a corruption event between forms.

evidence.text: For the lexical bright/target character, the page gives Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *[t-l]ˤewk and Middle Chinese tek, and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *pleːwɢ. The distinct systems yield substantially different Old Chinese forms; these are reconstructions rather than direct attestations. Standard Mandarin readings listed for this lexical sense include dì and dí; Cantonese Jyutping is dik1.
evidence.title: 的 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry 勺; reconstructions attributed to Baxter–Sagart (2014) and Zhengzhang (2003)
evidence.field: Pronunciation and historical comparisons for proposed sound component 勺
evidence.text: The 勺 entry gives multiple lexical readings: the noun ‘ladle’ has Mandarin sháo, Middle Chinese dzyak and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *m-tewk; a separate verb reading has Mandarin zhuó, Middle Chinese tsyak and Baxter–Sagart *t-ewk. Zhengzhang (2003) lists 勺 *bljewɢ for one reading and *pljewɢ for another. Since 的 is Zhengzhang *pleːwɢ and 勺 has *pljewɢ readings in that same system, the within-system comparison supports 勺 as a plausible phonetic element in 的; reconstruction mismatch across systems prevents claiming the precise original sound. 勺 is also an independently glossed ladle, but the sound-component claim does not require that referent to be the source of a whole-graph loan.
evidence.title: 勺 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry 白; reconstructions attributed to Baxter–Sagart (2014) and Zhengzhang (2003)
evidence.field: Pronunciation and history of semantic component 白

formation.text: The received account describes 知 as 口 plus 矢, assigning 口 a meaning role and 矢 a sound role. A modern paleographic study instead proposes an earlier graph shared with 智 that contained 大 and 子, and rejects 矢 as its phonetic. The evidence supplied does not establish the early construction or a sequence connecting these accounts.

components.text: In the received analysis, 口 contributes meaning. The explanation that it represents oral transmission is an interpretation, not an established account of the graph’s origin. The supplied readings differ from 知’s in modern Mandarin and in the Baxter–Sagart Middle Chinese and Old Chinese comparisons; those differences do not establish 口’s historical role.

components.text: The received analysis identifies this component as 矢, “arrow,” and modern accounts assign it a sound role. That assignment is disputed: a study proposes 大 and 子 in an earlier graph, and the supplied reconstructions of 矢 and 知 differ in both Middle Chinese and Old Chinese.

sound_limitation.text: The readings document a comparison but do not prove that 矢 was a sound component. Baxter–Sagart gives different Middle Chinese and Old Chinese forms for 矢 and 知, while the proposed earlier graph and the received analysis remain in dispute.

sound.text: The modern Mandarin readings differ; this pair neither proves nor disproves an earlier sound role.

evidence.text: The study reports that 知 and 智 were originally one graph and split after Shang; it argues that the original graph contained 大 rather than 矢, and 子 rather than 于. This is a specific modern analysis, not an uncontested account.

formation.text: 票 is a derived graph from 𤐫, whose lower 火 is identified with the gloss “fire flying” or “fire rising.” In clerical writing, the upper element was reduced to 覀 and 火 was written 示. The upper element’s referent is not securely identified.

components.text: In historical graph 𤐫, lower 火 is identified as the fire element in the gloss “fire flying/rising.” It was later written 示 through clerical change.
The upper element of historical graph 𤐫 is transcribed as 𦥑囟. Its depicted referent or action is not securely identified.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說文釋形; 字樣說明; 異體字研訂說明
evidence.text: The dictionary reports that Shuowen’s headform for 票 was 𤐫, glossed “fire flying,” and analyzes it as fire plus a second graphic element. It says the lower 火 changed to 示 through clerical transformation, and that the modern form was later written 票. Its variant note calls 𤐫 the original form of 票. This supports an older graphic form and a clerical change, not the dossier’s altar/offering interpretation.
evidence.title: [A02895] 票 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義通解; 字形資料
evidence.text: The account, citing He Linyi, describes the older form as 𤐫 with an upper [𦥑囟] element and lower 火; it says the upper part was reduced to 覀 and 火 was confused with 示, yielding the clerical form behind modern 票. It gives fire rising as the basic meaning, followed by light rising/wafting and rapid movement. Its displayed graph inventory has a seal form and bamboo-slip examples, but no oracle-bone or bronze examples; this is not evidence that no earlier forms existed.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 票

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary calls 𤐫 the original form of 票 and cites Guangyun’s statement that 𤐫 means “fire flying” and is now written 票. The entry also notes distinct sound and sense connections for 𤐫 in other variant records; those do not establish a phonetic component in 票. This supports a graphic predecessor and clerical change, not the dossier’s specific two-pairs-of-hands or sparks narrative.
evidence.title: [A02895-002] 𤐫 (票) - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry transcribes Shuowen’s analysis of 𤐫 as 火 plus [𦥑囟] and reports the reading 方昭切. It does not identify the upper graphic element as a particular object or establish a phonetic role for either visible part in 票. Its analysis is a source’s account, not independent proof of the depicted referent.

formation.text: The traditional analysis treats 穿 as an ideographic compound: 穴 is a hole and 牙 is a tooth shown within it, together suggesting penetration. A competing analysis proposes that an early spelling had a sound-bearing element written with 耳 and 串, later altered through confusion between 耳 and 牙. That reading and sequence remain disputed; available comparisons do not establish a phonetic role for 穴 or 牙.

components.text: In the traditional explanation, 穴 depicts the hole containing the tooth and contributes the setting for penetration. No sound comparison establishes a phonetic role for it.

In the traditional explanation, 牙 depicts the tooth within the hole. A competing account proposes that this visible form reflects confusion with an earlier 耳, but that graphic change remains disputed; no sound comparison establishes 牙 as phonetic.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 通也。从牙在穴中。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 穴 (“cave”) + 牙 (“tooth”) – to penetrate through, to pass through.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan [Term?]; cognate with Tibetan རྟོལ (rtol, “to bore; to pierce; to perforate”) (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 online text and 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry glosses 穿 as “通也” and explains its form as a tooth (牙) inside a cave or hole (穴). Duan Yucai quotes the Shijing line about a mouse boring through a wall. This is an early lexicographic analysis, not independent confirmation of the original graphic motivation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「穿」

evidence.source: Pan Deng, discussion of the Anda University Chu manuscript Shijing, citing the 2019 manuscript edition and other scholarship
evidence.text: The discussion reports an Anda Chu manuscript form in the Xing Lu passage with an 耳 component and 串 sound element, corresponding to received 穿. The author argues that this spelling records the word 穿 and proposes that Qin-Han graphic change, including confusion between 耳 and 牙, produced the familiar 穿 shape from a form written with 穴 and a reduced sound element. Another cited interpretation reads related Chu examples as 貫 or connects the form with 聯. This is a disputed paleographic argument reported in a specialist discussion, not a settled account; the source’s glyph images were not visually inspected.
evidence.title: 安大簡《詩經》初讀 — 简帛网

evidence.source: Japanese Wiktionary, 穿 entry
evidence.text: This entry presents a phonetic analysis: 穴 plus a reduced form associated with an 耳-plus-串 spelling, later altered by graphic confusion between 耳 and 牙. It gives 穿 Mandarin chuān, Middle Chinese tsyhwen, and Old Chinese *tʰon {*tʰo[n]}. The analysis points to 布之道’s 廣韻形聲考, but that cited page was not accessible in this research, so the etymological chain lacks direct verification here. The entry is secondary and its proposed analysis remains disputed.
evidence.title: 穿 — ウィクショナリー日本語版

evidence.source: Pan Deng, discussion of Anda manuscript evidence and phonological interpretation
evidence.text: The discussion compares reconstructed Old Chinese forms for 穿 and 貫 and describes the Chu manuscript spelling’s 串 element as phonetically related, while noting that the consonant relationship may appear distant under conventional initials. It advances a “special 昌 initial” account and treats 穿 and 貫 as related in sound and possibly cognate. This is the discussant’s analysis, not an independently confirmed reconstruction. No specific pronunciation for 穴 or 牙 is offered as support for their being sound components.
evidence.title: 安大簡《詩經》初讀 — 简帛网

evidence.source: Dong Chinese dictionary
evidence.text: Dong Chinese treats 穴 and 牙 as meaning components, with 穴 indicating a hole and 牙 a tooth, and describes the original sense as boring a hole. It gives Mandarin chuān, Middle Chinese tsyhwen, and Old Chinese *tʰo[n] for 穿. This is a secondary dictionary account; it supplies no separate same-system reconstructions for 穴 and 牙 that would establish a phonetic role for either component.
evidence.title: 穿 — Dong Chinese dictionary

formation.text: Lexicographic analyses describe 站 as phonosemantic: 立 contributes standing-related meaning, and 占 is proposed as the phonetic component. This structural interpretation is not a documented sequence of the character’s early forms.

components.text: 立 is the left component and contributes standing-related meaning in the reported analysis. No earlier form or graphic sequence for 站 is documented in the available evidence.
占 is the right component and is assigned a phonetic role. The historical comparison is relevant, but does not independently establish the component’s identity or sound role.

sound_limitation.text: The Modern Mandarin readings of 占 and 站 match, but that alone does not establish their historical sound relation. Baxter–Sagart lists 占 but has no 站 entry for comparison.

sound.text: The supplied local Unihan readings give both characters as zhàn, a present-day match that does not establish their historical relation.
Zhengzhang gives these Old Chinese readings as a comparison. They belong to that reconstruction system, not Baxter–Sagart, and do not by themselves establish the proposed sound role.

formation.text: The formation is disputed. Reported early forms are interpreted as 艸 above 犬, but the parts’ roles are unsettled. In one later received account, 竹 is paired with 夭: 竹 is linked to meaning through a questioned proposal that wind-bent bamboo resembles a laughing person, and 夭 is assigned a sound role. A distinct transmitted account instead pairs 竹 with 犬 without assigning 竹 that meaning role. Baxter–Sagart reconstructions for 夭 and 笑 share the sequence aw, but this resemblance does not prove the proposed sound role or explain how the forms relate.

components.text: In the 竹+夭 account, 竹 is assigned a meaning role, explained by the questioned proposal that wind-bent bamboo resembles a laughing person. A distinct Tangyun account pairs 竹 with 犬; it does not assign 竹 that role. No change from early 艸 to 竹 is established.

sound.text: In Modern Mandarin, 竹 is zhú and 笑 is xiào. This modern comparison does not establish an ancient sound role for 竹.

components.text: In one later received analysis, 夭 is proposed as a sound element; a distinct Tangyun account instead has 犬. The evidence does not establish that these occupy corresponding positions or that one changed into the other.

sound_limitation.text: The reconstructed rhyme resemblance and current Mandarin pair do not independently establish 夭’s identity or phonetic role in 笑.

sound.text: In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese, the reconstructed readings share the sequence aw. This resemblance does not by itself establish that 夭 supplied the sound in 笑.
In Modern Mandarin, 夭 is yāo and 笑 is xiào. This pair does not establish an ancient sound relationship.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. ⺮ represents the meaning and 夭 represents the sound. The connection between 竹 (bamboo) and 笑 (laugh) is unclear.

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, 說文解字·竹部
evidence.text: The received text gives “此字本闕” (“this entry was originally missing”). Its appended note says Sun Mian’s Tangyun quote gives a form from 竹 and 犬 meaning “喜也”; Li Yangbing’s recension instead uses 竹 and 夭 and offers the explanation that wind-bent bamboo resembles a person laughing. The note itself questions Li’s explanation.
evidence.title: 說文解字 : 卷六 : 竹部

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry (summarizing cited paleographic scholarship)
evidence.field: 字源; graph forms and analyses
evidence.text: The entry reports that excavated Warring States through Han manuscript forms are written with components interpreted as 艸 and 犬, contrasting these with received dictionary forms in the 竹 section and forms analyzed as 竹+犬 or 竹+夭. It presents a proposed history in which 艸 was confused with 竹 and 犬 with 夭, and also lists alternative proposals involving 芺 or a pictorial form. These are competing hypotheses summarized by the entry, not settled conclusions. It reports a Zhengzhang series assigning 笑 *sqʰows and 夭 *qoːwʔ, *qrow, *qrowʔ, and a separate Baxter–Sagart row for 笑.
evidence.title: 笑 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese University of Hong Kong）
evidence.field: 形義通解; 說文新附; 簡帛文字
evidence.text: The entry reports that early manuscript forms of 笑 are analyzed as 艸 over 犬, while later seal forms were transmitted as 竹+犬 and the Li Yangbing form as 竹+夭. It reproduces the Shuowen note that the entry was missing and quotes the competing Tangyin and Li Yangbing accounts, including the qualification that the latter’s explanation is uncertain. evidence.text: The article cites oracle-bone forms (Heji 71 and 32541) and Chu manuscript forms (Xin 2.029 and Bao 2.95). It reviews differing interpretations: Li Xiaoding's central sieve proposal, Cai Xinfa's scattered-grains pictograph, and Xu Jinxiong's interpretation as shelled grain kernels rather than a particular crop. The article concludes that 米 originally referred broadly to dehusked grain, not one specific grain, and that modern usage often specializes it to rice. It also cautions against a proposed reconstructed preform based only on writing convenience.

evidence.field: 考; formation analyses and examples, lines 171–179
evidence.text: The dictionary presents a 老-based account: early Western Zhou bronze writing used 老 for both ‘old’ and ‘father’; adding 丂 as a phonetic marker distinguished 考, and the 考 form commonly omits the lower 匕 of 老. It also reports a competing account in which 丂 was an original graph, borrowed for ‘father’, and 老 was added as a semantic classifier; the dictionary says early bronze use of 丂 for ‘father’ gives this account some support, but considers the 老-based account a better explanation of early Western Zhou evidence. It reports bronze 考 for ‘father’ in 兮仲鐘 and for ‘consider/estimate’ in 中山王鼎, alongside separate phonetic uses for 孝 and 巧 in named bronze and Warring States texts. The entry supplies no dates for those particular examples and does not establish a semantic bridge from ‘father’ to ‘examine/test’.

components.text: The graph is treated as one whole picture of a bear-like animal, with a head, body, limbs and short tail. The identification of damaged Shang forms as this character is disputed; the modern-looking parts are not separate components in this analysis.

evidence.text: 熊屬。足似鹿。从肉㠯聲。能獸堅中，故稱賢能；而彊壯，稱能傑也。凡能之屬皆从能。

evidence.source: CASE報科學 (National Taiwan University Center for Science Education)
evidence.text: The author identifies rare, damaged Shang oracle-bone forms as 能 and describes a bear-like pictograph: the head is reduced to an eye-shaped form, the limbs become more linear, and the short tail remains. The author says the few oracle-bone occurrences are too damaged to establish their use. From oracle bone to Western Zhou bronze, the head changes from an eye-like shape to 㠯, the body is simplified to 月 (肉), and the feet are rearranged side by side; the later bronze, Warring States, Chu-slip, Qin-slip, seal, and clerical forms are described as easier to relate. This conflicts with another paleographic account that considers securely identified 能 earliest in Western Zhou bronze; the Shang identification is therefore disputed, not settled.
evidence.title: 獼猴與黑熊：甲骨文的「夒」、「猱」與「能」

evidence.source: 劉雲, Fudan University Center for Unearthed Documents and Ancient Chinese Characters
evidence.text: The author says securely identifiable 能 in ancient writing first appears in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, and argues a disputed Shang animal-shaped graph is not 能 but 鷧, a cormorant: it differs in the supposed bear's neck, feet, tail, and head. The article's discussion establishes a material disagreement over whether a Shang form is 能; the identification remains contested. It supplies images of Western Zhou examples including 能匋尊, 鬲比簋, 毛公厝鼎, and 番生簋, but the web text does not provide a dated first inscription.

formation.text: 脑 is a simplified form of 腦, not a separately analyzed ancient compound. The traditional graph is linked to the older form 匘, glossed “head marrow.” Shuowen’s account, as reported in later sources, describes 匘 using 匕, 巛 as hair, and 囟; a competing account proposes a figure-and-axe picture involving 夒 and a sound role. The accounts conflict, and no inspected early glyph settles the construction.

It also gives later lexicographic senses including head, an object's center, brain-like material, and things functionally like a brain, with examples from the Huainanzi and Tang and Song texts. formation.text: The later graph combines a plant-category element, 艹, with 化 as a probable sound element. Mandarin huā and huà are similar, and Old Chinese reconstructions also show a partial sound match, though they do not directly record ancient speech or date the graph’s formation.

components.text: 艹 is the plant-category element in 花. It is a conventional side form of 艸, not evidence here of a separate historical stage.

化 serves as a probable sound element in 花. Mandarin 花 huā and 化 huà are similar but differ in tone and vowel; Baxter–Sagart reconstructions share a similar onset and medial sequence but differ in their ending.

In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstructions, 花 *qʷʰˤra and 化 *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s share a similar onset and medial sequence but differ in the ending. These are reconstructed forms, not direct records of ancient speech.

formation.text: 茶 is a later graphic form linked to 荼. The earlier graph 荼 is analyzed as a compound: 艸 marks the plant category, while 余 supplies a sound cue. This analysis does not assign a separate meaning to every stroke in 茶.

components.text: In 荼, 艸 marks the plant category. This role belongs to the earlier graph and does not make every stroke of 茶 a separate meaningful component.
In 荼, 余 is analyzed as its sound element. In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction, its reading is compatible with 茶’s; this comparison does not identify 余’s original referent.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction, 余 *la is compatible with 茶 *rlaː. Their modern Mandarin readings, yú and chá, differ.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes 茶 as a later graph, written earlier with 艸 and phonetic 余 as 荼. It gives 茶 as tea plant and tea drink, and cites Lu Yu’s Tang-period 茶經, which calls tea a fine southern tree. It also records later uses for other brewed drinks and, in Ming usage, as a verb ‘drink’. These glosses do not by themselves date each semantic extension.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：茶

evidence.source: Victor Mair, Language Log
evidence.text: Mair argues medieval manuscript forms vary in their lower strokes and that 茶 was not necessarily an independent replacement of 荼 at first. In his account, surviving Qieyun manuscript evidence around 700 CE generally writes the tea plant with a graph transcribed as 荼; a 706 CE manuscript gives no 茶 form in its cited line, while a reading that mentions 茶 in another manuscript requires image verification. He reports Guangyun (1007 CE) lists 茶 as俗 relative to the regular form. He also cautions that a Han tomb seal often read 茶陵 may instead read 荼陵. This challenges simple claims that 茶 was securely established in Han times or invented by Lu Yu.
evidence.title: Sinographs for “tea”

The page is a tertiary compilation; this does not independently establish the earliest shape or referent of 余.

formation.text: Phonosemantic: 艸 contributes the plant category and 采 supplies the sound. The character is defined as edible vegetation. A separate proposal derives the word from 采, “gather, pluck,” plus a nominal suffix; that word-history proposal is distinct from the graphic analysis.

components.text: 艹 is the conventional side form of 艸 here. It contributes the plant category, rather than depicting a plant within a scene.
采 supplies the sound in 菜. In its own graphic history, 采 depicts a hand picking from a tree or fruit; that picture is not the referent of 菜.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction, 菜 *sʰɯːs and 采 *sʰɯːʔ share an onset and rhyme; 菜 has an added departing-tone suffix. Modern Mandarin cài and cǎi retain a related initial and rhyme but differ in tone.

formation.text: The conventional analysis is phonosemantic: 虫 contributes an animal-related category, while 延 provides a sound cue. A competing account proposes that the graph developed from 蜑 around the Tang period. The relationship between that graphic history and the current component analysis remains unsettled.

components.text: 虫 is conventionally treated as the semantic element, contributing an animal-related category. This analysis does not establish that the character originally referred specifically to snake eggs.
延 is conventionally treated as the phonetic element. Its separate graphic history includes early forms interpreted as a person walking on a road; that does not identify an object depicted in 蛋.

sound_limitation.text: The cited sound-series comparisons support a phonetic relationship, but the individual 蛋 reconstruction record was not inspected; they do not establish the origin of the spoken word for egg.

sound.text: In the Zhengzhang Old Chinese system, 延 *lan/*lans and 蛋 *l'aːns are similar, although their modern Mandarin readings, yán and dàn, differ. The historical comparison is compatible with a sound cue, not proof of lexical borrowing.

components.text: 蜑 is a separate graph proposed as a predecessor of 蛋, not a component within it. It is recorded for a southern people and, in later usage, chicken egg. The proposed Tang-period graphic change rests on an account whose underlying examples have not been checked here.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 虫 represents the meaning and 延 represents the sound.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *l'aːns): phonetic 延 (OC *lan, *lans) + semantic 虫 (“snake, insect”) – "egg", with particular reference to snake eggs.
The non-contracted form is 蜑. In the current version, 延 is abbreviated to 疋.
This character was coined at a late stage in Chinese, since it is unattested on oracle bones, bronzes, Shuowen Jiezi and Guangyun.
From 彈 (MC danH, “pellet”) (Zhengzhang, 2003).

formation.text: A traditional pictographic analysis treats the whole graph as a bird’s nest, without dividing it into modern-looking parts. A competing explanation connects west with birds roosting at sunset. Another proposal links a different early form with 囟 through sound similarity; these analyses remain unsettled.

formation.text: Pictographic under the whole-scene interpretation: the early graph depicts a person holding the body's middle. Competing analyses disagree about the upper and hand-like forms, so the present shape should not be confidently split into modern-looking parts. The Han dictionary's analysis involving 𦥑 and phonetic 交省 is an ancient interpretation, not a settled account of the graph's construction.

evidence.text: 身中也。象人要自𦥑之形。从𦥑，交省聲。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形): a man 大 then drawn as a woman (女) with two hands pointing to his/her midsection. On top of the character there was huge eye 目, then stylized as a horn 角. The hands gradually shifted upwards; hence, a nearly-original version of the character is 𡢗. All the upper part was eventually stylized as 覀. Unrelated to 栗 but partly related to 票.
Original meaning was “waist” (now 腰 (OC *qew)).

evidence.source: 常用漢字二百字探源（金真姬）
evidence.text: The study lists 要 in Shang oracle-bone examples, including 合集8175, and in Western Zhou bronze examples, including 是要簋 and 伯要敦; it also lists Spring and Autumn, Warring States, Qin, and Han-period forms. Its analysis describes the oracle graph as 女 with two hands and a head-like upper element, and reports competing component analyses: Li Xiaoding rejects 交 as phonetic and reads the graph as a woman holding her waist; another cited proposal treats it as a compound involving 臼/女. The author concludes 要 is the original graph for 腰, with 肉 later added to distinguish the body-part word. These are scholarly interpretations, not a visually inspected glyph in this research.

formation.text: The traditional graph 見 is pictographic: an eye above a human figure depicts seeing. Ancient forms are analyzed with 卩, a kneeling person; the received form is parsed as 目 and 儿. 见 is the standardized simplified form of 見, though its particular path from cursive writing is not established here.

components.text: In 見, 目 is the prominent eye and part of the depiction of seeing. Both the ancient-form and received-form analyses identify this eye element.

In the ancient-form analysis of 見, 卩 is a kneeling person beneath the eye, completing the person-and-eye depiction. The received-form analysis instead identifies the lower figure as 儿; these are stage-specific analyses, not evidence of corruption.
In the received-form analysis of 見, 儿 is the human figure paired with 目 in the depiction of seeing. This differs from the ancient-form analysis, which identifies the lower figure as 卩.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨文、金文用例
evidence.text: The database analyzes the oracle-bone and bronze forms as 目 plus 卩, with 卩 representing a kneeling person and the eye emphasized to express seeing. It distinguishes 見 from 視 by the seated versus standing human figure, with a noted exception. Oracle-bone uses include seeing and audience; it also reports a reading as 獻 ‘offer sacrificial goods’. Bronze examples include seeing, audience, and a passive auxiliary use. These are source-reported interpretations and examples; no specific earliest dated inscription was verified here.

Separately, a proposed early graph is interpreted as a whole picture of an eye above a standing person; that interpretation does not establish a sequence of component changes.

components.text: In the received graph 視, 見 is the semantic element associated with seeing. This analysis describes that traditional graph, not the proposed early pictograph.
In the received graph 視, 示 is analyzed as phonetic. The cited historical comparison is compatible with that analysis but does not by itself prove the component’s role.

sound_limitation.text: The reported Old Chinese forms share the rhyme and differ by the reconstructed *s- prefix, but this comparison does not prove 示’s graphic role. The modern Mandarin match also does not establish the ancient relationship.

sound.text: In Baxter–Sagart’s reported Old Chinese forms, 示 and 視 share the rhyme and differ by the reconstructed *s- prefix, compatible with a phonetic relationship.
Both 示 and 視 are read shì in current Mandarin; matching current readings do not establish the historical relationship.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說明; 說文釋形; 釋義
evidence.text: The entry records the received Shuowen wording “瞻也。从見、示” and Duan Yucai’s reading “从見，示聲.” It glosses 視 first as looking, then gives attested extended senses including examining or observing, treating someone as, eyesight, caring for, administering, comparing, imitating, and a use通「示」. formation.text: Traditional 識 is a phonosemantic compound: 言 contributes a speech-related category and 戠 is its phonetic component. Standardized 识 renders 言 as 讠 and replaces 戠 with 只; this later substitution does not make 只 the historical phonetic of 識.

formation.text: Traditional 訴 is analyzed as phonosemantic: 言 contributes the speech or reporting category, and the right side is proposed as a sound element. The received Shuowen analysis names 厈省; Song editors reject that analysis, while Duan Yucai proposes a graphic path from 㡿 through 厈 to 斥. The path and historical sound fit remain uncertain.

components.text: In 诉, visible 讠 is the simplified counterpart of 訁 and contributes the speech or reporting category. Traditional 訴 uses 言 in that role; the evidence does not establish a direct positional-form relationship between 言 and 讠.

Traditional 訴 has visible 斥 on the right. The received Shuowen analysis identifies 厈省 as phonetic; Duan Yucai instead proposes that 㡿 changed to 厈 in clerical writing and was later miswritten as 斥. This proposed history is not confirmed by an early specimen.

evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *hljods, *hljod, *lod): semantic 言 + phonetic 兌 (OC *l'oːds).
All of the pronunciations of this character are in the same word family apparently derived from a root *lo meaning “to loosen; to relax” (Schuessler, 2007); based on this, STEDT compares the word to Proto-Sino-Tibetan *lot (“free; release; slip; dislocate”), whence also 脫 (OC *l̥ʰoːd, *l'oːd, “to peel off, take off (clothes), escape, etc.”). However, STEDT also offers an alternative derivation from a provisional Proto-Sino-Tibetan *b-tsyat (“to speak, say”), comparing Tibetan འཆད ('chad, “to say, explain”), which is semantically more appealing; the association with the words associated with "release" may be a case of phonetic pigeonholing.
According to the "release" theory, Pronunciation 1 is derived by causative devoicing of 悅 (OC *lod, “to relax; to be delighted”) (pronunciation 3).
Pronunciation 2 is probably the exoactive of pronunciation 1.

formation.text: 讀 is phonosemantic: 言 supplies a speech-related meaning, and its other component is analyzed as a sound cue. Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstructions compare 𧶠 *luɡ with 讀 *l'oːɡ, supporting that analysis. The transmitted phonetic form varies among 𧸇, 𧶠, and 𧷏; its original referent and spoken name are not established. The modern printed 賣 is not the ordinary word “sell.”

components.text: 讠 is the conventional compact side form of 言 in 读. 言 contributes speech-related meaning; this form relationship does not imply that one replaced the other over time.

In 讀, the phonetic element is printed 賣, but it is distinct from the ordinary word 賣 ‘sell.’ Accounts transmit the element as 𧸇, 𧶠, or 𧷏, and propose later confusion with 賣; they do not establish a complete sequence or which form came first. A reported comparison with 育 does not identify the element’s original referent or its spoken name.

formation.text: The traditional graph 謝 combines semantic 言, written 訁 on the left, with phonetic 射. Its dictionary gloss is “depart or resign.” In standardized 谢, 訁 is rendered as 讠 while 射 remains.

components.text: 訁 is the left-side form of 言 in 謝 and marks a speech-related category. In standardized 谢, this element is rendered as 讠.
射 is the phonetic component in 謝 and remains in 谢. Its early forms depict a bow and arrow, but this does not establish the depicted object’s name as the basis of the sound relation.

formation.text: The traditional analysis treats 貴 as phonosemantic: 貝 supplies a money-related meaning, while 臾 supplies a sound cue. A competing account describes early forms as hands holding earth and assigns the sound role to 中. These analyses differ, and the early graph’s depiction remains disputed.

components.text: In the traditional analysis of 貴, 貝 contributes a money association. The historical dictionary describes shells as currency; this does not by itself show that the early graph depicted hands carrying a shell.

The traditional dictionary identifies 臾 as the sound element and calls it an ancient form of 蕢; a later study associates it with the protoform of 簣. The sound role is part of this traditional analysis, though the cited reconstructions do not alone prove the historical correspondence.

sound_limitation.text: The cited Old Chinese forms are reconstructions, not direct ancient pronunciations, and do not by themselves establish that 臾 supplied 貴’s historical sound. Their current Mandarin readings also cannot establish that relation.

sound.text: The study reports Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese *gruds for 臾 and *kluds for 貴. These are reconstructions in the same system, not directly recorded pronunciations.
In Modern Mandarin, 臾 is yú and 貴 is guì; this current comparison does not establish their historical sound relation.

formation.text: The oldest proposed construction is pictographic: an early graph is interpreted as a person running with swinging arms. Some later bronze forms are analyzed as adding 止 to emphasize the feet. The received Shuowen account instead reads the seal-script form as 夭 plus 止, explaining 夭 as bending; this records a Han-era analysis and differs from the account of the earliest graph.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The database analyzes the oracle-bone and early bronze forms as a person running with arms swinging; later bronze forms add 止 to emphasize the feet. It assigns the basic verb sense “run” to the graph. It reports oracle-bone uses in place-name and personal-name contexts, including 合集17230 and 合集27939; its cited clear bronze verb example is 效卣, “夙夜奔走.” It says the upper running-person shape was later misread as 夭 in Shuowen. This is a modern paleographic account, distinct from Xu Shen’s historical analysis.

evidence.text: Lists oracle-bone, bronze, Warring States, Shuowen seal, clerical, and regular-script records, including oracle-bone Heji 27939, early Western Zhou 大盂鼎 (集成2837), and Western Zhou to Warring States bronze forms. This later phonetic-component interpretation is an analysis of later structures, not evidence that the oldest graph was a phonetic compound.

formation.text: 跟 is a phonosemantic compound: 足 contributes the foot-related category, and 艮 contributes sound. This analysis and the sense “heel” are recorded in the Han-period dictionary account; the graph’s prehistoric formation sequence is unresolved.

components.text: 足 marks the foot-related category, fitting 跟’s sense “heel.” No separate earlier form for this component in 跟 is recorded.
艮 supplies the sound cue. In the Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstruction, its initial and rhyme match 跟’s, while 艮 has an additional final suffix.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Old Chinese, 艮 *kɯːns and 跟 *kɯːn share the initial and rhyme; 艮 has an additional final suffix.

components.text: In the recorded alternative graph 𣥦, 止 fills the meaning-bearing position occupied by 足 in 跟. The two forms’ relative chronology is unresolved.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 足踵也。从足𥃩聲。

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 跟 as 从足、艮聲 and gives its original sense as the back of the foot/heel. It records the Shuowen alternative form 𣥦 as 从止、艮聲, noting 足 and 止 are semantically related shape elements. It supplies no oracle-bone or bronze examples for 跟, while listing one small-seal example; therefore the inspected entry does not establish a pre-imperial graphic chronology for 跟.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 跟

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The entry transcribes the Shuowen explanation as “跟，足踵也。从足，艮聲。〔古痕切〕𣥦，跟或从止。” Thus Shuowen attributes heel as sense, 足 as semantic element and 艮 as phonetic element, and records 𣥦 with 止 as an alternative form. This is evidence for what the Han-period dictionary reports, not direct proof of the graph’s prehistoric formation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 跟

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 跟
evidence.field: Glyph origin / Zhengzhang 2003 sound series and readings
evidence.text: This entry identifies 跟 as an 艮-series phonetic graph and lists 跟 Old Chinese *kɯːn and 艮 *kɯːns in Zhengzhang (2003). It gives 跟 Middle Chinese fanqie 古痕切 and category 見開一痕平, with Mandarin gēn and Cantonese gan1; it gives 艮 Mandarin readings gèn, gěn (among others) and Cantonese gan3. In the stated reconstruction, the related initial and rhyme support a phonetic role despite the departing tone suffix on 艮. The source also reports 跟 as cognate with 根 (Old Chinese *kɯːn), attributed to Wang (1982), but no primary text supporting that cognacy was inspected here.
evidence.title: 跟 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: 韻典網, 上古音系
evidence.text: For 艮 the displayed Old Chinese form is *kɯːns; its table supplies Middle Chinese kən in the named reconstruction systems. Compared with 跟’s Zhengzhang *kɯːn and Middle Chinese kon in Baxter notation, this supports historical sound similarity for 艮 as a phonetic component. It does not establish the pronunciation of any depicted object or imply a whole-graph phonetic loan.
evidence.title: 艮 - 字 - 上古音系 - 韻典網

formation.text: 路 is conventionally analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 足 is associated with the road or path meaning, while 各 is assigned a phonetic role. The received Shuowen wording names both components; a later commentary explicitly calls 各 the sound component. The available sound comparisons do not by themselves establish how the historical pronunciation matched.

components.text: 足 contributes an association with foot and the road or path meaning. The precise reason for its selection in this character is not specified.
各 is assigned the sound role in the conventional analysis, although the received Shuowen wording itself only names it as a component.

sound_limitation.text: The readings can be compared, but these comparisons do not by themselves establish the historical sound relation or prove the component analysis.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang's reconstruction, 各 and 路 have different onset notation; this pair alone does not demonstrate their proposed sound relationship.
The modern Mandarin readings are 各 gè and 路 lù; this present-day comparison does not establish their historical relationship.
In the Baxter–Sagart table, the Middle Chinese readings are 各 kak and 路 luH; this comparison does not by itself prove the phonetic analysis.
