formation.text: The whole graph depicts a human-like figure with a prominent midsection. Interpretations differ on whether the mark represents an abdomen or pregnancy, and the image alone does not settle the question.

components.text: The whole pictographic form: a person-like figure with a marked midsection. The mark is interpreted as an abdomen, possibly with a navel, or as a pregnant abdomen; the image does not decide between these readings.

evidence.source: 漢字構形資料庫 / Character Structure Database, Academia Sinica
evidence.field: evolution records; oracle-bone entry 合集822正, bronze entry 集成04025, seal-script entry 說文; interpretation
evidence.text: The page catalogs 身 forms under oracle bone (including 合集822正), bronze (集成04025), Chu manuscripts, and small seal script. It interprets the old graph as a woman with a large pregnant abdomen. This supports the existence and broad evolution of early forms, but the page’s brief interpretation does not date individual forms or establish that pregnancy, rather than abdomen, was the graph’s first meaning.
evidence.title: 漢字「身」：字形演變

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Character Structure Database

The early image is compatible with both descriptions; the inspected pages do not demonstrate that the image itself distinguishes a pregnant figure from an abdomen-marked person.
evidence.title: 漢字「身」：字形演變

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Character Structure Database

evidence.text: The record lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript and small-seal forms, including oracle-bone 合集822正 and bronze 集成04025. evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 / Multi-function Chinese Character Database, Chinese University of Hong Kong

evidence.text: The database analyzes early forms as 人 with the abdomen marked, possibly including a navel dot, and proposes 腹部 ‘abdomen’ as the original sense. It cites the oracle-bone use 合集822正 for the king's abdominal illness; bronze inscriptions for body/person, personal action, and era; and Guodian Laozi B strip 8 and Qinghua 程寤 strip 9 for body. It treats 有身 in 詩經·大雅·大明 as ‘pregnant’ and the body and self senses as semantic extensions. The page supplies citation labels but not absolute dates for each example.

formation.text: The traditional graph 車 pictures a vehicle as a whole. Early forms varied in the features shown; later forms selected and regularized some of them. The modern graph 车 derives from cursive 車.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Chinese Characters Database
evidence.text: The database describes Shang oracle-bone forms as variable, sometimes depicting wheels, carriage body, axle, yoke, pole and crossbar; later forms retain selected features, producing the regular 車 form. It lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript and seal-script evidence. This supports a pictorial graph, with reduction and stylization over time.
evidence.title: 漢字「車」：字形演變

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Chinese Characters Database
evidence.text: The author identifies 车 as a cursive form of 車, attested by the Sui dynasty at the latest and continuing in later cursive writing, but says it did not become generally used as a standard character until adoption in the first simplified-character list. The formal 1956 reform resolution states that the first table of 230 simplified characters was to be used from 1 February 1956; the 1964 table lists 车 as a simplified component corresponding to 車. These records support the relationship, but do not show the calligraphic exemplars themselves on the inspected page.
evidence.title: 从单个字符形体的简化看字形与繁简关系

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Chinese Characters Database
evidence.text: Describes Shang oracle forms as variable, with detailed and abbreviated depictions of vehicle features including wheels, body/frame, crossbar, and yoke; says later writing selected some features to form regular 車. Its page displays oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and seal-script categories. This supports pictographic formation and graphic reduction, without implying every version includes every named part.
evidence.title: 漢字「車」：字形演變

formation.text: 邊’s early construction is disputed. One analysis assigns movement meaning to 辵 and a sound role to 𦤝; another assigns “beside” to 方 and proposes sound roles for 自 and 丙. 边 is the simplified form of 邊.

components.text: One analysis of 邊 assigns 辵 a movement meaning. Its conventional left-side form is 辶; this proposed role in 邊 is not established for 边.
A Han-era dictionary analysis identifies 𦤝 as 邊’s sound element. Its graphic relationship to 臱 remains unresolved.

sound_limitation.text: Zhengzhang’s reconstruction compares 臱 *men with 邊 *mpeːn, but the evidence does not establish that 𦤝 is 臱. This pair therefore cannot validate 𦤝’s proposed sound role.

sound.text: The reported Mandarin readings are 𦤝 mián and 邊 biān. This modern comparison does not establish the proposed ancient sound role.
sound.system: Mandarin: CNS11643 reading for 𦤝 and Modern Standard Mandarin for 邊

components.text: One analysis of the bronze form assigns 方 the meaning “beside”; a competing analysis assigns meaning to 辵.
Some analyses propose that 自 supplies sound in early 邊. Its Mandarin reading zì differs from 邊 biān and does not establish that historical role.

sound_limitation.text: The current Mandarin readings do not establish an ancient sound relationship for 自 in 邊.

sound.text: The current Mandarin readings are 自 zì and 邊 biān; they differ and do not establish an ancient sound match.

components.text: Some analyses propose that 丙 supplies sound in early 邊. Its Mandarin reading bǐng differs from 邊 biān and does not establish that historical role.

sound_limitation.text: The current Mandarin readings do not establish an ancient sound relationship for 丙 in 邊.

sound.text: The current Mandarin readings are 丙 bǐng and 邊 biān; they differ and do not establish an ancient sound match.

components.text: 边 is simplified from 邊 and retains 辶, the conventional left-side form of 辵. This form correspondence does not establish the disputed movement meaning for 辶 in 边.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Simplified form of 邊.  Phonosemantic compound with two sound components and two meaning components. 辶 and 方 represent the meaning, while 自 and 丙 represent the sound. The traditional component 自 was removed for simplification. The traditional component 丙 was removed for simplification.

evidence.text: Simplified from 邊 (臱 → 力). Officially adopted as the simplified form of 邊 in the Chinese Character Simplification Scheme (《漢字簡化方案》) in 1956.

evidence.field: 形義通解 / bronze form and early uses
evidence.text: The database describes bronze 邊 as containing 辵, 自, 丙, and 方. It reports an analysis attributed to 張世超 in which 自 and 丙 both function as sound elements, and 方 contributes the sense ‘side’; it gives ‘beside’ as the original meaning. It cites the bronze inscriptions 大盂鼎 for a use meaning ‘frontier region’ and 散氏盤 for the place-name 邊柳. These are source assertions; the multiple-phonetic-element analysis differs from accounts that assign a single phonetic element.

evidence.text: The page quotes the Han-era Shuowen account: 邊, ‘行垂崖也’ (walking by a precipitous edge), ‘from 辵, sound from 𦤝,’ with fanqie 布賢切. It separately records Guangyun fanqie 布玄 and places 邊 in the level-tone 先 rhyme, grade IV, labial initial. Shuowen’s explanation is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the graph’s original composition.

evidence.text: The entry presents a sequence of Shang, Western Zhou, Warring States, and Shuowen forms and identifies 臱 as 邊’s sound-series member. It gives Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) Old Chinese 臱 *men and 邊 *mpeːn; in Baxter–Sagart (2014) it gives Middle Chinese ‹pen› and Old Chinese *pˁe[n]. The differing reconstructions belong to distinct systems and should not be collapsed into a single pronunciation. The entry also says the oracle-bone form consists of 自 and 丙, which may both be phonetic; that proposal differs from the bronze analysis assigning 方 a semantic role.

It cites 大盂鼎 for a use meaning a frontier region and 散氏盤 for the place-name 邊柳. These are the database’s analysis and readings of cited contexts, not an independently checked reading of the artifacts. The same page quotes Shuowen’s Han-era analysis ‘行垂崖也。从辵，𦤝聲’ and its fanqie 布賢切; Guangyun is separately listed with 布玄 and level-tone 先, grade IV, labial initial. Its account proposes that the oracle-bone form contains 自 and 丙, possibly both sound elements; for the bronze form it lists 辵, 自, 丙, 方, with 辵 and 方 possibly semantic and 自 and 丙 phonetic. It says the small-seal lower-right part of 𨘢 reflects a corruption of 方. The article also reports Schuessler’s proposed cognates 偏, 片, 諞; this is a disputed lexical proposal, not a demonstrated graphic or semantic chronology.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ŋrans): semantic 辶 (“walk”) + phonetic 言 (OC *ŋan).
The character was originally a verb meaning “to meet”, whose modern pronunciation is yàn. It was later borrowed for the proximal demonstrative “this/here”, by a confusion in medieval handwriting with 遮 (zhē, “this”).
First attested in the Tang dynasty; etymology unclear. Proposed etymologies:
* From 者 (OC *tjaːʔ, “one which”) (Lü, 1985). Wang (1990) notes that 者 always occurs after what is referred to, whereas 這 always before.
*: 者 (OC *tjaːʔ, “one which”) > 者 (MC tsyaeX, “this (possessive case)”) > 者 (MC tsyaeX, “this (general demonstrative)”) > Mandarin 這 /这 (zhè).
* From 之 (OC *tjɯ, “this; it”) (Wang, 1990). Norman (1988) notes that this derivation would be phonologically problematic.

components.text: 辶 is the conventional side form of 辵, which contributes a travel-related category in 道. This side/full-form relationship does not itself imply a historical sequence.

formation.text: This is a phonosemantic compound: 邑 contributes the settlement category, while 者 provides a sound cue for the city reading. 者 is the phonetic component for 都’s city reading. The reconstructed syllables are related but not identical, consistent with a sound cue; they do not establish the graph’s ultimate pictorial origin.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, 者 is reconstructed as *tjaːʔ and 都 as *taː. Their related initials and finals support a sound comparison, though the forms differ and are reconstructions rather than recorded pronunciations.

evidence.text: This dictionary states 里 first appears in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, formed from 田 and 土 and interpreted as a place where land and fields are habitable. It reports later bronze forms where strokes in 田 and 土 run together, with the stroke in 土 later extended into the seal-script shape. It cites bronze uses for a settlement head (令方彝), a distance measure (中山王鼎), and as a writing for 裏 in a garment-lining phrase (伯䢅鼎). It also cites Warring States Qin slips for settlement and distance-measure uses, and a Guodian slip where 里 writes 理. These are the dictionary's reported readings of cited artifacts; I did not inspect the glyph images or artifact editions independently.

formation.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary gives a phonosemantic analysis: 壬 contributes meaning and 東 supplies sound, alongside the whole-character gloss “thick/deep.” Distinct proposals picture a person carrying a load, or identify 東 as a sack with 土 beneath it as a weight. The original construction is unresolved; the sack proposal does not establish that 土 was added later.

components.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary identifies 壬 as the semantic element in 重. Its gloss for the whole character is “thick/deep”; this analysis does not establish the graph’s original referent.
The Han-dynasty dictionary assigns 東 a phonetic role. The available reading comparison is modern and does not independently prove that role or an ancient sound relationship.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 厚也。从壬東聲。凡重之屬皆从重。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *doŋ, *doŋʔ, *doŋs) and ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): semantic 人 (“man”) + phonetic 東 (OC *toːŋ, “bag”) – a man carrying a bag. A glyph 土 (“earth”) was later added to show that the bag-carrying man is standing on the ground. From this composition (𡍺) is the current form. In the modern form, the man on top can be seen as 亻 (however, the upper part of the character is unrelated to 千).
See also 以, in which a person is carrying something, 央, in which a person is carrying a pole, and 年, in which a person is carrying the harvest.
Schuessler (2007) notes that the etymology is uncertain and compares the word to Burmese စုံ (cum, “to be sufficient; pair”), which STEDT puts under Proto-Sino-Tibetan *dzum ~ tsum (“pair”).
Pronunciation 3 is the exoactive derivation of pronunciation 1.

evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi, online text and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary defines 重 as “thick/deep” (厚), analyzes it as 从壬東聲 (“壬 as semantic element, 東 as phonetic”), and treats characters in its series as written with 重. Duan Yucai says the senses “solemn/respectful” and “repeated/overlapping” are extensions from 厚, and comments that ancient usage had only the level-tone reading, without the departing-tone reading. This is a historical analysis, not independent confirmation of the graph's origin.

formation.text: The traditional graph 錢 is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 金 contributes a metal-related category, while 戔 supplies a sound cue. In simplified 钱, these are written with the corresponding forms 钅 and 戋. This is a historical dictionary analysis, not direct proof of the graph’s earliest formation.

components.text: In 錢, 金 is the left-side semantic component, marking a metal-related category. Its corresponding left-side form in 钱 is 钅.
In 錢, 戔 is analyzed as the right-side phonetic component. Simplified 钱 writes this part as 戋; the readings are compatible with a sound role but do not establish its full historical sound relation.

sound_limitation.text: The modern and reconstructed comparisons fit a phonetic role but do not establish a complete regular sound history or independently prove the component’s ancient role.

sound.text: In modern Mandarin, 戔 jiān and 錢 qián are similar but not identical; these readings alone do not establish their historical relationship.
In Baxter–Sagart 2014 Middle Chinese, 戔 dzan and 錢 dzjen are similar, a comparison compatible with a phonetic role.
In Baxter–Sagart 2014 Old Chinese, 戔 *[dz]ˤa[n] and 錢 *N-ts[a][n] are compatible with a phonetic role; this comparison does not establish a complete regular sound history.

formation.text: 錯 is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 金 contributes a metal-related meaning category, while 昔 supplies a sound cue. It notes that Shuowen instead analyzes 昔 as dried meat; CUHK regards that explanation as belonging to 腊, not 昔. formation.text: The traditional interpretation of 閒 is a semantic compound: 門 pictures a gate framing a gap, and 月 pictures the moon whose light enters through it. 間 is described as a later spelling of 閒, with 日 in place of 月, though the sequence and origin of this spelling are unsettled. Simplified 间 retains 日 and uses 门, the simplified form of 門.

components.text: In the traditional interpretation of 閒, 門 pictures the gate framing a gap; this account does not prove how the graph was first made.
In the traditional interpretation of 閒, 月 pictures the moon in the proposed moonlight-through-a-gap scene; this is a historical explanation, not proof of the graph’s creation.
日 occurs in 間 and 间. Some explanations picture sunlight passing through a doorway, but this interpretation is not established as the graph’s original construction.

evidence.source: 蔡一峰, “古文字所謂「閒」「外」通諧說辨議”
evidence.text: The article reports 間 as a later variant spelling of 閒 and cites a Warring States bronze inscription (間右戈, 集成 10974) as an attestation. It cites late Western Zhou bronze examples of 閒, including 㝬鐘 (集成 260), whose graph places 月 outside 門. The author presents the traditional semantic interpretation as a gap at a door, with moonlight entering, and discusses a separate graph with an added 卜 as a Warring States differentiation of 閒. The paper also explains that scholars have proposed phonetic relations involving 月/外, but argues that the sound-series evidence is not secure and favors treating the series separately. This is a secondary paleographic study, not direct inspection of the cited bronzes.
evidence.title: 古文字所謂「閒」「外」通諧說辨議

The quoted 段注 expands the sense from a gap or interval between two sides to spaces, intervals in speech, and leisure; it describes 閒 as a semantic compound and repeats the traditional moonlight-through-a-door-gap account. These are historical lexicographic explanations, not independent proof of the graph’s creation circumstances.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary treats 閒 as a variant of 間 in later standardized usage. Its note quotes the tradition that 閒 was the earlier spelling for ‘gap/interval’, and that 間 became the conventional form for interval/between while 閒 was used especially for leisure; it also cites an epigraphic note that 閒 follows 月 in Shuowen and that the popular spelling uses 日. This supports the later spelling relation, but the entry does not establish the exact date or a single mechanism for every 日-form.

evidence.text: The entry describes variable oracle-bone forms: often a stroke represents the sky, with two or three drops below; some drops join the upper stroke, and an extra stroke may be decorative. It says Western Zhou forms connect the outer rain shape into a line, resembling small-seal forms, and Warring States forms sometimes render the drops with a water-like shape. It identifies the original sense as rainwater and cites oracle-bone examples: 《合集》8329 往于河，㞢(有)雨; 《合集》20397 壬戌㞢(有)雨; and verbal uses 《合集》9757 今日雨 and 《合集》12598 今日其大雨. This supports a rain pictograph, but not a single invariant early design or the claim that the top stroke was simply added later. The cited inscription numbers are source locators; this page does not supply absolute dates for those individual records.

No phonetic component is identified for 雨 itself.

evidence.field: 形義通解; character forms; Middle Chinese reading
evidence.text: The database interprets the oracle bone and bronze graph as wings spread to either side; following Xu Shen and Lin Yiguang, it proposes ‘wings’ as the original sense and derives ‘turn against’ from the wings facing away from one another. It records oracle-bone 非 in 《合集》16927, ‘非𡆥(憂)’, as a negative meaning ‘without worry’, and also as a place name. For bronze inscriptions it gives 毛公鼎’s ‘余非’ as ‘my faults’ and 中山王方壺’s ‘寡人非之’ as ‘I judge it wrong’; Warring States bamboo slips use 非 as a negator. evidence.source: 漢典 / ZDIC

evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry says ‘違也。从飛下翄，取其相背’ (‘opposition; from the lower wings of 飛, taking their facing away from one another’). The Duan Yucai commentary argues that 非 means 背 (‘face away’) rather than 離 (‘separate’), glossing the old reading as 韋. This is a Han-era explanatory tradition and commentary, not independent proof of original referent or semantic chronology.

evidence.text: Wang argues that 非 and 北 were nearly homophonous in Old Chinese and that 非 split from 北 during the oracle-bone period. She reads the early forms as two people back-to-back, with short strokes added to distinguish the negative graph. She reports that extant oracle-bone examples of 非 include negation and a possible place name, and lists examples in 《合集》10977, 33147, 34707–34709, 24156, 33694, 33479, and 16927–16928. This is Wang’s analysis, not an uncontested account.

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for Studies of Unearthed Documents and Ancient Chinese Characters; Wang Qingju

evidence.text: The article summarizes Xu Shen’s Han-era account: 非 means opposition, formed from the lower wings of 飛 to express facing away; it also notes that this was taken to imply an extension to negation. Wang disputes that interpretation, observing that the oracle-bone use she surveyed is already negative and arguing that 飛 is later attested as a graph. She proposes a relation to 北 instead. Neither interpretation establishes a certain graphic origin or a dated semantic path from a pictorial referent.

formation.text: 页 is a derived form of the pictographic traditional graph 頁. That graph is analyzed as a kneeling person with the head emphasized; the analysis concerns 頁 and does not establish separate components in modern 页.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Simplified form of 頁.  Pictograph of a head (首) on top of a person (卩). Means "head" when pronounced xié. Has unrelated meaning "leaf" when pronounced yè, due to this character being adopted as a shorthand form of 葉.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.text: The database describes 頁 in oracle and bronze forms as 卩 plus 首: a kneeling human figure with the head visually prominent. It says the graph denotes ‘head’; 頁 and 首 differ in whether the body is drawn and are graphic variants. Its examples include oracle-bone uses meaning ‘pig’s head’ (合集15684) and ‘bowing the head’ (合集22215); it notes a Western Zhou bronze occurrence in 卯簋蓋 and a phrase 頁手 there, possibly abbreviated or erroneous. It reports that 頁 and 首 were originally one graph pronounced like 首, and that 頁 had acquired the reading 胡結切 by the Eastern Han at the latest. The source calls the paper measure use a俗字 for 葉. Its account of shape change says oracle-bone 頁 may show or omit hair; a W. Zhou bronze has hair; Warring States forms often distort the hair as 止; the small-seal form omits it. This is a database’s paleographic analysis, not direct visual inspection in this research.

evidence.text: The database analyzes oracle-bone and bronze 頁 as combining 卩 and 首, depicting a kneeling human with the head emphasized. It describes 頁 and 首 as graphic variants distinguished by whether the body is drawn, and reports oracle-bone examples for the head sense: 合集15684 豕頁 (“pig’s head”) and 合集22215 五子叩頁 (“the boys bow their heads”). Its shape account says oracle-bone forms may include or omit hair, a Western Zhou bronze form has hair, Warring States forms often distort the hair into 止, and the small-seal form omits it. It treats the paper measure use as a common form for 葉 and reports a change to 胡結切 by the Eastern Han at the latest. This is the database’s analysis, not a direct inspection of the ancient artifacts.

The head-sense evidence and paper-use account are separate; the page does not establish the earliest dated instance of the latter.

formation.text: The later form 風 is analyzed as phonosemantic: 凡 provides a sound cue, while the lower marks are interpreted as pictorial traces of tail feathers from the earlier bird-shaped graph. The early bird sign was used for “wind,” possibly because the bird’s name and the wind word sounded alike; that proposed sound match is unverified because the bird’s spoken name is uncertain.

components.text: 凡 is analyzed as the phonetic component in 風. Old Chinese reconstructions give related but nonidentical readings, suggesting a sound relationship; the comparison alone does not establish this graphic analysis.

sound_limitation.text: These reconstructions provide sound comparisons but do not by themselves establish 凡’s graphic identity or role in 風.

sound.text: The Baxter–Sagart reconstructions are related but nonidentical.
The Zhengzhang reconstructions are related but nonidentical.

components.text: In 風, the lower marks shaped like 虫 are interpreted as traces of bird-tail feathers, not as an original insect element. Chu forms preserve differing feather designs; Qin forms reshape the marks as 虫, a form continued in seal script. The Han-period insect explanation records a later interpretation.

evidence.source: CASE報科學, National Taiwan University science education center
evidence.text: The article analyzes the use of the bird graph for the wind word as a phonetic loan, motivated by wind's lack of a concrete shape. It says the words were close in Old Chinese: 風 has a labial initial in the 冬 group and 鳳 a related labial initial in the same group. However, the proposed original referent of the bird graph is only tentatively identified as green peafowl, and the article notes that clear oracle-bone examples of the graph meaning the animal are lacking or disputed. Thus the graphic-loan proposal does not independently establish the animal's original spoken name or pronunciation.

evidence.source: CASE報科學, National Taiwan University science education center

It reports that Chu forms preserve different parts of the feather design and that Qin forms reinterpret the lower feathers as 虫. This is an account of graphic development and corruption, separate from the early whole-graph loan.

Modern paleographic accounts reject this insect explanation as a retrospective interpretation of the corrupted feather shape; it remains important evidence for how the graph was understood in the Han lexicographic tradition, not proof of its original construction.

formation.text: The traditional graph 飯 is analyzed as 食, which marks the food category, plus 反, which supplies a sound cue. This structure is reported for a bronze form and in the Shuowen account. Simplified 饭 writes 食 as 饣 while retaining 反.

components.text: 饣 is the visible abbreviated form of the food component in 饭. In traditional 飯, the corresponding component is 食, which marks the food category. The available account identifies the simplification but does not explain how the abbreviated shape developed.

反 is retained in 饭 from traditional 飯 and serves as its phonetic component. In the Baxter–Sagart reconstructions, 飯 and 反 share a labial onset and nasal-rhyme material, though they are not identical. The precise historical sound motivation remains unresolved; modern Mandarin similarity alone does not prove the analysis.

sound.text: The Baxter–Sagart forms for 飯 (*bonʔ / *bonʔ-s) and 反 (*Cə.panʔ) share a labial onset and nasal-rhyme material, supporting a plausible, inexact sound relationship. Their Mandarin readings, fàn and fǎn, are similar as well, but that modern resemblance alone does not establish the historical link.

evidence.text: The database reports the bronze graph 飯 as 食 plus 反, with 反 functioning as phonetic. It quotes the Shuowen definition 食也，从食反聲 and two Guangyun spellings, 扶晚 and 符万. Its explanation, following Duan Yucai, takes the early verbal sense as ‘eat’ and the noun sense ‘what is eaten’ or cooked rice as an extension. A bronze inscription has 飯者月 as a Qi month name, but the database says which month it denotes is unknown. The page displays one bronze example and one Small Seal example; its text alone does not establish a detailed sequence of graphic changes.

evidence.text: For 飯 the page gives Mandarin fàn in its headword display and shows Guangyun fanqie 扶晚 and 符万, corresponding to two readings with voiced labial initials, rising and departing categories. For 反 it gives Mandarin fǎn and Guangyun entries 孚袁 and 府遠, with aspirated and voiceless labial initials in the listed categories. Modern same-syllable similarity alone does not prove the phonetic history; the medieval categories and Old Chinese reconstructions provide historical comparison.

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction 1.1 (2014)
evidence.text: In the Baxter–Sagart system as reported on the page, 飯 has readings reconstructed *bonʔ ‘eat’ and *bonʔ-s ‘cooked rice or millet’; 反 has *Cə.panʔ ‘reverse’ (and a separate reading). These reconstructions have related labial onset and nasal-final/rhyme material but do not make 反 and 飯 identical in every feature. They support a plausible phonetic relationship in the compound rather than a claim that 飯 is a whole-graph loan from 反. The page also lists Zhengzhang’s reconstruction for 反 as *panʔ; that is a different system and is not directly interchangeable with Baxter–Sagart.

formation.text: The traditional character 餓 is phonosemantic: 食 supplies the food-related meaning and 我 supplies a sound cue. In simplified 饿, 食 is written in its conventional left-side form 饣; this is a graphic standardization of the character, not a separate ancient construction.

components.text: 饣 is the simplified left-side form corresponding to 食 in traditional 餓. 食 marks the food-related category; the difference between these forms reflects simplification, not a historical sequence.
我 is the phonetic component in 餓. The Zhengzhang comparison supports this role, although the reconstructed forms differ in their endings; Mandarin readings wǒ and è are not identical today.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Old Chinese, 我 *ŋaːlʔ and 餓 *ŋaːls share a segmental base but differ in ending. These are system-specific reconstructions, not recorded pronunciations.

formation.text: The traditional analysis of 館 is phonosemantic: 食 contributes a food-related meaning category, and 官 provides a sound cue. In 馆, 饣 is the conventional side form corresponding to 食. An earlier use of 宛 for the lodging word is reported, but how it relates to the 食+官 analysis remains unresolved.

components.text: 饣 is the simplified side form corresponding to 食, the food-related meaning element in the traditional analysis of 館. The evidence identifies 馆 as simplified from 館 but does not date this spelling in the character.

官 is the phonetic element in the traditional analysis of 館. In the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese system, 官 is reconstructed as /*kʷˤa[n]/ and 館 as *[k]ˤo[n]ʔ-s, a broad historical sound relationship. The proposed sound merger and replacement of 宛 by 官 remain uncertain.

sound_limitation.text: The cited sound comparison supports a broad historical relationship, but the specific proposed sound merger and replacement pathway is a secondary account and is not independently verified.

sound.text: The Old Chinese reconstructions differ in detail but indicate a broad historical sound relationship; modern Mandarin readings alone do not establish it.

formation.text: The traditional graph 雞 is phonosemantic in later forms: 隹 or 鳥 contributes the bird category, and 奚 supplies a sound cue. Early forms are also interpreted as a whole chicken picture. The evidence does not give a fully dated sequence from picture to compound. The modern shape 鸡 does not establish a historical 又 + 鸟 construction.

components.text: Early forms of 雞 are interpreted as a whole picture of a chicken, with the crest and open beak emphasized. The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name, so the picture’s original referent is uncertain.

In 雞, 奚 supplies sound, not its separate lexical meaning. The Middle Chinese readings share a rhyme but differ in initial; the Old Chinese comparison is approximate and comes from a local cross-check.

sound_limitation.text: The exact Old Chinese forms in the local cross-check were not verified at the dataset publisher. The historical dictionary explicitly assigns 奚 a sound role in 雞.

sound.text: Modern Mandarin readings xī and jī differ. This modern pair alone does not establish the historical sound relation.
The supplied Middle Chinese forms share a rhyme but differ in initial.

components.text: 隹 contributes the bird category in Qin and later forms of 雞. Some Warring States Qi and Chu forms instead use 鳥; the evidence does not establish a single sequence between these bird elements.

鳮 is recorded as a simplified-style variant associated with 雞 and appears as 鳮（雞） in the 1956 simplification scheme. The precise graphic route to 鸡 is not documented; 又 has no supported historical role in 鸡.

evidence.source: 中央研究院漢字構形資料庫（Character Structure Database）
evidence.text: The database describes the bronze form of 雞 as a whole-figure pictograph of a chicken that later developed into a phonosemantic form with 隹 as semantic element and 奚 as phonetic element. It identifies a bronze specimen as 集成05802. This supports a development from pictorial graph to compound, but the page gives no date for that individual specimen.
evidence.title: 漢字「雞」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義通解; 早期用例
evidence.text: The database analyzes early oracle forms as chicken pictures, often emphasizing the comb and open beak; it says 奚 was later added as a phonetic marker because the picture could be confused with other birds. It reports an oracle-bone use as a place name in 《合集》37363 and cites Qin bamboo slips from the Shuihudi annals (簡45), “十二月甲午雞鳴時，喜產,” as a use referring to chickens. It separately reports Chicken as the ordinary sense in Warring States/Qin slips and a Mawangdui silk text. In Mawangdui 《老子乙本》 line 65, 雞 is used as a phonetic loan for 谿 “valley/stream,” with the A copy reading 溪 and the Fu Yi text 谿. The page distinguishes these written uses rather than presenting a gloss list as a chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：雞

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 《說文》; 字形分析; 音韻資料
evidence.text: The page transmits the Eastern Han Shuowen account: “雞，知時畜也。从隹，奚聲。鷄，籒文雞，从鳥。” Its account says Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥, while Qin forms and later use 隹, citing Ji Xusheng. This variation complicates a simple story that 鳥 was only a later substitute for 隹. It gives Guangyun fanqie 古奚 and Middle Chinese categories 見母, 平聲, 齊韻, 開口四等.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：雞

evidence.source: Local structured dataset: sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv; inspected rows 1444–1445 and 3613–3614. Verified against inspected external pages at the upstream dataset publisher could not be established.
evidence.text: Local rows give 雞 and 鷄 as Mandarin jī, Middle Chinese kej, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *kˤe; 奚 as Mandarin xī, Middle Chinese hej, Old Chinese *[g]ˤe (with one row also giving the note “dial. for 何 *[g]ˤaj?”). In this dataset the pair shares the rhyme and differs in reconstructed initial, so their Old Chinese comparison is approximate rather than identity. These spellings are the dataset’s own Baxter–Sagart notation and must not be merged with other Old Chinese systems. Local row metadata is not treated as externally verified evidence because no official upstream HTTP page for the exact rows was inspected.

It also records 鳮 as a variant and cites a cross-strait simplification comparison associating 鷄 with that form. evidence.text: This secondary reference lists modern Beijing pinyin jī, Middle Chinese Baxter transcription kej, and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *kˤe for 雞; it separately lists Zhengzhang *keː. The two Old Chinese reconstructions belong to distinct systems and should not be combined. The локal TSV cross-check described in the dossier gives the same 雞 Baxter–Sagart form but no externally verified exact upstream row was found in this run.
evidence.title: 雞 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese character entry
evidence.field: Mandarin and Old Chinese reading table
evidence.text: The inspected entry supplies Mandarin xī for 奚 and separate historical systems. The search/opened material did not verify the exact Baxter–Sagart row upstream; the repository TSV noted in the dossier records *[g]ˤe, while the secondary material surfaced in search appeared to give other-system forms. Therefore exact system-specific correspondence should be stated cautiously; the independent support for 奚’s phonetic role here is Shuowen’s explicit “奚聲,” not a claim of identical Old Chinese reconstructions.
evidence.title: 奚 - 维基词典

sense.text: 一 is also used with the present-day function “a, an.” Its date and development from the numeral sense are unresolved.
一 is also used with the present-day meaning “alone.” Its chronology and connection to the numeral sense are unresolved.

sense.period: Oracle-bone writing; exact date unresolved; additional senses attested in later cited textual sources
sense.text: An oracle-bone example uses 一 in the numeral phrase ‘one ox.’ The cited study describes the numeral as the smallest positive integer and discusses ordinal ‘first’ as well; these are attested uses, not proof of a hypothetical original meaning.
A specialized Japanese sense meaning “gambler” is recorded with an example dated 1744. The evidence does not explain its development from “seven.”

sense.period: Oracle-bone writing onward, as reported by a paleographic study
sense.text: A paleographic study reports 七 used for the numeral in oracle-bone writing and cites an oracle-bone example. This is an early attested numeral use; it does not rule out the disputed proposal of an earlier cut-related use.

sense.gloss: seven (Japanese readings なな and しち)
sense.period: Manyōshū example dated to the 8th century; later attestations also recorded
sense.text: Japanese lexical evidence records なな for “seven” in an 8th-century Manyōshū example and しち in an example from 1477. These Japanese readings and uses do not explain the origin of the Chinese graph.
A corpus study reports 三 writing the numeral three in Shang oracle-bone examples H.16189 and H.37453; it gives no precise date for either inscription.
三 continues to represent the numeral three.

sense.period: Zhou bronze inscription contexts reported; current use
sense.text: Reported Shang-period examples include 上帝, 上甲, and contrasts with 下; Zhou bronze examples include spatial ‘above.’ The cited dictionary definitions also support ‘above; upper side’ as a current meaning, without establishing priority among every lexical use.
Bronze-inscription accounts report this spatial use. Its relationship to “above” is not established.
Current dictionary definitions include rank-related “superior”; the reported historical uses do not establish its sequence relative to spatial “above.”
The graph indicates a lower position. Cited oracle-bone uses refer to lower deities and ancestral spirits; these examples attest use but do not establish either as the character’s original meaning.

sense.period: Warring States text; precise date unresolved
sense.text: A cited military passage uses 下 of a city that does not surrender. The account does not establish how this use developed from “below,” if it did.
Current glosses include “under,” “below,” and “down.”

sense.period: Later transmitted texts; precise date unresolved
sense.text: Later cited texts use 下 as a verb meaning “descend.” Their chronology within a sequence of meaning changes is unresolved.

sense.period: Later transmitted texts; precise date unresolved
sense.text: A cited later use expresses humility toward a superior. Its date and development from the lower-position sense are not established.
A cited bronze inscription uses 下 for the human world below.

sense.period: Later Archaic Chinese; examples cited from the Analects and Xunzi
sense.text: 不 is used as a general verbal negative in later Archaic Chinese. The intervening development from its earlier particle use is not traced in detail.

sense.period: Modern Chinese; usage varies by language and dialect
sense.text: 不 commonly expresses negation, including as a negative prefix; its distribution varies across modern varieties.
不 is attested as a negative particle in oracle-bone inscriptions. The corpus is dated broadly; no specific occurrence is dated here.
The common modern meaning is the east or something situated toward the east.

sense.period: Early inscriptional contexts reported; exact first attestation unresolved
sense.text: 東 is reported in an oracle-bone inscription for the eastern region, as well as in later early inscriptions referring to eastern territory. The received poem 小星 also uses it directionally, but its exact composition date and earliest physical witness are unresolved.

東 is also recorded with the meaning “host” or “landlord.” A traditional explanation links this sense to the host’s position on the east side, and a Tang literary example is reported. The first attestation and the path from “east” to this sense are unresolved.
两 is used for ‘both’, ‘pair’ and ‘couple’. The available evidence does not date these meanings or connect them to the early measure uses through a specific transition.
‘Ounce’ is recorded as a gloss for 两/兩, but its historical relation to the earlier weight-unit use is not traced here.
Western Zhou bronze inscriptions attest quantity and measure uses, including a measure associated with pairs of horses. These examples do not securely date the first abstract numeral use.

sense.period: Western Zhou bronze inscriptions; also recorded in Shuowen
sense.text: Bronze inscriptions attest a weight-unit use, and Shuowen defines 兩 as twenty-four zhu. How this sense relates historically to quantity or measure uses is unresolved.
A cited classical passage is associated by commentary with counting bamboo. It does not establish the first attestation or a transition to the general classifier.

sense.gloss: counting item or unit, like 枚
sense.text: A ritual counting context is recorded, with 个 glossed as comparable to 枚. The available evidence does not date this sense or connect it to bamboo-related counting.

sense.gloss: general classifier for individual people or things
sense.text: 个 is used as a general classifier for counting people and objects. Its emergence is not dated here.
A transmitted commentary reports this meaning for 个 as an alternate form; it is not established as the character’s earliest meaning.
A current sense meaning “single” or “individual” is recorded. Its historical relation to the classifier is not established here.

sense.gloss: uses in Shang-period contexts, precise values unresolved
sense.text: The graph is reported in dated Shang divination contexts, including 立中 and passages associated with warfare, weather observation, and ancestral rites. These attest graph use, but the exact word meaning in each passage is unsettled.

中 is reported with the meanings “hit the center” or “attain.” A departing-tone reading is associated with hitting the center, but the evidence does not establish when or how this use relates to “middle.”
The received Shuowen gloss is “inside.” The evidence supports this as a historical dictionary interpretation, but does not independently establish it as a lexical sense or settle its chronology.
中 commonly means “middle” or “center.” The evidence does not show that this was necessarily its earliest lexical meaning.

sense.gloss: interrogative or sentence-final particle; postposed element
sense.text: In simplified Chinese, 么 writes interrogative and postposed uses also written 麼 in traditional Chinese. Cited literary examples attest these uses but do not date the earliest surviving spellings.
A small or fine use is cited for 么, including in 么虫. The evidence does not establish whether this meaning continues a sense associated with 幺 or 麽.
九 is the current numeral nine.
A cited oracle-bone passage uses 九 for a body part read as elbow or wrist, consistent with the interpretation that the graph is an early form associated with 肘.
Later transmitted-text examples use nine to express a large or extreme quantity; the timing and path of this extension are unclear.
Oracle-bone examples use 九 for nine, including a count of oxen and a month date. These examples do not establish whether numeral use preceded or followed the body-part use.
九 is reported as a loan spelling for 鳩. This is a separate use of the graph, not evidence that the meaning “nine” developed into “dove”; the reason for reuse is not given.
Modern Chinese uses 也 as an adverb meaning “also” or “as well.” Dictionary glosses attest the use but do not establish when or how it developed from particle uses.

sense.period: pre-Qin texts; precise dating unresolved here
sense.text: A grammatical analysis identifies copular use in the Guodian corpus and proposes a path from focus particle to copula. This concerns the word’s grammatical use, not the graph’s origin, and does not establish a dated sequence here.
也 has classical grammatical uses. The earliest securely dated occurrence is unsettled; general glosses and transmitted examples do not establish it.
Guodian slips attest learning-related use of 習 in the Warring States period. The relationship of this use to repeated divination or flying is unresolved.
Practice is a current use of 習 and its standardized simplified written form 习. The evidence does not establish how it developed from the older reported uses.

sense.gloss: use in expressions glossed as repeated divinations
sense.text: Oracle-bone expressions 習一卜, 習二卜, and 習三卜 are reported with the gloss “repeated divinations.” These attest a use of the graph but do not establish it as the original or earliest meaning.

sense.period: received Shuowen account; date not specified here
sense.text: The received Shuowen entry defines 習 as repeated flying. This historical gloss does not show that repeated flying was the oracle graph’s earliest meaning.
“Book” is a current meaning of the character and also occurs in cited classical examples. The evidence does not date its development from “write” or “text.”
書 also means “letter” or “document.” The cited examples do not establish when these uses arose or how they relate chronologically to the other senses.
書 is also used to mean “record.” The cited example does not establish when this use arose relative to the other senses.
The character is used for writing or text; cited examples do not date this sense in relation to the others.
The traditional gloss associates 書 with writing or setting something down; the evidence does not identify this as the earliest attested use.
These glosses are listed for the character, but the supplied examples do not clarify their relation to “buy” or establish their chronology.
買 is used for “buy” or “purchase.” Texts cited for buying and selling do not establish the date of the surviving wording or the earliest securely dated use.
An early lexicographic account glosses 買 as 市, “market.” This is the gloss of that account, not a securely dated earliest meaning of the spoken word.

sense.period: later literary examples; origin date unresolved
sense.text: Later literary examples use 買 for seeking or obtaining, including fame or favor. They show this usage but do not date its emergence.

sense.period: dating unresolved; later than perfective use in the reported account
sense.text: Accounts describe this sentence-final use as a later development from the perfective particle. Its detailed path remains uncertain, including a proposed interaction with 也 in some dialects.

The received entry glosses 了 with 尦; later commentary interprets this as legs crossing or becoming entangled. This is a historical interpretation, not direct confirmation of what an early inscription depicted.

Historical dictionary citations include “finish; be completed”; a Tang poem uses 未了 for “not ended” or “not finished.” The earliest attestation and the connection between this meaning and the graphic interpretations remain unresolved.

sense.period: common by Tang; later stages summarized for Tang–Song
sense.text: Accounts describe the completed-action marker developing from the verb “finish,” with resultative uses between the verb and aspect marking.
Current uses include affair, matter, and business.
Bronze-inscription examples attest 事 for duty or office. The cited examples do not establish this use as earlier than the other attested uses.

sense.period: Bronze inscriptions and early texts; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: Bronze inscriptions attest an event sense, and cited early-text examples use 事 for matters or events. The evidence does not establish priority among these uses.

sense.period: Bronze inscriptions and early texts; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: Bronze examples attest a command or service use; cited early-text examples also attest serving and undertaking. They do not establish a linear development from duty or event.

sense.gloss: divided or disloyal (as in 二心)
sense.text: A cited Zuo zhuan usage has 二心 meaning ‘divided’ or ‘disloyal heart’; its semantic path and earliest date are unresolved.
A cited Tang poem uses 二 with the ordinal meaning ‘second’; this example does not establish when the sense first arose or how it developed from the numeral.
‘Twice’ is recorded as a current gloss, but its chronology and development are not established here.
二 is used for the numeral two. The cited summaries and quotations do not verify a dated earliest inscription or manuscript witness.

sense.period: Oracle-bone corpus; specific inscription dates unresolved
sense.text: Oracle-bone examples use 五 to count dogs and sheep in a sacrificial offering and in the date expression 五月. These establish numeral use in the cited corpus, not the first origin of the graph or word.
五 is the character for the number five; its modern Mandarin reading is wǔ.
The Shuowen account associates 五 with the Five Phases. This documents a historical explanation and use of the term, not a proven origin for the graph.

sense.gloss: graph used to write words represented by 伍, 吾, or 語 in reported manuscript contexts
sense.period: Qin slips and Mawangdui manuscript; exact dates and earliest examples unresolved
sense.text: Later manuscript evidence reports 五 in contexts read as 伍, 吾, and 語. These may reflect reuse of the graph to write other words; the sound basis and detailed borrowing history are unresolved.

sense.gloss: fifth; five in dates or sequence
sense.period: Oracle-bone corpus; specific inscription dates unresolved
sense.text: The cited 五月 example attests 五 in a month expression. The evidence does not establish priority between this and the cardinal use.

sense.period: dating unresolved; attested in the transmitted 招魂 text
sense.text: The transmitted 招魂 text places 些 at line ends, and its commentary glosses it as a particle. This attests the transmitted spelling and commentary, not the poem’s original manuscript spelling or composition date.
Current glosses include “rather” and “somewhat.” No historical development connecting these senses to another sense is established.
Current glosses include “little” and “few.” When this sense arose and how it relates to the particle or reported dictionary glosses are unresolved.

sense.period: sixth century, as reported for a 玉篇 entry
sense.text: A scholarly article reports that a sixth-century dictionary entry glossed 些 as “this” and “particle.” The report does not establish which sense came first or identify an original meaning.

sense.period: attested in a Tang poem by cited work; earliest use unresolved
sense.text: 京 means “capital city”; an example occurs in a cited Tang poem. This does not establish when the sense began or how it relates to the high-structure or mound interpretations.
京 is interpreted as a tall building or platform; the Shuowen account instead describes a high man-made mound. The evidence does not resolve which interpretation best captures its earliest meaning.
“Large” is recorded as a sense, but its chronology and connection to the other meanings are not established.
Bronze-inscription examples are glossed ‘common people’ and ‘people’. Their exact dates and priority relative to one another are not given.

sense.period: Oracle-bone inscriptions; individual specimen dates unresolved
sense.text: The graph depicts a person. Cited oracle-bone examples use it in contexts glossed ‘ten people’ and ‘I, the king’; the individual specimens are not dated here.

sense.gloss: the speaker or ruler referring to himself
sense.period: Oracle-bone inscriptions; individual specimen date unresolved
sense.text: One cited oracle-bone example is interpreted as a ruler’s self-reference. Its relationship to the sense ‘person’ is not established.
Dictionary entries record 什 with the value 十, but their examples do not establish when this use began.

sense.gloss: spelling used in interrogative words, as in 什麼
sense.period: Tang-Song onward in the cited account; transition dating unresolved
sense.text: A separate account says 甚 was reused to write interrogative words and 什 then served as another spelling. This proposed graph reuse depends on a sound resemblance; it is not a semantic development from “group of ten,” and the sound relation to the ten-unit word is not established.
什 is also recorded with miscellaneous and things-related senses. The examples do not show how these relate to the ten-unit sense.

sense.period: dating unresolved; early literary use cited
sense.text: A cited early literary passage uses 什 for a group organized in tens. The date of a surviving manuscript witness is not established.
One proposal connects the graph with groaning or chanting, but this is not established as the word originally written by 今.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone inscription; individual date unresolved
sense.text: The phrase 今夕其雨 attests the temporal meaning “now” or “today.” This is the earliest supported meaning, not proof of a hypothetical original meaning.
今 is also used for “present,” “current,” and “modern era,” but the examples available here do not date how these uses developed from the earlier temporal sense.

sense.period: early textual examples reported; individual dates unresolved
sense.text: Reported early textual examples use 介 for being situated between two states. This is the earliest meaning supported here, not proof of the graph’s original meaning.

sense.gloss: individual or item, in uses associated with 個
sense.period: Warring States use reported; exact transcription and date unverified
sense.text: A reported Warring States slip uses 介 where 個 is intended. The proposed explanation is that the sign 介 was reused to write the separate word 個 because the words may have sounded alike. The cited Mandarin readings jiè and gè, and Baxter–Sagart forms *kˤr[e]p-s and *kˤa[r]-s, do not establish that historical sound match.

sense.gloss: between; mediate or concern oneself with
sense.text: Modern dictionary data include “between,” “mediate,” and “concern oneself with.” They do not establish when these senses arose or how they developed.

sense.period: oracle-bone use reported; individual inscription dates and readings unverified
sense.text: Oracle-bone uses are reported with the meanings “junior” or “secondary,” but their readings remain disputed and the underlying inscriptions have not been verified.

sense.gloss: shell or scale; armor; assist; forerunner or intermediary
sense.text: These glosses occur in the supplied material, but no dated sequence links them to one another or to “between.”

sense.period: dating unresolved; reported in oracle-bone and bronze materials
sense.text: The paired figures are interpreted as one person following another. This is the earliest meaning supported by the graph analysis, though the earliest dated occurrence is not fixed.

sense.period: bronze uses reported; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: Bronze examples are reported for 从 meaning ‘follow’ and 從 meaning ‘accompany’. Their sequence relative to the other reported senses is not established.

sense.period: oracle-bone uses reported; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: Early uses are reported with ‘from’ senses, including examples glossed ‘from the west’ and ‘from the east’. Their timing relative to the ‘follow’ use is unclear.
These are supplied modern glosses. Their individual histories and development from earlier uses are not established.

sense.period: Han dictionary account; earlier chronology unresolved
sense.text: The Han dictionary glosses 从 as ‘heed’ and analyzes it as two 人. A later editorial account relates this sense to ‘follow/accompany’ by extension, but the transition is not securely dated.

sense.gloss: indulge (written with 從 as a loan for 縱)
sense.period: bronze use reported; exact date unresolved
sense.text: A bronze use of 從 is reported as a spelling for 縱 ‘indulge’. In this account, the graph was reused to write another word; ‘indulge’ is not shown to have developed from ‘follow’. The source word’s sound comparison and the borrowing’s date are not established.
Transmitted 詩經 and 孟子 passages use 他 for “other/else”; they do not date the first use of the graph.
他 is also used as a third-person pronoun. Its earliest attestation and the date this use arose are unresolved.

sense.gloss: plural marker used with personal pronouns and person-denoting nouns
sense.text: In modern Chinese, 们 follows personal pronouns or words for people to indicate plurality.

sense.gloss: plural marker used with personal pronouns and person-denoting nouns
sense.period: Song dynasty, reported; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: The plural-marker use is reported in Song-period sources; proposed Tang-period evidence is disputed. The exact dated occurrences have not been established in the cited account.
The common current meaning includes resting or taking a break.
Reported inscriptional uses include favor or reward. Their relationship to rest or shelter remains uncertain.
A competing graph analysis cites a bronze use glossed “good” or “commendable” and connects it with recognition of merit. This use does not settle the graph’s origin or the sense’s chronology.
Rest is supported by received-text examples and the transmitted 說文 definition; the cited examples do not establish that it was the earliest attested sense.
One proposed connection links resting in shade with shelter or protection, but the cited uses do not establish that development or its chronology.
休 is also used to mean “stop” or “cease.” The cited examples do not show when this use arose relative to “rest.”

sense.period: historical; chronology relative to meeting unresolved
sense.text: Historical dictionary citations attest 會 as a noun meaning “lid” or “cover.” This sense fits some proposed readings of the graph’s vessel-like forms, but does not prove that interpretation or establish which sense came first.

sense.period: Warring States and later securely reported; earlier oracle-bone use tentative
sense.text: Reported bronze and Warring States examples use 會 for meeting at a place, joining ideas, and meeting in alliance. A fragmentary oracle-bone example may have the sense “meet,” but that reading is tentative.
会 is also a noun meaning a meeting or gathering. In Japanese, え is recorded for a gathering, especially a religious assembly, in an early ninth-century text.
会 also means an organization or association. The development of this sense from “meeting” or “gathering” is not dated here.
Dictionaries record lodging and staying among the uses of 住, but the evidence does not date this sense or establish its precise relation to “stop/remain” and “reside.”

sense.period: Late Han–Three Kingdoms texts reported; attested more widely later
sense.text: A usage study reports residence uses in late Han–Three Kingdoms texts and says they became dominant by the Eastern Jin. These are literary-text attestations, not securely dated manuscript evidence.

sense.period: Western Han and later uses reported; secure earliest attestation unresolved
sense.text: A usage account reports a transmitted Western Han example for “stay/remain” and discusses early medical-text examples, while noting that transmission and dating do not settle the earliest attestation. Reference works also describe “stop/remain” as a basic or early sense.
体 is recorded as a variant spelling of 體, which is used for the whole human or animal body and its limbs. The earliest use of this sense is not dated.
A separate bèn reading of 体 is recorded with the meaning “coarse; inferior,” equivalent to 笨. Its relationship to the tǐ spelling of 體 is unresolved.
Current glosses include making, working, composing or writing, and acting or performing. The evidence here does not establish the full chronology from older uses.

sense.period: Shuowen lexicographic record; date of use unresolved
sense.text: The Shuowen glosses 作 as 起, ‘rise’ or ‘begin.’ A separate discussion reads 作 as ‘arise/recover’ in a disputed oracle-bone phrase; that reading does not settle the identity of all early forms.

Early examples associated with 乍/作 writing include clearing land, building a settlement, casting, and broader making or action. These support a work/action range but do not establish the earliest dated use of 作 itself.

sense.period: attested in cited historical examples; present-day status unresolved
sense.text: A character dictionary records bare 你 in plural examples such as 你兩個 (‘you two’) and 你眾人 (‘you all’). These cited examples are from historical works; their frequency or productivity in present-day speech is not established here. This is distinct from the ordinary modern plural construction 你们, formed from singular pronoun 你 with 们.
你 is a current singular second-person pronoun meaning ‘you.’ The exact earliest surviving occurrence and the date of quoted passages’ wording remain unresolved.
Modern dictionaries list “come” and “coming” among the character’s meanings.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone material; exact date unresolved
sense.text: Oracle-bone examples use 來 for movement, including coming and going. Their chronology relative to the wheat use is unresolved.

sense.period: Oracle-bone and bronze usage; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: 來歲 means “next year” in oracle-bone and bronze usage. A connection to movement has been proposed, but no dated sequence establishes that development.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone material; exact date unresolved
sense.text: Oracle-bone material also attests a return use. Its chronology and semantic relation to the other uses are unresolved.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone material; exact date unresolved
sense.text: Oracle-bone examples use 來 for tribute or bringing offerings. Their chronology and semantic relation to the other uses are unresolved.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone material; exact date unresolved
sense.text: A rare oracle-bone use of 來 is read as wheat. This attests the use but does not show that it was the graph’s earliest lexical use.
Visit and greet are recorded uses. Their relationship to the watching and waiting senses is not established.
候 is also used for waiting and expecting, including in an example of someone waiting at a door. Its relationship to the watching sense is not established.
候 is used for watching or reconnoitring in the received passage 武王使人候殷. The date of the surviving physical witness is unresolved.
候 also means climate, season, and weather. The earliest attestations and relationship of these meanings to the action senses are unresolved.

sense.period: classical text; composition and attestation dating unresolved
sense.text: A cited classical example uses 假 for borrowing a passage. A scholarly account interprets Qin-period writing as distinguishing 假 for borrowing from 叚 for lending; this does not show that borrowing was the earlier meaning of 假.
假 is glossed as “not true,” and a cited classical example uses it to mean “false” or “not so.” The example’s date and its priority among the character’s attested senses are unresolved.

sense.period: historical and current; first attestation unresolved
sense.text: Textual examples record temporary or acting uses, and modern definitions include “vacation.” Their dates and relationship to “borrow” or “false” are unresolved.
Dictionary accounts list uses glossed ‘become’ or ‘serve as’, but do not date them or connect them historically to the other senses.
Current dictionary glosses include ‘do’ and ‘act’. The evidence does not establish which use came first.
Current glosses also include ‘make’ and ‘work’. Their listing does not establish a development to or from ‘do’.
A dictionary lists a literary use glossed ‘pretend’; its date and relation to the other senses are unresolved.

sense.period: modern simplified writing; exact adoption date unresolved
sense.text: Simplified 儿 writes the child graph 兒 in reduced form. This graphic change does not show that its child meaning developed from the separate person-shaped use of 儿.

sense.gloss: address to a child or younger person; parental address or self-reference
sense.period: Han-attributed text and later examples; exact chronology unresolved
sense.text: 呼兒 in a Han-attributed poem addresses a child or household dependent. Later examples include parental address and self-reference, but the poem’s disputed attribution and later transmission do not establish a contemporary Han witness or a sequence of semantic development.

A historical dictionary glosses 兒 as a young child, and the graph is recorded in early inscriptional corpora. The semantic context of the earliest graph examples and the first occurrence of the spoken word are not securely dated.
Son is a recorded sense, but its emergence relative to the child sense is not dated.
Suffix use is recorded, but its emergence and any semantic path from the child sense are not established.
A young-person sense appears in later cited material, but its first date and connection to the child sense are unresolved.

sense.period: oracle-bone and Western Zhou bronze contexts; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: An oracle-bone example 元卜 is interpreted as ‘first divination,’ and a Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 元 in 元年, ‘first year.’ These are early attested uses; they do not establish priority over every other sense.

sense.period: bronze inscriptional use; exact date unresolved
sense.text: The bronze phrase 元德 is interpreted as ‘great virtue.’ Its relation to ‘head’ or ‘first/beginning’ is unresolved.
Early forms are interpreted as depicting a human head. The cited oracle-bone and bronze examples use 元 for other meanings; ‘head’ occurs in transmitted 左傳 and 孟子 passages.
“Former” and “previous” are recorded meanings of 先. Their chronology and connection to the Shang uses are unresolved.

Shang oracle-bone examples use 先 for going ahead or leading in hunting and military contexts. It is attested in the same broad period as precedence, but the evidence does not establish which use came first.

sense.gloss: precedence; first or earlier in time or order
sense.text: Shang oracle-bone examples use 先 for temporal or ordered precedence, including in references to ancestors, wine and years. They are dated broadly by corpus context, not by individual artifact dates.
Oracle-bone examples use 八 as a cardinal numeral, including in expressions for eight animals and in a month expression. These attest early numeral use, not a hypothetical original meaning.
Oracle-bone month usage and later examples show 八 in month and year expressions with ordinal value. The evidence does not date a distinct development from the cardinal sense.
Cited oracle-bone records use 六 as a cardinal numeral in “six sheep” and in a month name meaning “sixth month.” They attest both uses but do not establish which came first.
六 means the number six.

sense.period: early Zhou songs, broadly dated; poem described as late Western Zhou
sense.text: In 關關, the graph appears in an expression for a bird-call. The evidence does not show that this is the same word as 關 ‘barrier’ or that one meaning developed from the other.

sense.period: attested example attributed to Eastern Jin
sense.text: Dictionary evidence records 關 meaning ‘shut’ or ‘close.’ It does not establish every step connecting this use to the door-fastener sense.

sense.period: later historical use; exact development date unresolved
sense.text: 關 is used for connection, relation, and involvement. Dictionary examples attest these uses without establishing a complete sequence linking them to older physical or pass senses.
A historical dictionary glosses 關 as a wooden bar laid crosswise to secure a doorway. This meaning is supported, though no securely dated first occurrence is given.

sense.period: bronze-period use reported; precise date unresolved
sense.text: The graph is reported in an inscription for a frontier pass, and dictionaries also cite later uses of this sense. The inscription’s precise date is not given in the cited account.
Dictionary sources record a mechanism sense, but do not establish a dated development from the door-fastener or closing senses.
The character has recorded senses of flourishing and prosperity, also reflected in common modern glosses. The evidence does not establish a specific path from rising or mobilizing to this sense.

sense.period: bronze-inscription and manuscript contexts; precise dates unresolved here
sense.text: Bronze inscriptions and manuscript contexts are reported using the character for raising or mobilizing troops. Their chronological relationship to the rising sense is not established.

sense.period: dating unresolved; reported in oracle-bone and later textual contexts
sense.text: Early contexts are reported with a sense of rising or getting up; one oracle-bone use is described in connection with illness improving. This does not prove that rising was the character’s original meaning, and the chronology is incomplete.
Bronze inscriptions are reported using 再 to mean “again” or “a second time.” The evidence does not establish whether this use preceded “two.”
再 is currently used to mean “again” or “twice.” The evidence does not establish a complete sequence connecting these current meanings to the early uses.
A bronze inscription is reported using 再 to mean “two.” Its priority relative to the bronze use “again” or “a second time” is unresolved.

sense.period: Warring States manuscript; absolute date unresolved
sense.text: A Guodian slip may use 再 to write 在. If so, the graph was reused for a different word on the proposed basis of a sound similarity, rather than because 再’s meaning developed into 在. The reading comparison needed to demonstrate that match is not supplied.
写 is used with the meaning “write.”

A traditional dictionary glosses 寫 as 置物; later commentary explains this as transferring contents, including pouring from one vessel to another. The cited uses are undated, so this is not identified as the earliest attested meaning.
Later commentary records 寫 for writing and drawing and proposes a connection to transferring or pouring contents. The chronology and semantic link are not established by dated attestations here.
The Zhuangzi passage uses 冷 in 冷風, “cold wind.” It attests the cold sense in that passage, but does not securely date the text or establish the first occurrence.
“Cold” and “cool” remain current meanings.

sense.gloss: quiet or desolate; neglected; ironic or disdainful; severe; sudden; surname
sense.text: These additional senses are listed with literary examples, but their dates and development from “cold” are not established.
A cleanliness sense is cited in Mozi. This attestation does not show that cleanliness was the graph’s original meaning.
Historical examples use the word for making something clean and washing it clean. Their chronology and relation to the other recorded senses are unresolved.
Modern character records give these meanings for 净.

sense.gloss: pure or undiluted; entirely gone; other recorded senses
sense.text: Dictionary examples include “pure” or “undiluted” and “exhausted” or “entirely gone.” The evidence does not establish a continuous development among these senses.
A supplied definition gives ‘in accord.’ The evidence does not date this use or establish how it developed from meanings such as level or standard.
准 is used for permission and approval, including in 准許. A dictionary dates this document-related use broadly to the Tang–Five Dynasties period, without establishing its first occurrence.

sense.gloss: how many; how much; a few
sense.text: In simplified Chinese, 几 also writes quantity words represented by 幾 in traditional Chinese. This spells a distinct word; it is not a demonstrated development from the furniture meaning.
The earliest meaning supported here is a furniture term, traditionally glossed as a small stool or table. The precise object and the graph’s earliest date remain unresolved.

sense.period: dating unresolved; attested in oracle-bone examples
sense.text: The oracle-bone example 王出 uses 出 for going out. Its exact date is unresolved.
Bronze inscriptions use 出 in contexts involving paying or issuing cloth and issuing or transmitting commands. Their order and semantic links are unresolved.
出 is also glossed ‘produce’; its historical development from another sense is unresolved.

sense.period: dating unresolved; attested in oracle-bone examples
sense.text: The oracle-bone example 勿出兵 uses 出 in a context of sending out troops. Its chronology relative to the motion use is unresolved.
出 is also glossed ‘stand’; its historical development and chronology are unresolved.

sense.gloss: allocate fields and settlements; allotted duty or status
sense.period: early textual and inscriptional uses; individual dates unresolved
sense.text: An inscription records allocation of fields and settlements, and Warring States manuscript uses are reported for role or status. A separate historical reading is listed for “allotted duty,” but its relationship to the reading for “divide” is not demonstrated.
The Shang Yang measure inscription attests 分 in a fractional measurement expression by 344 BCE. This dates that use, but does not show when it arose or whether it preceded the separation sense.
分 is used for a unit of time. Japanese examples attest that use in 1798–1802, but do not date the corresponding Chinese sense.
分 has current senses including “part,” “share,” and “segment.” The available glosses do not establish when these senses arose or a specific path from “separate.”

The Shuowen glosses 分 as “separate” or “distinguish.” This is an attested historical dictionary gloss, not proof that it was the earliest ordinary use; a reported oracle-bone place-name use does not settle that question.
Historical phonological and textual discussions record an intransitive sense, “be separated.” Its chronology and relation to the transitive sense “separate” remain disputed.

The proposed bone-and-knife interpretation suggests cutting apart, and later textual examples include physically separating or opening. The disputed oracle-bone occurrence does not securely attest this as the earliest written sense.

sense.period: Warring States and Han examples reported; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: Reported manuscript examples use 別 for classifying and expressing distinctions. They attest those uses but do not establish a complete development from cutting apart.
“Other” is a recorded current sense. When and through what change it developed from separating or distinguishing remain unresolved.

sense.period: Yuan period proposed; prominence reported from Ming–Qing onward
sense.text: The prohibition sense is current. Proposed histories connect it with 不要, 不必, or an extension from “other/separate”; its source and proposed dating remain provisional.
The received 詩經·韓奕 phrase 靡國不到 is cited with the sense “reach/arrive.” It supports an early literary use, but does not date the poem’s composition or transmission.
A dictionary records this sense with a textual citation, but its date and semantic relation to “arrive/reach” are unresolved.
“Go to” is recorded as a sense, but its date and semantic relation to “arrive/reach” are unresolved.
Modern records include “arrive/reach” among the character’s meanings.
A dictionary records this sense with a citation, but its chronology and semantic pathway are unresolved.
This sense is recorded with textual examples, but its chronology and development from “arrive/reach” are unresolved.
前 also means earlier in time or preceding. Its historical development in relation to the spatial sense is not established.
前 is used for a position in front and for forward direction. The evidence does not securely date the historical emergence of these uses.
The transmitted gloss 作也 means ‘act’ or ‘do.’ Cited textual and manuscript examples also show action or movement, but are not dated precisely enough here to order them.
A cited Mawangdui manuscript example uses 動 for changing position or state. Its development in relation to the action sense is unresolved.
Modern records include ‘move’ and ‘happen,’ as well as the nouns ‘movement’ and ‘action.’ The evidence does not establish a single chronological path among these meanings.
包 is used for a package or bundle as well as for wrapping and packing. The history of this object sense is undated.

sense.period: Current use; classical example is transmitted, but its written-witness date is unresolved
sense.text: 包 is currently used for wrapping, packing, enclosing, or containing. The transmitted Shijing line 白茅包之 is an historical example of wrapping, but its written-witness date is unresolved.

sense.period: Qin–Han written use reported; spoken-sense chronology unresolved
sense.text: 北 was used to write “back”; 背 later became the usual graph. This change in written practice does not establish when the spoken word arose or prove a semantic path from “turn against.”

sense.period: Qin–Han written examples reported; exact chronology unresolved
sense.text: Written examples of 北 for “back side” are reported. Their attestation does not establish when the spoken sense developed or its precise relation to other proposed senses.

sense.period: Shang period onward (reported); exact first occurrence unresolved
sense.text: 北 is reported as a loan graph for the direction “north” from Shang-period writing, and this became its principal continuing function. A specific earliest inscription context is not supplied.

sense.gloss: turn against; turn one’s back on
sense.text: This proposed sense is associated with the back-to-back image and the Han dictionary gloss, but secure excavated examples writing it have not been identified.
医 is used for medicine, healing, and physicians. The evidence does not date these uses of 医 separately from its relationship to 醫.

sense.gloss: container for bows, crossbows, and arrows
sense.text: The received Shuowen entry gives this gloss and analyzes 医 as 匸 enclosing 矢. It is a historical dictionary account, not an independently confirmed earliest meaning.
“Complete” and “perfect” are listed as extended meanings, but their chronology and any specific development from the numeral sense are not established.

sense.period: Shang-period oracle-bone use reported; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: Reported oracle-bone examples use 十 for the numeral ten, including in date and quantity expressions. They show an early numeral use but do not establish the first occurrence or the graph’s original motivation.
The supplied definitions include “tenth,” and 十月 is cited among early examples. That example alone does not show when an ordinal use arose or whether it is the earliest such use.
These senses occur in dictionary tradition and in analyses relating 午 to 啎 and other forms. The evidence does not establish that they gave rise to the branch use or connect them to the midday sense.
A cited bronze inscription uses 午 in 庚午 as the seventh earthly branch. The vessel is undated in the account, so this attestation does not establish the earliest occurrence.

sense.period: historical examples from Jin and Tang texts; exact first occurrence unresolved
sense.text: 午 is used for the midday period, including 11 a.m.–1 p.m. Later textual examples attest this sense but do not establish when it began or its precise relation to the branch sense.

Paleographic accounts identify the early graph as a pestle or wooden stick for pounding rice, and as the original graph for the implement word 杵. This identifies the pictured object; its ancient name and pronunciation are not known.

sense.gloss: the sun at its daily highest point
sense.text: This is a recorded sense of 午; its chronology and relation to other senses are unresolved.

sense.gloss: half; one of two equal parts
sense.text: “Half” is the established current meaning and appears in historical examples, including the cited bronze numeral use 大半升. One proposal treats “half” as an extension of “split/open”; another treats “half” as the original meaning. The evidence does not settle the disagreement.
