This use is documented with later examples; its emergence and relation to other meanings are unresolved.

sense.gloss: middle point or part of a span or place
sense.text: Historical examples document use for a middle part or point in time or space. A separate proposal derives the “in the middle” sense from dividing an object; this does not establish a dated extension or show that the lexical sense “half” intervened.
Historical examples document the “partial; incomplete” use. A separate proposal derives “incomplete” from dividing an object; its date and relation to the lexical sense “half” are unresolved.

sense.gloss: 磐, in a reported manuscript spelling
sense.text: 半 is reported in a Mawangdui Zhouyi manuscript where the received text has 磐桓. The proposed borrowing mechanism is that 半 stood for 磐 because their spoken forms sounded alike or similarly. Reconstructions suggest similar labial onsets and -an material, but come from different systems and do not establish the manuscript token’s sound or the reason for the spelling. This is graph reuse, not a meaning of 半.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone inscriptions; exact earliest specimen date unresolved
sense.text: 南 is attested for the direction “south” in Shang oracle-bone inscriptions. This early documented use does not prove that “south” was the graph’s original meaning.
南 is also used for a southern part; its date relative to the directional sense is unresolved.
南 is also used to mean southward; its date relative to the directional sense is unresolved.

sense.period: Transmitted Zhouyi and Shijing passages, characterized as Western Zhou; exact manuscript dating unresolved
sense.text: The cited departure uses occur in transmitted Zhouyi and Shijing passages characterized as Western Zhou usage; the quoted lines are not independently dated manuscript attestations. Departure is not securely established in the oracle-bone examples discussed.
In current use, 去 commonly means “go away,” “leave,” or “depart.”

sense.gloss: put away; eliminate; get rid of
sense.text: Historical reading records associate 去 with “get rid of” as well as “depart” and distinguish readings for these uses, but do not establish when they arose or how they are related.
Assistance or cooperation is listed as a use, with no supplied chronology or supported link to other senses.
A dictionary records a verb meaning to make friends or become acquainted; the supplied example does not date this use.

sense.period: Western Zhou bronze contexts reported; individual witness dates unresolved
sense.text: Bronze inscriptions are reported using 友 for friend or friendly relations and for associates. These uses do not establish a semantic development from the reported name or sacrificial use.
友 is used for a friend or companion.
“Love” is listed as a use, with no supplied chronology or supported link to other senses.

sense.period: oracle-bone context; absolute dating of the cited witness unresolved
sense.text: The graph is reported in use as a personal name. This attestation does not establish its original meaning.

sense.period: oracle-bone context; absolute dating of the cited witness unresolved
sense.text: The graph is also reported in a sacrificial context, read as 侑, “assist in sacrifice.” Its priority relative to the personal-name use is unresolved.

sense.gloss: person counted as part of a household
sense.period: documented in cited texts; first occurrence unresolved
sense.text: Cited historical texts document uses of 口 for household population. They do not establish its first occurrence or a semantic path from the mouth sense.
The graph depicts the human mouth, described as used for speaking and eating. The mouth sense remains current.

sense.gloss: opening of an object; open end, entrance, or gate
sense.period: documented in a Han-period cited text; first occurrence unresolved; current use attested
sense.text: Current definitions include an open end, entrance, or gate, and a cited Han-period text uses 口 for an object's opening. The evidence does not date the sense's beginning or show how it developed from the mouth sense.

sense.gloss: make an animal cry or sound
sense.text: Literary examples use 叫 for animal cries. They do not establish when or how this use relates to shouting or calling.
Current glosses include calling, hailing, greeting, and summoning. Their chronology in relation to older uses is unresolved.
A cited Shijing phrase uses 叫 in an expression of shouting or calling; the date of this attestation is unresolved.

sense.gloss: call or summon someone; name; causative or passive uses
sense.text: Examples attest summoning, naming, causative, and passive uses, but do not establish their chronological order or development from earlier senses.
Classical citations record uses meaning help or assist. They are not dated here well enough to establish priority or development from the directional sense.
Dictionary records include uses for blessing or protection, without establishing their chronology or a semantic link to direction or assistance.
High status or rank is recorded among historical uses, with no chronology or development established here.

sense.gloss: right; right hand or right-hand side
sense.text: The character is recorded for the right hand and right side, but the evidence does not identify either as its earliest sense.
The modern political sense is recorded, but no date or account of its development is supplied.
A banquet-related use is recorded and glossed as 侑. The evidence does not establish whether this is an extension of meaning or a distinct word written with 右.
West is recorded as a sense of 右; the evidence does not date it or explain its relation to “right.”
These modern glosses are recorded for 号/號. Their listing does not establish a chronological sequence among them.
The separate historical dictionary entry for 号 gives this sense. It is an attested lexicographic meaning, not proof of the graph’s hypothetical original meaning.

sense.gloss: command; order; assigned number or sequence
sense.text: Dictionaries record commanding and numbered or ordered uses for 號. They do not give a complete dated path from crying or calling to these senses.

sense.period: early textual examples cited in dictionaries; surviving witnesses undated here
sense.text: Dictionary-cited examples for 號 include crying and calling. They document meanings associated with 號, not a dated transition from the separate graph 号.
Examples and dictionary commentary associate 號 with names and titles. An extension from calling to what is called is plausible, though its chronology is incomplete.
吃 commonly means “eat”; “drink” is also recorded. How this use relates to the older speech sense remains unresolved.
吃 is recorded for eating or drinking and is associated with 喫. Its earliest spelling and relationship to the speech sense remain unsettled.

sense.period: dating unresolved for 吃; Yuan-text examples are reported for 喫
sense.text: “Suffer” and “endure” are recorded glosses for 吃; Yuan-text examples are reported specifically for 喫. Their chronology and semantic path to 吃 are not established.

sense.period: attested in the received Shiji text; physical witness dating unresolved
sense.text: 吃 is defined as difficult or halting speech, and a transmitted Shiji passage describes Han Fei as 口吃. These attest the speech sense, not an eating sense.

sense.period: Oracle-bone inscriptions; exact dates not supplied
sense.text: An oracle-bone example is interpreted as “along with.” The evidence does not establish whether this use predates the meeting sense.
Later examples attest uses glossed as following or assenting. Their connection to the other senses is unresolved.

sense.period: Oracle-bone inscriptions; exact dates not supplied
sense.text: Cited oracle-bone examples are interpreted as meeting or joining. This is the earliest use documented here, not necessarily the original meaning.

sense.period: Bronze inscriptions and later examples; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: Bronze examples include a use interpreted as making things alike; later examples attest “same” or “alike.” Their relationship to the earlier uses is unresolved.
Current definitions include “same,” “similar,” and “together with”; these glosses do not establish a chronology among the senses.
Later examples attest a transitive use meaning to make things the same or unify them. Its development from another sense is not established.
One bronze use is glossed as 銘, “inscription.” The evidence does not resolve whether this is a meaning development or 名 used to write a related word.

sense.period: Western Zhou bronze and Warring States manuscripts
sense.text: A Western Zhou inscription uses 名 as a verb meaning “name” or “designate”; Warring States manuscripts also attest name or designation uses. These examples do not establish when the sense first arose.
名 also means to name or designate; the evidence does not establish its chronology relative to the noun sense.
名 is used for a person’s name, though the cited material does not date the first occurrence of this sense.
The earliest cited use is a token in a place name; its precise interpretation is unresolved.
Dictionary sources list reputation and status-related meanings, but do not establish when they arose or how they developed.

sense.period: Classical spelling use reported; precise chronology unresolved; current in simplified Chinese
sense.text: In simplified Chinese, 后 writes the separate word “after/behind,” represented by 後 in traditional Chinese. This is a spelling loan, not a documented change in 后’s meaning. An ancient sound match is reported but not established here.

sense.period: Late Spring and Autumn bronze inscriptions; primary examples not independently verified
sense.text: A late Spring and Autumn bronze use is reported with the meaning “ruler.” Any earlier oracle use of the same graph and word is not securely dated here.

sense.period: Received textual usage; transition date unresolved
sense.text: Received-text examples document 后 for a ruler’s principal wife. They do not establish when, or whether, this sense developed from “ruler.”
The traditional-character entry also records a pause or topic-marking use. Its chronological or semantic relation to the question-particle use is unresolved.
吗 is used at the end of a statement to form a question. The traditional 嗎 entry also records this use and cites a literary example whose date is unresolved.
A separate lexical use records 嗎 as a colloquial form of 罵. Its 口＋馬 analysis belongs to this “scold” use, not the question particle.
吧 is used in the Chinese loanword for English bar as a separate use of the whole character. The borrowing date and the relevant English pronunciation are not established.
A Qing-novel example uses 吧 to imitate the sound of a cup being set down. The example is not precisely dated, and no historical link to the sentence-final particle is established.

sense.period: attested in historical sources by the eighteenth century; exact emergence and development disputed
sense.text: 吧 serves as a sentence-final particle for agreement, suggestions or commands, conjecture or questions, and pauses or conditions. One account proposes that the conjectural use developed by contraction of sentence-final 不是, while the imperative use derives from 罢; the two were later conflated in writing rather than semantically developing from one another. Other accounts propose derivation from 罷/罢, including a proposal involving 夫 and 不乎. These histories remain unsettled, and reported eighteenth-century spellings do not date the formation of 吧.

sense.period: Song–Yuan vernacular use attested; beginning date unresolved
sense.text: By the Song–Yuan period, 听 was used to write the separate word 聽, meaning “hear” or “listen.” The reason for this reuse is unresolved; the proposed 𠯸/厅 account has not been verified from primary manuscript evidence.

sense.period: Han-period example cited; exact first attestation unresolved
sense.text: A cited Han-period literary example uses 听 for a smiling appearance. It attests this use by that period but does not establish when the word or graph first arose.

sense.period: Western Zhou examples reported; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: Accusatory use is reported among Western Zhou bronze examples; its relationship to “report” is not established.

sense.period: Western Zhou examples reported; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: Western Zhou bronze examples are reported with uses for reporting and admonishing. Their development from earlier senses is not established.
Current uses include telling, announcing, informing, and accusing. The supplied glosses do not establish their chronology or semantic connections.

A Southwestern Mandarin use meaning “try” or “check out” is attested in a 1909 example. One proposed account is that 告 borrowed the graph for 校 to write a similar-sounding word, rather than developing this meaning from “tell.” The borrowing direction and sound pathway remain uncertain.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone and later examples reported; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: A reported oracle-bone example concerns a deer report, and later examples use 告 for reporting or telling. These attestations do not establish one original meaning or a sequence of semantic change.
呢 is used as an interrogative or emphatic sentence-final particle.

sense.gloss: sentence-final particle, including interrogative and emphatic uses
sense.period: Southern Song and Yuan examples reported; later examples also cited
sense.text: A Southern Song example is reported for a topic-question use; Yuan examples include interrogative-strengthening and other sentence-final uses. Later examples show question-final and affirmative sentence-final uses. These records do not establish the first appearance of each function.

sense.period: Medieval lexicographic record; exact date unresolved
sense.text: A medieval dictionary glosses 呢喃 as soft, low, much speech. This records an older use but does not establish the character's original meaning or earliest attested use.
A separate noun sense for woollen cloth is recorded. Its first attestation and any relationship to the particle graph remain undetermined.
和 is also used as the conjunction “and; with.” Its chronology and connection to the other senses are unresolved.
Classical examples use 和 for coordinating or adjusting, including in culinary and musical contexts. They do not establish an ordered development from these uses to social harmony.

sense.gloss: harmony; a valued social or ritual quality
sense.period: traditionally pre-Qin textual setting; precise dating unresolved
sense.text: In the Analects passage “禮之用，和為貴,” 和 describes a valued social or ritual quality commonly rendered “harmony.” The passage does not establish the first use of this sense.
和 also means peaceful, calm, or mild. The examples do not establish how these senses developed from response or harmony.
A historical dictionary glosses 和 as “responding.” This records a dictionary meaning but does not show that responding was the word’s earliest use.
Historical accounts report use for “father” and broader male address, but do not establish a complete chronology or a secure development from “elder brother.”

sense.period: written attestations reported from Tang; exact earliest use unresolved
sense.text: 哥 is used for “elder brother,” with written kinship use reported from Tang-era material. Its proposed borrowing origin is disputed, and the sense is not shown to derive from the song use.

sense.gloss: song; to sing (use of 哥 for 謌/歌)
sense.period: Han-era use reported; precise earliest attestation unresolved
sense.text: Shuowen records that 哥 was used for 謌, and historical accounts report song-related use. The evidence does not establish whether this was sound-based reuse, what older word the graph represented, or whether that word sounded like the song word.
The received Shuowen entry glosses 哥 as “sound”; a later note says this sense was no longer in use at the annotator’s time. This gloss does not establish the character’s earliest meaning.

sense.period: Qing citation; exact first use unresolved
sense.text: A Qing play citation records 哪 used rhetorically to mean “how”; it does not establish the first occurrence.
Later lexicographic testimony describes 哪 as a spelling for a particle, originally written 那. The first use of 哪 for this word is not dated.

sense.gloss: personal name element in 咄哪
sense.text: 哪 is recorded in the personal name 咄哪. This compound citation does not establish an independent single-character meaning.

sense.gloss: sound made by performers in nuo exorcism rites
sense.text: 哪哪 is recorded as the sound made by performers in nuo exorcism rites; the cited record does not date this use.
哪 is used for “which” and “where”; the beginning of this written usage is not dated.
Calling or shouting is reported in cited examples, but its chronology and relation to the other meanings are unresolved.
A traditional gloss gives “lead or guide”; a cited example describes the yu leading while the other instruments follow. The date of the surviving written form remains unresolved.
Singing and chanting are reported uses. Their dates relative to “lead” are not established.
唱 is also used as a noun meaning “song” or “tune.” When this meaning developed is unresolved.

sense.period: bronze inscriptions reported; precise dating unresolved
sense.text: Bronze inscriptions are reported to use 商 for a musical note; its chronology relative to the name uses is unresolved.

sense.period: dating unresolved; oracle-bone corpus examples reported
sense.text: An oracle-bone corpus example is reported to use 商 as a personal name; the specimen’s date is unresolved.

sense.period: dating unresolved; oracle-bone corpus examples reported
sense.text: Oracle-bone examples use 商 as a place name and in 大邑商 for a polity. The evidence does not establish which use came first.

sense.period: classical sources cited; witness dates unresolved
sense.text: Classical citations record trade and trader uses, but the dates of their textual witnesses and their relation to the polity name are unresolved.
商 is commonly used for commerce, business, and trade.
Oracle-bone examples are reported with the meaning joy or rejoicing. Name uses are also reported in this corpus, so the evidence does not establish which attested use came first.
Modern dictionary summaries include these glosses, but the available historical account does not establish their date or a semantic path from joy.

sense.period: Bronze inscriptions; examples undated in supplied evidence
sense.text: Bronze uses include a music term. Its relation to the joy sense is not established.
Personal and polity-name uses are reported among oracle-bone examples; their priority relative to joy or rejoicing is unresolved.

sense.period: Bronze inscriptions; example undated in supplied evidence
sense.text: A bronze inscription is reported with a ritual use read 喜(饎). This distinct reading does not by itself show development from joy.
喝 is also used for calling aloud or scolding. The evidence does not derive this use from drinking or hoarseness.
喝 is used for drinking; the earliest attestation of this use is unresolved.

sense.gloss: be hoarse; have a hoarse voice
sense.period: Han-era texts are cited; exact attestation dates unresolved here
sense.text: Hoarseness is documented as a distinct use, with dictionaries citing Han-era texts.
One account proposes “thirsty” as an original sense associated with 㵣, but the cited material does not independently confirm it.
The ordinary present-day meaning is ‘four.’ A middle Western Zhou bronze inscription is reported in a four-horse context. The evidence does not establish the earliest use or how 四 originated.
回 can refer to one time or occurrence and serve as a counter. The evidence does not date this use or show how it developed.
“Return” is a common current meaning. Its historical relationship to the turning sense is unresolved.
Turning or revolving is proposed as the graph’s early meaning, but no securely dated contextual occurrence establishes it as the earliest attested sense.

sense.period: Western Zhou inscriptions reported; exact earliest attestation unresolved
sense.text: Western Zhou bronze inscriptions are reported to use 國 for “country/state.” This supports the sense in that period, though the disputed He zun reading of 或 leaves the word’s earliest attestation unsettled.
The character is currently used for “nation” and “country.” The evidence does not date how this range developed from the older country/state sense.
Modern definitions include diagrams, charts, maps, and pictures.
A passage in the received Zhouli uses 圖 for maps in the context of administering lands; the wording’s date is unresolved.
Dictionary evidence records picture or image as a noun sense of 圖, without establishing when it arose or how it relates chronologically to the map sense.
Dictionary evidence records planning and drawing among verb senses of 圖. Their chronology and relation to the map sense are unresolved.

sense.gloss: be at, in, or on; consist in; rest
sense.text: Current definitions include being at, in, or on a place, as well as consist in and rest. These glosses do not establish the chronology or derivation of historical senses.

sense.period: Early bronze usage reported; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: Reported bronze uses include existence and location; the Han dictionary glosses 在 as 存, “exist” or “be present.” The evidence does not establish when this sense arose relative to locative use.

sense.period: Bronze usage reported; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: A reported bronze example uses 才 read as 在 in a past-time expression. The evidence does not establish a semantic path from the locative or existence uses to this use.

sense.gloss: be at; be in; be located
sense.period: Shang oracle-bone and bronze usage reported; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: A reported oracle-bone date phrase uses 才, read as 在, in the sense “in”; reported bronze examples also show a locative use. The evidence supports an early locative or temporal use, though the phrase’s exact date and reading remain unresolved.

The earliest inspectable account describes 地 as the heavy, turbid yin counterpart to heaven and as the place where things are arrayed. This attested account does not establish the word’s hypothetical original meaning.
Cited texts show noun uses for ground, cultivated land, territory, place, and region. They do not establish when each sense arose or a complete sequence of change.

sense.gloss: grammatical particle after an adjective, commonly read de
sense.period: Song citation; exact first use unresolved
sense.text: A Song text is cited for 地 following an adjective. This attests the use in that textual tradition, but does not show how it arose from the noun or another form.

sense.period: Yuan citation; exact first use unresolved
sense.text: A Yuan text is cited for a postverbal use glossed as ‘stand there/remain’; its precise relation to other uses of 地 is unclear.
Classifier use is recorded, but its date and development from another sense are unresolved.
A figurative use meaning a domain is recorded, but its date and development from a physical-place sense are unresolved.

sense.gloss: ground for processing or drying grain
sense.text: A further gloss describes ground for grain processing, and cited texts use 場 for a grain-drying or threshing floor. The timing of this use relative to the other early glosses is unresolved.
Textual examples record 場 for a general place and other venues. Modern glosses include open space, field, and market, but their order and semantic links are unresolved.
An early dictionary account describes 場 as a way or ground for sacrificing to spirits; another explains it as level ground used for ancient sacrifice. The first surviving occurrence is not dated.
An early dictionary account also gives 田不耕, an uncultivated field, as an alternative gloss. Its timing relative to the ritual-ground sense is unresolved.

sense.period: Bronze inscription context; absolute earliest attestation unresolved
sense.text: A cited bronze inscription uses historical 坏 for a mound or high place. This attests the use but does not establish that it was the word’s original meaning.

sense.gloss: spelling of a place name read as 褱德
sense.text: A cited Qin bronze writes a place name with 壞, read as 褱德. This use does not show a semantic development from “ruin.”

sense.gloss: written form for 壞: bad, spoiled, ruined
sense.period: Modern standardized usage; standard table published 1986
sense.text: The standard table maps 坏 to 壞 as a simplified form. This spelling use is distinct from the older mound and unbaked-material uses. Sound-based reuse is proposed: the older word written 坏 may have sounded like the word written 壞. The older word’s pronunciation and the reuse’s exact history remain unresolved.

sense.period: Historical lexicographic and classical references; precise chronology unresolved
sense.text: A historical dictionary glosses 坏 as unbaked tile; other references record unbaked-material uses for 坯 or related 坏 forms. Their order and connection to the mound use remain unresolved.
A causal use is reported in poetic texts; its development from another sense or by another process is not established.
Cited examples record uses meaning stay or keep watch, without establishing when they arose or whether they developed from sitting.

sense.gloss: be implicated or convicted; legal confrontation
sense.text: Classical examples are cited for these legal uses, but their chronology and relationship to the sitting sense are unresolved.

sense.gloss: ride or travel by a vehicle
sense.text: 坐 is also used for riding or traveling by vehicle, but the cited examples do not establish how this use developed.
Cited texts show 坐 used for a seat or place; they do not date this use relative to the sitting sense.

sense.gloss: sit; remain in a seated or kneeling posture
sense.text: Classical textual examples are reported for sitting or kneeling, but the surviving witnesses are not dated here, and this use is not thereby established as the character’s original meaning.
Uses of 塊 meaning “alone” or “settled” are documented, but their chronology and connection to the clod sense are unresolved.
凷 is defined by reference to a clod, and a cited Zuozhuan passage uses 塊 for a clod given to a traveler. The passage’s composition date and manuscript witness are unresolved.
塊 is documented as a measure word for block-like things; its date and development from the clod sense are unresolved.

sense.gloss: money measure equivalent to yuan; dollar
sense.text: 塊 is documented as a money measure in later literary usage. Its development from “piece” or “lump” is unresolved.
块 is used for a piece, lump, chunk, or mass. The available examples do not establish a complete dated sequence for this sense.
Dictionary citations include uses glossed ‘all’ or ‘entirely’; the supplied evidence does not establish this use as current or date its emergence.

sense.period: received lexicographic tradition; date of spoken sense unresolved
sense.text: The received dictionary tradition records ‘cautious’ or ‘careful’; the supplied evidence does not establish this use as current.
The current dictionary records 备 for 设备 (‘equipment’). Cited examples also use 備 for equipment or facilities; the evidence does not establish a particular path from earlier meanings.
The current dictionary records 备 for 预备/准备 (‘prepare’). Earlier reported uses of 備 include ‘for use’; the available evidence does not establish that these uses form a dated sequence.
The current dictionary records 备 for 具备/完备 (‘have; complete’). Reported bronze uses of 備 are glossed ‘equipped’ or ‘complete’; their relation and chronology are not established here.
A bronze example is reported with this use; its development from “outside” is not established.
“Foreign” is a current gloss; its date and development are unresolved.
A bronze example is reported with this kinship use; its semantic connection to “outside” is not established.

sense.period: Western Zhou bronze inscriptions; precise dating unresolved
sense.text: Bronze examples use 外 for “outside,” including in contrast with 內. This is identified as the basic sense; priority among all early uses is not established.

sense.period: Warring States text; exact date unresolved
sense.text: 多言後 is cited as an adverbial or frequentative use in a Warring States bamboo text. This example does not establish a complete path from the “many” sense.
Oracle-bone and bronze inscription contexts are reported with 多 meaning “many.” The cited oracle-bone inscription has no exact date established here.
“More than” and “over” are recorded meanings, but their dates and development from “many” are not established here.

sense.period: Bronze inscription (reported use; earliest status unresolved)
sense.text: 大 is attested meaning “big,” opposite 小, in a reported bronze-inscription phrase; this example does not establish the earliest attestation.
大 is currently used with senses including “big,” “great,” “vast,” “large” and “high.”

sense.gloss: divine or sovereign uses, including “Heaven” in compounds
sense.period: Bronze inscriptions and later Warring States texts; individual token dates unresolved
sense.text: Reported examples include 天帝, 天命, 天子, and 天下. Their contexts attest divine, sovereign, or “under heaven” uses, but compound meanings alone do not establish separate single-character senses or a dated sequence of change.

sense.gloss: “great” or use in a name expression
sense.period: Shang-Zhou material; individual token dates unresolved
sense.text: 天邑商 is cited alongside 大邑商, and an older gloss reads 天 as “great” in one phrase. This supports early interchange or close relation in usage, not an original meaning of “great.”

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone corpus; individual token dates unresolved
sense.text: A head-related use is reported in an oracle-bone context. Paleographic analyses connect it with the graph’s marked head, but its relationship to the word for sky or heaven remains unsettled.

Sky or heaven is an established meaning of 天, and one account proposes it as the word’s original meaning. Early inscription evidence and its interpretation are contested, so this records an attested sense category rather than a proven original meaning or priority over head-related use.

太 is used as a degree word meaning ‘very’ or ‘much’. Interpretations of excavated texts report degree uses written with 大, and sometimes 泰, before 太 became a distinct graph; this does not establish one linear semantic development.
The sense ‘too’ or ‘excessive’ is reported both for 太 and in interpretations of early degree-word uses written 大. The evidence does not securely order it relative to ‘very’ or ‘great’.
太 is associated with ‘great’ and ‘big’. Earlier texts often wrote 大 for words later written 太, so the meaning of any particular 大 occurrence depends on its context.
Dictionary and definition records list these meanings, but do not establish when they arose or how they developed from “woman.”

A separate lexical reading is recorded with the meaning “give as a wife.” The supplied historical readings distinguish it from 女 “female,” but do not date this use or establish how the meanings are related.
Early inscription accounts report 女 used for 母, including cited oracle-bone examples. This documents an early use or overlap, but does not establish a semantic development from “woman.”

sense.gloss: reported uses for 毋, 每/悔, 汝, 如, and place names
sense.text: Inscription accounts report these uses of the graph. Some may be spellings borrowed for other words, but the available accounts do not provide enough context or sound evidence to explain each use.

Early inscription accounts report female-related uses, and the Han-period Shuowen glosses 女 as “woman.” The cited inscription examples are not precisely dated here, so this is the earliest documented sense in these accounts, not proof of the graph’s original meaning or priority among early uses.
“Breast” is a recorded sense, with a cited literary example; the material here does not date its earliest use.
Modern dictionary records include the sense “milk”; the supplied readings include Mandarin nǎi.
奶 is recorded for “milk,” including in 牛奶. The cited literary example is undated here, so it does not show when this use began.
Nursing is a recorded use with a cited literary example. Its date and chronology relative to the breast and milk senses are unresolved.

sense.period: Early twentieth century; reported use by 1918
sense.text: A dated modern account records a proposal to use 她 alongside 他 in 1918; later use and standardization establish the feminine pronoun sense. This is the earliest use documented here, not necessarily the character’s first attestation.

sense.gloss: old mother or female-kin term, in the reported relation to 姐
sense.text: Later dictionary reports describe 她 as an old form of 姐 and associate 姐 with a word for mother or female kin. The exact date, distribution, and earliest attestation of 她 in this use remain unresolved.
A bronze inscription is reported with 好 in 好朋友, meaning ‘friendly’. Its chronological relation to the ‘good/beautiful’ use is not established.

In modern Chinese, 好 means ‘good’. The consulted dictionaries also list current adverbial uses meaning ‘very’ or ‘very much’; they do not establish a general standalone sense ‘well’. The evidence does not show the dated steps from the selected inscriptional uses to current usage.
A bronze inscription is reported with 好 meaning ‘good/beautiful’. The vessel is not absolutely dated in the account, so this example does not establish the earliest attested ordinary use.

A Warring States bamboo text is reported with 好 meaning ‘like’. A proposed Old Chinese suffixal relationship between the verbal reading and the ‘good’ reading does not establish which meaning came first.

sense.gloss: form of address for female elders, older women, and servants in northern usage
sense.text: Dictionaries record these forms of address but do not date them or establish that they developed from the mother sense.
A dictionary excerpt lists an obsolete “mare” sense as a single-attestation use, without a dated citation linking it to the mother sense.
媽 is cited with the meaning “mother” in 龍龕手鑑; the exact wording and date have not been verified from the primary page.

sense.period: oracle-bone and bronze inscription readings; phrase interpretation disputed
sense.text: Some early forms and a bronze phrase are interpreted as 妹 used to write 昧, “before daybreak” or “dawn twilight.” If this is borrowing, the graph was reused for a different word because the words sounded alike or similar; the old word’s pronunciation and its relation to the kinship word are not established.

sense.gloss: modest first-person reference by a woman
sense.period: later literary use; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: Historical examples attest 妹 as a woman’s modest first-person reference. The evidence does not establish when or how this usage developed.
A broader use meaning “young woman” is attested, but its chronology and relation to the kinship sense are not established.

sense.gloss: younger female relative of the same generation
sense.text: Historical dictionary examples attest 妹 for a younger female relative of the same generation. The evidence does not date this sense or derive it from “younger sister.”

sense.period: attested in bronze inscriptions; exact date of the cited example unresolved
sense.text: A bronze inscription is read with the kinship sense “younger sister,” also given in the historical gloss 女弟. This does not establish the spoken word’s earliest meaning.
The current definition includes elder sister and young woman. Their historical relationship to the regional mother use remains unresolved.

sense.period: Attested in a Song-dynasty example; earlier chronology unresolved
sense.text: A Song-dynasty example uses 大姐 in a sibling-age context. An adjacent dictionary entry glosses 姊 as elder sister, but does not establish when 姐 acquired this sense.

sense.period: Han-dictionary account; exact word and graph attestation date unresolved
sense.text: The Han-dictionary entry records 姐 as a Shu regional term for mother and 社 as the corresponding Huainan term. This attests a reported regional meaning, not the character’s first graphic appearance.
A Yuan-dynasty example uses 姐姐 for an older woman. Its historical relationship to the regional mother use is unresolved.
A Yuan-dynasty song uses 姐儿 for a young woman. The evidence does not establish a semantic path from the regional mother term.
子 is reported as used for a child in Shang contexts. This fits the infant interpretation, though the evidence does not establish a precise date or a separate transition from “infant.”
A Shang use for a same-surname clan leader is reported. How it developed from or relates to “infant” is unresolved.

子 is attested as the first earthly branch, but the identity of the graph used earlier and the reassignment sequence are disputed. One account places 𢀈 before 子; another proposal identifies 甾. Its relationship to the infant sense is unresolved.

sense.period: Shang; exact earliest token date unresolved
sense.text: A paleographic account identifies “infant” as the graph’s original sense and reports a Shang pregnancy-related use in 有子. This is the earliest supported sense here; the exact reading and calendar date of that example remain unresolved.
“Offspring” is a supplied dictionary gloss; its chronology and connection to the earliest infant sense are not documented here.
In 君子, 子 is reported as a suffix referring to a person. A semantic path from the child sense to this use is not established.
“Seed” and “fruit” are supplied glosses; their history and development from “infant” or “child” are unresolved.
A later use meaning “young” or “immature” is reported, as in 子薑. Its date and development from the child sense are unresolved.

sense.period: Han lexicographic account; earlier dating unresolved
sense.text: A Han lexicographic account glosses 字 with birth or nurture. This records that account, but does not establish the original meaning or when this use arose.
“Word” is also recorded as a meaning of 字, but its chronology and relationship to the birth or nurture sense are unresolved.
字 commonly means a written character. The available evidence does not date the earliest use of this sense.
The Qin-slip phrase 成學 is reported with the meaning “complete one’s studies”; it illustrates a contextual use of traditional 學.
A bronze-inscription example uses traditional 學 in a passage about archery instruction. This evidence does not establish a full semantic sequence from learning to teaching.
學 and its standardized simplified counterpart 学 are currently used for learning and study.

sense.gloss: feel; perceive, written with the graph 學
sense.text: A source reports traditional 學 used in Han slips as a borrowed spelling for 覺, “feel” or “perceive.” The reason for choosing this spelling is not established. This is a reported spelling loan, not a meaning that developed from “learning.”

sense.period: current; school use attested for 學 in bronze inscriptions
sense.text: Traditional 學 is reported in bronze inscriptions in a school context. In present-day compounds such as 小學、中學 and 大學, 學—and its standardized simplified counterpart 学—is a morpheme naming an educational institution or place of learning; these examples do not establish 学 as a standalone word meaning “school.” The evidence does not establish when the school use began.

sense.period: attested in cited classical and later texts; exact earliest attestation unresolved
sense.text: Cited uses include 孩提之童 in the Mengzi and 生孩六月 in a Jin-era memorial. Guangyun glosses 孩 as a newborn or very young child, but these sources do not date the first use of 孩 for this noun.
The received Shuowen account assigns this meaning to 咳 and records 孩 as its old spelling. The earliest use of 孩 for this word is not dated.
孩蟲 is cited for young or immature creatures. Its chronological or semantic relationship to the infant noun and child-laugh use is unresolved.

sense.gloss: arrive (written with 客 in a reported bronze example)
sense.period: Bronze example reported; exact date unresolved
sense.text: A reported bronze example uses 客 for the separate word 各, “arrive.” This is a borrowed spelling, not a meaning shown to develop from “guest”; the material does not provide a sound comparison confirming why the graph was reused.

sense.period: Western Zhou bronze uses reported; inscription context not supplied
sense.text: A character-specific historical record reports bronze uses of 客 for “guest.” The cited material does not reproduce the inscription, so it does not settle whether this was the earliest sense.

sense.period: Received 說文 lexicographic account; exact attestation date unresolved
sense.text: The received 說文 glosses 客 as 寄, “lodge” or “reside.” This historical sense does not demonstrate the graph’s original motivation.
Reference material records visitor, traveller, and commercial customer senses, but does not establish a complete sequence connecting them.

sense.period: Oracle-bone uses are reported; dates of individual examples are unresolved
sense.text: Uses for human dwelling are reported in oracle-bone contexts. A pig-enclosure origin has been proposed, but is not established as the earliest meaning.
家 commonly means house or home, and also family. How these senses relate chronologically to the reported early uses is unresolved.

sense.gloss: ancestral temple, family, royal house or court, or counted household
sense.period: Oracle-bone and bronze uses are reported; sequence unresolved
sense.text: Reported uses include ancestral temple and family, royal house or court, and households counted as 家. Their order and relationships are unclear.

sense.gloss: meaning in early bronze formulas disputed
sense.period: Early Western Zhou; 大盂鼎 dated 998 BCE by the cited chronology
sense.text: An inscription uses 對 in a formula following royal rewards. Interpretations include response, acknowledgment or repayment, praise, and ritual action; its precise force remains disputed.
Modern usage includes “correct” and “right.” When or how these meanings developed is not established.

Oracle-bone uses have been proposed as a sacrificial or place name, but no specific specimen, context, or meaning is established. The proposed land-working interpretation is not a secure earliest sense.
Modern usage includes “facing” and “opposed.” When or how these meanings developed is not established.

sense.period: Early Western Zhou bronze formulas attest 對; later literary citations are transmitted texts
sense.text: Early Western Zhou bronze inscriptions use 對 in response or acknowledgment formulas, though their precise force is disputed. Later transmitted texts use the word to mean “reply” or “answer”; they do not directly date the surviving graph to the narrative settings they describe.
小食 is reported as an expression for an afternoon time. Its relation to the sense “small” is unresolved.
小采 is reported as an expression for dusk. Its chronology and relation to the sense “small” are unresolved.

sense.period: Oracle-bone and bronze uses reported; absolute dates unresolved; also current
sense.text: 小 is used for ‘small’ in present-day Chinese. The character appears with this meaning in oracle-bone and bronze examples, including 小雨; the examples’ absolute dates are unresolved and they do not establish the graph’s hypothetical original referent.

sense.period: Oracle-bone usage reported; bronze usage also reported, with precise dates unresolved
sense.text: Early forms transcribed as 少 or 小 are reported for “few”; bronze examples include use in contrast with 多. The evidence does not establish this as the earliest sense or its priority relative to “small.”
Current meanings include “few” and “less.”
Historical dictionary entries record “insufficient” or “lacking”; development from another sense is not established.
Historical dictionary entries record “short time”; its emergence and relation to the other meanings are unresolved.

sense.period: Oracle-bone usage reported; bronze examples occur sometimes, with precise dates unresolved
sense.text: Early forms transcribed as 少 or 小 are also reported for “small,” and some bronze uses are reported. Their overlap does not establish which meaning came first.

sense.period: Bronze inscription usage reported; precise date unresolved
sense.text: Bronze examples and historical dictionary entries record “young” or “youthful”; how this sense developed is not established.
‘Approach’ and ‘near’ are current glosses; their dates and development from earlier uses are not documented here.

sense.gloss: graph used to write 造 in a travel context
sense.text: One analysis proposes that 就 was used in a Warring States travel context to write the different word 造. This would be a reuse of the graph because the words were thought to sound alike or similarly, not a change in the meaning of 就; the cited evidence does not establish the source word’s pronunciation or the proposed sound match.
The phrase 申就乃命 is reported as a verbal use with a sense near ‘complete.’ Its connection to the early place-name use or the proposed ritual-at-height interpretation is not established.
‘Just’ and ‘simply’ are current glosses; their dates and development from earlier uses are not documented here.

sense.period: oracle-bone inscriptions; exact dating and identification unresolved
sense.text: The earliest reported examples are mostly place names. Their identification with the later verbal character is unsettled, so this use does not establish the word’s original meaning.

山 means a mountain or hill, a landscape sense found in early inscriptional and literary contexts and still in ordinary use. It refers to a high, pointed landform. The earliest attestation and deeper chronology remain unresolved.
“Age” is among the supplied glosses; its emergence and development from earlier uses are not established.
A historical dictionary defines 歲 as Jupiter and describes its circuit through the lunar mansions over twelve months. This recorded sense does not establish the earliest spoken meaning.

sense.period: Oracle-bone period, as reported in supplied paleographic accounts; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: Paleographic accounts report oracle-bone use for “year,” but the evidence does not establish it as the earliest attested sense; ritual interpretations are also reported for this period.

sense.gloss: achievement, written with 工 for 功
sense.period: bronze inscriptions and Warring States bamboo slip; artifact dates unresolved here
sense.text: In cited contexts, 工 is read as 功, ‘achievement’. This is graphic interchange or borrowing in those contexts, not proof that 工’s work sense developed into achievement.

sense.period: early examples and received Zhouli tradition; dating unresolved
sense.text: Reported examples use 工 for craft workers, including 百工. The received Zhouli tradition also uses it for skilled makers, but these attestations do not date the sense’s beginning or show how it relates to the tool interpretation.

sense.gloss: official title, status, or occupation term
sense.period: oracle-bone and bronze examples; dating unresolved
sense.text: Reported examples use 工 for status or occupation and in official titles. Their relationship to craft and work uses is unresolved.
Reported oracle-bone examples use 工 as a state or place name. This use is not connected to the proposed tool meaning.
The graph is interpreted as picturing a tool, but the precise object is disputed. The cited account does not date the relevant artifacts, so this is not a securely dated earliest word meaning.

sense.gloss: tribute or offering, written with 工 for 貢
sense.text: In reported oracle-bone contexts, 工 writes 貢. This proposed whole-graph loan means the sign was reused for another word because the words were said to sound alike or similarly, not because the tool meaning changed into ‘tribute’. The early sound match is not independently established by the cited account.
工 currently means work or labor. The evidence does not give a dated sequence showing how these senses developed from the proposed tool or craft-worker senses.

sense.period: dating unresolved; reported in bronze inscriptions
sense.text: Bronze inscriptions are reported to use 左 for “assist,” as an early written form of 佐. The evidence does not establish when this use began relative to the directional sense.

sense.period: dating unresolved; reported in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions
sense.text: 左 is reported for the direction “left” in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions. The available reports do not date an individual example closely enough to establish the absolute first use.
Modern dictionaries record difference and distinction among the senses of 差. When these became associated with mismatch is unresolved.

sense.period: historical and current; earliest dating unresolved
sense.text: A distinct reading tradition records selecting, dispatching, and a dispatched person or task. The evidence does not establish a semantic path from mismatch or difference to these uses.

sense.period: historical and current; earliest dating unresolved
sense.text: Error and discrepancy are recorded senses. A pre-imperial Xunzi passage uses 差 in a divergence- or error-related context, though the precise nuance is uncertain.

sense.period: Han lexicographic account; graph attested in Western Zhou bronzes
sense.text: The received Shuowen gloss and analysis record 差 as mismatch. This is a historical lexicographic interpretation, not necessarily the earliest spoken meaning.

sense.period: historical and current through the spelling 瘥; dating unresolved
sense.text: A separate reading tradition records recovery, also later written 瘥. No semantic transition linking it to the other senses is established.
A ritual passage uses 差 for rinsing, glossed as rice-washing. This is a distinct reading and lexical use, with no established connection to difference or the proposed wheat-rubbing origin.

sense.period: early textual use; precise composition date unresolved
sense.text: In the transmitted Odes passage ‘既差我馬,’ 差 is read as selecting the horses. This early attested use does not prove that selection was the word’s original meaning.

sense.period: early compound use; precise dating unresolved
sense.text: The compound 參差 is attested in an Odes line and glossed as uneven or irregular. This attests the compound meaning, but does not date the standalone sense or show that it developed from mismatch.
Reported among bronze-inscription uses of 師. People bearing 師 titles had varied duties, not all directly military.
A current gloss; its chronology and connection to earlier senses are unresolved.
Dictionary glosses include teacher and master, but the first use and its development from another sense are unresolved.
Reported among bronze-inscription uses of 師. Its date and priority relative to the official-title use are unresolved.

Help and assist are current meanings of 帮. The current dictionary evidence cited here supports this sense; the separate current uses for a group or organization, an object-side part, and a classifier are not included in this sense record.

sense.gloss: constant, regular, frequent; customary or ordinary
sense.period: historical and current; first-use dates unresolved
sense.text: 常 is used with these meanings. The available accounts do not give a fully dated chronology among them or establish a single semantic path from the garment sense.
A specialist reference reports a bronze use for custom or law, and dictionary entries document senses involving rule and ethical order. They do not establish a first-use date.

The traditional gloss identifies a lower skirt or garment, and specialist references report garment uses in bronze and Warring States materials. The available accounts do not establish which use is earliest or date them.

sense.period: Early inscriptional and textual use reported; exact first date unresolved.
sense.text: A defensive or protective use is reported in an oracle-bone example and a later bronze inscription. Its relationship to the shield sense is not established.

sense.gloss: dry (written 干 in simplified Chinese; traditionally 乾)
sense.period: Current simplified spelling; the word sense’s onset is undated here.
sense.text: 干 is the current simplified spelling of 乾 for “dry.” The dry reading is recorded as gān, and its first-use date is unresolved. The Book of Odes passage is cited for the dry word written as 乾; 干 is its current simplified spelling. No semantic development from “shield” is established here.

sense.period: Recorded in a Han-period dictionary; date of the word sense unresolved.
sense.text: The Han-period Shuowen account gives “offend” or “violate” as a sense and analyzes the graph as 反入 plus 一. It does not explain how or when this sense arose.

sense.period: Securely attested by the mid-Western Zhou; proposed earlier Shang attribution is disputed.
sense.text: The graph is interpreted as a shield pictograph. A bronze inscription meaning “shield” is reported; the earliest secure attestation identified here is mid-Western Zhou.

sense.gloss: trunk; main stem (written 干 in simplified Chinese; traditionally 幹)
sense.period: Current simplified spelling; historical examples of 幹 do not date this spelling correspondence.
sense.text: In simplified Chinese, 干 writes the word traditionally written 幹. Cited early examples of 幹 mean a tree stem or the body's frame; they do not show that this word developed from the shield sense.
年 is used for a person's age. The cited definitions do not establish when or how this use developed.
In an oracle-bone divination, 年 is interpreted as the harvest the speaker hopes to receive. Another cited Shang example is also read as harvest.
New Year is documented as a sense, but its emergence and development from the harvest meaning are not dated here.

sense.period: Shang and Zhou usage as described in the source; absolute dates unresolved
sense.text: One account distinguishes 年 as harvest, 歲 as harvest season, and 祀 as a regnal-year count in a Shang inscription. It reports that Zhou usage later replaced 祀 with 年 for regnal dating.

sense.period: Shang use is reported; later Western Zhou examples are cited
sense.text: A grain cycle may have come to stand for a year. A possible Shang time-count use is reported with a caution about its reading, and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions use 年 in wishes for long duration; these examples do not date every step in the development.
Bed and couch are documented meanings of 牀/床, but the earliest use of the bed word is not securely dated here.
Classifier use is documented, but its development from another sense is not established.

sense.gloss: place for sitting or resting the body
sense.text: 牀 is glossed as a place for sitting or resting the body. The earliest securely dated witness for this sense is unresolved.

sense.gloss: rack, support, base, or bed-like surface
sense.text: These meanings are recorded, but their dates and any path linking them to the resting-place sense are unresolved.

sense.period: Jin-attributed gloss; exact composition and textual witness date unresolved
sense.text: The earliest historical gloss supplied here describes 店 as a place for keeping goods, distinguishing it from a place where goods are displayed for sale. This is the earliest attestation in the evidence, not proof of the character’s original meaning or first use.

sense.period: Tang poem attribution; exact composition date unresolved
sense.text: A Tang poem uses 店 for an inn or roadside lodging. The evidence does not show how this sense relates historically to the goods-place senses.

sense.period: Tang legal text attribution; exact composition date unresolved
sense.text: A Tang legal distinction uses 店 for a place of sale and 邸 for a place where goods are kept. This attests the selling-place sense but does not show when or how it developed from the storage-place sense.
店 is used today to mean a shop or store. The evidence does not establish when this use arose or how it relates chronologically to the historical storage-place and selling-place senses.
开 also means “begin,” “initiate,” or “start.” Its chronological relation to “open” is unresolved.
A paleographic argument proposes these as early uses of 開 and suggests 啟 was more commonly used for opening doors. This proposal does not establish a settled chronology.
开 means “open”; its earliest occurrence is not dated here.
The received Shuowen entry glosses 開 as “stretch/open.” This is a historical dictionary interpretation, not a dated first meaning.

sense.period: Attestations cited from a Tang poem and later literature; witness dates not checked
sense.text: In literary contexts, 弟 can serve as humble self-reference among peers. Its earliest use and path from a junior designation are unresolved; this sense does not show that the character originally meant “I.”

sense.gloss: junior; younger person or lower in rank
sense.text: 弟 is used for a younger person or one junior in status. When this use began, and whether it developed from the sibling sense, is unresolved.

sense.period: Western Zhou bronze inscription evidence; exact date unresolved
sense.text: A cited Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 弟 in 兄弟. This is the earliest securely sourced sibling use here, but it does not show that the earliest oracle-bone forms already had this meaning.
Classical citations are reported for female younger-sibling or junior uses. Their dates and relationship to the broader junior sense are unresolved.
Dictionary records include image-related uses such as figures or portraits. Their first dates and a complete development from “shadow” are not established.
影 is used with the sense “photograph”; the beginning of this use and its path from “shadow” are not dated here.
A museum catalog transcribes 影命不長 on a rubbing of the 爨寶子碑 dated 405; the date and reading are mediated by the catalog and later scholarship.

sense.period: Han usage proposed; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: Reference works record adjectival uses meaning fierce or perverse. One scholarly account places this adjective after earlier noncompliance usage, though the chronology is uncertain.

sense.period: current; emergence proposed for Yuan, exact dating unresolved
sense.text: 很 commonly means “very” or “quite.” Its development has been explained as grammaticalization from adjectival constructions or as connected with Yuan-period contact and a degree word written 哏; the route is unsettled.
The Shuowen also gives “difficult to walk.” One dictionary treats this as the original sense and connects obstruction with later defiance, but that proposed path is uncertain.
The Shuowen glosses 很 as “not obeying.” The transcription comes from an indexed search result, so exact textual details warrant caution.

sense.gloss: meet, use, understand, finish, suffice, reach, be able; auxiliary and particle functions
sense.period: Historical; individual developments and dates unresolved
sense.text: These meanings and grammatical uses are recorded, but their order and development from “obtain” are not established. One study argues that pre-Qin examples still mean “obtain” and that auxiliary use had not yet developed; other descriptions place a possibility use earlier, leaving the chronology disputed.
Modern usage includes “obtain,” “get,” “gain,” and “acquire.” These meanings alone do not show when or how the other historical uses developed.

sense.period: Dating unresolved; attested in Warring States manuscript examples
sense.text: The hand-taking-shell interpretation proposes “obtain” as the graph’s original sense, though its earliest secure attestation date is unresolved. Warring States manuscript examples use 得 to mean “obtain” or “get” by that period.

sense.gloss: not to recognize or know; forget
sense.period: Han lexicographic tradition; earliest attestation dating unresolved
sense.text: The Han lexicographic gloss is 不識也, “not to recognize or know.” It does not establish this as the graph’s earliest attested use.
Current reference glosses include “neglect,” “miss,” and “omit” alongside “forget”; their chronology and relationship to “forget” are not established here.
Current glosses include being busy or pressed for time. A dated path from the other recorded senses is not established.
A dictionary account records 心迫, meaning inner urgency. The date of this gloss and whether it represents 忙’s earliest use are unresolved.

sense.gloss: occupied with many affairs; having no free time
sense.period: historical and current; exact chronology unresolved
sense.text: 忙 is recorded with the sense of having many affairs and no leisure, including a cited use in 北魏《齊民要術》. Its chronological relation to inner urgency is unclear.

sense.gloss: to do something urgently or quickly
sense.text: A literary use is cited for doing something urgently. Its date and relation to the other recorded senses are unresolved.
A cited gloss associates 快 with uninhibited or self-indulgent behavior; its relation to other senses is unresolved.
The traditional gloss gives ‘joyful’ as an early sense, though a securely dated first attestation is not established.
A cited passage uses 快 to mean pleased or satisfied; it does not establish a securely dated first witness.
A cited exclamation uses 快 to express pleasure; its chronological position is unresolved.
‘Rapid’ is a common current sense. A commentary describes it as an extension from ‘joyful’, without giving the intervening steps or date.
A Tang literary example is cited for ‘sharp’, but its development from other senses is not established.
An adverbial use meaning ‘soon’ is cited, but its chronology and semantic development are unresolved.
A dictionary lists an illness-related sense, but no use or development connecting it to the core senses is cited here.
A cited use in 快戰 describes vigorous or decisive action; its relation in time to the other senses is unresolved.

sense.period: Song period and later examples cited; graph’s first attestation unresolved
sense.text: 怎 is used interrogatively to ask how or in what way; cited examples include a Song poem and later literary works. These examples do not date the graph’s first appearance.
Modern dictionary data also glosses 怎 as “what?”; the timing and relationship of this use to “how” are not established.

The received 說文 gloss gives 息 as breathing or panting. Separately, accounts of the proposed early graph interpret it as breath moving through the nostrils; that graphic interpretation does not establish when the sense was first attested.
息 is also recorded with the meaning “interest on money.” Its date and relation to the other senses are unresolved here.
息 is also recorded with the meaning “son.” Its date and relation to the other senses are unresolved here.
息 is also used for rest and for ceasing or ending. The available evidence does not date these uses or establish how they relate to the breathing sense.
您 is used as a respectful second-person form. Its emergence is not securely dated, and whether it developed from the earlier plural use remains unsettled.

sense.period: Jin and Yuan periods (dictionary-cited examples; earliest surviving use unresolved)
sense.text: Dictionary-cited Jin and Yuan examples use 您 as a second-person pronoun, including when addressing a group. These reports establish pronoun use, not the origin of the spoken word or priority among early uses.
Inventories record conjecturing or estimating, without establishing chronology or a semantic pathway.
A dictionary lists hope and want among 想’s uses, without establishing their chronology or a semantic link to thinking.
Lexicographic inventories list imagining among 想’s uses, but do not date it or establish how it developed from thinking or pondering.
Inventories record a sense of missing or longing, without dating it or establishing its development.
A dictionary lists a resemblance sense, without dating it or establishing its relation to the other meanings.
Thinking and considering are established current meanings of 想.
The Han dictionary glosses 想 as 冀思也, and a received 楚辭 passage uses it in a context associated with thinking or pondering. The passage does not establish a securely dated earliest use.
Textual uses are glossed as disrespect, arrogance, and treating lightly. Their dates and relationships to the other senses are unresolved.
慢 is glossed as laziness or neglect. The cited examples do not establish that this sense preceded other recorded senses.
Current glosses include “leisurely” and “sluggish,” alongside “slow.” The evidence does not establish a dated path linking these meanings with one another or with laziness and neglect.

sense.period: received Shijing use; manuscript dating unresolved
sense.text: In the received Shijing phrase 叔馬慢忌, 慢 describes horses moving slowly near the end of a hunt. This textual use does not date when the sense first arose.

sense.gloss: first-person self-reference (“I/me”; an early example is also interpreted as “we/us”)
sense.period: Oracle-bone and bronze inscription use; exact first-attestation date unresolved
sense.text: The graph is reported in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions for first-person reference. One oracle example is interpreted as plural self-reference, but this does not establish the number scope of all early uses.

sense.gloss: first-person self-reference (“I/me”; also used in first-person plural forms)
sense.text: Modern glosses include “I,” “me,” “we,” and “us.” The available evidence does not establish a full chronology connecting early number scope with these current uses.

sense.period: Dating unresolved; interpretation concerns early pictographic forms
sense.text: Early forms are interpreted as pictures of a toothed implement with a long handle. Whether it was a saw, axe-like weapon, ritual implement, or another object is disputed; this proposed pictured meaning does not establish a securely recovered spoken name.
“House” or “dwelling” is a recorded current sense. Its chronological relation to the side-room and room senses is unresolved.

sense.period: attested by the Three Kingdoms period in a cited literary example
sense.text: A cited Three Kingdoms-era poem uses 空房, “empty room.” This attests the room sense by that period, but does not establish how it developed from the side-room sense.
The traditional lexicographic gloss defines 房 as a room beside the main room. This is an attested historical interpretation, not proof that it was the character’s original meaning.
Shuowen glosses 手 as 拳 (“fist”). Its commentator explains hand and fist as mutually explanatory; this account does not establish that “fist” was the original meaning.

sense.period: Western Zhou bronze materials (earliest graph evidence identified; semantic context unverified)
sense.text: The graph is interpreted as depicting a hand, and later lexicographic evidence supports this meaning. The bronze occurrences themselves lack verified semantic contexts, so they do not establish a securely dated earliest use with this meaning.
手 is used for “hand.”
A historical dictionary records this use with a citation to 漢書, without establishing its date or a semantic pathway from the bodily sense.
A historical dictionary records 手 as a verb meaning “hold,” with a citation to 公羊傳. Its chronological relation to the hand noun is not established here.
A historical dictionary records this use with a citation to 宋書, but the evidence here does not establish when it arose or how it developed from the hand sense.

sense.period: Examples cited from the Liang period and later
sense.text: Later dated examples document uses for attacking and fighting. They establish these uses, but not a direct semantic path from one to the other or from a particular earlier sense.
A Song example records ‘take/catch fish.’ The evidence does not show when or how this sense developed from other uses.

sense.gloss: a dozen; a unit of twelve
sense.text: Mandarin dá is a separate word for a dozen, associated with English dozen and the reported spelling 打臣. The graph was reused to write this word, rather than the sense developing from ‘strike.’ The first Chinese attestation and chronology of the intermediate form are unresolved.
A Song-period example records a use meaning ‘make’ or ‘manufacture’; its development from the striking sense is not established.
A Tang example documents a prepositional use marking place, direction, or time; its semantic development is not demonstrated by that example.

sense.period: Han-period use is cited, but textual transmission and exact dating are debated
sense.text: A cited Han-period poem uses 打 for striking. Early dictionary citations and a gloss roughly meaning ‘to knock or strike out’ are also discussed, but transmission leaves the earliest attestation unsettled.
This is identified as a distinct later sense, without a dated first occurrence or established development from another sense.

sense.gloss: write 划 for propelling a boat with a pole
sense.period: Song-era rhyme-dictionary material cited; exact dated attestation unresolved
sense.text: 找 is recorded as an alternate spelling of 划 in this sense. This use does not show that the later seeking sense developed from boat-poling.
This is identified as a distinct later sense; its first occurrence and relation to the other senses are unresolved.
This sense is placed among uses current from the Ming period onward, though no first dated example is established here.
The common current meaning is “seek” or “look for.”

sense.period: Later literary examples; precise dates unresolved
sense.text: Later cited examples include forceful taking and apprehending; their order relative to ordinary taking is unresolved.

sense.period: Later literary examples; precise dates unresolved
sense.text: Later examples include grasping or control. A precise development from the taking sense is not established.

sense.period: Song-period use reported; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: A Song poem is cited for 拿 meaning “take.” This is the earliest use reported in the supplied evidence, not proof of the word’s origin or exact first occurrence.
Current dictionary glosses include taking, holding, and grasping.

sense.gloss: with, by, or related prepositional uses
sense.period: Later literary examples; precise dates unresolved
sense.text: 拿 also appears in instrumental and other prepositional uses, including meanings corresponding to “with” or “by.” A study describes development from verb to preposition and bound morpheme, but does not give the dates or full steps.

sense.period: Dating unresolved; reported in the transmitted Shuowen account and a classical-text tradition dated approximately to the fourth century BCE
sense.text: The transmitted Shuowen account glosses 放 as 逐, “expel” or “drive away.” The approximate date assigned to a classical example does not date a surviving manuscript.
A distinct reading meaning “imitate” is recorded. Its chronology and historical relationship to the release reading are unresolved.

sense.gloss: place or set down; expand; distribute; emit or shoot; play a recording
sense.period: Later and current uses; sequence unresolved
sense.text: These uses are recorded, but their chronology and direct semantic links are not established.

sense.period: Historical use reported in Mencius; underlying word’s first attestation unresolved
sense.text: Several Mencius uses have been interpreted as “reach,” with a proposed development from “banish” or “send away.” This connection remains disputed.

sense.period: Historical and current; precise chronology unresolved
sense.text: “Release,” “let go,” and “set free” are recorded meanings. Their chronology and a complete path from “expel” are not established.
A dictionary records “admonition”; its chronology and relation to teaching are unresolved.
“Class” is listed as a current meaning; its development and chronology are unresolved.

sense.period: Oracle-bone command/cause interpretation reported; manuscript command use also reported; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: One oracle-bone context is interpreted as command or cause, but that reading is not settled. Command is also reported in Warring States manuscript contexts. The relation of these uses to teaching is unresolved.
Doctrine and religious teaching are recorded meanings, but their development from the teaching sense is not dated here.
A historical dictionary records the sense “school,” but no dated example establishes when it arose.

sense.period: Current; teaching and instruction are reported in bronze and Warring States manuscript contexts; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: "Teach" is a current meaning. Teaching and instruction are reported in bronze and Warring States manuscript contexts. Oracle-bone occurrences are interpreted as “instruct,” alongside reported personal or place-name uses and readings such as transmit, cause, or command. These reports do not establish which early use came first or the graph’s original meaning.

sense.gloss: use in names and as an honorific modifier
sense.period: Late Shang; exact first instance unresolved
sense.text: The earliest uses reported here occur in personal and place names, especially as an honorific modifier in royal names. This use does not establish the graph’s original meaning; “great” is one proposed interpretation.
The Shuowen account interprets 文 through crossed markings or interwoven pattern. It describes the seal form rather than proving the referent of the Shang graph.

sense.gloss: honorific use in royal posthumous names and for ancestors
sense.text: 文 is reported in royal posthumous names and ancestor honorifics in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions.
文 is used with the meanings writing, literature, and culture. The evidence does not date their emergence or establish a progression among them.
A historical gloss and graph analysis connect 新 with taking or chopping wood for fuel, but a dated standalone use of 新 meaning ‘firewood’ is not established.
An oracle-bone example, 新鬯, is glossed ‘newly brewed wine’, attesting ‘new’ in the Shang corpus. This early use does not establish the character’s original meaning.
‘Recent’ and ‘modern’ are current glosses; the available account does not date their development from ‘new’.
These are supplied modern glosses; their listing does not establish when or how each sense developed.

sense.gloss: direction, including west and the four quarters
sense.text: Reported Shang inscription uses include a western-direction context and 四方. These attestations establish early directional use, but do not show whether it continues the graph’s original meaning or reflects borrowing for a similar-sounding word.
A period-labeled bronze example is glossed “just/now.” The evidence does not establish its development from another sense.
A Western Zhou bronze example is reported for land measurement; its relation to the square, direction, or polity senses is not established.
Later lexicographic records include method and law. The evidence does not date their emergence or securely connect them to earlier attested uses.
Reported Shang examples use 方 for polities and polity leaders. Their relationship to the directional use is not established.

A Western Zhou bronze example is reported with the square sense. One analysis proposes that the graph was reused to write “square” because that word sounded like the name of the depicted object. The name and sound match are unknown, so the borrowing account remains hypothetical.

sense.period: late Warring States to early Qin context
sense.text: A Shuihudi Qin slip is reported to use 方 for a writing board. No semantic link to the other senses is established.
The traditional dictionary glosses 旁 as 溥; later commentary interprets this as “broad” or “abundant.” This account does not establish the graph’s original meaning.

sense.gloss: reported place name, polity name, or personal name; directional use for 方
sense.period: oracle-bone, bronze, and Spring-and-Autumn inscription contexts
sense.text: Early occurrences are interpreted as place, polity, and personal names, and a directional use for 方 is reported. These readings do not show that the common sense “side” developed from them.
旁 is used with the meanings “side,” “beside,” and “near.” Early manuscript examples are reported, but the first occurrence of these meanings is not dated here.

sense.period: Shang-period oracle-bone inscriptions; current Chinese use
sense.text: An oracle-bone example attests 日 for a five-day period, and present-day Chinese dictionaries list day as a calendrical unit. The evidence does not establish when or how this use relates to the sun and daylight uses.

sense.period: Shang-period oracle-bone inscriptions; current Chinese use
sense.text: Oracle-bone examples use 日 for daylight, including in contrast with evening, and a present-day Chinese dictionary lists daytime as a sense. The evidence does not establish whether this use developed from the sun sense.

sense.period: current Chinese use; origin date unresolved
sense.text: Present-day Chinese dictionaries list 日 as an abbreviation for Japan, with examples such as 日貨 and 中日條約. The evidence does not establish when this abbreviation originated.
The cited corpus includes 日 as a sacrificial name. Its relation, if any, to the sun, daylight, or day-unit uses is not established.

sense.period: Shang-period oracle-bone inscriptions; current Chinese use
sense.text: Oracle-bone examples attest 日 for the sun, and present-day Chinese dictionaries list this sense. Its use in the earliest documented corpus cited here does not prove it was the graph's first-ever use.
“Already” appears in a dictionary sense inventory, but no dated example here establishes when this use arose.

sense.period: Later bronze inscription; exact date unresolved
sense.text: A later-bronze inscription is cited for 早 used with the sense “early” or “sooner.” This documents a use of the graph, not the earliest attestation of the spoken word.
The Shuowen account glosses 早 as “morning,” and the character is also defined with this meaning in current reference data. This does not identify it as the earliest attested use of the spoken word.
A demonstrative use is reported, but its relationship to the time noun remains complex.
The character also means an era, age, or period; the development of these senses is not dated here.
A Warring States inscription uses 旹 in a sense glossed “regularly.”
The character is used for a season or quarter, but the development and chronology of this sense are unresolved.
Abstract time is treated as the lexical core. Early transmitted texts use the word, though the precise date of the earliest lexical example is unresolved.
Current meanings include bright, light, and clear.
Brightness is reported among the uses of oracle-bone examples. The evidence does not show whether this use preceded or followed the attested dawn use.
Clear or manifest uses are reported in bronze inscriptions. How this sense developed from brightness or dawn is not shown.
Dawn is reported among the uses of oracle-bone examples; a Shijing line also illustrates daybreak. Its chronological relation to the brightness sense is unresolved.

sense.period: oracle-bone period; dating and reading disputed
sense.text: An oracle-bone example is interpreted as 星 used for 晴, “clear weather.” A Shijing phrase is also read this way, but that interpretation is disputed; neither establishes a secure first occurrence or a semantic path from “star.”
