A Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 星 in a personal name; this does not establish the first use of 星 for “star.”
Later scattered and numerous uses are recorded, but their first occurrences and development from the star sense are not established.

sense.period: dating unresolved; oracle-bone-period forms are reported
sense.text: The character analyses identify “star” as the original sense. Reported early forms do not establish a precise first occurrence.

sense.period: Warring States/Qin slips and Han silk manuscripts
sense.text: In these manuscripts, 星 is reported as a borrowed graph for 腥. The written sign was reused for a different word; this is not a development of “star” into “fishy.” The old object-name and sound match are not established here.
A brief gloss gives “day,” but the evidence does not establish an independent historical use of 昨 with this meaning.

sense.period: Eastern Jin and later examples cited
sense.text: 昨 also refers more broadly to the past, as in the Eastern Jin phrase 覺今是而昨非 and a Tang poem. These examples attest the sense but do not show when it developed from “yesterday.”

sense.period: Dating unresolved; cited in the Shiji passage 昨暮夜
sense.text: In the cited Shiji passage 昨暮夜, 昨 means “yesterday.” The citation establishes this use, but not the first occurrence of the character or word.
An affirmative-response use is recorded, but the examples do not establish its chronology.

sense.period: Eastern Han onward (reported periodization; earliest example unresolved)
sense.text: A published account describes copula use emerging during the Eastern Han, developing from demonstrative uses through constructions with copula-like properties. This is a periodization, not a dated first example. Zero-copula and verbal-copula constructions continued in parallel, and copula constructions later became more frequent.
是 commonly serves as a copula in modern Chinese. The account describes its later expansion and widespread use in modern narrative.

sense.period: Western Zhou–Warring States bronze-inscription range (11th–3rd centuries BCE); individual earliest token unresolved
sense.text: A study of bronze-inscription uses reports early pronominal and anaphoric uses; the individual examples and first token are not available here.

sense.period: Western Zhou–Warring States bronze-inscription range (11th–3rd centuries BCE); individual earliest token unresolved
sense.text: A study reports focus-marking uses in its bronze-inscription material, without identifying a checkable first instance here.
Historical dictionary entries record “right/correct,” including use opposite 非, but their examples do not establish when this sense began.
The traditional Shuowen account glosses 是 as 直, “straight”; the first use of this sense is not dated here.
Dusk or sunset is identified as the character’s original sense. The earliest attestation of this sense is not dated in the cited material.
“Evening” is recorded among the character’s current glosses.
Historical examples document 晚 meaning “late”; the cited material does not date this use or trace its development from dusk.
“Late” is recorded among the character’s current glosses.

sense.gloss: later in a period or succession; successor
sense.text: Historical examples document uses for something later in a period or for a successor. Their chronology and connection to the dusk sense are not established.

sense.period: Six Dynasties use reported; first occurrence unresolved
sense.text: A cited Southern Liang poem uses 晚 for night. A corpus survey reports this sense in Six Dynasties material but does not establish its first occurrence.
A cited historical example uses 晚 for old age. Its first occurrence and development from the dusk sense are not established.
最 also means “extremely” or “exceedingly.” Its relationship to the “most” sense is not established.
A cited use in 燕丹子 refers to a foremost person or thing. Its chronology relative to the current superlative use is unresolved.
最 occurs in a passage whose commentary gives the sense “gather.” This does not establish it as the original meaning or connect it securely to “most.”
最 commonly means “most”; the cited material does not identify the first attestation of this sense.

sense.gloss: offend or force one’s way and take
sense.text: The received account gives this gloss and explains it through 冃 and 取. It is not established as the word’s original meaning or earliest attested use.
最 appears in the administrative expression 課殿最; this use does not establish when the current superlative sense arose.
小爾雅 glosses 最 as 要, “summary” or “essential”; no development to or from another sense is established.
A cited 史記 passage uses 最 in a totaling sense. Its chronology relative to other uses is unresolved.

The current Chinese dictionary records 月 with the meaning ‘each month’. Shang inscriptions also attest its use for a calendar month, associated with the moon’s waxing and waning cycle; the chronology relative to the moon sense is unresolved, and these examples do not establish the sense’s first occurrence.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone period; precise dating unresolved
sense.text: 月 is used for the moon in current Chinese, and Shang oracle-bone examples attest the same use, including in an eclipse context. These are early examples, but the precise first dated occurrence is not established here.
Reported oracle-bone uses, including 有虎? 亡其鹿?, are interpreted as existential. Their exact date and priority over every other early use are unresolved.
A bronze inscription is cited for possession, though the vessel’s date is unresolved here.
The supplied definition records the current senses “have,” “own,” “possess,” and “exist.”

sense.period: Received classical text and historical dictionary tradition
sense.text: The received 說文 discussion cites 有 in 日月有食之 and interprets the passage as something that should not occur but does.
朋 commonly means friend or companion. A connection with pairing or paired valuables is proposed, but its direction, timing, and path are unresolved.
朋 is recorded with group and association uses. Their chronology relative to the counting-measure and friend senses is unresolved.
A traditional explanation records a phoenix use through a graph described as an ancient form of 鳳. It does not establish that the valuables-measure graph originated from that form.
朋 is recorded for people of the same kind, but the evidence does not date this use relative to group or friend.

sense.gloss: counting measure for valuables, traditionally cowries
sense.period: Book of Odes textual tradition; surviving witness date unresolved
sense.text: 朋 is recorded as a currency-counting measure in the Book of Odes textual tradition. Traditional explanations differ over how many cowries made one 朋 and how they were grouped; its date relative to other recorded senses is unresolved.
Current glosses include ‘clothes’ and ‘wear’.
服 is reported in a bronze inscription in a context interpreted as succession to office or duties. The evidence does not establish a development from ‘subdue’.

sense.period: historical use in a compound; earliest date unresolved
sense.text: 箕服 is attested with the meaning ‘arrow case’ or ‘quiver’. Whether this reflects a distinct word, a semantic development, or graph borrowing is unresolved.

sense.period: oracle-bone use reported; precise dating unresolved
sense.text: An analysis of 𠬝 reports an oracle-bone verb meaning ‘conquer’ and a noun for conquered people. The reading and interpretation of individual occurrences are not uncontested.

sense.period: classical textual attestations; manuscript dating unresolved
sense.text: Transmitted classical quotations attest 服 meaning ‘wear’ and ‘clothing’. Their historical relation to ‘subdue’ or ‘office’ is not established.

sense.period: Spring-and-Autumn bronze inscriptions; individual dating and priority unresolved
sense.text: A bronze inscription is interpreted as using 期 for a calendrical interval, though this example does not show that this use preceded other early meanings.

sense.period: Spring-and-Autumn bronze inscriptions; individual dating and priority unresolved
sense.text: Bronze examples are reported for a limit or deadline. A modern study also cites transmitted poetry for appointed-time uses, though it identifies no dated manuscript witness.
Shuowen glosses 期 as 會, “meeting”; this dictionary gloss does not establish it as the earliest meaning.

sense.gloss: period of time, date, or time limit
sense.text: Current definitions include a period of time, a date, and a time limit.

In a Mawangdui manuscript passage, 木 is reported as a sound-based spelling for 沐. This borrows the graph for another word rather than extending the meaning ‘tree’ or ‘wood’; the first use of this spelling is unresolved.

木 is currently used for ‘tree’. An oracle-bone phrase, 埶(藝)木, is reported as a tree-planting use; the rubbing was not independently checked. This evidence does not establish whether ‘tree’ or ‘wood’ came first.

The graph is currently used for ‘wood’ or ‘lumber’. 木枋 in a bronze inscription is interpreted as a wooden writing board, supporting an older wood or timber use; its chronology relative to the tree-planting phrase is unresolved.
The character is also currently used with the sense ‘wooden’. The cited evidence lists this current meaning but does not establish its historical development from ‘tree’ or ‘wood’.
Current dictionary definitions include root, origin, source, and basis. Older cited examples also record foundation uses, but they do not date when this sense arose.

A Japanese lexical account proposes that 本 meaning ‘original’ or ‘source’ came to refer first to an exemplar manuscript and then to books generally. This proposed Japanese word history is separate from the documented Chinese senses and from the character’s graphic origin.
Current definitions include root, origin, source, and basis; this list does not establish their chronology.

The transmitted Shuowen explanation and a cited Book of Odes passage associate 本 with a plant’s root or lower part. The passage’s composition date is unresolved, and these sources do not establish this as the earliest attested use.
Current dictionary entries list source, cause, and basis among 本’s meanings. Their precise development from the root or foundation sense and their first occurrence dates are not established.
A cited Zhuangzi passage records 本 for a tree trunk. Its first occurrence and precise relation to the root sense are undated.
Reference data list 机 with the meaning “desk” or “table.” They do not establish a chronological path from the wood-related or small-table senses.

In mainland simplified writing, 机 is used for the mechanism word written 機 in the traditional graph. Historical accounts describe this as sound-based reuse of a written sign, not a meaning change from “wood” or “table.” The old tree name and its pronunciation remain unverified.
“Moment” appears among definitions for 机, but its chronology and whether it belongs to an independent sense history or to the later use for 機 are unresolved.
A phonological dataset associates 机 with “small table” or “stool.” Its date and relationship to the wood-related gloss are unresolved.

The historical gloss for 机 is 木也, and its recorded analysis pairs 木 with sound-bearing 几. This is the earliest sense supported here; it identifies neither a particular tree nor the date of an inscription bearing this sense.
Classifier use is reported in later transmitted material. Its chronology and any connection to the branch sense are not established.
An orderly-structure sense is reported in transmitted material, but its chronology and development from the branch sense are not established.
In a transmitted 詩經 example, 條 refers to a branch, distinguished in the accompanying gloss from a trunk. This is an attested use, not necessarily the character’s original meaning.

sense.gloss: sorrowful thought (a use read as 悠)
sense.text: In one reported Warring States Chu-slip passage, 條 is read as 悠, meaning “sorrowful thought.” This is reported as a use of the 條 graph for the different word 悠; the evidence here does not establish why that graph was chosen. It is not evidence that the meaning “sorrowful thought” developed from “branch.”
Current meanings include stripe and item or clause. Their chronology and connection to the earlier branch use are not established here.
A throughgoing or unobstructed sense occurs in transmitted material. Its chronology and relationship, if any, to the branch sense are not established.

sense.period: oracle-bone use reported; exact semantic chronology unresolved
sense.text: “Come” is an attested use of the graph. A common explanation is that the wheat sign was reused to write a different word because their sounds were similar; this proposed historical connection remains unverified.

sense.gloss: future, past, and other grammatical or extended uses
sense.text: Records include uses for future and past time, along with other extended and grammatical functions. The gloss lists do not establish their chronology or a continuous chain of development.
“Return” is a recorded sense, but its date and any specific development from “come” are not established.

The graph is traditionally explained as a picture of wheat, and lexicographic and transmitted literary evidence records it in grain terminology. The earliest securely dated use of 來 alone for wheat is unresolved.

sense.period: current; historical examples include the received Mencius passage
sense.text: 杯 is currently used as a classifier for cupfuls, as in 一杯水 and 兩杯麵粉. The received Mencius passage also documents an older textual use; its manuscript date and the classifier’s development relative to the vessel sense are unresolved.

sense.gloss: award or trophy, especially in the form 盃
sense.text: 杯 is currently used for a cup-shaped competition prize, including in 獎杯; one dictionary notes that 盃 is more common in this context. The chronology of this use is unresolved.

sense.period: attested in the received Mencius passage; manuscript date unresolved
sense.text: In the received Mencius passage, 一杯水 means “a cup of water,” documenting 杯 used for a vessel. The citation does not date the surviving physical witness or establish the word’s earliest occurrence.

Fruit is identified as the graph’s original meaning in the pictographic analysis and historical dictionary account. Early forms are reported, but a securely dated inscriptional context for this word meaning is not established.

An account reports oracle-bone use in 果然 and proposes a development from the fruit sense; another discusses early adverbial use. The examples do not establish a dated path or settle the relation to the fruit word.
Dictionary citations document uses such as 果敢, “brave and decisive.” The timing and development of this sense are unresolved.
Classical textual citations show uses meaning “result” or “accomplishment.” They do not show when or through what steps these meanings developed from “fruit.”
樹 is recorded with the sense “establish” or “set up,” but its date and relationship to the other senses are unresolved.
樹 is also recorded for planting or setting upright. The evidence does not establish whether this use preceded the tree sense or developed from it.
樹 is recorded with the noun sense “tree.” The evidence does not establish when this sense first appeared.
Classical citations attest a distinct barrier use, but do not establish when it began or how it relates chronologically to the restraint sense.
Classical citations attest uses meaning checking or collation. They do not date the sense’s beginning or connect it securely to the other uses.
Classical citations attest military organizational uses, but do not establish their first dates or a semantic path from restraint or barrier.

sense.period: transmitted Mengzi text; dating of sense onset unresolved
sense.text: The transmitted Mengzi associates 校 with a teaching place. This attests the use in that text but does not show that the graph originated with the meaning “school” or explain how the sense arose.
School is a current gloss for 校, but the evidence does not establish the chronology or specific semantic transition leading to it.

sense.period: Han-period dictionary account; dating of underlying use unresolved
sense.text: The traditional dictionary explanation gives this sense for 校. The evidence does not independently establish it as the earliest attested use or original meaning.
A current dictionary records 樣 as a classifier, as in 六樣小菜; the origin of this use is undated.
A cited Tang poem uses 樣 for form or shape. This establishes an example by the Tang period, not when the sense originated.
A cited Song poem uses 樣 for kind or type. This establishes an example by the Song period, not when the sense originated or its chronology relative to other senses.
A historical dictionary account glosses 樣 as an oak fruit; this is not established as the earliest meaning or as a dated use.
A dictionary account lists this sense for 樣. Its cited literary examples are not verified as dated attestations here.

sense.gloss: a tableful; a table as a count of dishes or people
sense.text: A cited example uses 桌 as a classifier for a meal or for people counted by tables. Its date and development from the furniture noun are not established.
桌 names furniture such as a table, desk, or stand. Historical reports cite earlier furniture spellings, but do not show that 桌 itself was used in those early passages.

sense.gloss: building of two or more stories
sense.text: The current definition retains the multistorey-building sense.

sense.gloss: building with two or more stories
sense.text: This is given as the basic meaning of traditional 樓 and remains a current meaning of 楼. The available evidence does not identify it as the graph’s first historical meaning.

sense.gloss: commercial or entertainment premises, including teahouses or taverns
sense.text: Cited examples use 樓 for premises such as teahouses or taverns. They do not establish when this use arose or how it relates to the other senses.
A cited literary example uses 樓 for a building storey; when this use arose is unresolved.

sense.gloss: upper structure on a vehicle, ship, or wall
sense.text: Cited examples use 樓 for elevated structures on vehicles, ships, or walls. Their dates and relationship to the multistorey-building sense are unresolved.
Japanese references list watchtower and lookout meanings; their development from the traditional basic sense is unresolved.
Current uses include “next,” “order,” and “sequence.”

A Han silk manuscript is reported to use 次 to write 恣. This is another word represented by the graph, not a demonstrated development in 次’s meaning. The account proposes sound-based borrowing, but supplies no pronunciations to compare; the proposed sound match therefore remains unverified here.

A Mawangdui manuscript is reported to use 次 where the transmitted Zhouyi has 濟. This is another word represented by the graph, not a demonstrated change in 次’s meaning. The account proposes sound-based borrowing, but supplies no pronunciations to compare; the proposed sound match therefore remains unverified here.
Transmitted texts use 次 for lodging or tents. How these uses relate to ranked and ordered meanings is unresolved.

sense.gloss: in sequence; next or second in rank
sense.text: Qin- and Han-period manuscript citations attest 次 for ordered transmission and successive rank. These uses are established by that period, but do not show that they were the graph’s original meaning.
A cited song uses 歡 as an address for a lover. The evidence does not establish how this use relates historically to ‘joy’.
A cited historical example uses 歡 for being on friendly terms. The evidence does not establish how this use developed from ‘joy’.
歡 is recorded with the basic sense ‘joy’ or ‘happiness’; the earliest secure date for this sense is unresolved.

sense.period: Tang example reported; precise witness date unresolved
sense.text: A later example uses 歡 with the sense ‘vigorously’. No supported transition linking this sense to the other listed meanings is established.
A cited classical passage uses 歌鐘 as a bell name. The evidence does not explain the naming or connect this use to the other senses.
Praise is recorded among the character’s uses, but the citations do not date its emergence or show how it developed from another sense.

A dictionary cites the Shijing line “心之憂矣，我歌且謠” for the verbal sense “sing.” The poem’s date is not established here, so this is an early textual citation rather than a secure date for the written graph.
Historical citations use 歌 for a song and describe singing as lengthened utterance. They do not establish when the noun sense arose relative to the verb.
A dictionary records a singable poetic genre among the senses, without establishing its chronology or semantic path.
正 means “correct,” “right,” or “proper.” The received Shuowen entry glosses it as 是, but the evidence does not date a transition from the early travel-related or first-month uses.
Oracle-bone examples use 正 for first-month dating. The evidence does not establish whether this use preceded the travel-related use.
Later bronze examples are reported in governmental or political-order contexts. The evidence does not establish how this use developed from the earlier attested uses.

正 is interpreted as travel or a journey; another account specifies military campaigning. Oracle-bone expedition contexts support an early travel-related use, though they do not settle the graph’s original meaning.
A Zhouyi commentary glosses 比 as “assist” or “support.” This resembles one proposed reading of the Shang phrase, whose meaning remains disputed.

sense.gloss: associate with; attach to a group or person
sense.text: A classical passage is conventionally understood as referring to partial association or factional attachment. Association and following uses are also recorded, but their chronology is unresolved.
A reconstruction table distinguishes a reading glossed “combine; all” from the reading glossed “compare,” but does not establish how the uses relate or when they arose.
比 is used to compare or match. A poem uses it of matching a team of horses, but this example does not date the sense’s beginning or show how it relates to other meanings.
In the early Shang phrase 王比望乘, 比 has been read as “follow” or “lead,” “form a close alliance,” or “assist” and “support.” Its precise sense is disputed.
This sense has been explained as an extension from the small, fragmentary nature of hairs, though its date and development are unresolved.
The Shuowen account defines 毛 with reference to eyebrows, hair, and animal hair; other interpretations include feathers. The first dated common-noun use is unresolved.

In a reported bronze use, 毛 writes 旄, a word for a tail ornament on a standard. This proposed sound-based borrowing is separate from a meaning developing from ‘hair’; the historical pronunciation of 旄 is not independently established.
气 is used for breath and air; the supplied phonological entry also glosses it as vapor. The evidence cited here does not date the beginning of these uses.
Traditional lexicography assigns 气 the meaning “cloud vapor” and calls it pictographic. Specialist discussions caution that this meaning is not secure for the reported oracle-bone occurrences.
One reported oracle-bone use is read as a verb involving either leveling ground with water or washing a temple. Its reading and any connection to the noun “water” remain unresolved.

A bronze inscription is reported to use 水 to write the different word 乞, “request.” This proposed borrowing reuses the sign because the words may have sounded alike or similarly; water did not develop the meaning “request.” The historical sound match is unconfirmed.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone examples; individual dates unresolved
sense.text: One analysis proposes ‘river’ as 水’s original meaning, while another gives the broader meaning ‘water’; which meaning was original remains unresolved.

sense.period: Current; also reported in Shang oracle-bone examples
sense.text: The common current meaning is “water.” Shang oracle-bone examples are also reported for water or flooding; their individual dates are unresolved. Other recorded glosses include liquid, lotion, and juice, whose chronology is not established here.

sense.gloss: Han dynasty or its political label
sense.text: 漢 is used for the Han dynasty and its political label. A naming account connects the dynasty with the Han fief and Hanzhong, which it associates with the Han River, but this does not establish a direct semantic transition or complete chronology.

sense.period: Early Western Zhou attribution; absolute date argued
sense.text: The 京師畯尊 inscription is read as using 漢 for the Han River. This is the earliest supported use here, though its dating is argued rather than established absolutely.
漢 appears in terms for the Chinese language. The date and semantic route to this use are unresolved.

sense.period: Book of Odes quotation; first date unresolved
sense.text: A Book of Odes quotation uses 漢 for the Milky Way. The available examples do not show that this meaning developed from the river name.

sense.period: Process reported from around the sixth century CE; stabilization later
sense.text: 漢 became an ethnic or cultural label associated with the prestige of the Han dynasty. The timing and stabilization are debated, and the earliest securely dated example is unresolved.

sense.gloss: vapor and gas in modern compounds
sense.text: Modern 汽 occurs in compounds for water vapor and gasoline; these compound meanings do not by themselves establish separate single-character senses.
“Tears falling” is recorded as an alternative older gloss; its chronology relative to the other senses is unresolved.
An older dictionary account glosses 汽 as “water dried up.” The evidence does not date this use, so it cannot be identified here as the earliest attested meaning.
A dictionary reports “water vapor” through Jiyun, but the attestation is not dated here.

Duan Yucai interprets “complete entry into water” as extending to “end” or “exhausted,” citing classical examples. This is his account of a semantic development; the earliest use and chronology are unresolved.

In the common reading méi, 沒 is used for “not have” and “none.” One contested proposal is that the graph used for “sink” or “drown” was borrowed to write this different word because the words may have sounded alike. Other accounts propose connections involving 勿, 未, or 有; the older word’s sound, proposed match, borrowing path, and first use remain unresolved.

The received 說文 glosses 沒 as 沈, “sink” or “submerge”; dictionary accounts also record sinking and drowning. These uses are documented, but their earliest attestation and the graph’s original meaning are not established.
The character is also recorded with the meanings clean and purify; when these uses arose and how they developed are unresolved.
An early lexicographic gloss associates 洗 with washing the feet, and cited transmitted texts also document this use; they do not establish the exact first occurrence.
洗 is used for washing and rinsing, including washing the head, feet, hands, and body. The evidence does not establish a linear development from the foot-washing gloss to broader washing.
A cited text uses 洗 for washing a ritual vessel; its precise date and chronology relative to other washing uses are unresolved.

sense.gloss: a vessel associated with wash water
sense.text: A cited ritual text uses 洗 for a vessel receiving wash water. Its chronology relative to the washing sense is unresolved.
Dictionaries list 清 for clarity and clear or fine weather. Their chronology and relationship to the clear-water sense are unresolved.
The received historical explanation describes 清 as clear water. This identifies a traditional account of the sense, not its earliest surviving occurrence.
Dictionaries also list “peaceful”; its origin and connection to the other senses are unresolved.
A bronze use is interpreted as “drying up” or “exhausted,” with the graph reported as writing 竭. The Fanghu transcription itself prints 竭 and does not independently confirm the graph identification.
A cited Tang usage has the sense “dry” or “parched.”

sense.period: Cited in 詩·王風·君子于役; earliest physical witness date unresolved
sense.text: A cited Shijing passage uses 渴 to mean “thirsty.” The date of the passage’s earliest surviving physical witness is unresolved.
Current dictionary definitions include “thirsty” and “parched.”
A cited 公羊傳 passage uses 渴 to mean “urgent”; its relation to the other senses is not established.
The modern Mandarin dictionary records 火 in a verb use meaning ‘become angry’; its date and historical relation to the noun ‘fire’ are unresolved.
The modern Mandarin dictionary records 火 as a verb meaning ‘burn’; its date and historical relation to the noun ‘fire’ are unresolved.

sense.period: Shang-period oracle-bone use; individual inscription dates unresolved
sense.text: Oracle-bone examples include 火 in a literal fire context. The whole graph is analyzed as depicting light and flames from a burning object. Fire remains a current noun sense.

sense.gloss: a star name, 大火 (Antares / 心宿二)
sense.period: Shang-period oracle-bone use; also attested in the Classic of Poetry
sense.text: Oracle-bone 火 in 合集 11503 may refer to 火星, without specifying 心宿二 or the planet Mars. Here 火星 is identified as the historical name for 大火/心宿二. The name’s motivation and its link to literal ‘fire’ are not established.
点 is used for a point; current definitions also include degree and decimal point. The evidence does not establish how each use developed from the older mark sense.
The reported original sense of traditional 點 is ‘small black mark’; its earliest lexical attestation is not securely dated.

sense.period: Jin-period example cited; exact earliest attestation unresolved
sense.text: A Jin-period text uses 點 for a spot on otherwise unblemished white jade. Other cited uses include writing over a character, ornamenting, textual punctuation, a liquid drop, and checking or counting. These examples do not establish a chronological chain among the senses.
A cited Mencius passage uses 熱中 for an emotionally urgent or intense state. Its relative chronology with the temperature sense is unresolved.
Cited examples use 熱 in references to illness and bodily heat. They do not establish a precise semantic sequence from the general temperature sense.
热 is used for heat and the state of being hot.

sense.period: dating unresolved; cited in pre-imperial transmitted works
sense.text: 熱 is defined as warm, and cited examples use it for something hot or for heat. Some examples come from transmitted pre-imperial works, but surviving witness dates and a secure earliest attestation are unresolved.

Modern 爱 means love, affection, fondness, and liking; 愛 is its traditional counterpart. Transmitted literary passages also use 愛 for affection, including examples in the Zuozhuan and Classic of Poetry. These examples do not establish when the sense began or the earliest physical witness; the evidence does not establish a dated sequence among the current senses.
The traditional construction points to the meaning “father.” A later dictionary quotation of 玉篇 associates 爺 with calling one’s father, but the earliest use is not securely dated.
The character is used for “father,” including in the cited Mulan Poetry example; that example does not establish the poem’s composition or manuscript date.
A dictionary-reported Ming source glosses 祖 as 爺, documenting a grandfather use.
“Grandfather” is among the character’s recorded meanings.

sense.gloss: honorific for a man of rank or an elder
sense.text: A dictionary-reported citation from the Old Book of Tang documents 爺 used as an honorific.

sense.period: Three Kingdoms era (reported dating of the Guangya record)
sense.text: A Guangya entry is dated to the Three Kingdoms era and glosses 爸 as “father.” This records use of the word, though it does not provide a dated physical witness for the graph.
Modern references gloss 爸 as “father” and “papa”; no separate historical stage for “papa” is established.
A modern dictionary lists this figurative sense, but its date and development from the animal sense are unresolved.

sense.period: Shuowen Jiezi; date of use not established here
sense.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry glosses 牛 as a large sacrificial animal. This dictionary gloss does not establish a separate earlier sense or the graph’s original meaning.
A modern dictionary lists this use, but its chronology and development are unresolved.
A modern dictionary lists a lunar-mansion sense; its chronology and development are unresolved.

The graph is interpreted as depicting the animal, and 牛 is reported in an inscription referring to cattle. The earliest securely dated occurrence is unresolved; this is the earliest supported sense, not a dated first use.
Personal-name use is reported in bronze inscriptions; the examples are not individually dated here.
A modern dictionary lists surname use, but its date and development are unresolved.
A modern dictionary lists a zodiac use; its chronology and relation to the animal sense are unresolved.

sense.period: Warring States literary citation reported by a later dictionary
sense.text: A Warring States literary citation uses 玩 in a sense of handling or appreciating. The citation does not establish when this sense began or how it relates chronologically to other uses.

sense.period: dating unresolved; cited in the received Shuowen account
sense.text: The received Shuowen gloss 弄也 records a historical sense of manipulating or playing with. It does not establish the character’s original meaning or earliest attestation.
Modern definitions include playing, joking, and enjoying. They do not establish a historical path from the cited older uses.
A phonological table gives 玩 the gloss “plaything.” This does not date the sense or show that a plaything was the character’s original referent.

sense.period: historical literary use; dating unresolved here
sense.text: A literary citation records 玩 for studying or becoming familiar with lines. Its date and semantic connection to other uses are unresolved.
Dictionary and character-record evidence gives 現/现 the sense ‘appear; become visible.’ The earliest dated attestation is not identified.
A dictionary records a noun sense for stone regarded as inferior to jade. Its date and relationship to the other meanings are unresolved.
A historical lexicographic quotation glosses 現 as ‘jade luster’; another dictionary records the same sense. Its date and priority relative to ‘appear’ are unresolved.
The character is also used with the meanings ‘present,’ ‘existing,’ and ‘actual.’ The listed meanings alone do not establish how they developed from ‘appear.’

The received-text phrase 班瑞于群后 is conventionally read as distributing jade tokens. The proposed original sense ‘divide auspicious jade’ is a traditional graphic interpretation, not a meaning established by the early bronze name uses; the date of the received text is unresolved.
The earliest cited bronze contexts use 班 in a personal name, including 毛班 on 班簋. These attest name use, not the proposed meaning ‘divide jade’.
Historical records include senses of rank or order; 班 currently also means a class, group, or squad. The evidence does not establish a full chronology or semantic bridge among these meanings.
Historical records include 班 meaning ‘separate’, as in 班馬之聲. The cited examples do not show that this sense developed from ‘divide’ or ‘distribute’.

球 means a ball or spherical object. Its use for the ball word associated with 毬 is explained as borrowing, not as an established semantic extension from jade; the earliest dated use remains unresolved.

sense.period: late nineteenth century in cited Japanese examples
sense.text: Japanese examples from 1872 and 1873 use 球 for a geometric sphere, including the sun. They document usage at those dates, not the sense’s earliest appearance.
Historical dictionary accounts gloss 球 as jade. The reported Qin-period writing does not securely establish the earliest attested sense.
In 戛擊鳴球, 球 is interpreted as a jade chime. The passage does not securely date the surviving wording or graph.
A historical dictionary glosses 生 as “advance”; a later interpretation treats this as an extended sense. The evidence does not date this sense or show its development.
生 is reported in an oracle-bone prayer for childbirth. Other early uses are also reported, so this does not establish childbirth as the character’s first meaning.
生 is reported as an adjective for fresh or live animals; separate historical phonology entries record “fresh, raw.” No chronology connecting this sense to the others is established.

sense.period: Warring States manuscripts and later usage
sense.text: A Warring States manuscript uses 生 for living in opposition to dying. Later lexicographic evidence also records life and living, without establishing a complete development from earlier uses.
A bronze-inscription example is reported with the sense “lifespan.” No transition from the other attested senses is established.
生 is reported as an adjective describing live animals in oracle-bone inscriptions. This does not establish its priority relative to the childbirth use.
One interpretation reads 生月 as “following month,” but other readings are contested. This phrase does not establish a semantic development from plant growth.
Bronze-inscription examples are reported with the sense “occur” or “produce.” The evidence does not show when or how this use developed from other senses.
用/不用 is reported after divination statements to indicate whether a proposed action was carried out. This attested use does not establish the graph’s original meaning.
One Qin-slip context is read 桶, “container” or “measure.” It preserves a container-related use but does not establish the graph’s original meaning or when this use arose.

sense.gloss: preposition equivalent to 以; sequential or causal conjunction
sense.text: Bronze-inscription examples include prepositional and conjunctive uses alongside the verb “use.” The examples do not establish their relative chronology or development.
用 has the current meaning “use” or “employ.” The evidence does not establish a complete path from the attested inscriptional uses to its present range.

sense.period: modern; scientific sense reported from the late nineteenth century
sense.text: 電 is used for electricity and related modern meanings. The precise development from atmospheric lightning to the scientific sense remains unresolved.

sense.period: received Book of Songs; composition date unresolved
sense.text: 電 is used for lightning in a received Book of Songs passage. The poem’s composition date is not independently established, and the late Western Zhou bronze example does not by itself show the word’s meaning there.
男 is used today to mean “male” and “man.” How these meanings developed from earlier uses is not dated here.
Bronze examples are reported in contexts interpreted as referring to male persons. This does not establish that the graph first meant “man.”
A personal-name use is reported, without an established semantic or chronological connection to the other uses.

sense.gloss: rank or domain, including 男服
sense.period: Oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions; individual dates unresolved
sense.text: An oracle-bone use for 男服 and bronze examples interpreted as rank or domain are reported. These uses do not determine the graph’s original meaning or later semantic development.
A bronze example is reported with 男 used for “son.” Its chronological relation to the other reported uses is unresolved.
男 is also recorded with the current meaning “son”; its development from earlier uses is not dated here.

sense.period: present-day usage; earliest noun attestation unresolved
sense.text: Illness, sickness, or disease is a common present-day meaning. The earliest word sense remains disputed: 字源 proposes “serious illness,” Shuowen glosses 病 as illness worsening, and another study proposes hardship as the original meaning. These are competing analyses, not established stages in a single history.

Dictionaries attest uses involving fatigue and withered foliage, including later examples. Other listed meanings such as difficulty, resentment, distress, harm, and defect are recorded in dictionaries, but this evidence does not establish that they are all historical-only senses or show when they arose.

sense.period: transmitted classical texts; precise dating unresolved
sense.text: Transmitted examples use 病 for being troubled or affected by burdens, and for being concerned about one’s shortcomings. They attest these uses but do not show that they developed from the illness sense.
This is a current dictionary-listed sense. A proposed link from daylight to brightness is undated and not established here.
An ancient use meaning “hundred” is reported, but its chronology and any semantic connection to the color word are unresolved.

sense.period: Oracle-bone period; individual dated attestations unresolved
sense.text: A place-name use is reported, but its reading, meaning, and relation to the color-word and 伯 uses are unresolved.
This is a current dictionary-listed sense. A proposed development from “white” through purity is undated and not established here.

sense.period: Oracle-bone period; individual dated attestations unresolved
sense.text: The color meaning is reported in oracle-bone inscriptions and remains a current sense. Its first dated example and whether it was the graph's original referent are unresolved.

sense.period: Oracle-bone period; individual dated attestations unresolved
sense.text: Use for 伯 is reported in oracle-bone inscriptions. One account connects it with the thumb's proposed leading position; another proposes that the sign was reused because 白 and 伯 sounded alike. The relationship and sequence remain disputed.

sense.period: A Book of Odes example is cited; its composition and manuscript dates are unresolved
sense.text: 百 is recorded with an inclusive sense, including in a cited Book of Odes example. Its chronological and semantic relation to the numeral and abundance senses is unresolved.

sense.period: Current Mandarin use; oracle-bone contexts are also reported, and a Western Zhou bronze example is cited
sense.text: 百 denotes the numeral one hundred in present-day Mandarin. Specialist accounts also report oracle-bone numerical examples and cite a Western Zhou bronze example; the cited artifact contexts have not been checked against the objects.

sense.period: A bronze-context example is cited; its interpretation and earlier chronology remain unresolved
sense.text: 百 is also recorded with the sense “many.” A cited bronze-context example is interpreted as a possible extension from the numeral, but does not prove that development. When this sense arose remains unresolved.

sense.period: Late Middle Chinese onward; precise chronology disputed
sense.text: In Mandarin, de marks possession or links a modifier to a noun. Historical accounts report 底 as an earlier spelling before 的 replaced it; the spoken word’s origin remains disputed.

Dictionary sources record 的 with the meanings ‘mark in a target’ and ‘target.’ A traditional commentary proposes that the target sense extended from the brightness associated with 旳, while another account allows an independent root; the relationship and chronology remain unsettled. The Han gloss ‘bright’ belongs specifically to 旳 and is not established here as a sense of 的.

sense.gloss: gaze or look into the distance
sense.text: The received Shuowen gloss 睎也 is explained in later commentary as shading the eyes with the hand to gaze. This is the earliest sense supported by the cited account, though the earliest historical occurrence of the spoken word is unresolved.

sense.period: transmitted early medieval text examples; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: A transmitted early medieval text gives an example of watching or keeping observation. The evidence neither dates the origin of this use nor connects it sequentially to “gaze.”
Looking, seeing, and observing are recorded meanings. Their relationship to the gaze gloss and to one another is not dated here.

sense.period: later literary examples; exact chronology unresolved
sense.text: Dictionary and later literary examples record these uses. The evidence does not establish a dated semantic chain linking them to the gaze or look senses.

sense.period: transmitted early medieval text example; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: A transmitted early medieval text gives an example glossed “visit.” The evidence does not show whether or how this use developed from “look.”
Modern definitions include ‘real,’ ‘actual,’ ‘true,’ and ‘genuine.’ The supplied evidence does not trace a complete path from the cited early uses to these current meanings.

sense.period: Text cited from Xunzi; exact date and witness relation unresolved
sense.text: 真 is cited as an adverb meaning ‘indeed.’ Its chronology relative to the other cited senses is not established.

sense.period: Texts cited from Zhuangzi and Lüshi Chunqiu; exact composition and witness dates unresolved
sense.text: 真 is cited in uses meaning ‘original nature’ or ‘inherent nature.’ Their chronology relative to the ‘true/actual’ use is not established.

sense.period: Qin Shuihudi legal-question bamboo manuscript cited for slip 49; exact manuscript and composition dating unresolved
sense.text: A cited legal discussion uses 真 to mean ‘actual’ or ‘true.’ The bronze personal-name use does not identify its spoken sense or establish this meaning for that use.

sense.gloss: grammatical particle marking ongoing or persistent action
sense.text: 着 is used as a particle marking ongoing or persistent action. The evidence does not establish when this use arose or how it relates to other uses of 著.

sense.period: Qing example recorded; exact chronology unresolved
sense.text: A later example is glossed “lie down.” The evidence does not establish a semantic path from sleeping to lying down.

sense.period: attested in transmitted classical examples; dating unresolved
sense.text: Transmitted text examples use 睡 for sleeping or dozing. The evidence does not establish when this broader use arose relative to the sitting-sleep gloss.
The modern definition includes “sleep” and “doze.”

sense.period: dating unresolved; gloss in the transmitted Shuowen account
sense.text: The traditional gloss is “sleep while sitting.” It provides an early lexical framing but does not establish manuscript dates or that this was the word’s original meaning.

A secondary account reports a bronze-inscription use glossed “know,” but its context and date were not verified. This is a reported historical use, not a securely established first attestation or original meaning.
Modern glosses include knowing, perceiving, and comprehending.

sense.period: later traditional usage; precise dates unresolved
sense.text: Historical dictionary examples include knowing, awareness or sensation, and understanding. Their relative chronology and development from one another are not established.

sense.period: later traditional usage; precise dates unresolved
sense.text: 知 is recorded in a wisdom-related use corresponding to 智. When this use arose and how it relates chronologically to other uses are unresolved.

sense.gloss: written or printed credential; ticket or ballot
sense.period: Ming-era and later examples; earliest attestation unresolved
sense.text: 票 is used for documentary credentials and in modern compounds such as 車票, 門票, and 選票. The examples do not establish its first use or a direct development from the fire or motion senses.

sense.period: dating unresolved; gloss reported in Shuowen
sense.text: The older graph 𤐫 is associated with the gloss “fire flying” or “fire rising.” This does not establish that the gloss was the earliest attested use or the graph’s original meaning.

sense.period: Qin and Han examples reported; earliest priority unresolved
sense.text: Older examples record light movement and shaking. A Qin-slip use 票風 is interpreted as a strong or rapid wind, but the evidence does not demonstrate a dated transition from the fire gloss.

sense.period: Qing-era and later examples; earliest attestation unresolved
sense.text: Paper-money uses are recorded in Qing-era and later examples. Their relationship to the fire, motion, or credential senses is not established.

sense.period: Qin and Han examples reported; earliest priority unresolved
sense.text: The character occurs in expressions associated with rapid movement, including the reported Qin-slip 票風 and Han shu examples. A separate Shuihudi phrase, 票行, has disputed readings and is not secure support for this sense.
This meaning is recorded in the supplied definition, without a dated example establishing its chronology or relation to the credential and ticket senses.

sense.gloss: dig or excavate, including a canal
sense.text: Historical sources attest digging, including digging a canal. They do not establish a semantic path connecting these uses to the piercing sense.
Historical sources attest uses meaning “pass through.” They do not establish a precise development from the piercing sense.

sense.period: pre-Qin Shijing corpus; exact composition date unresolved
sense.text: The earliest textual use located is in the Shijing passage Xing Lu, where 穿 describes boring through a house or wall. This attests the word in that text, though the poem’s precise composition date is unresolved.
Texts attest uses for threading or joining, but do not show when or by what steps these uses developed from “pierce through.”
Later texts attest the clothing and footwear sense. Its precise development from the older senses is not established.
Sources separately attest a worn or broken sense, but do not show how it developed from the other senses.

sense.period: Historical use cited in 元史; exact passage date unresolved
sense.text: A dictionary cites 站 in a 元史 passage for a relay or post station. The evidence does not establish how this use relates historically to the standing sense.

sense.period: Medieval lexicographic evidence; precise earliest date unresolved
sense.text: Medieval dictionary accounts record standing senses, including standing alone and standing upright. They do not identify the first dated use of the character or word.

sense.gloss: station, including modern transport or service stations
sense.text: 站 is used for stations in modern contexts, including transport. Proposed borrowing accounts disagree about whether Chinese or Mongolian and Turkic forms came first; neither direction is established here.
A flower-opening use is recorded, but its chronology and relationship to the laugh/smile sense are not established.

笑 is reported in a Mawangdui manuscript in a laugh-related context; the exact passage’s physical graph has not been verified. Quotations in received classical texts attest the word but do not date surviving graph material.
Ridicule and joking uses are recorded, but their dates and development from the laugh/smile sense are not established.
Modern dictionary metadata gives smile, laugh, giggle, and snicker as meanings.
A text dated 815 uses 第 to refer to the time after passing an examination. How this use developed from sequence or rank is unresolved.
Dictionary accounts record an adverbial “only” or “just” sense. Its history and any relation to “sequence” are unresolved.
第 commonly precedes a numeral to mark an ordinal. The first occurrence of this use is not dated here.

sense.period: Han text example; broader dating unresolved
sense.text: A Han text uses 第 to rank performances. Dictionary accounts also record examination rank and evaluation; these uses do not establish the graph’s original meaning.
Dictionary accounts record a residence sense and offer a rank-related explanation, but its date and development are unresolved.

Dictionary accounts give “sequence” or “order,” but the earliest attestation is unsettled: one quotation has 第，次也, while an inspected transcription has 弟，次也. The text’s composition date and witness history are unresolved.

sense.gloss: and so forth; enumeration or plural marker
sense.period: historical attestations; earliest date unresolved here
sense.text: 等 is attested in enumerative and plural uses, including “and so forth.” The evidence does not establish a specific path from rank or equality to these uses.

sense.period: early textual examples cited by dictionaries; exact dates unresolved here
sense.text: Dictionary citations attest the meaning “equal.” The proposed link to arranging slips evenly is an interpretation, not a documented sequence of change.
The received Shuowen entry glosses 等 as 齊簡, conventionally rendered “orderly bamboo slips.” This is the earliest meaning supported here, not a proven original meaning at the graph’s creation.

sense.period: early textual examples cited by dictionaries; exact dates unresolved here
sense.text: Dictionary citations attest uses for rank, class, or grade. They do not establish when this sense arose relative to the orderly-slip gloss or equality.

sense.period: attested in a transmitted Tang poem; earliest dated use unresolved
sense.text: A waiting-related use appears in a transmitted Tang poem. Its earliest occurrence and relation to 待 remain unresolved; manuscript spellings of 待 with 寺 do not establish that 等 meant “wait” at that time.
Received Shijing and Mengzi passages show answer-related use. They do not identify the graph in the earliest manuscript witnesses or date the first use of 答 itself.
Assenting is among the recorded meanings, but its date and connection to answering or replying are unresolved.
Dictionary records include “return” and “recompense.” Their dates and any development from “answer” or “reply” are unresolved; the reported use of 荅 for recompense does not establish such a sequence.

米 is reported in oracle-bone use for rice or grain. Scholarly discussion identifies its early referent as probably dehusked grain broadly, rather than a single crop; the precise first-use date and inscription context are unresolved.

In Japanese, 米 is used for the length unit metre following the use of 米突 to render French mètre by sound. This is a separate word use, unrelated in meaning to grain. The exact route by which 米 alone became current is unresolved.
米 commonly means rice in modern usage.
Binding or connection is proposed as the sense of a hand holding connected silk. This is an interpretation of the graph’s origin, not a dated earliest use.

sense.period: historical; cited in a Han-dynasty text
sense.text: A source proposes an extension from connection to lineage and cites a Han-dynasty example, but intermediate stages are not documented.
System is a recorded modern gloss. Its historical development is not shown by this evidence.
Thread is a recorded gloss and fits the interpretation of silk held by a hand. The evidence does not identify it as the earliest attested lexical use.

sense.gloss: use of 系 to write 奚
sense.text: A Warring States use of 系 for 奚 is reported. This is a proposed reuse of the graph for another word, not a meaning developing from 系. The older word’s sound and any sound match are not given.

累 is used for accumulation and increase in cited textual traditions. 絫 is also associated with increase, but the evidence does not show that these uses developed from the rope and binding meanings associated with 纍.

Dictionary glosses include tiredness, involvement, and trouble. The evidence does not establish how these uses relate to accumulation and increase, or to the distinct traditions associated with 纍 and 絫.
Modern references retain the senses “continue,” “carry on,” and “inherit.”

Traditional 紹 is glossed “continue” or “inherit.” A received Shang Shu passage uses it for carrying on the former kings’ enterprise; the wording’s composition date and earliest occurrence are unresolved.
紹 is also used for introducing or mediating between people. The cited received-work examples do not establish when this sense arose relative to “continue/inherit.”
An old dictionary glosses 紹 as “tighten and twist”; its relation to the inheritance sense is unresolved.
A dictionary also lists “wind around,” without dating the use or connecting it to the inheritance sense.
給 is used to mean “give.” The evidence here does not establish when this sense arose or how it developed from the older recorded glosses. The origin of colloquial Mandarin gěi remains disputed.
A research abstract proposes that prepositional and complementizer uses developed through grammaticalization from a verb. The cited evidence gives no dated attestations or complete pathway.

sense.gloss: make up what another lacks; suffice
sense.text: The received Shuowen account glosses 給 as 相足也, explained as one side making up what another lacks. This is the earliest meaning supported here, not a securely established original meaning.
Dictionary entries record supply and grant senses with examples from named works. Those examples do not establish their dates or their chronological relation to the received gloss.
Oracle-bone examples use 网 as a verb for catching game. This attests the verb use, not the earliest noun use for a net.

sense.period: attested in cited classical examples; first occurrence unresolved
sense.text: A figurative constraint or legal “web” sense is recorded in cited classical examples. The evidence does not date its emergence or establish a secure development from the physical net sense.
The graph depicts a net, and lexicographic records also use it for the net noun. The first attestation of that noun use is not established.
Lexicographic records include uses for net-like forms or things, without establishing their first occurrence.
Modern network meanings are recorded, but their first use and the full semantic path from “net” are not established.

sense.period: bronze inscriptions; absolute dates not supplied here
sense.text: Reported bronze examples use 老 for an elderly person and as an adjective meaning “old.”
“Experienced” is also recorded as a current sense; its development is undated here.

sense.gloss: father, written with 老 for 考
sense.period: bronze inscriptions; absolute dates not supplied here
sense.text: Bronze examples reportedly use 老 to write 考 “father.” Whether this was a semantic development or a writing substitution is unresolved.
The common current meaning is “old” or “aged.”
The earliest cited oracle-bone instance uses 老 as a place name; it attests that use, not the lexical meaning “old.”
A reported bronze example uses 考 for “consider” or “estimate”; its date and relation to the “father” use are unresolved.
Current definitions include “examine,” “test,” and “investigate.” Their chronology relative to the reported historical uses is unresolved.
Reported bronze examples use 考 for “father,” often, though not always, referring to a deceased father.
A traditional lexicographic analysis glosses 考 as “old”; whether this was the graph’s earliest meaning is unresolved.
A dictionary records 肉 for fruit pulp, with a citation from 齊民要術. The date and any development from the meat sense are unresolved.

The received Shuowen account glosses 肉 as 胾肉, interpreted in its later annotation as a large piece of animal meat. Dictionary citations document uses for meat and bodily flesh but do not establish their exact dates or which use came first.
In current Chinese, 肉 means meat or flesh; the supplied record gives the Mandarin reading ròu.
A dictionary records a use of 肉 for musical voice or timbre. Its date and any semantic path from the meat sense are unresolved.

sense.gloss: solid part of a perforated ring
sense.text: Dictionary explanations and citations record 肉 for the solid part of a perforated ring. They do not establish when this use arose or how it relates to the meat sense.
Historical reports cite ability-related noun uses in Warring States-era texts. Modern definitions include “ability,” but do not establish a further dated stage.
A reported Western Zhou bronze use has 能 as a verb meaning “be able to.” This is the earliest ability use identified here; it does not establish the character’s original meaning.

The Han dictionary defines 能 as a kind of bear, and historical pronunciation records distinguish bear readings. The proposed Shang examples do not securely date this use because their identification and use are disputed.
The character is used for “brain.” The available evidence does not date the earliest use.
A later dictionary lists brain-like material among the character’s senses, without dating it or connecting it chronologically to the other senses.

sense.period: attested in a Song text; exact date unresolved here
sense.text: A later dictionary records a “central part” use in a Song poem. Its relationship to the bodily sense is not established.

sense.period: attested in the Huainanzi and Tang works; exact dates unresolved here
sense.text: A later dictionary records uses meaning “head” in the Huainanzi and Tang works. The evidence does not show that this sense developed from “head marrow.”
An older dictionary glosses 匘, a form associated with 腦, as “head marrow.” This dictionary gloss does not establish the graph’s hypothetical original meaning or earliest attested use.

sense.gloss: flower-like objects and other figurative or extended senses
sense.text: Later recorded senses include flower-like objects, beauty, patterns, and expenditure. Their dates and paths of development from “flower” are unresolved.

sense.period: Tang citations; earlier first use of 花 unresolved
sense.text: Tang citations attest 花 for the noun “flower.” The older graphs 𠌶 and 華 have flower-related definitions or reported uses, but those do not establish an early attestation of 花 itself.
A Tang citation attests 花 as a verb meaning “to flower.” The evidence does not establish when this use arose relative to the noun.
茶 is recorded as a metonym for betrothal gifts associated with tea; when this use began is undated.
茶 commonly names tea, including the plant and its prepared drink.
A Ming example uses 茶 as a verb meaning ‘drink’; how this use developed from the noun is not established.

sense.gloss: infusion made from ingredients other than tea leaves
sense.text: 茶 is also recorded for brewed drinks made with other ingredients; the start of this use is undated.
Tang-period sources use 茶 for prepared tea. Proposed Han references written with 荼 remain disputed as evidence for this sense.

sense.period: Tang period attested; earlier date unresolved
sense.text: 茶 is recorded for the tea plant. A Tang text describes tea as a fine southern tree, but the earliest date of this sense is unsettled.
Modern glosses include vegetables, dishes, and food. The supplied definitions do not establish that every gloss is a distinct, chronologically ordered sense.

sense.period: Han dictionary definition; Qin-period spelling evidence
sense.text: The Shuowen definition identifies 菜 as edible vegetation. Qin slips reportedly spell the vegetable word with 采; this supports the word’s use but does not date the first appearance of the full graph 菜.

sense.period: Qin-period example; later Chinese use; Japanese example dated approximately 1120
sense.text: 菜 is used for prepared food or a dish. Qin-period slips reportedly spell the vegetable word with 采, and later Chinese evidence records collective uses for dishes; Japanese sources separately cite a side-dish use around 1120. The evidence does not establish a sequence from vegetables to dishes.
Abusive uses are recorded, including examples attributed to Ming-Qing and later texts. Their development from another sense is not established.

蛋 is used for an animal egg in textual examples, including one from a work attributed to the Southern Song. The earliest date remains unresolved: one account proposes Northern Song onset, while the cited transmitted example is Southern Song-attributed.
Uses for egg-shaped things are recorded, but the evidence does not date this sense or show whether it developed from “egg.”
蛋 is also recorded for southern coastal people. The evidence documents this use but does not establish its chronological or semantic relation to “egg.”
Warring States inscriptions and Chu slips are reported with 德行, where 行 has a conduct-related use.
The crossroads graph and cited oracle-bone contexts support a road-related use in this period; reading those contexts as ‘road’ is an interpretation.
Later rhyme-book records distinguish a reading glossed ‘row/rank’ from readings associated with walking, order, and conduct; they do not establish when this sense arose.
Verbal uses for movement are reported in oracle-bone inscriptions. They attest this use by that period but do not show it was the earliest spoken sense.
衣 is used for clothing generally as well as for an upper garment.
Dictionaries record a covering or wrapping use, but do not establish when it arose or how it relates historically to the garment sense.
Early graphic analyses identify the depicted object as an upper garment; the earliest dated word use with this meaning is unresolved.
衣 is also used as a verb meaning “wear” or “put on.” The cited examples do not date its relationship to the clothing noun.

“Nest” is proposed as the referent of the pictographic analysis, and one graphic-history account describes it as an original meaning no longer used. This is not established as the earliest attested single-character use.

sense.period: Oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions; precise dates unresolved
sense.text: The graph is also reported in place and palace names in these inscriptional periods. Their order relative to the directional use is unresolved.

sense.period: Oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions; precise dates unresolved
sense.text: 西 is reported for the western direction in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions. The available account gives no individually dated examples establishing a precise first use.
要 has these current uses, but the evidence does not establish when they arose or how they relate historically to the waist or want/need uses.

sense.period: dating unresolved; attested in transmitted pre-imperial texts
sense.text: Transmitted pre-imperial works use 要 for the waist. These examples attest the sense but do not establish its earliest date.

The familiar “want” and “need” uses are explained as a proposed borrowing: the sign used for “waist” was reused to write a different word thought to sound similar. This is not established as a meaning change from “waist.”
Audience is reported among oracle-bone and bronze uses. Its date and chronological relation to “see” are unresolved.

sense.gloss: offer sacrificial goods, written with 見 and read 獻
sense.text: One oracle-bone use is reported as 見 read 獻, “offer sacrificial goods.” The proposed explanation is borrowing the graph for a similar-sounding word, not a demonstrated semantic extension; the inscription evidence and sound comparison are unavailable.
A passive auxiliary use is reported for bronze inscriptions. Its date and development from the seeing sense are unresolved.
Seeing is the core meaning assigned in the received dictionary account and reported for oracle-bone and bronze uses; no specific earliest inscription date is established.
The current simplified character is glossed with meanings including seeing, observing, and perceiving.
Current definitions include looking at, observing and seeing.

The received traditional graph is glossed as looking toward, and dictionary examples include examining or observing. When this use developed in relation to the basic looking or seeing sense is unresolved.

sense.period: Shang oracle-bone evidence; individual token date unresolved
sense.text: The cited paleographic analysis identifies Shang oracle-bone contexts, including 視師 and 視方, as uses involving observing. The date of any individual token is not specified.
Cited texts use 覺 for awakening or understanding, becoming aware, and discovery. These uses are attested, but their first dates and order of development are unresolved.
觉 is used with the sense “conscious” or “aware.” How this current sense developed from earlier uses is unresolved.
A sense of prompting or informing is cited from the 《孟子》. Its date relative to the waking and awareness uses is unresolved.
A separate jiào reading is listed for sleep and an episode of sleep. Its historical relation to the waking sense is unresolved.
In 尚寐無覺, a cited 《詩經》 passage, 覺 occurs in a sleep context and means “wake.” The passage’s date is unresolved.

sense.gloss: agree or accept; regard as; form a non-blood kinship relation
sense.text: These senses are listed for 認, but their dates and relationships to one another or to “identify” are not established.
A cited Song poem uses 認 to mean “identify carefully.” This is the earliest dated use documented here, not necessarily the earliest attestation or the word’s original meaning.
The character is glossed “know” and “understand.” The evidence does not date these senses or show how they relate to the Song-era identifying use.
Modern dictionary glosses include both recording and retaining an impression in the mind.

sense.period: Later range includes a cited Ming example
sense.text: A dictionary records a narrative genre and cites a Ming example. This documents the sense but does not establish how it developed from the verbal or documentary senses.

sense.period: Attested in a cited Hanshu context; exact date of surviving witness unresolved
sense.text: A cited Hanshu passage uses 記 for “record.” This attests the use in context, but does not establish a semantic transition from “remember” or from the Shuowen gloss.

sense.period: Attested in a cited Hou Hanshu context; exact date of surviving witness unresolved
sense.text: A cited Hou Hanshu passage uses 記 for remembering. This attests the use in context, but does not show when the sense began or how it relates to the Shuowen gloss.
Dictionary entries include “written record” or “document” among the noun senses. Their ordering does not establish when this sense arose or its precise relation to the verbal senses.

sense.period: Eastern Han dictionary account; exact earliest use unresolved
sense.text: The received Shuowen entry gives this gloss. A later commentary and an edition variant differ in interpreting or transmitting it, so it records the dictionary’s account rather than proving the character’s earliest word sense.
Traditional 識 is used with meanings including “know” and “recognize.” The cited glosses and examples do not establish when these uses began.
Current glosses include “recognize,” “understand,” and “know.” The evidence does not establish how these uses developed from remembering or other historical senses.

Remembering or retaining is identified as an early sense and illustrated with classical examples. The evidence does not establish that it was the earliest attested sense or preceded knowing and recognizing.
Historical citations include uses glossed as accusation or denunciation; their chronology relative to grievance reporting is unresolved.
Current dictionary glosses include accusation, suing, informing, and narrating; this range does not establish a chronological sequence of meanings.
Cited examples are glossed as expressing or telling feelings. Their chronological relationship to reporting or accusation is unresolved.

sense.gloss: report a grievance; bring a complaint
sense.text: A passage cited from the Hanshu Chengdi annals uses 訴 for reporting grievances at court, supporting an early imperial attestation of this use.
The Shuowen glosses 訴 as 告, “report” or “tell,” and cites an Analects passage. The citation is a traditional textual reference, not a securely dated manuscript witness.
A recorded use means seeking recourse, but its date and relationship to the other uses are unresolved.
Current dictionary glosses for 试 and 試 include “test,” “try,” and “experiment.”
Dictionaries record uses glossed as probe, examination, and testing, without establishing when they arose or how they relate to use or appointment.
The received Shuowen account glosses 試 as 用也 (“use”); dictionaries also record uses meaning use or appointment. These are reported uses, not securely dated attestations here.

sense.period: Later examples are reported; precise chronology and semantic links unresolved
sense.text: Later examples show uses for narrated stories and informing or telling, but do not establish how or when these uses developed from the words-or-speech sense.

sense.period: Current usage; chronology of these senses unresolved
sense.text: Current meanings include speech, talk, language, and dialect. The available examples do not establish when these uses arose or a dated path from “good words.”

sense.period: Textual example in 《詩·大雅·抑》; precise composition and witness dates unresolved
sense.text: In 慎爾出話, from 《詩·大雅·抑》, 話 is glossed as 善言, “good words.” This gives an early textual context for the words-or-speech sense, but does not date the graph’s earliest use.

Current dictionary meanings include language, words, saying, and expression. The evidence does not establish when these uses developed in relation to the cited speak-or-discuss and tell uses. [E4, E11, X-f0406cd650ab46caf66f]

sense.period: dating unresolved; cited in an Analects example
sense.text: An Analects passage uses 語 for speaking or discussing. The surviving witness is not dated here, so the example does not establish the earliest attested use. [X-54c077aa35264a3b494e, X-f0406cd650ab46caf66f]

sense.period: dating unresolved; cited in an Analects example
sense.text: A separate Analects passage uses 語 for telling or addressing. Its chronological relation to the speak-or-discuss use is unresolved. [X-54c077aa35264a3b494e, X-f0406cd650ab46caf66f]
The traditional graph is recorded in admonishing and persuasion contexts. Their chronology relative to other senses is unresolved.
The traditional dictionary account records uses meaning “explain” and “discuss”; it does not establish their chronological relationship to speaking or saying.
The character is also glossed “scold” and “upbraid”; no chronology or development from another sense is established.
The character is used with the meanings “speak,” “say,” and “talk.” No securely dated earliest occurrence is established, so these meanings are not identified as the earliest attested sense.
A historical lexicographic gloss is 謁也. This gloss does not establish the earliest attested use or a hypothetical original meaning.
Invite is a recorded use of 請; its chronology relative to asking or requesting is unresolved.
請 is also used for a respectful request, including as “please.” The evidence does not date this use or establish how it developed from other uses.
The character is used to ask, request, or entreat. These are recorded uses, but their earliest attestation is not established here.

sense.gloss: a pause within a clause that remains unfinished
sense.period: historical use cited in later commentary; dating unresolved
sense.text: The reading dòu denotes a pause where the clause remains semantically unfinished. The cited example does not establish when this use or reading began.
A cited later example uses 讀 in connection with pronunciation, but its date and relation to the other uses are unresolved.
讀 and its simplified form 读 are used with the meanings “read” and “study.”

sense.period: early textual contexts reported; composition dates unresolved
sense.text: Examples associated with the Mencius and Strategies of the Warring States use 讀 in contexts of reading or studying books. Their chronology does not show when this use began relative to saying or uttering.

sense.period: early textual contexts reported; composition dates unresolved
sense.text: Examples associated with the Book of Odes and Zhuangzi use 讀 for saying or uttering. Their dates are unresolved, so this is the earliest use reported here, not a securely dated first meaning.
An administrative-division sense is recorded, but its date and connection to examination or educational meanings are unclear.
Current definitions include lesson, course, and classwork. Their historical connection, if any, to testing or official assessment is unclear.
A reported Former Han citation uses 課 in the context of assessing officials; the citation’s full textual dating details were not verified.
A traditional dictionary presents “order or rank” as an extension from testing or examination, without dating the development.
A traditional dictionary presents taxation as an extension from testing or examination, without dating the development.
A traditional dictionary glosses 課 as “test” or “examine.” This does not establish that meaning as the graph’s original meaning or earliest use.
Dictionary entries record an assertive use meaning “anyone,” but do not date it or establish whether it developed from the interrogative sense.
A dictionary records a rhetorical use, but its example is undated and its development from another sense is not established.
The traditional gloss 何也 and cited examples support an interrogative use for a person. The earliest surviving witness is not dated in the cited accounts.
Apologizing appears among cited uses of 謝. Its first attestation and connection to the other senses are not established.
Declining or refusing appears among the cited uses of 謝. The citations do not establish a first-use date or a definite development from resignation.

sense.period: Shuowen Jiezi gloss; first-attestation dating unresolved
sense.text: The Shuowen gloss for 謝 is “to depart or resign.” It records a dictionary meaning, but does not date the graph’s first use or establish this as its earliest attested sense.
“Thank” is a current gloss for 谢 and 謝. Its first use and historical relation to resignation or refusal are not established by the cited evidence.
Dictionary records list esteem, honor, and high social status. Their chronology and semantic path from the price sense are unresolved.
A traditional dictionary glosses 貴 as “not cheap”; current records also give “expensive” and “costly.” The dating of this sense in primary texts is unresolved.
Current dictionary records list “valuable” and “precious.” Their dating and whether they developed directly from “expensive” are unresolved.
Classical citations use 走 for fleeing or escaping. Their witnesses are not securely dated here, and they do not show when this sense developed in relation to “run.”
A historical sense “go or tend toward” is recorded, but the cited material does not establish its chronology relative to “run” or “flee.”
A clear verbal use is reported in the bronze-inscription phrase 夙夜奔走. The cited oracle-bone examples are reported as names or place names, not secure verbal attestations.
In modern use, 走 commonly means walking or going on foot. The evidence does not establish when this broader sense became current or how it developed from the older “run” sense.
Classical citations attest 起 used for beginning. A later philological interpretation treats this as an extension, but its timing and path through intermediate meanings are unresolved.
A classical citation documents a use for departure. Its chronology relative to standing, rising, or beginning is unresolved.
In the Chu manuscript phrase 天下之兵大起, 起 is interpreted as troops being raised or mobilized. The cited account gives no precise date and does not identify this as the earliest sense.

sense.gloss: rise; stand up; go up; begin
sense.text: These are recorded current meanings; their relative chronology is not established.
