Classical citations and dictionary definitions document rising or getting up, including rising from sitting or lying. They do not date this use relative to other meanings.
The transmitted gloss is “able to stand,” and classical citations document standing up. They do not establish this as the earliest use or original meaning.

sense.gloss: go about business; go or arrive
sense.text: Sources record business-related uses, and a modern dictionary also gives “go” or “arrive.” Their development from the movement sense is not established in detail.

sense.gloss: flee or leave in a hurry
sense.text: Historical examples and a modern dictionary record uses meaning to flee or avoid. The path from running to fleeing is not established in detail.

sense.period: attested in 龍龕手鑑; date of the relevant graph witness unresolved
sense.text: A dictionary records 跑 as a Qin usage meaning “kick.” Its relation to the pawing sense and its chronological priority are unresolved.

sense.gloss: paw or scrape the ground with the feet
sense.period: attested in Guangyun, compiled 1008; dates of earlier cited examples and graph witnesses unresolved
sense.text: The earliest gloss directly reported here describes feet pawing the ground. Cited examples include a horse pawing the ground and a Tang poem about a hungry horse pawing snow, but they do not establish a secure first-use date for the graph.

Historical examples use 跑 for running, and a modern dictionary lists rapid forward movement. Sources connect this use with pawing, but the examples do not establish the transition’s precise chronology.

sense.period: historical and current; first attestation unresolved
sense.text: 跟 means to go along after someone, attend, or accompany them. It is described as a later common sense, but its first attestation and a fully dated path from “heel” are unresolved.
The historical dictionary account gives “heel” or “back of the foot” as the sense. The received text includes 頭痒搔跟, but the consulted edition does not securely date that wording.

sense.gloss: rear or bottom part of an object; shoe heel
sense.period: historical and current; first attestation unresolved
sense.text: 跟 is also used for the rear or bottom of an object and for a shoe heel. A dated transition from the heel of the foot is not established.
跟 also functions as a preposition or conjunction, meaning “with,” “and,” or “to/toward.” The chronology and precise development of these uses from “follow” are unresolved.
Later examples attest figurative uses including method, approach, order, and route, but do not establish their chronology or precise development from the road or path sense.
Modern references include “journey” and “distance.” Their chronology and development from “road” or “path” are unresolved.
The received Shuowen definition glosses 路 as 道, “road” or “path.” This attests the sense but does not date its first use or show that it was the earliest sense.
An oracle-bone inscription is cited in a context concerning the king’s abdominal illness. This supports an early abdomen-related use; it does not establish abdomen as the original meaning.

sense.period: bronze inscriptions and Warring States manuscripts; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: Cited bronze inscriptions and Warring States manuscript examples use 身 for the body. “Body” remains its familiar current meaning.

sense.period: 詩經·大雅·大明; exact dating unresolved here
sense.text: The phrase 有身 is cited with the meaning “pregnant.” A development from an abdomen sense is proposed, but the examples do not show every step.

sense.gloss: self; one’s own person or action
sense.period: bronze inscriptions and later textual citations; exact chronology unresolved
sense.text: Cited bronze uses include one’s own action, and later textual examples use 身 for “self.” These uses are analyzed as extensions from body or person, though their full chronology is not established.
The common modern meaning includes vehicle and car.

sense.gloss: wheeled machines; transporting by cart; cartload measure
sense.text: Later dictionaries record these uses, but the evidence does not date their emergence or establish a continuous development from the vehicle sense.
An oracle-bone example is identified as a place-name use. Its meaning and any connection to the vehicle sense are unresolved.
Oracle-bone examples use 車 for vehicles, and bronze examples include vehicles and war chariots. These attest early vehicle-related use but do not establish a calendar-dated first occurrence.
One analysis proposes “beside” as an original sense of 邊; its earliest attestation and date remain unresolved.
边 and 邊 commonly mean a side or edge, including a margin or border. Their first occurrence and any continuous development from “beside” remain unresolved.
A use of 邊 meaning “frontier region” is reported in a bronze inscription, but its date and place in the word’s history remain unresolved.

sense.gloss: while, in the paired construction 邊…邊…
sense.text: 邊 is also used in the paired construction 邊…邊… to mean “while.” Its chronology and development from spatial meanings remain unresolved.
Classical citations show 過 used to mean “exceed,” but do not date the emergence of this sense.
A later commentary interprets “fault” or “error” as an extension of the passing sense. The timing and precise path of that development are unresolved.
The common current meaning includes passing, passing through, and going across.
The received Shuowen entry glosses 過 as 度也, interpreted as measuring or crossing a distance. The date of the earliest use is unresolved.

sense.period: later cited uses; exact chronology unresolved
sense.text: Cited uses include “also,” “more,” and “besides.” Their individual chronology and any path from “return” are not established.

sense.period: bronze and classical attestations; exact dates unresolved
sense.text: 還 is attested with the sense “go around” or “circle.” Its chronological relation to “return” is not established.
A classical citation uses 還 to mean “immediately.” Its relation to “return” or other senses is not established.
The received dictionary glosses 還 as 復, “return/repeat,” and cited classical material records “return.” Exact dates for the cited works and artifacts are not given here.

sense.period: Tang citations and later uses; exact chronology unresolved
sense.text: Adverbial uses include “still” and “yet”; a Tang citation has the sense “still/again.” No dated chain connects these uses to “return.”
The character can refer to a nearby place as well as a nearby thing; the evidence does not establish a separate chronology for this use.

sense.period: Warring States manuscript proposal; exact attestation unresolved
sense.text: A Warring States manuscript graph has been proposed as 這 used for a verb meaning “meet” or “receive,” but the identification remains an interpretation. This distinct lexical use has no demonstrated development into the demonstrative.
A reported Yuan drama example uses 這 as an empty metrical filler. Its relation to the demonstrative is not established.
The proximal demonstrative is reported in Tang material, including the expression 這回. This is the earliest attested period reported here, not proof of the word’s original meaning.
Entering is a current dictionary meaning; its emergence and connection to earlier uses are undated.

sense.period: Warring States Chu-slip examples reported; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: Forward or upward movement is reported in Warring States Chu-slip examples. This is the earliest meaning supported here, but it is not established as the graph’s hypothetical original meaning or as a development from earlier reported uses.

sense.period: Oracle-bone and bronze contexts; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: An oracle-bone use has been interpreted as an offering, while bronze uses are reported for recommending and presenting. These accounts establish neither a chronological development among these uses nor a connection to forward movement.
Making progress is a current dictionary meaning; its chronology and connection to earlier uses are not established.

sense.period: Warring States texts; later lexicographic attestation also recorded
sense.text: Warring States examples include figurative contexts, and a later lexicographic record lists figurative depth. The evidence does not date a development from the spatial sense to this use.
A dictionary records a verbal use meaning “keep away,” but the evidence does not date it or connect it historically to the spatial sense.
Warring States examples document 遠 in kinship contexts; the evidence does not date its development from spatial distance.
Modern definitions include spatial distance and figurative depth; their chronology is not established here.
Oracle-bone examples use 遠 for spatial distance, including a hunting context that contrasts it with near. This is an early attested use, not necessarily the character’s hypothetical original meaning.

sense.period: early received Shijing text; composition date unresolved
sense.text: A received poem uses 送 in a context interpreted as accompanying someone to a place. It attests an early accompanying or sending context, without settling the precise distinction between accompanying and seeing someone off.
A supplied modern definition includes ‘give,’ but no dated usage here establishes when this use arose or how it relates to sending.

sense.period: Han-dynasty lexicographic record and medieval dictionary record
sense.text: Shuowen glosses 送 as 遣; a medieval dictionary record gives the same gloss and a fanqie reading. These records attest the gloss in those dictionaries, not when the sense began.
Dictionary entries record guiding and speaking uses, but do not establish their chronology or relationship to the road and method senses.
道 is used for a method or principle, including philosophical Dao. The available examples do not date these senses or establish how they developed from “road; way.”

道 is defined as a way people travel, and a transmitted poem uses it in a road context. “Road; way” is the earliest meaning supported here, though the poem’s composition date and the graph’s first attestation remain unresolved.
Dictionary entries also record “route” and “journey.” Their listing does not establish when these uses arose or how they relate to the road sense.

sense.period: Tang poem cited; exact date unresolved
sense.text: A Tang poem uses 那 as a distal demonstrative, referring to something at a distance. This attests the use but does not establish when it began.
Interrogative 那, especially in rhetorical questions, is attested from the Eastern Han. Its origin and relation to the distal demonstrative remain disputed.

sense.gloss: name of a state or place
sense.text: The Shuowen entry describes 𨙻 as the name of a western state and mentions a place name. This establishes the recorded state-name account, not that it preceded the demonstrative.

sense.period: Reported in a lexicographic source; exact earliest attestation unresolved
sense.text: The totalizing word is written 都 and read dōu in Mandarin. Its proposed connection to 諸 concerns a possible reuse of the graph for a different word, not a demonstrated change from “city” to “all.” The early sound match remains uncertain.

sense.period: Western Zhou bronze use reported; exact dating of the spoken sense unresolved
sense.text: A bronze inscription associated with the 㝬鐘 is reported to use 都 for a city. This supports an early city use, not the claim that “city” was the word’s first meaning.
A classical citation records an elegant or beautiful sense, but its relation to the settlement and city senses is undetermined.
A cited Zhou ritual text records 都 as a territorial or fief category. Its chronological relation to the shrine-bearing settlement sense is undetermined.
Classical citations record large-city and capital uses. Their chronology relative to the institutional settlement and fief senses is undetermined.
In modern Mandarin, 都 is also read dōu for “all” or “the whole.” Its proposed historical connection to 諸 remains uncertain.
In modern Mandarin, 都 is read dū for city and capital meanings.

sense.gloss: settlement containing a former ruler’s ancestral temple
sense.period: Han lexicographic account; underlying spoken sense dating unresolved
sense.text: A traditional dictionary account defines 都 as a settlement containing a former ruler’s ancestral temple. This is a historical definition, not proof of the word’s earliest meaning.

sense.period: attested in bronze inscriptions; first occurrence unresolved
sense.text: A bronze use for a distance measure is reported. This establishes an attestation, not when the sense began or how it relates to settlement.

sense.gloss: inside or interior, in the use associated with 裏/裡
sense.text: 里 is reported writing 裏 in a bronze phrase about garment lining. This is use of the graph to write another word, not evidence that “inside” developed from the settlement sense. The interior sense is associated with 裏/裡 in later usage.

sense.period: Western Zhou bronze inscriptions (earliest reported graph attestation; first occurrence of this sense unresolved)
sense.text: The traditional account glosses 里 as habitation, and a Western Zhou bronze use for a settlement-related title is reported. This supports an early settlement sense, though the precise original referent remains interpretive.

sense.period: attested in historical uses; first occurrence unresolved
sense.text: Village and neighborhood are recorded senses, with settlement uses reported in early sources. The evidence does not establish a dated development from habitation to village or neighborhood.
“Double” is a documented current meaning, and historical phonology data associate a reading with “repeat; double.” The evidence does not date this sense or show that it developed from “thick; deep.”
“Heavy” is a documented current meaning; its emergence relative to the dictionary gloss “thick; deep” is undated.
A historical commentary proposes this sense as an extension of “thick; deep,” but its timing is not established.

sense.period: Han-dynasty dictionary gloss; dating of word use unresolved
sense.text: The transmitted dictionary glosses 重 with 厚, “thick; deep.” This historical gloss is not an established earliest use or proof of the graph’s original meaning.
Historical phonology data record a noun meaning “weight”; its chronology relative to “heavy” is unresolved.
A recorded use refers to coin-shaped objects; its chronology and connection to other senses are unresolved.
A recorded use has the meaning “fees”; its date and connection to other senses are unresolved.

sense.period: dating unresolved; cited in transmitted Odes wording and defined in the Han-era Shuowen account
sense.text: The Shuowen account defines 錢 as an ancient field implement, and a cited Odes line names it among agricultural tools. The wording’s exact date is unresolved.

sense.period: attested in cited Guoyu and Shiji passages; first use not dated
sense.text: 錢 occurs in cited monetary contexts, including passages about casting large coins and marked copper coins. These attest the money sense in the cited texts but do not date its first use.
钱 means money, currency, or coins.
A recorded use is a unit of weight; its date and connection to other senses are unresolved.
An alternating use is attributed to Wang Bo’s verse. This example does not establish a sequence connecting the other meanings.
An intercrossing use is cited in the Book of Odes, but the date of the textual witness and its relation to other senses are unresolved.

sense.period: Shuowen gloss; exact date of wording not established here
sense.text: The gloss 金涂也 describes metal coating or inlay. It does not establish whether this sense predates or follows the whetstone sense.
A mixed or disordered use is cited in the Classic of Documents. Its chronological relation to the whetstone and intercrossing senses is not established.

sense.gloss: whetstone or tool for working jade or stone
sense.text: A dictionary analysis identifies this as 錯’s original meaning and cites 錫貢磬錯, interpreted as working jade or stone. The date of the textual witness is not established here.
Wrong or error is among the recorded senses, with an example attributed to Mozi. The evidence does not show a continuous development from the other listed senses.
A verbal use meaning “to attack a city gate” is reported. Its relation to the gate noun and its chronology are unresolved.

sense.period: oracle-bone corpus examples; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: Oracle-bone corpus examples are reported using 門 for gates, including a temple gate and a hall gate. These attest the gate meaning but do not establish the graph’s first occurrence.
Uses meaning “lineage” or “category” are reported, but their chronology and semantic path from the gate sense are unresolved.
Current glosses include “gate,” “door,” “entrance,” and “opening”; these glosses do not establish a chronology among the meanings.
Uses meaning “path” or “key point” are reported, but their chronology and connection to the gate sense are unresolved.

sense.period: Late Warring States, as reported for the earliest clear graph in the surveyed evidence
sense.text: The earliest clear graph for the word meaning “ask” or “inquire” in the surveyed evidence is reported in late Warring States Qin slips. The received Shuowen gloss 訊 supports this meaning but does not itself establish the earliest use.
Current definitions include “ask about” and “inquire after.”

sense.gloss: discuss, investigate, interrogate, visit, give, and uses glossed as 通聞
sense.text: Historical dictionaries list these additional uses. Their dates and pathways from “ask” or “inquire,” or from one another, are not established, so they cannot be arranged as a sequence.

sense.period: Warring States evidence reported; exact dating of sense unresolved
sense.text: Warring States bronze and manuscript forms are interpreted as 間 meaning ‘between’. Older textual citations also show interval or between uses, but do not settle their precise chronology.
‘Place’ or ‘locality’ is listed as a meaning of 间; the evidence does not establish its development from ‘interval’ or ‘space’.
Later dictionary examples include ‘room’, but do not establish when or how this sense developed.
Historical explanations gloss 閒 as a gap and describe related uses for spaces or intervals. Their chronology relative to ‘between’ is not established.
Transmitted literary examples attest 院 in the courtyard sense. The evidence does not establish its first occurrence or a complete development from wall to courtyard.
Transmitted examples use 院 in institutional names and contexts, including an official institution and an academy. They do not establish every step connecting this use to the wall or courtyard senses.
School is a current dictionary gloss. Its first occurrence and development from earlier uses are not established here.

A cited Qin manuscript passage uses 院 in a context concerning boundaries between lanes and buildings; later glosses equate it with a wall or surrounding wall. This is the earliest use supported here, not proof of the character’s original meaning.
Historical lexicographic accounts record 難 as a bird name; the earliest surviving occurrence is not dated here.

Bronze contexts are reported for 難 meaning “difficult,” including uses glossed as difficult to do and difficult to approach. The inscriptions are not dated here, so priority among early senses is unresolved.
難 is also used as a noun meaning “difficulty”; the evidence gives no first attestation for this use.
Later literary examples use 雨 as a transitive verb. They attest this use but do not establish its chronology or development from the intransitive verb.
Cited oracle-bone inscriptions use 雨 as a noun for rainwater. This is an early attested use, not necessarily the graph’s original meaning.
雨 has the current gloss “rainy”; its development and chronology are not established here.
Other cited oracle-bone inscriptions use 雨 as a verb meaning “to rain.” The noun and verb are attested in the same broad corpus; which use came first is not established.
Cited commentary and later examples use 零 for falling, including the falling of rain, snow, frost, or dew. Their dates and relation to the rain sense are unresolved.

The Shuowen glosses 零 as “remaining rain,” and the Shijing phrase 零雨其濛 uses it with 雨. The poem’s date is unresolved, so this is the earliest sense supported here, not necessarily the word’s original meaning.
Dictionary examples attest scattered or residual quantities, fragments, and remainders. Their dates and connection to the falling-rain sense are not established as a single development.
零 is used for the number zero in standardized numeric notation. Its first use with this meaning is unresolved; the reported 1248 placeholder account is unverified.
A later dictionary records an ‘avoid’ sense; its relation to the other senses is unresolved.
Reported oracle-bone examples use 非 as a negative. Oracle-bone script is the earliest script class identified here, though the examples’ absolute dates are unresolved.
Modern references give negative meanings including ‘not’ and ‘non-’.

sense.period: Han-era dictionary explanation; earlier use unresolved
sense.text: The received Shuowen explanation gives 非 the sense ‘opposition’ and connects it with wings facing away. This does not establish opposition as an earlier lexical stage.
Later dictionary records include uses meaning reproach or criticize, but do not establish their path from the negative sense.

sense.gloss: fault or wrongness; judging something wrong
sense.period: bronze inscriptions reported; absolute date unresolved
sense.text: Reported bronze examples use 非 for faults and for judging something wrong. Their semantic or chronological relation to the negative use is unresolved.

sense.period: oracle-bone script period; individual attestations undated
sense.text: The oracle graph is interpreted as depicting a face; the Shuowen gloss describes the area before the face. This is the earliest supported sense here, though the individual inscriptions are undated.

sense.period: Chu-slip text cited by a modern database; date not supplied
sense.text: 面 is recorded with the sense “face toward” in a Chu-slip text.

sense.gloss: flour, dough, noodles (written 面 in simplified Chinese for 麵)
sense.text: In simplified Chinese, 面 writes the flour and noodle word for which traditional Chinese uses 麵. This is a writing substitution; the evidence does not establish semantic development from “face” or sound-based borrowing from the face word.
Dictionary records list “surface,” “side,” and “dimension.” Their dates and links to the face and facing senses are unresolved.

sense.gloss: head, including pig’s head in the cited oracle-bone contexts
sense.text: Oracle-bone contexts are interpreted as referring to a pig’s head and to bowing the head. These are documented early uses of traditional 頁; they do not identify the original spoken name of the pictured head.
“Leaf” is listed alongside page and sheet, but its dating and whether it is an independent single-character use are unresolved.
Modern 页 writes the page or sheet word through traditional 頁, which was used as a common spelling for 葉. This is a borrowed spelling, not an established semantic development from “head.”
In modern Chinese, 风 means wind or air.

sense.gloss: customs, demeanor, style, atmosphere, and related uses
sense.text: Older dictionary material records these senses, but does not establish their dates or a development from “wind.”

sense.period: late Shang (attested with an early bird-shaped graph)
sense.text: Late Shang divinations are reported to use an early bird-shaped graph for the word “wind.” A sound-based borrowing from a bird sign is proposed, but the bird’s referent and spoken name are uncertain.
飛 is glossed as a bird in flight, and early literary examples use it for flying. The composition dates of those works and the earliest secure surviving written attestation are unresolved.
The common current meaning is “fly.”
“High” or “elevated” is recorded as a sense; its chronology and relation to “fly” are unresolved.
Rapid movement is recorded as a sense, but its chronology and whether it developed from “fly” are unresolved.
Current meanings include cooked rice, food, and meal. The evidence does not date the first appearance of these noun senses.

sense.period: early literary use; precise date unresolved
sense.text: A transmitted Analects passage uses 飯 as a verb meaning “eat.” The passage’s composition date and the first occurrence of this sense are unresolved.
A historical interpretation connects the noun meaning “what is eaten” to the verb “eat.” No dated intermediate attestations are given.

sense.gloss: make hungry; cause to suffer hunger
sense.text: A literary citation records a causative use meaning “make hungry.” Its timing relative to the intransitive sense “be hungry” is unresolved.
“Greedy for” appears among modern glosses, but its chronology and relationship to “hungry” are unresolved.

The traditional character 餓 is glossed as 飢, “hungry,” and literary citations show its use for being hungry. These are the earliest supported sense and attestations here, though their dates do not establish when the character was first used.

sense.gloss: poor; lacking, including lack of water
sense.period: later dialectal usage; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: Later dialect examples use the word for being poor or lacking, including fields short of water. The evidence does not show when this sense arose or how it developed from “hungry.”

sense.period: some early literary usage; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: Some reported early passages distinguish 餓 from 飢 by degree, using 餓 for more severe hunger. This limited contrast is not a complete account of their historical meanings.
A traditional dictionary glosses 館 as lodging for guests and quotes a description of route stations holding provisions for visitors. The earliest securely dated attestation is unresolved.
馆 is used for public buildings and institutions. The available examples do not establish when or by what sequence this broader use developed from the lodging sense.
The character’s common meaning is “horse.” The earliest lexical use is not dated here.
The character is also used as a surname. Its earliest attestation and relation to the word “horse” are unresolved.
The traditional pictographic interpretation connects the tall structure with “high.” No verified inscription context securely establishes this as the earliest attested lexical sense.
The common current meaning is “high” or “tall.”

sense.gloss: high place or ridge; excellence, esteem, high price, old age, or a high or forceful voice
sense.text: Textual citations and dictionary records attest these uses, but do not establish when they arose or how they developed from “high” or “tall.” Their pathways are left unspecified.
A Qin bamboo-slip passage is reported to use 雞 for chicken. The oracle-bone place-name use does not show whether this was the graph’s earliest animal meaning.
The common current meaning is chicken.

sense.period: oracle-bone script tradition; exact dating unresolved
sense.text: An oracle-bone use of 雞 is reported as a place name. This shows a use of the graph but does not establish the place-name’s referent or the graph’s original lexical meaning.

sense.gloss: 谿, valley or stream, written with 雞
sense.period: Mawangdui manuscript witness; exact borrowing date unresolved
sense.text: In a Mawangdui text, 雞 is reported as a phonetic loan for 谿, “valley” or “stream”; another manuscript copy has 溪. The written sign was reused for a different word, apparently on the basis of sound similarity, rather than “chicken” developing into “valley.” The reported account supplies no contemporary pronunciations to demonstrate the sound match.

edges.subject: character:一
edges.text: An oracle-bone example uses 一 in the numeral phrase ‘one ox.’ The cited study describes the numeral as the smallest positive integer and discusses ordinal ‘first’ as well; these are attested uses, not proof of a hypothetical original meaning.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology Database, CUHK)
evidence.text: The entry reports oracle-bone 一 used as a numeral and gives the example 《合集》21575「一牛」 (‘one ox’). This supports an early numeric use, but the accessible result does not provide a date for that inscription.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — Oracle-bone entry for 一

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology Database, CUHK)
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 一 entry
evidence.text: The entry says oracle-bone and bronze forms represent the concept of one with an abstract horizontal stroke, and that these forms and the small-seal form use one horizontal stroke for the number one. It cites oracle-bone 《合集》21575「一牛」 as a numeral use. The page also discusses 弌 as a more complex form: it reports the received Shuowen label 古文一, then gives a later proposal deriving the shape through 戈 and 一, and marks the suggested 戌-based precursor as unattested and tentative. This is a source account, not independent verification of every proposed graphic transition.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 一

evidence.source: 李學勤主編, 字源, 2012, 天津古籍出版社／遼寧人民出版社
evidence.field: PDF p. 13, headword 一; printed page not visible/identified; scan SHA-256 ca587c8650396b510459c0da1f819d61c79392b822061989f317be87bc9fb70a
evidence.text: Inspected the attached scan pixels. The actual headword is 一, with reading yī and phonological labels “影组、质部; 影组、质韵、於悉切.” The entry calls it a 指事字, says the ancient graphs 一 through 四 use one to four horizontal strokes as primitive counting symbols, and identifies its basic meaning as the smallest positive integer. It cites 玉篇 and 尚書《洪範》 for “one as the beginning of number” and ordinal use. It says that from the Spring and Autumn/Warring States period 一 could be written with added strokes/components as elaborated forms, analogous to forms of 二 and 三, and that these spellings later fell out of use. This paraphrase relies on the scan-verified claims, not an emendation of its printed forms.
evidence.title: 字源, edited by 李學勤, 2012 edition

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Chinese Etymology Database)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 一; historical explanation and oracle-bone uses
evidence.text: The entry says oracle and bronze forms, as well as small seal, use a horizontal stroke for the number one. It records oracle-bone uses as a numeral in 《合集》21575「一牛」 and ordinal “first” in 《合集》2703「今一月」, and also gives the usage 《合集》41027「余一人亡(無)𡆥(憂)」. It does not supply an absolute date for those cited inscriptions on this page. Its discussion of 弌 is separate from the basic 一 graph: it reports a traditional Shuowen label 古文一 and describes later competing or tentative analyses of the added form.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析：一

edges.subject: character:一
edges.text: 一 is also used with the present-day function “a, an.” Its date and development from the numeral sense are unresolved.

evidence.source: Unicode Consortium
evidence.text: Official record for U+4E00 gives current kMandarin yī and kDefinition “one; a, an; alone.” This is present-day character metadata; it does not date those senses or establish their semantic order. The local Unihan_Readings.txt row checked for 一 is kMandarin yī, in agreement with this official page.
evidence.title: Unihan data for U+4E00

edges.subject: character:一
edges.text: 一 is also used with the present-day meaning “alone.” Its chronology and connection to the numeral sense are unresolved.

evidence.source: Unicode Consortium
evidence.text: Official record for U+4E00 gives current kMandarin yī and kDefinition “one; a, an; alone.” This is present-day character metadata; it does not date those senses or establish their semantic order. The local Unihan_Readings.txt row checked for 一 is kMandarin yī, in agreement with this official page.
evidence.title: Unihan data for U+4E00

edges.subject: character:七
edges.text: A paleographic study reports 七 used for the numeral in oracle-bone writing and cites an oracle-bone example. This is an early attested numeral use; it does not rule out the disputed proposal of an earlier cut-related use.

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Research on Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study reports that 七 has recorded the numeral from oracle-bone writing through early Western Han clerical forms. It describes the early graph as crossed horizontal and vertical strokes, and says a bent lower vertical stroke appears after the Eastern Han. Its proposed explanation for the graphic change is avoidance of confusion with 十. The article cites specific examples, including oracle-bone 合集10650, Western Zhou 小盂鼎 inscription 集成2839, Qin Shuihudi slips, and Eastern Han-period Wuwei medical slips. It also discusses alternate spellings 桼、漆、柒 and copy or printing errors in those forms; these are numeral spellings, not necessarily stages in 七’s graphic development.
evidence.title: 数词{七}的用字研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Research on Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study identifies 七 as the long-standing graph for the numeral. It reports crossed horizontal and vertical strokes from oracle-bone writing through early Western Han clerical forms, citing oracle-bone 合集10650 and Western Zhou bronze 小盂鼎 (集成2839). It describes later differentiation from 十, with a rightward bend in the lower vertical becoming established after the Eastern Han. This account treats the history as numeral writing and graphic differentiation; it does not establish an earlier ‘cut’ meaning.
evidence.title: 数词{七}的用字研究（一）

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Research on Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study cites oracle-bone 合集10650, Western Zhou 小盂鼎 bronze 集成2839, Qin Shuihudi slips, and Wuwei medical slips from around the Eastern Han transition. It says the pre-Eastern-Han crossing form persisted until early Western Han clerical writing and that the lower vertical later bent right. These cited objects supply examples in a graphic sequence, but the web page does not provide a directly inspectable image of each example in this research pass.
evidence.title: 数词{七}的用字研究（一）

edges.subject: character:七
edges.text: Japanese lexical evidence records なな for “seven” in an 8th-century Manyōshū example and しち in an example from 1477. These Japanese readings and uses do not explain the origin of the Chinese graph.

evidence.source: Kotobank, entry citing 精選版 日本国語大辞典 and 普及版 字通
evidence.field: Japanese lexical attestations and later senses
evidence.text: The dictionary gives a Manyōshū example (8th century, poem 4.743) for なな ‘seven’; 古事記 (712) for a use meaning that seven people perform an action; and 史記抄 (1477) as an example of the Sino-Japanese reading しち for the number seven. It also records a specialized later sense ‘gambler’ with a 1744 example. These are Japanese word and usage histories, not evidence for the origin of the Chinese graph.
evidence.title: 七(シチ)とは？ 意味や使い方

edges.subject: character:七
edges.text: A specialized Japanese sense meaning “gambler” is recorded with an example dated 1744. The evidence does not explain its development from “seven.”

edges.subject: character:上
edges.text: Reported Shang-period examples include 上帝, 上甲, and contrasts with 下; Zhou bronze examples include spatial ‘above.’ The cited dictionary definitions also support ‘above; upper side’ as a current meaning, without establishing priority among every lexical use.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析 / 上 / 字形與用例
evidence.text: The database describes the oracle-bone graph as a short stroke above a baseline, which could be curved in early forms and was often straightened in later forms because straight horizontal lines were easier to carve. It reports that early oracle-bone and bronze forms were similar to 二, with a vertical stroke added in late Spring-and-Autumn bronze forms to distinguish 上 from 下 and 二. It gives the original meaning as 'above/upper side.' Its examples include oracle-bone 上帝 (Heji 16703), 上甲 (Heji 6384), and a paired 上/下 passage (Heji 6204); Zhou bronze examples include 上 meaning 'above,' as in 㝬鐘, and 'on/at the side of,' as in 啟尊. These are source-reported readings and examples, not direct inspection of the inscribed artifacts here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Etymology)
evidence.field: 上 / semantic uses by inscriptional period
evidence.text: The dictionary separately reports Shang oracle-bone uses in 上帝, 上甲, and 上/下 contrasts; Zhou bronze uses include spatial 'above,' 'at/on the side of,' and 上帝, and it cites a Spring-and-Autumn-period tally where 以上 means 'more than.' It also notes a Chu-script form with 辵 added as a semantic element for movement upward. These reports show that spatial and lexical uses are attested in inscriptional contexts, but the listed examples do not establish a precise chronology for every later sense such as 'superior,' 'ruler,' or the verb 'ascend.'

edges.subject: character:下
edges.text: The graph indicates a lower position. Cited oracle-bone uses refer to lower deities and ancestral spirits; these examples attest use but do not establish either as the character’s original meaning.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 下 as an indicative graph: the Shang oracle-bone form places a short stroke below a longer reference stroke, expressing the lower position. It reports that the curved reference line was later commonly written as a horizontal line; early oracle-bone and bronze forms are identified as 𠄟. The entry says a vertical stroke was added in late Spring and Autumn forms to distinguish it from 上 and 二, and that Warring States regional forms no longer used 𠄟. Chu forms may add a short decorative stroke above. This conflicts in detail with the Academia Sinica account, which describes the reference as a horizon and puts the distinguishing change in small seal writing.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 下

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.field: 甲骨文 / bronze and transmitted-text uses
evidence.text: The entry cites oracle-bone 《合集》7428「下上若(諾)，受(授)我又(祐)」, interpreted as the agreement of lower deities and upper deities, and 《屯南》1115「下示五牢」, a sacrifice to the lower ancestral spirits. For bronze inscriptions it cites 番生𣪕蓋「廣啟厥孫子于下」 as 下 referring to the human world below, and records 下官 as an office and 下淢 as a place name. It describes later transmitted uses for humility toward a superior, then the verb sense ‘descend’, with ‘capture/take (a city)’ exemplified by 《戰國策·齊策六》「唯莒、即墨不下」. These attestations show multiple uses but do not establish a complete dated semantic sequence.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 下

evidence.source: 中央研究院文字學資料庫 / Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The graph-history note says the oracle-bone form has two horizontal strokes: the longer upper stroke represents the horizon and the shorter lower stroke is an indicative mark for ‘below’. It says a different 下 form arose in small seal script to avoid confusion with 二, changing the lower horizontal stroke to a vertical stroke. The page lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu bamboo-and-silk, small-seal, and Shuowen-seal sections, but its machine-readable text does not identify a dated specimen for each stage.
evidence.title: 漢字「下」：字形演變

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes the oracle-bone form as two horizontal strokes: the upper, longer line represents the horizon and the lower, shorter line is an indicative mark for ‘below’. It says a small-seal form changed the lower horizontal to a vertical stroke to avoid confusion with 二. This account is not fully aligned with CUHK’s placement of the added vertical stroke in late Spring and Autumn forms.
evidence.title: 漢字「下」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.field: 《說文》 entry and 形義通解
evidence.text: The entry quotes the received Shuowen explanation: 「丅，底也。指事。下，篆文丅。」 It interprets the oracle graph as a short stroke placed below a curved line, later often made horizontal; it says late Spring and Autumn forms commonly added a vertical stroke to avoid confusion with 上 and 二. It cites oracle-bone uses 《合集》7428 and 《屯南》1115, bronze uses including 番生𣪕蓋, and later extensions to humility, ‘descend’, and ‘capture/take’ (《戰國策·齊策六》). These examples show uses, but the entry does not provide a complete dated semantic sequence.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 下

edges.subject: character:不
edges.text: 不 is attested as a negative particle in oracle-bone inscriptions. The corpus is dated broadly; no specific occurrence is dated here.

evidence.source: Hilary Chappell and Alain Peyraube
evidence.text: The authors place 不 as a general negative marker in oracle-bone inscriptions of the 14th–11th centuries BCE. They give an oracle-bone example 王不往于田, ‘the king will not go hunting,’ and note that scholarship has proposed several distinctions between 不 and other early negatives, including 弗; the distribution is debated. For later Archaic Chinese they identify 不 as a general verbal negative and cite examples from the Analects (dated in the article to 479–400 BCE) and Xunzi (4th century BCE). This documents the negative word’s uses, not the graphic origin of the sign.
evidence.title: A Typological Study of Negation in Sinitic Languages: Synchronic and Diachronic Views

evidence.source: Chinese Character Database (CUHK)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析 / shape and meaning history
evidence.text: The database presents competing analyses: a horizontal ground line with root-like strokes, with Chen Shihui linking the graph to 茇, and a flower-calyx interpretation, with earlier scholars linking it to 柎. It quotes Shuowen’s bird-flying-upward account separately. Its entry reports oracle-bone use as a negative adverb, including 今至丁丑，其雨不？, and also as place, personal, and state names. Bronze examples are reported for negative use and readings/uses as 丕 ‘great’ and 邳, plus names. These are lexicographic reports, not a settled derivation or a dated chronology of semantic extensions.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析：不

evidence.source: Hilary Chappell and Alain Peyraube
evidence.text: The authors report 不 as a general negative marker in oracle-bone inscriptions of the 14th–11th centuries BCE. They cite 王不往于田, ‘the king will not go hunting,’ and date this corpus broadly rather than assigning a specific date to the inscription. They describe 不 as a general verbal negative in later Archaic Chinese, while discussing competing scholarship on the distribution of early negatives. This documents word use, not the graph’s pictorial origin.
evidence.title: A Typological Study of Negation in Sinitic Languages: Synchronic and Diachronic Views

They give an oracle-bone example 王不往于田, ‘the king will not go hunting,’ and note that scholarship has proposed several distinctions between 不 and other early negatives, including 弗; the distribution is debated. For later Archaic Chinese they identify 不 as a general verbal negative and cite examples from the Analects (dated in the article to 479–400 BCE) and Xunzi (4th century BCE). This documents the negative word’s uses, not the graphic origin of the sign.
evidence.title: A Typological Study of Negation in Sinitic Languages: Synchronic and Diachronic Views

evidence.text: Pictograph of a basket or a bag. The current meaning "east" is a phonetic loan. The simplified character 东 was adapted from the cursive form of the traditional character 東.

evidence.source: wiktionary

evidence.source: Outlier Linguistics
evidence.field: 東西南北, part 1, sections 東 and 束/橐
evidence.text: The article proposes bag-like origins for 東, 束, and 橐, reports 東 and 束 used interchangeably in bronze inscriptions, and analyzes east as a sound loan. It compares Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese forms 東 *tˤoŋ and 束 *s-tʰok, describing shared initial/root material despite differing codas. It also explains simplified 东 as derived from a cursive shorthand of 東. This is a modern specialist account; the specific name and pronunciation of the pictured sack are not independently recovered, so the phonetic pathway from the object's name to the word for east remains a proposal.

edges.subject: character:两
edges.text: Western Zhou bronze inscriptions attest quantity and measure uses, including a measure associated with pairs of horses. These examples do not securely date the first abstract numeral use.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, character entry 兩
evidence.text: The entry says bronze forms appear as 㒳, sometimes with an added top stroke; it presents the yoke/chariot-front explanation as a proposal attributed to 于省吾, and reports early bronze uses as a quantity word (‘two’) and a weight unit. It also notes a Warring States form with 羊 inside, interpreted as a sound marker. The page reports no oracle-bone forms for 兩, so its ancient examples are bronze, seal, and manuscript forms.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 兩

evidence.source: 李運富, “兩字職用演變研究（一）,” 河南大學漢字文明研究中心
evidence.text: The article cites early Western Zhou examples using 兩/㒳 as a measure for horses: 《小臣宅簋》 (8.4201), “金車，馬兩”; 《小臣守簋盖》 (8.4179–4181), “宾马两”; a mid-Western Zhou example 《㒼簋》; and 《𤼈鼎》. It says this dedicated horse-pair measure declined by late Western Zhou. The article identifies its own publication as 2014 and later inclusion in a 2016 volume. These examples support early quantity/measure use, but their dating does not by itself prove the proposed graphic motivation.

evidence.text: The entry reports bronze forms written 㒳, sometimes with a top stroke, and says a Warring States bronze form writes 羊 in the middle as a sound marker. It presents the chariot-front/yoke interpretation as a proposal attributed to 于省吾. It reports bronze uses for a quantity (‘two’) and a weight unit, including 小臣宅簋 and 平宫鼎, and records no oracle-bone form in the entry.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 兩

evidence.source: 李運富、何余華, “两”字职用演变研究（一）
evidence.field: sections on graphic history and early use, published 2017-05-09
evidence.text: The authors report initial 㒳 forms in early Western Zhou bronzes, including 盝驹尊 and 卫盉; a form with a top stroke appears by the Spring and Autumn period and gradually replaces 㒳, becoming dominant after the Han. They review the traditional distinction between 㒳 for ‘two’ and 兩 for the weight unit, but adopt the view that they are one graph. Their own proposal derives the shape by modifying part of 車 to mark a pair of horses as a dedicated measure; they explicitly describe this as a hypothesis after raising objections to a straightforward vehicle depiction. They cite Western Zhou uses: 《小臣宅簋》 ‘金車，馬兩’ and 《小臣守簋盖》 ‘宾马两’ (early Western Zhou); 《㒼簋》 and 《𤼈鼎》 (mid-Western Zhou). The date and examples establish early measure uses, not the proposed graphic motivation or a secure semantic chain to all later senses.
evidence.title: “两”字职用演变研究（一）

edges.subject: component:中
edges.text: The early graph is described as a whole pictorial form; this does not claim that it divides into separate modern components.

evidence.source: CASE 報科學（國立臺灣大學）
evidence.field: 最早的「中」字及其造字初義、用法
evidence.text: Reports late-Shang oracle-bone and bronze forms with a long vertical shaft and sometimes attached streamers, plus a central circular or square feature; it also notes forms without streamers. It cites oracle-bone examples of 立中 in military, weather-related, and ancestral-ritual contexts. The author reviews competing interpretations of the center feature (including drum, central marker, sundial-related feature, and attachment) and says the evidence does not settle its referent. The article rejects the arrow-and-target account as unsupported by the graph and describes several other functional reconstructions as partly conjectural. Thus the dossier's flag-and-drum story is one proposal, not a secure component analysis.

evidence.source: CASE 報科學（國立臺灣大學）
evidence.field: 最早的「中」字及其造字初義、用法
evidence.text: The article describes late Shang oracle-bone and bronze forms with a long shaft, sometimes with streamer strokes, and a circular or square feature at the center. It reports variants without streamers; Western Zhou bronze forms continue both types, and some omit the central feature. The article reviews flag, marker, wind instrument, gnomon, arrow-and-target, drum, and ritual-pole interpretations. It rejects the arrow account for lack of an arrow shape and describes several other functional explanations as conjectural. The article ultimately favors a ritual pole bearing an ancestral inscription, but that is its conclusion, not a settled referent.

edges.subject: character:中
edges.text: 中 commonly means “middle” or “center.” The evidence does not show that this was necessarily its earliest lexical meaning.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形) – a flagpole, as depicted in its original form 𠁩. Based on archaeological evidence, the middle box has been interpreted as a drum (建鼓). This flagpole with a drum was placed in the center of a field to gather people and to detect the direction of the wind. In addition, the pronunciation of 中 (OC *tuŋ, *tuŋs) is reminiscent of the beating of a drum.
Shuowen interprets the character as a vertical stroke 丨 passing through the center of 口, indicating the center.
It has also been interpreted as an arrow in the center of a target.
“Middle; centre” (Pronunciation 1) > “to hit the centre; to attain” (Pronunciation 2).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *t/duŋ. Cognate with Tibetan གཞུང (gzhung, “middle, center”).
Related to:
* 衷 (OC *tuŋ, *tuŋs, “middle; inner garment; inner feelings”);
* 仲 (OC *duŋs, “second (of the brothers or months)”).

edges.subject: character:九
edges.text: A cited oracle-bone passage uses 九 for a body part read as elbow or wrist, consistent with the interpretation that the graph is an early form associated with 肘.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese Character Database: With Word-formations）
evidence.field: 甲骨部件分析 / 九 / 形義通解
evidence.text: The database reports that oracle-bone 九 depicts an arm and is the original graph for 肘; it says the same form continued in Shang–Zhou bronze and Warring States writing. It cites 《合集》13677正「疾九(肘)」 as an oracle-bone use for elbow, and 《合集》358「𤉲(燎)九牛」 and 《合集》8108「九月，才(在)鯀」 as numeral uses. It also cites a bronze vessel inscription recording the king’s nineteenth year. The database attributes the elbow analysis to 丁山、明義士、李孝定, and says the graph was later borrowed for the numeral.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

edges.text: One proposed explanation links practice with repeatedly flapping wings, but this development is not established by the reported attestations.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 羽 (“wings”) + 日 (“sun”) – to learn to fly, to practice flying.
In the current form, 日 (rì, “sun”) has changed to 白 (bái, “white”), so the present form is 羽 (“wings”) + 白 (“white”).
Alternatively, the original form may have been a phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ljub): phonetic 彗 (OC *sɢʷeds, *ɢʷeds, *sɢʷids) + semantic 日 (“sun”).
Two general semantic fields are found in the senses: "to flap the wings; to flutter" and "to practice". They are generally considered to be the same word, with the link being "to repeatedly flap the wings (in order to learn to fly)", a sense attested in Liji.
Area word:
* Proto-Sino-Tibetan *sV-ləp (“to learn”): Tibetan སློབ (slob, “to learn”), སློབས (slobs, “exercise; training”); Mizo tlip (“to repeat; to do again; to perfect”),
* Mon-Khmer: Khmer ធ្លាប់ (thlŏəp, “to become accustomed to; to have the habit of; marker of continuous action in the past”); Proto-Mon *le̤p ("to know how to, be skilled in") > Mon လေပ် (lèp, “to be versed in”).

evidence.text: The dataset gives 書 as Middle Chinese syo, Old Chinese *s-ta (“write”), and 者 as Middle Chinese tsyaeX, Old Chinese *tAʔ (“nominalizing particle”). edges.subject: character:了
edges.text: Historical dictionary citations include “finish; be completed”; a Tang poem uses 未了 for “not ended” or “not finished.” The earliest attestation and the connection between this meaning and the graphic interpretations remain unresolved.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
According to the Shuowen Jiezi, a pictogram (象形) of a baby without arms. Compare with 子, where the arms are visible. The Shuowen defines 了 as "the crossing of lower legs".
In the Shuowen Jiezi Zhu, a commentary to the Shuowen Jiezi, it is said that the pictogram instead depicts entangled legs (了戾).
Its relation with the meaning "to finish" is likely via sound loan, but an argument can be made about "entangled legs" → "tie"→ "finish".
Unrelated to 亨.
Verb “to finish; to be completed” > perfective aspect particle (了₁, weakened form) > change-of-state modal particle (了₂). It eventually replaced classical 矣 (OC *ɢlɯʔ).
Two kinds of particle uses of 了 can be distinguished: the perfective aspect particle after verbs (conventionally written as 了₁) and the sentence-final modal particle (了₂). It is generally accepted (Wu, 1998) that these two uses of 了 are derived from the concrete verb “to finish”. The grammaticalisation of this verb had become common in the Tang Dynasty, initially in the form of ‹verb + (object) + perfective 了› to indicate the completion of an action.
The perfective particle subsequently underwent further grammaticalisation to become the sentence-final change-of-state modal particle; Liu (1985) has demonstrated that this last step may have involved the coalescence of sentence-final 了 with 也 in certain Mandarin dialects, as the pronunciations of 了₁ and 了₂ are distinct in these dialects, with 了₂ rhyming with 也.
Contrary to the suggestion in Schuessler (2007), this word is not related to Vietnamese rồi, due to the non-existent correspondence between any given phonemes. Thai แล้ว (lɛ́ɛo, “to be finished; already; then, afterwards”), Lao ແລ້ວ (lǣu, “to finish; to be completed; perfective particle”) are loans from Chinese.

edges.text: Bronze-inscription examples attest 事 for duty or office. The cited examples do not establish this use as earlier than the other attested uses.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: Historical attestations and semantic uses of 事
evidence.text: The database cites bronze inscriptions for 事 meaning duty/office, event, and serving/commanding. It cites transmitted early texts for matters/events (including Analects 為政, ‘有事，弟子服其勞’) and for serving/undertaking (Analects 顏回, ‘請事斯語矣’; Xunzi 非相). Its examples distinguish evidence for word senses from the account of graphic development. The site gives inscription names and received-text citations but not exact archaeological dates or a complete textual dating argument; semantic chronology beyond the attested examples remains uncertain.

evidence.text: The database reports bronze-inscription uses for duty/office (麥鼎, 克鼎), event (琱生簋), office (小盂鼎), and command or service (小臣守簋). edges.subject: component:二
edges.text: In this character, the complete two-stroke sign indicates the quantity two; this edge records its function as a whole sign, not an internal division.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Two horizontal strokes, representing the number two.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogram (指事) - two parallel strokes. Compare with 一, one stroke meaning one, 三, three strokes meaning three, and 亖 (sǐ), four strokes meaning four. Duplication of 一 (“one”).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *kV-ni-s. Cognate to Tibetan གཉིས (gnyis), Sikkimese ཉི (nyi), Tangut 𗍫 (*njɨ̱¹), Burmese နှစ် (hnac), and Nuosu ꑍ (nyip). See also: 次 (OC *sn̥ʰis, “second; next”), a cognate within Chinese languages.

evidence.source: 漢典 (zdic.net), 二 entry
evidence.text: The dictionary characterizes 二 in ancient writing as two horizontal strokes used as a primitive counting sign, and lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu slip/silk, Shuowen, Qin slip, clerical and regular-script form categories. This supports a straightforward numeral-sign analysis; its simplified listing is not a dated inscriptional history.

edges.text: A scholarly article reports that a sixth-century dictionary entry glossed 些 as “this” and “particle.” The report does not establish which sense came first or identify an original meaning.

evidence.source: 羅忱烈, “楚「些」字的形音問題”
evidence.field: earliest lexicographic record; competing graphic histories
evidence.text: The article says the earliest surviving dictionary record it identifies is the sixth-century Yupian entry under 此, with readings 息計切 and 息箇切 and glosses 此也、辭也. edges.subject: character:京
edges.text: 京 is interpreted as a tall building or platform; the Shuowen account instead describes a high man-made mound. The evidence does not resolve which interpretation best captures its earliest meaning.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 人所爲絕高丘也。从高省，| 象高形。凡京之屬皆从京。

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database labels the graph forms as oracle-bone, bronze, and small-seal script. Its explanation identifies the oracle-bone and bronze forms as a tall building: roof above, tower in the middle, and wall below; it says the small-seal form simplified the tower element to 口. This supports a building interpretation, but the database does not provide dated individual attestations in the accessible text.
evidence.title: 漢字「京」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database reports a high platform / tall tower interpretation and quotes Shuowen’s high-mound analysis. It also gives a related-size interpretation (large) and reports 郭沫若’s comparisons linking 京 to large mounds, granaries, animals, and strength. These are dictionary interpretations, not a demonstrated dated chain from mound to capital.

edges.subject: character:京
edges.text: 京 means “capital city”; an example occurs in a cited Tang poem. This does not establish when the sense began or how it relates to the high-structure or mound interpretations.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry cites 詩經·小雅·甫田, “曾孫之庾，如坻如京,” with Mao’s Han-period gloss “京，高丘也” (‘京, a high mound’). It also cites 管子·輕重丁 for a granary sense, 左傳·莊公二十二年 for “equal/compare,” and 白居易·琵琶行 for capital-city use. The latter is a Tang poem; this is an attestation by cited work, not an exact manuscript date. The sources available here do not establish when capital use began or whether it arose through mound-to-settlement semantic extension, another path, or a distinct word sense.

edges.subject: character:人
edges.text: The graph depicts a person. Cited oracle-bone examples use it in contexts glossed ‘ten people’ and ‘I, the king’; the individual specimens are not dated here.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 甲骨文 and 金文 usage
evidence.text: The database describes 人 in ancient forms as a person standing in profile with hands lowered; it gives the original sense as ‘person’. It cites Shang oracle-bone examples 《合集》22626 ‘伐十人’ (ten people killed) and 《合集》20328 ‘余一人’ (the king’s self-reference), and bronze-inscription uses including ‘庶人’ (common people) and ‘人民’. It also reports a bronze-inscription phonetic loan 人 for 年 in one vessel inscription, a separate graph borrowing from 人’s role as sound element in 年.

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》
evidence.field: 人 entry; printed p. 698; PDF p. 711
evidence.text: The 人 entry identifies the graph as pictographic, resembling a person in side view, and gives its basic sense as ‘person.’ It describes two early graphic variants—one joining head-like and torso-like parts, another joining head-like and arm-like parts—as equivalent in meaning; it says the former underlies the Shuowen Small Seal form, while the latter was more common in clerical script and developed into regular 人. edges.subject: component:十
edges.text: In the traditional 人+十 analysis, 十 contributes the number ten to the group- or unit-of-ten sense associated with 什.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 相什保也。从人、十。

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.text: The entry says the basic sense is “taking ten as a unit,” quotes the Shuowen account “相什保也。从人、十,” and cites *Zuo zhuan*, Duke Zhao year 1: “以什共車，必克.” It also reports a later use of 什 as 十 and an interrogative use from Tang-Song onward. This supports an analysis of the graph as 人 plus 十 associated with a group of ten, while Shuowen’s wording remains a historical explanation rather than independent proof of the formation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 字頭「什」

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry records the Shuowen explanation for 什 as “相什保也。从人、十” with fanqie 是執. It separately lists the ten-unit sense, cites 管子 for “十家為什，五家為伍,” and records a miscellaneous sense with a 後漢書 example. This supports reporting the historical 人+十 analysis and associated ten-unit sense, without assigning 十 a phonetic role or treating the Shuowen account as independent proof of formation.
evidence.title: A00070 什 — Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 《說文》; 形義通解; 《廣韻》; 中古音
evidence.text: The entry repeats the Shuowen 人、十 analysis and calls the basic sense “以十個為單位,” citing 左傳·昭公元年 “以什共車，必克.” It gives the later use equal to 十 with a 賈誼 example and says the interrogative-pronoun use is found from Tang-Song onward, citing Su Shi. Its Guangyun information is 是執; the listed Middle Chinese categories are voiced retroflex sibilant, entering tone, third division, 侵/緝. The entry does not label 十 as phonetic, and its entries provide cited literary examples rather than dated physical witnesses.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 字頭「什」

edges.text: A separate account says 甚 was reused to write interrogative words and 什 then served as another spelling. This proposed graph reuse depends on a sound resemblance; it is not a semantic development from “group of ten,” and the sound relation to the ten-unit word is not established.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: This entry treats 什 as a variant of 甚 specifically in interrogative use. It says 甚 had an earlier meaning glossed “尤安樂,” was later borrowed for interrogative words such as 甚麼, and 什 became a spelling used for that interrogative use. This gives a distinct whole-graph borrowing/spelling history for the interrogative use; it is not evidence that 什 originated as a phonetic component in its original 人+十 graph.

edges.subject: character:今
edges.text: 今 is documented as a phonetic element in 吟. In the Zhengzhang system, 今 is reconstructed as krɯm and 吟 as ŋɡrɯm: their rhyme sequences are comparable, though their initials differ. This later role does not establish 今’s proposed original word.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The 吟 entry quotes the Shuowen analysis 从口，今聲. In that later graph, 口 is the semantic element and 今 is explicitly the phonetic element. This independent phonetic role does not depend on resolving what the older graph 今 originally depicted.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.text: The database describes 从 in oracle-bone and bronze forms as two 人 figures arranged one after another, the early graph for 從, with the sense ‘follow’. edges.text: The Han dictionary glosses 从 as ‘heed’ and analyzes it as two 人. A later editorial account relates this sense to ‘follow/accompany’ by extension, but the transition is not securely dated.

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》, Taiwan Ministry of Education
evidence.text: The dictionary reports that 說文 treats 从 and 從 as separate entries: 从 is glossed 相聽也 with 二人, while 從 is 隨從也 and analyzed as 从 plus 辵, with 从 also serving as phonetic. The editor notes that the meanings are related by extension and that oracle-bone material uses only 从; in this account, the split into two 說文 entries reflects later usage. This is an editorial historical interpretation, distinct from simply repeating Xu Shen’s Han-dynasty analysis.

edges.subject: component:亻
edges.text: 亻 is commonly analyzed as the person-category component of 他.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 亻 represents the meaning and 也 represents the sound.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *l̥ʰaːl): semantic 亻 (“man”) + phonetic 也 (OC *laːlʔ).
Corrupted form of 佗 (OC *l̥ʰaːl, *l'aːl), which is found in Zuozhuan.
Etymology not clear (Schuessler, 2007). Perhaps cognate with 誃 (OC *l'al, *l̥ʰjalʔ, “to separate”).
The modern sense of "he, she, it" only emerged after the Han period in colloquial passages, and displaced classical 其 (OC *ɡɯ) and 之 (OC *tjɯ) in Mandarin dialects (Pulleyblank, 1995).
The phonological development from Middle Chinese was irregular. The expected reflex is tuō, which is sometimes used in literary contexts for the classical "other" sense, but in most Mandarin dialects it is read like tā.

edges.text: A common structural analysis assigns 也 a phonetic role, but the supplied historical readings do not establish a close match or prove that role.

edges.subject: character:佗
edges.text: Dictionary accounts report 佗 as used for 他 and describe 他 as a later form, without fixing the date or precise graphic mechanism.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 佗 entry: explanatory notes and cited forms
evidence.text: The entry gives 佗 a Shuowen analysis, “from 人, with 它 as sound,” and cites 左傳 隱公元年 “佗邑唯命” for 佗 meaning “other place,” plus later cited uses. Its note under the tā reading says 佗 is also used for 他 and quotes the Shuowen note that 佗 was borrowed for 它 and later俗作他. This supports a historical association between 佗 and 他 in “other” usage, but the entry does not establish a precise date or mechanism for the graphic change.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *l̥ʰaːl): semantic 亻 (“man”) + phonetic 也 (OC *laːlʔ).
Corrupted form of 佗 (OC *l̥ʰaːl, *l'aːl), which is found in Zuozhuan.
Etymology not clear (Schuessler, 2007). Perhaps cognate with 誃 (OC *l'al, *l̥ʰjalʔ, “to separate”).
The modern sense of "he, she, it" only emerged after the Han period in colloquial passages, and displaced classical 其 (OC *ɡɯ) and 之 (OC *tjɯ) in Mandarin dialects (Pulleyblank, 1995).
The phonological development from Middle Chinese was irregular. The expected reflex is tuō, which is sometimes used in literary contexts for the classical "other" sense, but in most Mandarin dialects it is read like tā.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声): semantic 亻 (“person”) + phonetic 門 (OC *mɯːn).
First attested in the Song dynasty (Lü, 1940). Various other glyphs representing *mVn have been attested in Song dynasty texts, including 懣, 滿, 瞞, 門.
It is probably related to 弭 (MC mjieX) (in 我弭) and 偉 (MC hjw+jX) (in 兒郎偉 /儿郎伟 (érláng wěi)) attested in the Tang dynasty (Lü, 1940); it is related to 每 (měi), as in 我每 (wǒměi), common during the Jin (Jurchen), Yuan and early Ming dynasties (Lü, 1985).
Proposed etymologies:
* From the personal pronoun plural marker 輩 (OC *puːls) (Lü, 1985; Feng, 1997; Li, 2013).
* From 門 (MC mwon, “door; clan; family”) (Ota, 2003; Yu, 1989; Li and Shi, 2000).
* From 每人 (MC mwojX nyin, “everybody”) (Norman, 1988); compare Eastern Min 各儂／各侬 (“everybody”), used in 我各儂／我各侬 (“we; us”), 汝各儂／汝各侬 (“you (plural)”), 伊各儂／伊各侬 (“they”).
* From 物 (MC mjut, “thing”) (Jiang, 1995).
* From plural features in Dravidian languages, cf. Classical Tamil -m, -mar, -mār suffixes, Tamil நாம் (nām, “inclusive we”), via Indic languages by means of Buddhist transmission (Chen & Ye, 2020).
Also compare 您.

edges.subject: character:会
edges.text: Reported bronze and Warring States examples use 會 for meeting at a place, joining ideas, and meeting in alliance. A fragmentary oracle-bone example may have the sense “meet,” but that reading is tentative.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.field: 形義通解；字形分類；出土用例
evidence.text: The database describes 會 in oracle-bone and bronze forms as 合 plus a container-like element: a lid covering a vessel and its contents, with the proposed original sense ‘fit together’. It reports oracle-bone 《合集》1030正「會我」 as a damaged, uncertain possible ‘meet/assemble’ use; bronze inscription 𠫑羌鐘「入長城，先會于平陰」 uses it for meeting at a place. The database also reports a bronze form with 彳 in some inscriptions and interprets it as meeting on a road. Warring States bamboo texts use 會 for joining, e.g. 郭店《語叢一》36 「所以會天道人道也」. These are separate records of graphic analysis and lexical uses; the oracle-bone ‘meeting’ reading is explicitly tentative.

evidence.text: This account identifies a passage in the early medical text 《灵枢经·邪客》, ‘邪气恶血固不得住留；住留则伤筋络,’ as an early known example of 住, and says late Han–Three Kingdoms texts use it more often for stopping or remaining (including combinations such as 住车、住马、住船、住军). It distinguishes this early ‘remain/stop’ use from the later or separately documented dwelling sense. The accessible page does not give a manuscript date for the cited 《灵枢经》 line, and the cited text’s transmission history prevents treating the quoted phrase alone as a securely dated earliest graph attestation.
evidence.title: 汉语词汇史漫谈 | 汪维辉：古代人如何“居住”

evidence.source: 汪維輝, 漢語詞彙史漫談
evidence.field: 住的早期用例與語義變化
evidence.text: The author identifies a Western Han passage in Jia Yi’s 新書 as an early ‘stay/remain’ use and a line in 靈樞經 as another early example, while cautioning that the latter text’s dating is uncertain. The account places frequent ‘stop/remain/stand’ uses in Eastern Han Buddhist translations and traces residence uses from late Han–Three Kingdoms texts, becoming dominant by the Eastern Jin 法顯傳. These are literary-text attestations reported by a modern secondary study, not securely dated manuscript attestations; its proposed semantic path is stop/remain or stand → stay/lodge → reside.
evidence.title: 汉语词汇史漫谈 | 汪维辉：古代人如何“居住”

edges.text: Early examples associated with 乍/作 writing include clearing land, building a settlement, casting, and broader making or action. These support a work/action range but do not establish the earliest dated use of 作 itself.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（香港中文大學）
evidence.field: 乍；形義通解、甲骨文與早期用例
evidence.text: The database describes 乍 as an early graph for clearing vegetation, citing oracle-bone examples 乙8502 for clearing land and 合集13509 for building a settlement. It traces extensions to labor, construction and casting, and says 人 was added to distinguish 作 (labor/work) after 乍 was used for sudden or temporary meanings. It also cites bronze inscriptions for casting, building, making law and ‘serving as’ a standard, plus Warring States bamboo slips for both ‘serve as’ and ‘suddenly/temporarily.’ These are source analyses and cited examples, not a chronology inferred from a gloss list.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary reproduces two Shuowen textual forms: the Great Xu text says 从几, while Duan’s edition reads 从儿; both give the infant/fontanel explanation. edges.subject: character:元
edges.text: Early forms are interpreted as depicting a human head. The cited oracle-bone and bronze examples use 元 for other meanings; ‘head’ occurs in transmitted 左傳 and 孟子 passages.

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for Excavated Texts and Paleography, preface to Bi Xiujie, *Shangdai jinwen quanbian*
evidence.field: discussion of 元 oracle bone and Shang bronze forms
evidence.text: The article identifies the graph’s original sense as ‘human head.’ It describes two oracle-bone forms, Heji 00006 and 18747: a head rendered as a linearized square or as a long horizontal stroke with a short stroke above. It compares a Shang bronze form on the *Bei Yuan zuo fu Wu you* and says it depicts a human head. This supports the head interpretation, but does not establish that the strokes specifically represent a person 儿 plus the numeral 二.
evidence.title: 畢秀潔博士《商代金文全編》出版

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, 元 entry
evidence.field: 形義通解; dated graph uses and citations
evidence.text: The entry analyzes early forms as 人 with a round point or square highlighting the head, with the mark sometimes reduced to a horizontal stroke; an extra short stroke could be added decoratively. It reports oracle-bone 元卜 in Heji 23390 as ‘first divination’; bronze uses include 元年 on the Western Zhou mid-period 師酉簋 (‘first year’), 元德 on 番生簋蓋 (‘great virtue’), and other senses ‘first,’ ‘eldest,’ and ‘special-use.’ It notes the graph is not attested with the literal ‘head’ sense in its cited oracle-bone or bronze examples, while that sense occurs in the transmitted *Zuo zhuan* and *Mengzi*. The account reports a proposal that 元 and 兀 are a split from one graph, and separately records an alternative proposal taking the two upper strokes as 上 over 人; it argues the latter is not based on the most pictorial early shape, which has a dot.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：字頭「元」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, 元 entry
evidence.text: The entry distinguishes graph history from lexical senses: the oracle-bone citation 元卜 is interpreted as ‘first divination’; bronze inscriptions use 元 for ‘first/beginning’ and also ‘great.’ It cites *Zuo zhuan*, Duke Xi 33, 狄人歸其元, for ‘head,’ and *Mengzi*, Teng Wen Gong II, 勇士不忘喪其元, for ‘head.’ These transmitted-text citations establish older documented usage in their respective texts, but this research did not verify composition dates or manuscript dates and does not treat them as dated physical inscriptions.

evidence.text: The database reports competing explanations: early 六 and 入 are graphically alike and may once have been one graph, with added strokes later distinguishing the numeral; another proposal treats 六 as a shelter picture and an earlier graph for 廬; a third treats it as a conventional early counting mark. It regards the Shuowen explanation through 易 numerology as unlikely to preserve the graph’s original meaning. It cites oracle-bone numeral uses as cardinal in 合集 32320 (‘燎六羊’) and ordinal in 合集 7775 (‘今六月王入于商’), then gives numeral examples from bronzes and Warring States texts. edges.subject: character:兴
edges.text: Early contexts are reported with a sense of rising or getting up; one oracle-bone use is described in connection with illness improving. This does not prove that rising was the character’s original meaning, and the chronology is incomplete.

evidence.source: CUHK 漢語多功能字庫, 漢字甲骨部件分析
evidence.text: The entry describes the oracle-bone form as 舁 plus 同: four hands jointly lifting a tube- or bucket-like object; the center may also have a 口 below. It gives the basic sense as “rise/get up.” It reports oracle-bone uses as a personal or state name, cites a reading of 同 as 興 in a divinatory text about an illness improving, and records bronze-inscription uses as a personal or clan name and in the sense “mobilize/raise troops.” It also cites bamboo and silk manuscript uses for “arise,” “raise troops,” and “levy labor,” as well as received-text examples.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：興

evidence.source: 復旦大學出土文獻與古文字研究中心, 裘錫圭
evidence.field: discussion of 興 graph structure and ancient forms
evidence.text: The article argues that 興 depicts people jointly lifting a heavy object, but cautions that the object and its name cannot be confidently identified. It notes that an abbreviated 興-like form occurs in Wu Ding period oracle-bone inscriptions and discusses forms with an added 口; it treats the received 說文 analysis 从舁从同 as an old interpretive account, not settled proof of the original structure. It explicitly allows that the object’s name might have been 興, 同, or another word. The article discusses a later inscriptional reading of 興 as rising/recovering from illness, but does not establish a complete dated sequence of senses.
evidence.kind: scholarly article discussing primary inscriptional evidence
evidence.title: 裘錫圭：大豊（禮）簋銘新釋

edges.subject: character:再
edges.text: Bronze inscriptions are reported using 再 to mean “again” or “a second time.” The evidence does not establish whether this use preceded “two.”

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: 《說文》 entry and dated usage discussion
evidence.text: The database quotes Shuowen’s analysis ‘一舉而二也。从一，冓省’ and Duan Yucai’s later gloss that 冓 means 架. It reports bronze inscriptions with 再 meaning ‘second time/again’ (including 陳璋方壺 and 叔尸鐘) and ‘two’ in 𠫑羌鐘 (‘twenty-two’); Warring States bamboo texts include 再三 and the Zuozhuan phrase 一鼓作氣，再而衰，三而竭. It separately reports a possible loan of 再 for 在 in a Guodian slip and marks the interpretation as uncertain. The page does not supply absolute dates for each cited artifact/text, so none are assigned here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 字頭「再」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: 形義通解; graphic analysis and historical usage
evidence.text: CUHK says 再’s oracle and bronze construction and original meaning are unsettled. It reports competing proposals: Xu Zhongshu’s fish interpretation, with 冓 as two fish meeting (but the graph differs from 魚 and the proposal remains unverified); Shirakawa Shizuka’s cord-making tool interpretation; and Xu Shen’s account of one act yielding two, hence two/repetition. Warring States forms may add 二 or 口 decoratively, with 二 possibly also contributing the meaning ‘two’. The oracle-bone context is fragmentary and unclear. CUHK reports bronze uses for ‘second time/again’ (陳璋方壺; 叔尸鐘) and ‘two’ (𠫑羌鐘, twenty-two), Warring States bamboo use 再三, and a possible whole-graph loan for 在 in a Guodian slip, marked as uncertain.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 字頭「再」

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 置物也。从宀舄聲。

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 entry, with 段玉裁注
evidence.field: 寫 entry; form, gloss, component analysis, and historical notes
evidence.text: The entry says 寫 means 置物 and is formed 从宀舄聲 (宀 as semantic element, 舄 as sound element). Duan Yucai explains 置物 as transferring contents from one place to another, cites the *Liji* for pouring contents between vessels and the *Shijing* phrase 我心寫兮 for pouring out the heart, and says writing and drawing later also came to be called 寫. His claim that 宀 was included because 寫之則安矣 is a traditional explanation, not independent paleographic confirmation of the graph’s original semantic motivation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「寫」
