edges.subject: component:子
edges.text: 子 contributes child-related meaning in 孩; early forms depict an infant, supporting its suitability as the meaning element.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 子; graphic history and early uses
evidence.text: The database describes 子 in oracle-bone and bronze forms as a depiction of an infant, including forms emphasizing the large head and moving arms. It reports that the graph was used for children and also borrowed for the first earthly branch; another early graph was used for the sixth branch, later represented by 巳. This independently supports 子’s semantic suitability as the meaning element in 孩.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 子

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 孩 entry, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) and Baxter–Sagart (2014) reconstruction tables
evidence.text: The page classifies 孩 as a phonosemantic compound, semantic 子 plus phonetic 亥. It gives Mandarin Pinyin hái and Cantonese Jyutping haai⁴, with dated hoi⁴ also recorded. It gives Middle Chinese Baxter hoj and Old Chinese Zhengzhang *ɡɯː versus Baxter–Sagart *[ɡ]ˤə. Compared with 亥, Zhengzhang has the same onset and rhyme with a final glottal stop on 亥; Baxter–Sagart likewise differs principally in the 亥 final glottal stop. This is strong independent phonological support for 亥’s phonetic role. Modern sound similarity alone is not the basis for the classification.
evidence.title: 孩 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 子; early forms and semantic role
evidence.text: The database describes oracle-bone and bronze forms of 子 as depictions of infants, with forms emphasizing a large head and moving arms. It reports uses for children and other early uses, including borrowing for earthly-branch notation. This makes 子 semantically suitable in 孩, though it is evidence about the component, not an early inscription of the compound.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 子

edges.subject: component:亥
edges.text: 亥 cues the sound of 孩, supported by close Old Chinese reading comparisons within both cited reconstruction systems.

sound_comparisons.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, 孩 is *ɡɯː and 亥 is *ɡɯːʔ; in Baxter–Sagart’s system, they are *[ɡ]ˤə and *[ɡ]ˤəʔ. In both, the readings closely match, with 亥 chiefly differing by a final glottal stop. These readings compare the characters’ sounds; they do not identify the original referent of 亥 or its spoken name.

edges.subject: character:孩
edges.text: The received Shuowen account records 孩 as an old spelling of 咳, with 子 in place of 口. This spelling relationship does not establish the origin of the child noun.

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcribing the received Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai’s commentary
evidence.field: 咳 entry; graphic and lexical account
evidence.text: The received entry defines 咳 as “a young child’s laugh,” analyzes it as 口 plus phonetic 亥, and records 孩 as its old-form spelling with 子 in place of 口. Duan Yucai notes that Liji · Neize and Mengzi write this word with 孩. This supports an old graphic spelling relation between 孩 and 咳, but does not establish whether the separate child-noun 孩 arose by semantic extension from “laugh” or was an independent word using the same graph.
evidence.title: 說文解字「咳」

evidence.source: Received Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai’s commentary, transcribed at Shuowen.org

evidence.text: The received entry defines 咳 as a young child’s laugh, analyzes it as 口 plus phonetic 亥, and gives 孩 as an old form written with 子 instead of 口. Duan Yucai says Liji · Neize and Mengzi use this spelling. This supports a historical spelling relation between 孩 and 咳, but does not establish that the child noun developed from the laugh word.

evidence.field: 咳; lexical senses and cross-spelling evidence
evidence.text: The specialist entry distinguishes 咳 meaning a baby’s laugh from the child noun and notes that the latter was written with 孩 in sources including Shiji · Bian Que biography. It cites the pre-imperial Liji · Neize wording “咳而名之” for the laugh-related use, and a Western Han Mawangdui Laozi silk manuscript, dated 2nd century BCE, with “若嬰兒未咳.” It also warns that the later cough sense of 咳 is a homograph and semantically unrelated. Thus attestations of the child-laugh word should not be conflated with later cough or with all child-noun uses.

edges.text: Cited uses include 孩提之童 in the Mengzi and 生孩六月 in a Jin-era memorial. Guangyun glosses 孩 as a newborn or very young child, but these sources do not date the first use of 孩 for this noun.

evidence.text: The database reports no displayed oracle-bone, bronze, seal, or bamboo-slip forms for 孩 in its entry; its cited Shuowen material is 咳, with 孩 as the old spelling. It analyzes the later compound as 子 semantic plus 亥 phonetic and glosses 孩 primarily as infant/young child. It cites Guangyun, compiled in 1008, “始生小兒” (newborn/very young child); Jin poet Guo Pu and Li Mi’s 3rd-century memorial for infant uses; Liji · Yue Ling for “young” in 孩蟲; and the old child-laugh use as another sense. evidence.text: The Guangyun entry glosses 孩 as “始生小兒” (newly born or very young child) and gives 戶來切. The available page search result identifies it as Songben Guangyun, page 100, entry 49; opening the CText page failed, so this was not independently inspected beyond the returned result.

edges.text: 宀 contributes the house setting in the phonosemantic analysis of 客.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 宀 represents the meaning and 各 represents the sound.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 寄也。从宀各聲。

evidence.source: 小學堂文字學資料庫（中央研究院）
evidence.field: 客字形演變與構形說明
evidence.text: The entry catalogs 客 under Western Zhou bronze inscriptions (including 集成04214), Chu manuscripts, and Small Seal/說文. Its account says 宀 represents a house, while 各 has a ‘coming’ sense and also serves as the phonetic; the whole graph refers to someone arriving from outside. This supports a phonosemantic analysis, though the page does not reproduce a dated inscription text or establish that 各’s ‘coming’ sense was graphically intended in 客.

It analyzes 宀 as a house and 各 as both ‘coming’ and phonetic, with the whole graph referring to someone arriving from outside. edges.subject: character:对
edges.text: An inscription uses 對 in a formula following royal rewards. Interpretations include response, acknowledgment or repayment, praise, and ritual action; its precise force remains disputed.

evidence.source: 中國國家博物館
evidence.text: The museum identifies 大盂鼎 as an early Western Zhou vessel and dates it, under its cited chronology, to King Kang’s twenty-third year (998 BCE). Its inscription ends “盂用對王休，用作祖南公寶鼎.” The museum describes the text as a royal investiture and rewards, followed by Yu’s commemorative vessel. This securely dates the written formula but does not by itself settle whether 對 here means answer, repay, acknowledge, or another related act.
evidence.title: 大盂鼎

evidence.source: 鄭州大學文學院 article on Western Zhou bronze inscriptions
evidence.text: The article reports that 對揚 and related formulas occur hundreds of times in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, often in the transition from recorded royal gifts or commands to the reason for making and inscribing the vessel. It summarizes traditional explanations as a recipient’s response and praise or thanks, and also describes a dissenting ritual interpretation. Thus bronze “對” evidence is early and abundant, but its precise pragmatic force is disputed.
evidence.title: 西周铜器铭文文学功能观初论

evidence.source: 中國社會科學網
evidence.text: This article lists multiple early and middle Western Zhou vessel examples containing 對揚 and related phrases, with vessel catalogue references and proposed readings as expressions of thanks or acknowledgment. It supports early bronze use of 對 in the formula, but does not establish a land-working-to-reply semantic chain.
evidence.title: 金文“休”字意义补说

evidence.text: The official variant dictionary notes the Shuowen variant explanation but observes that ancient writing and clerical script often show 土, and that Duan Yucai acknowledged editions and rhyme books read 土. edges.subject: character:小
edges.text: 小 is reported as a sound element in 雀, which is also described as contributing the sense “small bird.” This proposed sound role is not explained by the supplied Baxter–Sagart forms: 小 *[s]ewʔ and 雀 *[ts]ewk show no obvious rhyme match, and no sound-change account is established.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes 小 in 雀 as both contributing the sense ‘small bird’ and functioning as a sound element. This is evidence for a phonetic role of 小 in that compound, but it does not establish that sand was the original object represented by 小. No comparison of 雀’s and 小’s readings in one reconstructed system was verified in this research.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—小

evidence.source: Repository supplied local_primary_readings
evidence.text: Exact supplied rows: 小 xiǎo, MC sjewX, OC *[s]ewʔ (‘small’); 少 shǎo MC syewX OC *[s.t]ewʔ (‘few’) and shào MC syewH OC *[s-t]ewʔ-s (‘young’); 雀 què MC tsjak OC *[ts]ewk (‘sparrow’). These are Baxter–Sagart 2014 table notations, checked as local rows. The *[s]ewʔ and *[ts]ewk forms do not support an obvious rhyme match for a proposed 小→雀 sound role in that system; CUHK's component-role assertion can be reported as source-attributed, without treating the local forms as proof of a sound change.

edges.text: Accounts report that 小 and 少 shared an early graph before later graphic differentiation; one account describes 少’s lower mark becoming a diagonal stroke. evidence.field: 少 entry, graphic and usage account
evidence.text: It says oracle-bone forms of 小/少 could have four dots and were used in the same way; later the three-dot graph was used for 小 and four-dot form for 少. In bronze forms, the lowest dot of 少 extended into a diagonal stroke. The page cites bronze uses of 少 for ‘few’ and ‘young,’ and a later case where 少 is read as 小. This supports graphic differentiation and shared early use, but does not settle the more specific proposed sand-grain referent.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Character Database
evidence.text: The database states that 少 and 小 were originally one graph depicting fine sand grains, with ‘small’ as the original meaning; in bronze inscriptions the bottom dot of 少 became a diagonal stroke, distinguishing it from 小. This is a clear assertion of the shared-origin analysis, while CUHK presents that relationship alongside competing accounts of 小’s earliest formation.

evidence.source: 李學勤主編,《字源》
evidence.field: 小 headword; PDF p. 76, printed p. 64; continuation PDF p. 77, printed p. 65
evidence.text: The inspected entry calls 小 pictographic, interpreting its marks as tiny dust or sand particles and describing 小 as an early graph of 沙. It says the graph extended to mean ‘small,’ opposite 大, and reports that sense in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions, citing 《粹》1004 for 小雨. It describes later extensions to low status, contempt and youth. It says the graph had become corrupted in bronze inscriptions and treats Shuowen’s 八-plus-丨 account as an explanation of that altered form. The adjacent 少 entry says 小 and 少 were originally one graph, used similarly in oracle-bone texts, and later differentiated; its account continues on printed p. 65. Both attached page images were inspected. Forms checked against scan pixels: 小, 少, 沙, 八, 丨, 大, and 《粹》1004. This verifies what this author claims, not the disputed sand-grain interpretation.

evidence.field: 字形探源 and 字義探源, pp. 20–21
evidence.text: The book lists oracle-bone and bronze examples and says both scripts write 小 with three dots. It reports disagreement over what the dots depict, including raindrops, scattered objects, or fine smallness; it judges an abstract indicator-of-smallness analysis plausible. It says later dots lengthened into lines and rejects Shuowen’s parsing of the seal form as 八 plus 丨 as an error based on the later shape. It cites oracle-bone examples 小雨, 小風, and 小牢 for the ‘small’ use. This provides another account of the dots and the alleged graphic reinterpretation, not independent proof that they depict sand.
evidence.title: 常用漢字二百字探源

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 構形初義; 甲骨文用例; 金文用例
evidence.text: The database records two competing origin analyses: three dots representing smallness, attributed to Shang Chengzuo and Yu Xingwu; or 小 as an early graph of 沙 depicting fine sand, attributed to Ma Xulun. It says 小 and 少 were one graph before differentiation. It cites oracle-bone 小雨 (《粹》1004), 小食 for afternoon, 小采 for dusk, bronze 小鼎, and 小子/小臣 for young nobles or lower officials. It gives no absolute dates for the cited artifacts or semantic developments.

evidence.source: 李學勤主編,《字源》
evidence.field: 小 headword; PDF p. 76, printed p. 64; continuation PDF p. 77, printed p. 65
evidence.text: The inspected entry calls 小 pictographic, interpreting its marks as tiny dust or sand particles and describing 小 as an early graph of 沙. It says the graph extended to mean ‘small,’ opposite 大, and reports that sense in oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions, citing 《粹》1004 for 小雨. It describes later extensions to low status, contempt and youth. It says the graph had become corrupted in bronze inscriptions and treats Shuowen’s 八-plus-丨 account as an explanation of that altered form. The adjacent 少 entry says 小 and 少 were originally one graph, used similarly in oracle-bone texts, and later differentiated; its account continues on printed p. 65. Both attached page images were inspected. Forms checked against scan pixels: 小, 少, 沙, 八, 丨, 大, and 《粹》1004. This verifies what this author claims, not the disputed sand-grain interpretation.
evidence.title: 《字源》, 李學勤主編, 天津古籍出版社／遼寧人民出版社, 2012, PDF pp. 76–77; printed pp. 64–65

evidence.text: 不多也。从小丿聲。

evidence.source: 段玉裁《說文解字注》, accessed via Shuowen.org
evidence.text: Shuowen glosses 少 as ‘not many’ and parses it 从小丿聲. Duan Yucai explains that what is not many is small, so 少 and 小 were mutually glossed in old usage. He comments that the phonetic analysis may be based on ancient initial-consonant relations. This is evidence for the received Shuowen and Qing commentary, not direct confirmation of the graph’s original design.
evidence.title: 說文解字「少」

evidence.source: Nohara Masaki, ‘The reconstruction of the word shao (少) in Old Chinese Phonology’
evidence.field: sections 2.2–3.1; table 2; discussion of oracle-bone, bronze and manuscript usage
evidence.text: The 2015 study surveys competing phonological analyses. It reports Zhengzhang and Pan analyses that connect 少 to the 明母 series, with Zhengzhang proposing an intermediate nasal relationship to 小; it reports that Schuessler and Baxter–Sagart do not accept the 少–眇 relationship and consequently do not accept 小 as a phonetic relative in that series. The author finds early spelling usage complex: oracle-bone forms conventionally transcribed 少 or 小 can represent either ‘few’ or ‘small’; cited examples include oracle-bone Heji 12711 and 33920, Chu manuscripts, and Qin slips. The study says Qin usage distinguishes 少 from 小, but the precise point when the distinction became stable is uncertain. It also notes that the received Shuowen assigns phonetic status to 丿, not 小. This leaves historical sound-series claims disputed and does not establish that 小 was the phonetic element of the original graph.
evidence.title: 「少」の上古音再構について

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解 / 小, 少
evidence.text: The entry reports two analyses of 小’s early dots: marks for smallness, or fine sand grains. It says early oracle forms conventionally read as 小 and 少 overlap in shape and use; bronze 少 adds a 丿-like stroke and is attested for ‘few’ against 多, for ‘young’, and sometimes for 小. It records the received Shuowen parsing 从小丿聲. These are source assertions; neither a sand-grain referent nor Shuowen’s original graphic analysis is independently settled by the record.

edges.subject: component:亯
edges.text: In the proposed early 亯 + 京 analysis, 亯 depicts a temple in a scene interpreted as ritual at height; both the scene and its link to the later verb remain unsettled.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.field: 形義通解；就 的字形與早期用例
evidence.text: The database reports that oracle-bone and bronze forms of 就 are composed of 亯 and 京, interpreted as a temple form placed above a high platform, with the proposed sense ‘sacrifice at a high place.’ It says Chu forms share strokes between 亯 and 京, while the Qin slips first show the form 京 + 尤 that informed small-seal 就. Later bronze forms include year/years, and later bronze variants add 月 or bamboo-slip forms add 日. edges.text: One analysis proposes 左 as a phonetic note in a distinct early form of 差; the role is form-specific and not established for every form.

sound_comparisons.text: For the proposed phonetic role in one early form, Baxter–Sagart reconstructs 左 as *tsˤa[j]ʔ and 差 chā as *tsʰraj. Their initials differ, so this is a related sound-series proposal, not an identical reading; the role is form-specific.

evidence.source: 甘木, “說字（九則）,” Fudan University Center for Excavated Texts and Paleography
evidence.text: Discussing a distinct ancient form associated with 差, the author proposes that its lower part represents two hands out of alignment and that an added 左 serves as a phonetic note. The graph and reading are discussed separately from the proposed bundled-fuel form. This supports reporting multiple paleographic analyses; it does not establish one linear origin for every 差 reading.
evidence.title: 甘木：說字（九則）

evidence.field: 差 and 左 Old Chinese pronunciations
evidence.text: The dataset lists 差 chā as Middle Chinese transcription tsrhæ and Old Chinese *tsʰraj, glossed “distinction; to select”; 差 cī as tsrhje and *tsʰraj, glossed “參差 uneven”; and 差 cuō as tsha and *[tsʰ]ˤaj, glossed “rub, polish, file.” In the same system, 左 zuǒ is tsaX and *tsˤa[j]ʔ, glossed “left (side).” These forms show that sound-component claims must specify the 差 reading and reconstruction system; the readings are not identical.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese characters database, CUHK)
evidence.text: The entry explicitly shows 師 as the traditional form and 师 as its simplified counterpart. The dossier’s relationship 師 → 师 is therefore supported as standard simplification; this statement concerns graphic standardization, not an ancient ancestor relationship.

edges.subject: component:𠂤
edges.text: One analysis treats 𠂤 as a meaning-bearing element of 師 and interprets it as a mound; other accounts dispute its referent and construction.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese characters database, CUHK)
evidence.field: 形義通解; 甲骨、金文用例; 《說文》; 繁簡對應
evidence.text: The entry describes 師 as composed of 𠂤 and 帀, with 帀 identified as the phonetic and 𠂤 as a semantic element; it offers an army-camps-on-a-mound explanation for the army sense. It reports that 𠂤 has been interpreted as a small mound or as buttocks, and also reports the proposal that 𠂤 and 帀 were abbreviations of 師. The entry says oracle-bone uses of 師 are unclear; bronze uses include an official title and troops/army, with examples named as 仲枏氏鬲 and 中山王圓壺. It reproduces the Shuowen account of a 2,500-person unit and its 帀 + 𠂤 analysis, and shows 師 as the traditional counterpart of 师. These are the database’s summaries and reported interpretations, not independent proof of the graph’s original construction or a dated chronology of sense development.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 師

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese characters database, CUHK)
evidence.field: 形義通解; 甲骨、金文用例;《說文》引文
evidence.text: The entry reports two oracle-bone examples for 師 but says their use is unclear; it reports bronze-inscription uses for an official title and for troops/army. Its analysis takes 𠂤 as a small mound and 帀 as the phonetic, while noting competing interpretations of 𠂤 (mound, following 孫海波, or buttocks, following 加藤常賢). It also reports a scholarly proposal that 𠂤 and 帀 were abbreviated forms of 師. The entry quotes 說文: “二千五百人爲師。从帀从𠂤。𠂤，四帀，眾意也。” These are source-reported analyses and examples; the page does not establish that the mound-and-military-camp semantic explanation is historically certain.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 師

evidence.source: 臺灣學術期刊開放取用平台 (Taiwan Academic Journal Open Access Platform)
evidence.field: search result abstract on the graph 師
evidence.text: A competing proposal says 𠂤’s original shape represents buttocks and refers to a place to sit or rest; a stopping place for travelers or armies could then be called 𠂤, hence an association with multitudes. The result also notes early Western Zhou bronze evidence for 太師 and 師氏. This is a search-result abstract rather than an opened article, so the proposed graphic and semantic derivation remains secondary and incompletely verified here.
evidence.title: 臺灣學術期刊開放取用平台 result on 師

Modern Mandarin readings are 帀 zā and 師 shī; supplied Baxter–Sagart 2014 forms are 帀 tsop / *[ts]ˤ[ə]p and 師 srij / *srij in Middle and Old Chinese respectively. edges.subject: component:巾
edges.text: In 帮, 巾 is analyzed as the semantic component, contributing a broad cloth-related category.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 幫/帮: variant-form classification and component account
evidence.text: The editorial note treats 帮 as a variant of 幫 and says both are phonosemantic structures: 幫 has phonetic 封 and semantic 帛, while 帮 has phonetic 邦 and semantic 巾. It regards the two semantic elements as belonging to the same broad meaning class. This supports a nonchronological variant relation between the forms; it does not show that 帮 was created by directly replacing the parts of 幫 at a specific date.
evidence.title: [A01190-003] 帮 (幫) - Ministry of Education《Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants》2024

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 帮: variant status and form account
evidence.text: The editor classifies 帮 as a variant of 幫, not as evidence of a dated simplification route. The note says both are phonosemantic: 帮 uses 邦 as phonetic and 巾 as semantic element; 幫 uses 封 and 帛. It treats the semantic elements as belonging to a related meaning class. The entry says 帮 is not found in Shuowen and its paleographic table marks oracle, bronze and bamboo-slip collections unavailable.

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》；scan directly inspected
evidence.field: PDF p.708, printed p.695; headword 幫(帮) and explanation
evidence.text: The entry is headed 幫(帮), gives the paired reading bāng, and calls 幫 a phonosemantic character formed from 帛 with 封 as phonetic. It gives the original sense as the edge of a shoe; cites 集韻·唐韻 “帮，治履边也”; then describes extensions to raised sides of objects, assistance, groups, and a classifier. It says 帮 had appeared by the modern period as a俗字 of 幫, formed by simplifying the lower 帛 component to 巾. This is the book author’s analysis, not a dated first attestation or a documented step-by-step history. The scan’s printed page number 695 is visible. The entry and its continuation are on p.708; p.709 begins other entries. Checked the visible headword, component clause, sense discussion, and simplification statement against the supplied scan pixels.
evidence.title: 字源, 李學勤主編, 天津古籍出版社 / 遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692

edges.subject: character:常
edges.text: 常 is used with these meanings. The available accounts do not give a fully dated chronology among them or establish a single semantic path from the garment sense.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *djaŋ): phonetic 尚 (OC *djaŋ, *djaŋs) + semantic 巾 (“cloth”).
The character originally referred to a "lower garment" similar to a skirt, before being phonetically borrowed to mean "long-lasting; frequently". The original sense is now represented by the character 裳 (OC *djaŋ, “lower garment”).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan; perhaps related to Tibetan ཡང (yang, “again, once more”) (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.field: 乾 formation, readings, senses, dated textual examples
evidence.text: The Ministry dictionary records 乾 as a distinct traditional graph, with 干 among its variants and 干 as its simplified correspondence. It quotes Shuowen’s “上出也。从乙；乙，物之達也。倝聲” and identifies 倝 as the sound element and 乙 as semantic. It records modern Mandarin qián for the ‘emerge upward/heaven/yang’ reading and gān for ‘dry’; it cites the *Book of Odes*, 王風·中谷有蓷, “中谷有蓷，暵其乾矣,” for the dry sense, and the *Zuo zhuan* (僖公十五年) and *Shan Hai Jing* for parched/dried-up senses. This separates the dry word and the cosmological/heavenly use; the source gives no date for when the dry reading began.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.text: The database describes 幹 as also written 干 and gives early textual examples for ‘main stem/trunk’: *Liji*, 月令, 羽箭幹; *Zuo zhuan*, 昭公二十五年, 幹 for the body’s frame/bones; and *Yi*, 乾卦, “貞者，事之幹也,” extended metaphorically to the basis or mainstay of affairs. It also records later ‘ability,’ ‘manage/take charge,’ and ‘business/matter’ senses with citations from *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, *Han shu*, and Song writings. Its entry supplies Guangyun 古案切 and Middle Chinese 見母 level/去-tone-category data; this is separate from the original shield graph and does not make 干 a component in 幹 a sound element.

edges.subject: character:干
edges.text: The graph is interpreted as a shield pictograph. A bronze inscription meaning “shield” is reported; the earliest secure attestation identified here is mid-Western Zhou.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Characters Database)
evidence.field: 形義通解 / graphic formation and usage
evidence.text: The database interprets oracle-bone and bronze 干 as a shield, reportedly with feather decoration, and says its protective sense developed from the defensive object. It cites an oracle-bone example from 合集 28059, 弜令戍干衛, glossed as defensive/protective use; a bronze-vessel example 豦簋「干戈」 uses it for the weapon. It also records the *Book of Documents*, “稱爾戈，比爾干，立爾矛,” with the traditional commentary glossing 干 as a shield. The database reports a competing proposal by Xu Zhongshu that oracle-bone 干 and 單 are variant forms representing a forked hunting implement. These are source interpretations; I did not inspect the glyph images.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 干

evidence.source: CASE Press / National Taiwan University science communication
evidence.text: The author argues that the earliest forms proposed for 干 are Shang oracle-bone signs, with earlier and later Shang shapes differing in a way interpreted as reflecting shield-decoration change. The article says 干 is securely attested by the mid-Western Zhou bronze inscription on the 豦簋, shaped like a round shield with a forked top; a related shape occurs on the late-Western Zhou 毛公鼎. By later Western Zhou the upper round feature is written as a short horizontal stroke, and this form continues through Spring-and-Autumn and Warring States scripts, small seal, Qin clerical and Western Han clerical forms; the forked top is regularized to a shorter horizontal stroke by Eastern Han. evidence.field: 牀 entry; component analysis and definition
evidence.text: The entry gives 牀, ‘安身之坐者’ (‘a seat/resting place for the body’), and analyzes it as 从木、爿聲: 木 is the semantic element and 爿 the phonetic. 徐鍇 offers a different historical explanation, treating 爿 as a shortened form of a reclining-person shape; 段玉裁 rejects the claim that the compound should be reanalyzed as 牀省聲 and discusses 爿 as a distinct element. edges.subject: character:床
edges.text: Bed and couch are documented meanings of 牀/床, but the earliest use of the bed word is not securely dated here.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Originally an unorthodox variant of 牀. Now made up of 广 (“house”) + 木 (“tree”), an ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意) representing a wooden furniture item (a bed) in a house.
Schuessler (2007) suggests that it may be related to Khmer រង (rɔɔng, “to support from below”), Old Mon [script needed] (joṅ, “couch; bedstead”). Compare also Burmese စင် (cang, “platform, stage”) (Luce, 1981).
Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstructs OC prefixal *k- based on Vietic evidences: cf. Maleng [Brô] kacɨəŋ, Maleng [Kha Pong] kəcɨːŋ² , Chut [Sách, Rục] kəcɨːŋ².

evidence.text: Reports Zhengzhang Old Chinese 店 /*tiːms/ and 占 /*tjems/ in the relevant departing-tone readings, and Baxter–Sagart 店 /*tˤem-s/ and 占 /*tem/. evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry gives 開 as 張也 (“to stretch/open”) and analyzes it as 从門从幵. This documents competing analyses; it does not independently prove the popular two-hands-and-latch interpretation of 開.

edges.subject: character:开
edges.text: A paleographic argument proposes these as early uses of 開 and suggests 啟 was more commonly used for opening doors. This proposal does not establish a settled chronology.

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for the Study of Excavated Texts and Paleography, Wang Ning
evidence.field: Discussion of 開 and excavated manuscript forms, especially paragraphs 97-127
evidence.text: Wang argues that 幵 may itself be an early form used for the word 開, and cites occurrences interpreted as 開 in Warring States manuscripts, the Qin Shuihudi 日書 slips, and a Western Zhou bronze inscription. The article disputes proposals that the 門 component plus 幵 form arose through scribal corruption: it points to Warring States manuscript forms with 門 and 幵. It further proposes that early uses of 開 could favor senses such as instruct, explain or release, with 啟 more common for opening doors, while acknowledging growing overlap later. This is a scholarly argument, not uncontested proof of the graph's origin or a complete first-attestation record.

edges.text: 弟 is reported as the phonetic element in 第. Mandarin dì is shared, and the cited reconstructions also report Middle Chinese 弟 dejX / 第 dejH and Zhengzhang Old Chinese 弟 *diːlʔ or *diːls / 第 *diːls; these readings support the reported sound-series relationship in 第, not a phonetic analysis of 弟 itself.

evidence.text: The entry analyzes 第 as a phono-semantic compound: 竹 ‘bamboo’ as semantic element and 弟 as phonetic element; it also notes that sequence may alternatively have been written 弟. This supports a phonetic role for 弟 within the later graph 第; it does not make 弟 itself a phonetic compound.

edges.text: A cited Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 弟 in 兄弟. This is the earliest securely sourced sibling use here, but it does not show that the earliest oracle-bone forms already had this meaning.

evidence.source: Hong Kong Baptist University repository, study excerpt citing bronze inscriptions
evidence.field: 殳季良父壺; bronze inscription usage
evidence.text: The inspected excerpt quotes the 殳季良父壺 inscription (catalogue no. 集成9713) using 兄弟 among the inscription’s recipients of ritual offerings. The specialist character database dates the vessel to Western Zhou late. This is evidence for the sibling sense in bronze inscription usage by the Western Zhou; it does not establish that the late Shang oracle-bone occurrences had that sense.
evidence.title: Hong Kong Baptist University repository PDF, excerpt on bronze inscriptions

edges.subject: character:弟
edges.text: 弟 is used for a younger person or one junior in status. When this use began, and whether it developed from the sibling sense, is unresolved.

evidence.source: 臺灣教育部《異體字字典》
evidence.text: The dictionary gives the Shuowen account: 弟 means the successive order of leather bindings and follows an ancient form; its cited old-text variant is analyzed there as abbreviated ancient 韋 plus 丿 as phonetic. Its entry quotes classical sources separately by sense: sequence/rank is cited from 呂氏春秋 and 漢書; younger brother from 爾雅, 左傳, and 史記; younger sister/female junior use from 孟子 and 史記; and humble self-reference to a peer from a poem attributed to Tang poet 王季友 and 紅樓夢. These references establish transmitted textual attestations, not the date of surviving manuscripts. The entry presents the 悌-related ethical reading under a separate pronunciation and gives 論語 and 禮記 examples.
evidence.title: 教育部《異體字字典》— 弟

evidence.source: Wiktionary
evidence.field: Chinese: glyph origin; pronunciation; historical phonology
evidence.text: The page labels 弟 a pictogram of a spear handle wrapped in a leather strap and claims the wrapping suggested sequence, extended to younger brother. These are reconstructions for 弟, not for the pictured implement or its name. Its gloss list includes junior and a literary humble “I/me” between male friends; those senses require separate semantic histories.

edges.text: 景 is the phonetic element in the conventional analysis. Modern Mandarin has 景 jǐng and 影 yǐng; Baxter–Sagart gives comparable Middle Chinese and Old Chinese forms that differ in initial notation. These comparisons support but do not independently prove the historical role.

evidence.source: 漢典 / zdic.net
evidence.text: For modern Mandarin, 景 has readings jǐng and yǐng; the dictionary analyses its graph as 从日、京声. This is dictionary evidence, not evidence that the ancient phonetic relationship must have been identical to modern pronunciation.

edges.subject: character:影
edges.text: A museum catalog transcribes 影命不長 on a rubbing of the 爨寶子碑 dated 405; the date and reading are mediated by the catalog and later scholarship.

evidence.source: 2025 article in 杜甫研究学刊, hosted as PDF
evidence.field: pp. 1–2: dating and early attestations of 影
evidence.text: The article reviews competing proposed first attestations: a Han-end attribution to Gao You’s 淮南子 commentary, a claim based on the lost Zhang Heng stele, and Ge Hong’s 字苑 as reported by Yan Zhitui. It argues that the earliest presently supportable example is the Eastern Jin 爨寶子碑, dated 405, whose preserved rubbing has “影命不長”; it also notes Tao Yuanming’s 形影神 poem titles. The article cautions that ancient-text editions sometimes replace 景 with 影. The 405 date and reading are reported through later scholarship and a Qing rubbing, so this is not an extant contemporary original inspected here.
evidence.title: 论杜诗中的“景”字不同于“影”

evidence.source: 杜甫研究学刊, 2025, article PDF
evidence.field: pp. 1–3, lines 61–111: disputed first attestations and early 景/影 usage
evidence.text: The study reviews proposed first attestations for 影: an attribution to Ge Hong’s Jin-era 字苑, a claim based on a Han-end 淮南子 commentary, and a lost Zhang Heng stele. It favors the 405 Eastern Jin 爨寶子碑, quoting “影命不長,” while noting the inscription survives here through a Qing rubbing and the date is scholarly attribution. The article warns that later editions sometimes replace early 景 with 影. It cites pre-Qin works where 景 can mean a shadow and discusses later literary examples; this does not establish a complete dated semantic path from shadow to image/photograph.

edges.subject: character:很
edges.text: Reference works record adjectival uses meaning fierce or perverse. One scholarly account places this adjective after earlier noncompliance usage, though the chronology is uncertain.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɡɯːnʔ): semantic 彳 + phonetic 艮 (OC *kɯːns).
“Cruel (~ 狠); to disobey; to defy” > “very; quite” (since Yuan dynasty). Compare 蠻／蛮 (mán).

evidence.text: The dictionary records 很戾 as “fierce/violent and perverse” and cites “趙王之很戾無親” from Shiji, Zhang Yi biography. It also records a Song-dynasty sense of hard and brittle in Su Shi’s 思治論. These show later adjectival uses; they do not by themselves prove a direct semantic transition to the degree adverb.

evidence.source: Journal of Chinese Language and Literature Translation, Lim Gyunghee (2012), abstract page

This is a distinct scholarly account from the Yuan 哏 language-contact proposal.

edges.subject: character:得
edges.text: The hand-taking-shell interpretation proposes “obtain” as the graph’s original sense, though its earliest secure attestation date is unresolved. Warring States manuscript examples use 得 to mean “obtain” or “get” by that period.

evidence.source: CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: form analysis and dated usage examples
evidence.text: The database interprets early 得 forms as 貝 plus a hand element 又 (with other hand forms also attested), sometimes with 彳 to suggest getting shell currency while travelling. It cites oracle-bone 《合集》8928 ‘弗其得’, bronze 《懷特》359 ‘得馬’, and the Zhongshan King square pot phrase ‘敄(務)才(在)得賢’. It says later forms sometimes reshape 貝 toward 目 or 日, the received small-seal form toward 見, and 又 toward 寸. These are the database’s paleographic interpretation; individual artifacts and images were not inspected in this run.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 得

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Knowledge Database
evidence.text: The database’s evolution page includes categories for oracle bone, bronze, Chu slips and silk, and small seal, labels bronze record 集成03976 and refers to the Shuowen form. Its summary says the old graph pictures a hand taking a shell, symbolizing obtain, and may add 彳 for action. The page’s text does not provide a dated list of individual sense extensions.

edges.text: These meanings and grammatical uses are recorded, but their order and development from “obtain” are not established. evidence.text: The database describes the old graph as a hand holding a shell, representing obtaining; 彳 may be added to show an action. evidence.field: pre-Qin corpus analysis and semantic history
evidence.text: The 2010 abstract reports quantitative and qualitative analysis of 1,319 occurrences of 得 in six pre-Qin texts. It cites 集韻《唐韻》, “忙，心迫也,” and records later uses for being occupied with many tasks (北魏《齊民要術》) and doing something quickly (《兒女英雄傳》). It gives 廣韻 fanqie 莫郎 and Middle Chinese category 明母、平聲、宕攝唐韻、開口一等. This supports the compound analysis and attested sense distinctions, but does not establish a precise date for the cited 集韻 gloss or the earliest occurrence of 忙.

evidence.source: 中華民國教育部《異體字字典》 (Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants)

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声): phonetic 乍 (OC *zraːɡs) + semantic 心 (“heart”).
First attested in the word 怎生 [10th c.] (Yuan et al., 1996).
Contraction of 作 (MC tsak) + some variant of 物 (MC mjut, “thing; what”), literally “to do what” (Norman, 1988). This is evidenced in forms found in the Tang and Song dynasties (Yuan et al., 1996): 作勿生 (MC tsak mjut sraeng) [8th c.], 作沒生 (MC tsak mwot sraeng) [8th c.], 作摩 (MC tsak ma) [10th c.], 作麼 (MC tsak maX) [10th c.].

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 自 (“nose”) + 心 (“heart”) – to breathe (life) through one’s nose. Note that 自 originally meant “nose” and was later borrowed for “self”.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *sək (“breath; life; to breathe”). Cognate with Jingpho sa' (“to breathe”), Burmese အသက် (a.sak).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese Character Database）
evidence.text: The page shows bronze, seal, and standard forms. Its account treats 自 and 心 as semantic elements: 自 represents the nose, while 心 reflects the ancient belief that breathing originated in the heart. This supports a semantic-component analysis, not 自 as phonetic.

evidence.source: 甲骨文每周识字（citing 甲骨文常用字字典）

It reports bronze forms continuing the older shape and says Spring and Autumn/Warring States forms regularized the lower strokes toward 心; the seal form inherited that shape. The page offers no dated individual inscription or citation sufficient to verify a particular earliest occurrence.

evidence.source: 賈若琛, “『您』来了：『您』作为现代汉语普通话第二人称敬称成因新释” (ResearchGate-hosted thesis text)
evidence.field: corpus search; earlier proposals; historical use
evidence.text: The author reports that searches of CCL, BCC, and Academia Sinica corpora found 您 as a pronoun from Yuan onward, while a Tang/Five Dynasties epitaph instance “并州您管” was judged a likely textual error and not a pronoun. The text reviews competing derivations: contraction of 你們/你每, contraction of 你老 or 你老人家, nasalization/contact proposals, and a possible relation between plural and honorific use. It also presents disagreement about whether the modern honorific descends from the earlier plural pronoun and when the honorific use arose. These are the thesis author's review and corpus-search claims, not independent verification of the corpora or epitaph witness.
evidence.kind: secondary scholarly review and corpus-search report

edges.subject: sense:您:second_person_pronoun
edges.text: A development from plural use to honorific use has been proposed, but competing explanations and disagreement about timing leave the transition unresolved.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 你 (“you”) + 心 (“heart”). 心 (MC sim) may also phonetically signify the original -m ending (Yuan et al., 1996).
This character was not listed in Sui/Tang rhyme books. First attested in Jin/Yuan-era literature, when it was also written as 恁 and probably pronounced as *nim at the time (Lü, 1940; Norman, 1988). The pronoun was used both in the singular and the plural.
The pronoun used in Jin/Yuan-era literature is generally thought to be a fusion of 你們／你们 (nǐmen, “you (plural)”) or 你每 (nǐměi, “you (plural)”) (Lü, 1940; Norman, 1988). Compare 怹 (tān, “he, she (polite)”) ( < 他們／他们 (tāmen, “they”)).
The honorific usage may simply be a development of the plural usage (Norman, 1988); compare English you, French vous. However, others have argued for a different etymology for the honorific pronoun. Wang (1984) and Lü (1985) argue that it is a contraction of 你老 (“you (honorific for seniors)”): /ni lau/ → /nil/ → /nin/. Alternatively, Zhang (2001) suggests that it comes from 仁 (MC nyin), an honorific used in Buddhist texts from the Han dynasty.
In Cantonese and Hakka, this character is simply read as 你; in Teochew, it is read as 汝.

evidence.field: historical corpus search and review of previous proposals
evidence.text: The article reports that searches of CCL, BCC, and Academia Sinica corpora found no pronoun use of 您 before Yuan; a Tang/Five Dynasties epitaph occurrence (“并州您管”) is judged a likely textual error and not a pronoun. It reviews competing explanations: contraction of 你們/你每; contraction of 你老; a relation to Buddhist 仁; nasalization or contact proposals; and development of honorific meaning from plural use. It also reports disagreement over when the honorific sense arose, with claims ranging from late Qing to early twentieth century. These are the article's review and corpus-search assertions, not independently verified transcriptions of the underlying corpora here.

edges.subject: component:相
edges.text: 相 is identified as the sound component. In Baxter–Sagart, 相 reading 1 (MC sjang, OC *[s]aŋ) compares with 想 (MC sjangX, OC *[s]aŋʔ), sharing onset and rhyme with a difference in the final glottal stop. The modern Mandarin pair xiāng/xiǎng is a current-reading comparison only.

sound_comparisons.text: Baxter–Sagart compares 相 reading 1, MC sjang and OC *[s]aŋ, with 想, MC sjangX and OC *[s]aŋʔ. The shared onset and rhyme, with a difference in the final glottal stop, support a plausible sound relationship.

evidence.text: The supplied local table row gives 想 MC sjangX, OC *[s]aŋʔ, gloss ‘think’. edges.subject: character:我
edges.text: Early forms are interpreted as pictures of a toothed implement with a long handle. Whether it was a saw, axe-like weapon, ritual implement, or another object is disputed; this proposed pictured meaning does not establish a securely recovered spoken name.

evidence.source: CUHK 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: Early 我 resembles a long-handled toothed implement, interpreted as a saw or related weapon. It was borrowed as a first-person pronoun. Oracle examples include a plural self-reference; bronze inscriptions also use it for the speaker. Specific identifications of the implement differ.
evidence.title: 我 — historical form and meaning

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.text: The database describes oracle-bone and bronze forms as a toothed, long-handled implement, interpreted as a saw or saw-like ancient weapon. It reports oracle-bone uses for diviner names and a state name as well as a first-person plural pronoun, citing 合集 9688 我受年 (“May we receive a harvest”). It reports bronze use as a first-person pronoun and gives the Mao Gong ding phrase 虔夙夕惠我一人 (“diligently assist me, one person”). Its account also records competing identifications: Guo Moruo linked the implement to 錡 in the Odes; other scholars identify it with a three-toothed axe-like weapon or a multi-ge halberd. These are source interpretations, not settled object identification.
evidence.title: 我 — 漢語多功能字庫, oracle-bone component and form/meaning history

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, National Taiwan University
evidence.text: The article argues that early 我 depicts a toothed, axe-like ritual or ceremonial implement, while noting that no Shang object matching the graph has yet been found. Similar three-toothed weapons are known from Middle Western Zhou contexts, including the 1975 Zhuangbai find, but this does not prove that the depicted Shang-era object was identical. It records Guo Moruo and Lin Yun’s proposed identification with 錡, while a different proposal associates 我 with a ring-shaped jade or stone axe form; the article questions the latter fit. It also argues that 義 and 羲 preserve the weapon sense, an interpretation presented as indirect corroboration rather than proof.
evidence.title: 戚戚我心 – 古漢字的「戚」與「我」

edges.subject: sense:我:implement
edges.text: The likely account is that the implement picture was reused to write the first-person pronoun because the words sounded alike; the meaning “implement” did not develop into “I.” Early pronoun use is reported, but the implement’s spoken name is unknown, so the sound match cannot be demonstrated.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Pictograph of a weapon or farming tool with a forked blade and long handle. The meaning "I; me" is a phonetic loan.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
A pictogram (象形) of a trident-like weapon or tool (note the oracle bone script form 𢦐). Jao & Zeng (1985, pp. 289–290) conjecture about its similarity to a kind of three-bladed polearm found at archaeological sites. Cf. 戈 (“polearm”), which is the same weapon but with a single blade instead of three. It was already borrowed for sound as an instance of jiajie (假借) for the pronoun 我 (OC *ŋaːlʔ, “I”) since the oracle bone script.
Guo Moruo considers it to be the original character for 錡 (OC *ɡral, “a kind of war axe with three blades or teeth”).
Folk etymology considers it to be an ideograph of a hand (手) holding a weapon (戈) to protect oneself.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ŋa. Cognate with 吾 (OC *ŋaː), Burmese ငါ (nga, “I”), Hakka 𠊎 (ngài). The expected Mandarin pronunciation is ě (now only found in a few Northern dialects); wǒ is "a col[loquial] archaism" (Schuessler, 2007).
Schuessler further decomposes 我 *ŋâiʔ (his reconstruction) into *ŋa + *i, which he terms an "independent suffix" which also appears in some Tibeto-Burman cognates of this pronoun. DeLancey and Benedict believe that the *-i here was an "information structure marker". But given how Sagart believes 我 was originally plural (Sagart 1999:142) and DeLancey discovered that first-person plural compounds of *ŋa (“I”) and *i (“we”) exist in e.g. Raji and Stau, it is also possible that the -iʔ element is actually *i (“we”) fused onto the singular.

edges.subject: character:房
edges.text: The traditional lexicographic gloss defines 房 as a room beside the main room. This is an attested historical interpretation, not proof that it was the character’s original meaning.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 室在㫄也。从戶方聲。

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, 說文解字 entry with Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.field: historical gloss and received graph analysis
evidence.text: The entry defines 房 as a room beside the main room and analyzes it as 从戶方聲. Duan Yucai explains that the central room of a hall is flanked by east and west rooms, and notes an extended use for a compartment of a ritual vessel. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the graph's first formation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「房」 - Shuowen.org

edges.subject: character:房
edges.text: A cited Three Kingdoms-era poem uses 空房, “empty room.” This attests the room sense by that period, but does not establish how it developed from the side-room sense.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education Revised Mandarin Dictionary
evidence.field: modern senses and cited literary examples
evidence.text: The entry lists 房 as ‘dwelling/house’, ‘a room within a dwelling’, house-like structures, family branches, and spouse/concubine senses. It cites Cao Pi’s Three Kingdoms-era poem 燕歌行 with 空房 (‘empty room’), and later medieval and imperial-era examples for other senses. These examples attest uses by their cited literary periods, but the dictionary list alone does not establish a chronological chain of semantic change.

edges.subject: character:手
edges.text: The graph is interpreted as depicting a hand, and later lexicographic evidence supports this meaning. The bronze occurrences themselves lack verified semantic contexts, so they do not establish a securely dated earliest use with this meaning.

This qualifies broader claims that 手 itself is securely attested on oracle bones; the excerpt supplies no specific date for the cited bronzes.

edges.subject: character:打
edges.text: A cited Han-period poem uses 打 for striking. Early dictionary citations and a gloss roughly meaning ‘to knock or strike out’ are also discussed, but transmission leaves the earliest attestation unsettled.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database analyzes 打 as from 手 with 丁 phonetic and identifies striking/collision as its basic sense. It cites Han-period 王延壽’s 賦 poem use “撞縱目，打三顱,” and later examples for attack and fighting in 梁書, making early lexical use potentially earlier than the Shuowen New Attached entry. It reports no oracle-bone or bronze examples in its form table; one small-seal form is listed. The citations do not establish an uninterrupted semantic chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「打」

evidence.source: 徐時儀, 「打」的形、音、義衍變遞壇探微
evidence.field: earliest attestation and disputed textual history
evidence.text: The paper states that present Shuowen lacks 打 and that it appears in the Song-era 徐鉉 New Attached section. It discusses claims of earlier occurrences in Han and Tang materials, including citations in 玄應’s Buddhist lexicon and an alleged Shuowen quotation, but notes uncertainty about whether these reflect an earlier Shuowen text or later transmission. It reports an early definition in 通俗文 as “撞出曰打” (roughly, an object knocked/struck out is called 打). Thus the claim that Shuowen is the earliest extant use is not secure; earlier textual evidence exists but its transmission and exact dating need caution.
evidence.title: 「打」的形、音、義衍變遞壇探微

evidence.source: 徐時儀, 「打」的形、音、義衍變遞壇探微
evidence.text: The article states that 打 is absent from the received Shuowen and appears in the Song-era 徐鉉 New Attached section. It discusses early references attributed to 玄應 and 慧琳, including a 通俗文 gloss “撞出曰打,” but notes that witnesses and alleged Shuowen quotations do not securely establish the wording of an earlier Shuowen edition. The article therefore complicates any simple claim that the Song New Attached entry is the earliest extant lexical use.

evidence.text: This database analyzes 拿 as 从手、合声 (“手” semantic, “合” phonetic), with original meaning “take with the hand.” It cites a Song poem by Wang Zhidao, “老夫僵不掃，稚子走爭拿,” and Water Margin chapter 5 for the taking sense; it then cites later novel passages for forceful taking, apprehending, grasping/control, and a prepositional use. edges.subject: character:拿
edges.text: A dictionary account describes 拏 as the earlier standard graph and 拿 as its popular form, later made independently standard.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A01571 拿; explanation and variant research notes
evidence.text: The dictionary says 拿 is not recorded in Shuowen. Its current standard form is written with 合 above 手. Its research notes report that 拏 was the older standard graph: Shuowen analyzes it as 手 plus 奴 phonetic, “to pull/lead”; a later clerical form is 拏. The notes call 拿 a popular form of 拏, say it became an independent standard graph as its use expanded, and cite Four-Sound Pianhai for the equation 拿, sound 拏, and Ming dictionaries for calling 拿俗拏字. The same entry records 挐 separately: Shuowen analyzes it as 手 plus 加 phonetic, “to hold”; later sources merge its meaning with 拏 and treat it as a variant. This supports a historical relationship among the graphs but does not establish that 合 in 拿 was historically a phonetic component.
evidence.title: [A01571] 拿 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants, research notes

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary describes 拏 as the earlier standard graph: Shuowen analyzes its source graph as 手 semantic plus 奴 phonetic, with the sense “pull/lead.” It reports 拿 as a popular form later established as an independent standard graph, citing Song–Yuan vernacular character records and later dictionaries. It separately describes 挐 as 手 plus 加 phonetic, originally “hold,” and later associated with 拏. These are the dictionary’s historical assertions, not proof of a single uninterrupted semantic path to every use of 拿.

evidence.text: This database analyzes 拿 as 从手、合声 (“手” semantic, “合” phonetic), with original meaning “take with the hand.” It cites a Song poem by Wang Zhidao, “老夫僵不掃，稚子走爭拿,” and Water Margin chapter 5 for the taking sense; it then cites later novel passages for forceful taking, apprehending, grasping/control, and a prepositional use. evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: 字形 / 甲骨部件分析 / 形義通解
evidence.text: The database presents 教’s oracle-bone form as 攴 + 子 + 爻, identifies 爻 as phonetic, and reports the graph’s core sense as teaching. It gives a proposed pictorial interpretation of 攴 as a teaching implement and爻 as materials for teaching counting or divination; this is an interpretation attributed to Shen Pei, not a directly established description of the object. It says some bronze forms use 攴 + 學, and some Warring States bamboo forms use 言. It reports oracle-bone use as a personal or place name, bronze and manuscript use for teaching, and cites manuscript examples for teaching, instruction, and command. Its reading of the later left component as 爻+子 (𡥉), with 孝 as a later graphic corruption, is one source’s analysis.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 教

evidence.source: CUHK Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 形義通解; 甲骨文字形; 說文; 廣韻
evidence.text: The entry analyzes oracle-bone 教 as 攴 + 子 + 爻, with 爻 also serving as the phonetic; its interpretation of 攴 as a teaching implement and the scene of teaching children to count or divine is attributed to Shen Pei. It reports oracle-bone use for personal and place names; bronze use for teaching; and Warring States manuscript examples for teaching, instruction, and command. It says some bronze forms use 攴 + 學 and some Warring States slips use 言; it calls 孝 a later corrupted graph for the left-side 爻+子 form. It quotes Shuowen 敎 as ‘上所施下所效也。从攴从𡥉’ and lists Guangyun 古肴切. These are the database's reported readings and examples; cited texts were not independently dated here.

edges.subject: character:教
edges.text: "Teach" is a current meaning. Teaching and instruction are reported in bronze and Warring States manuscript contexts. Oracle-bone occurrences are interpreted as “instruct,” alongside reported personal or place-name uses and readings such as transmit, cause, or command. These reports do not establish which early use came first or the graph’s original meaning.

edges.subject: character:文
edges.text: The earliest uses reported here occur in personal and place names, especially as an honorific modifier in royal names. This use does not establish the graph’s original meaning; “great” is one proposed interpretation.

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, Jiang Baiyi
evidence.text: The article reports 文 used in oracle inscriptions in personal and place names and chiefly as an honorific modifier in Shang royal names; it reports that Western Zhou bronze inscriptions use it in royal posthumous names and ancestor honorifics. The author presents Liu Yuan’s interpretation of 文邑 as 大邑 and 文 as ‘great’ as a live analysis, not a settled consensus. The article also notes that the ‘great’ account does not explain the chest mark.
evidence.title: 甲骨和金文的「文」字真的和「文身」有關嗎？

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, Jiang Baiyi
evidence.text: The article reports the earliest known 文 forms in Late Shang oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions, describing standing human-shaped graphs similar to 大, with chest marks that vary or are absent. It traces the marks through reduction to dots or short strokes and eventual disappearance in later forms. It reports early use in personal and place names, especially as an honorific modifier in Shang royal names, followed by Western Zhou royal posthumous names and ancestor honorifics. These are the article’s summaries; its inscriptional examples were not independently checked against primary editions here.

The article therefore documents a live disagreement; it does not establish that the graph originally meant ‘tattoo’ or ‘great’. Its proposed semantic developments to writing, literature, and culture are not independently dated by the evidence inspected.

edges.subject: component:斤
edges.text: One early-form analysis identifies 斤 as an axe and places it in the proposed wood-cutting scene.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 甲骨、金文用例
evidence.text: The database analyzes early 新 as 斤 (axe) plus 辛, with 辛 also serving as a sound component; some forms add 木, sharing strokes with 辛. It reports a Shang oracle-bone example, 《合集》30973, 新鬯 (‘newly brewed wine’), and later bronze uses including 新邑 and 新君. Thus the attested oracle-bone use already includes ‘new’; the sequence ‘firewood first, then borrowed for new’ is an etymological interpretation, not a chronology established by these examples. The account also records a proposal that 新 is an expanded form of 𣓀, whose graph is interpreted as splitting wood with a wedge.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：新

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解; 甲骨文、金文、戰國文字用例
evidence.text: The entry analyzes early 新 as 斤 plus 辛, with 辛 functioning as a phonetic component; some later forms add 木 below 辛, sharing strokes at their boundary. It reports variants in Shang oracle-bone and Zhou bronze forms, and Warring States slips that separate 木 and 辛 differently. It offers the firewood graph/loan-to-new explanation, but also records the alternative that 新 expands 𣓀, interpreted as splitting wood with a wedge. Oracle-bone 《合集》30973 already uses 新 in 新鬯, glossed as newly brewed wine; the entry also reports later bronze uses 新邑 and 新君. Those attestations show use for ‘new’ but do not date a proposed borrowing event.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 斤 represents the meaning and 辛 represents the sound. The 木 (wood) component was added later. Based on the original meaning "firewood", now written as 薪. The current meaning "new" is a phonetic loan.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 取木也。从斤新聲。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *siŋ): phonetic 辛 (OC *siŋ) + semantic 斤 — to chop wood. Original form of 薪 (OC *siŋ, “firewood”). The character was later borrowed to represent 新 (OC *siŋ, “new”) as an instance of jiajie (假借).
A semantic 木 was later added in the bronze inscriptions which merged with the 辛.
Shuowen misinterprets the character as 𣓀 + 斤.
Sino-Tibetan; cognate with Burmese သစ် (sac, “new”). Compare the cognacy between 薪 (OC *siŋ, “firewood”) and Burmese သစ် (sac, “wood; timber”).
This word may belong to the Sino-Tibetan stem Proto-Sino-Tibetan *sreŋ (“alive, fresh, green”) and may hence be related to 青 (OC *sʰleːŋ, “green”) as well as 薪 (OC *siŋ, “firewood”) (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 online text and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry says ‘取木也。从斤新聲’ (‘taking wood; from 斤, with 新 as phonetic’). Duan Yucai argues the text should instead be read ‘从斤木，辛聲’ (‘from 斤 and 木, 辛 as phonetic’), rejecting the received component analysis. Shuowen is an early historical account of the graph, but its component wording conflicts with later paleographic analysis and is not independent proof of the graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「新」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: Records the received Shuowen form ‘从斤，(新)[𣓀]聲’ and contrasts it with the analysis of early forms as 斤+辛, sometimes with an added 木. It says the latter represents chopping wood for fuel, and interprets 薪 as later marked with 艸 after 新 was used for ‘new’. The dossier’s alternatives therefore remain: a firewood graph later used for ‘new’; an analysis of 新 as an expanded 𣓀; and Shuowen/Duan’s differing phonetic-component accounts. The object-name and original pronunciation of any depicted chopping implement are not independently established by the cited material.

edges.text: Reported Shang inscription uses include a western-direction context and 四方. These attestations establish early directional use, but do not show whether it continues the graph’s original meaning or reflects borrowing for a similar-sounding word.

evidence.text: The database cites Shang oracle-bone records: 合集 28190 uses 方 in a west-direction context; 合集 30394 has 四方 in a ritual context; 合集 36536 and 屯南 2301 use 方 for polities; and 合集 28086 has 方伯 for polity leaders. evidence.text: 溥也。从二，闕；方聲。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *baːŋ): semantic 同 + phonetic 方 (OC *paŋ, *baŋ).
The upper component, which perhaps indicates the semantic field, is unclear and has evolved significantly in time, including 冖 (Shang), 同 (Western Zhou), or forms resembling 辛 (Spring and Autumn bronze of Wu) or 用 (Warring States bronze inscription of Wei and proto-clerical script of Qin). In the Chu Silk Manuscript the form was much simplified.
The modern form was a descendant from the clerical script. Hence, a knife or chisel to mark prisoners 辛 is written above the phonetic component 方, perhaps to indicate the concept of moving to remote. However, as already stated, the semantic component in this character is unclear and evolved during time, hence more explanations linked to the earlier versions can be formulated.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *paŋ ~ *pak (“side”) (STEDT). Cognate with Mizo bǎng (“wall, stockage”), as well as possibly Burmese ဘက် (bhak, “side”).

edges.subject: character:旁
edges.text: 旁 is used with the meanings “side,” “beside,” and “near.” Early manuscript examples are reported, but the first occurrence of these meanings is not dated here.

evidence.source: merged_record
evidence.text: side; by side, close by, near

evidence.source: 說文解字 online, Guangyun and pronunciation metadata on the character page
evidence.text: The page records the Guangyun fanqie 步光切 and Middle Chinese-era reading tradition, alongside modern páng; it quotes Duan Yucai’s interpretation of the old gloss 溥 as ‘broad/abundant’ and his observation that later writers used the sense ‘side.’ This does not date the first occurrence of the side sense, nor establish when or how ‘broad’ developed into ‘side.’

evidence.source: CUHK 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 旁; 形義源流通解; oracle and bronze usage
evidence.text: The entry says oracle forms comprise 方 plus an unidentified element, with a proposal that this element is a reduced 凡. It describes Western Zhou bronze forms as 方 plus 凡, says the upper part of 方 may carry a decorative stroke, and notes that later forms can share a stroke. In Warring States forms 凡 may be miswritten as 用. It reports oracle uses as a place name (合集36945) and a polity name 旁方 (屯南918), and a bronze use as a personal name; a Spring-and-Autumn bronze inscription uses 旁 for 方 in a directional expression. These cited early uses do not establish the later common meaning ‘side/near.’

edges.subject: character:日
edges.text: Oracle-bone examples attest 日 for the sun, and present-day Chinese dictionaries list this sense. Its use in the earliest documented corpus cited here does not prove it was the graph's first-ever use.

evidence.source: Multi-function Chinese Character Database, Academia Sinica
evidence.field: Oracle-bone character entry; paleographic account and cited inscriptions
evidence.text: The database describes 日 as a depiction of the sun, with early round forms sometimes squared because a circle was difficult to carve on bone; it says the central mark distinguished the graph from 囗. It cites Shang oracle-bone examples for the sun and sunrise (合集34163), eclipse (合集11480), daylight contrasted with evening (合集33871, 合集34036), and a period of five days (合集12314). It also notes later bronze-inscription uses for the sun, daylight, and calendar-day unit. The inscription citations substantiate distinct early uses; they do not by themselves establish the order in which those senses developed.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：日

evidence.source: Multi-function Chinese Character Database, CUHK

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》, 天津古籍出版社／遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692; scan inspected
evidence.field: 日部 entry, printed p. 599 / PDF p. 612; headword, glyph sequence, and prose checked against the supplied scan. The entry ends on this page; the next page begins the unrelated 旻 entry.
evidence.text: Under the actual headword 日, the entry describes the graph as pictographic and its initial form as resembling the sun. edges.subject: component:棗
edges.text: A later-bronze analysis identifies 棗 as a sound element, sometimes reduced to 朿. evidence.source: Chen Jian, “說「時」,” Bulletin of the Jao Tsung-I Academy of Sinology 4 (2017)
evidence.text: Chen reports no secure 時/旹 graph or time-word use in known Shang oracle-bone, Western Zhou oracle-bone, or pre-Spring-and-Autumn bronze evidence. The earliest known 旹 graph is Eastern Zhou; it is often elaborated with 寺 as a phonetic element to form 時. Chen says alleged oracle-bone 時 examples are generally misread combinations of 之 and 日 (‘this day’). The article distinguishes the old time word in transmitted early texts such as the Shangshu from the later secure graph evidence, and cautions that a four-season division may be later than the abstract time concept.

evidence.text: Chen treats abstract time as the lexical core and surveys extensions including time/moment/duration, time unit, season or quarter, era, timely conditions, and calendrical time. He regards a proposed relation with 之 as more plausible than a relation with 待, while saying the account need not be limited to solar motion. The demonstrative 時 (‘this/that’) is treated separately because its usage differs; its relationship to the time noun remains complex. These lexical arguments do not demonstrate that the graph depicts movement of the sun.

It separately records 明 borrowed for ‘next’ in a Tsinghua manuscript and as a loan for 盟 in Houma covenant texts. These are source-reported readings and interpretations; the underlying inscription images were not inspected here.

edges.text: Shuowen identifies 明 as an ancient form of 朙, whose analysis joins 月 and 囧. This does not show that 朙 was the only early construction.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說文釋形；字樣說明；釋義

edges.subject: component:囧
edges.text: 囧 is proposed as a sound element in 朙. Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstructions for 囧 (*k-mraŋʔ) and 明 (*mraŋ) differ in initial and final; current Mandarin jiǒng and míng resemble one another but do not settle the historical analysis. The window’s ancient spoken name is not established.

evidence.text: The entry reports four oracle-bone forms: 日+月, interpreted by Xu Zhongshu as the sun rising while the moon remains, hence dawn; 月+囧, with 囧 also phonetic and depicted as a lattice window, interpreted as moonlight entering a room; 目+月, with the oracle-bone examples too fragmentary to confirm as 明; and 田+月, where 田 may be a corruption of 日 or 囧. It says oracle-bone examples include dawn in 合集481 (‘乙巳明雨’) and brightness in 合集21037 (‘不喪朙’). Bronze examples include dawn in 大盂鼎, and ‘clear/manifest’ uses in other inscriptions. The entry reports that the Qin Shuihudi manuscript’s 目-form was judged by Qiu Xigui to be a corruption of 囧. It separately records 明 borrowed for ‘next’ in a Tsinghua manuscript and as a loan for 盟 in Houma covenant texts. These are source-reported readings and interpretations; the underlying inscription images were not inspected here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 明

evidence.source: CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨文及金文用例
evidence.text: The entry reports several early analyses. One oracle-bone form joins 日 and 月; Xu Zhongshu interprets it as dawn, while Shen Pei proposes brightness. The entry says 目+月 examples are too fragmentary to identify securely, and 田+月 may reflect corruption of 日 or 囧. It cites oracle-bone examples for dawn (合集481) and brightness (合集21037), and bronze examples for dawn and later senses including clear, manifest, and morally upright. evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；字形分析與用例
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 星 as 从晶、生聲: 晶 depicts an array of stars and 生 is the phonetic. It reports the original sense as stars, a Western Zhou bronze inscription 麓伯簋 using 星 in a personal name, and an oracle-bone example 合集15625反 read as “晴” (clear weather). It also cites 星言夙駕 in the Shijing as clear-weather use, but that interpretation is disputed. The entry records later borrowing of 星 for 腥 in Warring States/Qin slips and Han silk manuscripts, and extensions such as scattered or numerous. These attestations do not establish a precise first-occurrence date for each sense.

evidence.text: The database analyzes 昨 as 日 semantic + 乍 phonetic and glosses it as the day before today, extended more generally to the past. It records the Shuowen gloss 壘日也 and its component analysis 从日、乍聲, and Guangyun fanqie 在各. Its examples for the ‘yesterday’ sense include the Shiji 外戚世家 passage 昨暮夜; its broader past sense is illustrated with Tao Yuanming's 東晉-era phrase 覺今是而昨非 and a Tang poem. This supports those senses and citations, but the page does not date the earliest attestation of 昨 itself.

edges.text: A published account describes copula use emerging during the Eastern Han, developing from demonstrative uses through constructions with copula-like properties. evidence.source: Silpakorn University Journal of the Faculty of Arts
evidence.text: The article describes a development from demonstrative pronoun, through a demonstrative with copula-like properties, to copula use during the Eastern Han period. It reports that zero-copula and verbal-copula constructions continued in parallel, with copula constructions increasing substantially after the Tang and replacing the zero-copula pattern in modern narrative after the May Fourth Movement. These are the article's periodization claims; the abstract does not supply individual dated examples.

evidence.text: The dictionary identifies 㝡 as a nonstandard/later variant of 最, citing a Sui Longzangsi stele and references that describe this spelling in Six Dynasties usage. evidence.field: 形義通解; 《說文》; 《廣韻》; character form tables

edges.subject: character:最
edges.text: 最 appears in the administrative expression 課殿最; this use does not establish when the current superlative sense arose.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Multi-function Dictionary), character entry 最
evidence.field: 形義通解; dated textual examples
evidence.text: The entry separates later attested uses: 《漢書·宣帝紀》 has 最 in the administrative ranking expression 課殿最; 《燕丹子》 uses it for a foremost person or thing; 《小爾雅·廣詁》 glosses 最 as 要 (“summary/essential”); 《管子·禁藏》 uses it in a context glossed by the commentator as 聚 (“gather”); 《史記·絳侯周勃世家》 has a totaling sense; and 《墨子·經上》 uses 最 as “foremost.” The page also cites a Tang poem for a “just/exactly” adverbial use. These examples show distinct uses, but the page supplies no first-attestation chronology for the modern superlative sense; gloss order must not be read as chronology.

edges.subject: character:月
edges.text: 月 is used for the moon in current Chinese, and Shang oracle-bone examples attest the same use, including in an eclipse context. These are early examples, but the precise first dated occurrence is not established here.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry gives oracle-bone uses for 月 as ‘moon’, including 合集11483正, glossed as ‘之夕，月有食’ (an eclipse of the moon), and as a calendrical month, citing 合集5658正 ‘今十一月帝不其令雨’ and the bronze inscription 曶鼎 ‘唯王元年六月’. It describes the month sense as arising from the moon’s waxing-and-waning cycle. These are source-reported readings and glosses; they do not establish that ‘month’ was later than ‘moon’ solely by list order.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析; 月 entry
evidence.text: The entry describes oracle-bone and bronze forms as a half-moon pictograph with ‘moon’ as the original meaning. It gives an oracle-bone eclipse example, 合集11483正, and Shang oracle-bone and bronze examples using 月 for calendar months: 合集5658正 and 曶鼎. It connects the month use to the moon’s waxing and waning cycle; the page does not independently establish that one Shang use predates the other.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》, 2012, 天津古籍出版社／遼寧人民出版社
evidence.field: 月部 entry; printed p. 618; PDF p. 631; original scan visually inspected
evidence.text: The entry describes 月 as a pictograph whose early form resembles a half moon, with ‘moon’ as its meaning. It says 月 and 夕 were sometimes confused, bronze forms continued the earlier line, and the small-seal form underwent graphic change. It cites an oracle-bone eclipse passage as 《合集》11485, then explains the calendar-month use through the moon’s waxing and waning and mentions a later ‘time’ sense. The entry and its discussion are visible on this page; the next page begins with the following headword 朔, so no continuation of 月 is indicated.

edges.subject: component:又
edges.text: The bronze-form account treats 又 as the hand in a proposed hand-holding-meat scene; this structure is not established for every early form.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 有 entry
evidence.text: The entry distinguishes the transmitted 說文 analysis (从月，又聲) from a modern graphic account: bronze forms are analyzed as 又 (hand) plus 肉, depicting a hand holding meat; it calls the 月 account a misreading. It cites the bronze inscription 叔尸鐘「咸有九州」 for possession and notes 有𤔲 as a title corresponding to later 有司. This supports a competing graphic account, but does not by itself establish that the hand-and-meat scene is the earliest meaning.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 不宜有也。《春秋傳》曰：“日月有食之。”从月又聲。凡有之屬皆从有。

evidence.source: 說文解字 online transcription with 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The transmitted 說文 says 「不宜有也」, quotes 「日月有食之」, and analyzes 有 as 从月又聲. 段玉裁 interprets the gloss as ‘what should not occur but occurs’, says it extended to the general sense of 有, and explains the 月 association through eclipses; his note on 又聲 gives 云九切 and says 有 was often borrowed for 又 in ancient texts. This is evidence for the historical account, not confirmation of the early graph's components.
evidence.title: 說文解字「有」

edges.subject: character:有
edges.text: Reported oracle-bone uses, including 有虎? 亡其鹿?, are interpreted as existential. Their exact date and priority over every other early use are unresolved.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: 甲骨文 semantic-use discussion, citing 楊逢彬 2003 and 張玉金 2001
evidence.text: A 2024 linguistics article reports that oracle-bone examples of 有 are used for existence, not possession, citing 有虎? 亡其鹿? (《合集》893正); it says the traditional hand-holding-meat interpretation is possible as possession or as existence, since possession presupposes existence. This is a scholarly semantic analysis, not a direct independent inspection of the cited inscription image.
evidence.title: 外

evidence.source: CUHK article in 外
evidence.text: The article reports the oracle-bone example 有虎? 亡其鹿? (《合集》893正) as existential. It gives 有大雨? / 無雨? as contrasting existence examples and cites the received text 《老子》「有無相生」 and 《玉篇》 (梁代, 543 CE) glosses 有、不無 and 無、不有. Its argument is that existence is the earliest recoverable sense and possession developed from it; the earliest examples support use, but do not alone date the later semantic extension.
evidence.title: 外

edges.subject: character:朋
edges.text: 朋 is recorded as a currency-counting measure in the Book of Odes textual tradition. Traditional explanations differ over how many cowries made one 朋 and how they were grouped; its date relative to other recorded senses is unresolved.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry lists uses for phoenix, group, people of the same kind, friend, association, comparison, and a currency-counting measure. It cites 《詩經·小雅·菁菁者莪》 for the hundred-peng currency expression and transmits Zheng Xuan’s gloss that five cowries made one 朋; it also quotes Wang Guowei’s view that five made a string and two strings made a 朋. These glosses and citations do not by themselves establish when the senses arose.
evidence.title: [A01844] 朋 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說文釋形; 字樣說明; 釋義
evidence.text: The entry transmits Shuowen's account that a graph was an ancient form of 鳳 and was used for 朋黨 because many birds follow a phoenix; it also says regular 朋 is written like two adjacent 月 forms. Separately, it lists phoenix, group, same-kind persons, friend, and a currency-counting measure. For the measure it reports Zheng Xuan's five-cowries gloss and Wang Guowei's analysis of five cowries per string and two strings per 朋. This is a record of traditional explanations and listed senses, not proof that the distinct early valuables-unit graph descended from the phoenix graph or a dated chronology for the senses.
evidence.title: [A01844] 朋 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry cites the Book of Odes line ‘既見君子，錫我百朋’ under the currency-measure sense and transmits Zheng Xuan's gloss that five cowries made one 朋, alongside Wang Guowei's alternative grouping analysis. This supports describing the measure as attested in the Odes tradition; it does not establish a date for the surviving text witness or the measure's relative chronology against other senses.
evidence.title: [A01844] 朋 - 教育部《異體字字典》 臺灣學術網路十四版（正式七版）2024

evidence.source: Wikisource, 詩經/菁菁者莪
