evidence.text: The poem text includes “既見君子，錫我百朋” (“having seen the noble guest, grant me a hundred peng”). This attests the currency-related expression in the Odes textual tradition; the opened text page does not date its surviving textual witness or independently date the sense.

evidence.source: CUHK Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes bronze forms of 期 with 日 and 其, and also forms with 月 and 其. It treats 日 and 月 as time-related semantic elements, and 其 as the phonetic. It reports bronze uses for a calendrical period, a limit or deadline, and a personal name. It cites 吳王光鑑 for 既字白期 (interpreted there as a lunar-phase period) and 王子午鼎 for 萬年無期.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 期

evidence.source: 出土春秋文獻中一詞對應多字現象的初步考察 (名詞篇)
evidence.text: The study treats 期 as a temporal limit or deadline and cites 《詩·王風·君子于役》不知其期 and 《詩·鄘風·桑中》期我乎桑中. It separately notes the 春秋中晚期祝寿 formula 萬年無期/眉壽無期 and says earlier Western Zhou and early Spring-and-Autumn materials used 萬年無疆/眉壽無疆 for similar blessings. It does not establish from those examples a simple chronological development from a lunar “period” sense to “deadline.”
evidence.kind: secondary study citing transmitted and excavated texts
evidence.title: 出土春秋文獻中一詞對應多字現象的初步考察（名詞篇）

evidence.source: Southwest University study of excavated Spring-and-Autumn texts
evidence.text: The study cites transmitted Shijing phrases 不知其期 and 期我乎桑中 for the temporal-limit or appointed-time usage, and reports Spring-and-Autumn bronze祝寿 formulae 萬年無期 and 眉壽無期. It compares these with earlier祝寿 formulae using 無疆, but does not establish a simple chronological semantic progression from a lunar period to deadline.
evidence.kind: secondary study citing transmitted and excavated texts
evidence.title: 出土春秋文獻中一詞對應多字現象的初步考察（名詞篇）

edges.subject: character:木
edges.text: 木 is currently used for ‘tree’. An oracle-bone phrase, 埶(藝)木, is reported as a tree-planting use; the rubbing was not independently checked. This evidence does not establish whether ‘tree’ or ‘wood’ came first.

evidence.source: merged_record
evidence.text: tree; wood, lumber; wooden

evidence.source: kanjidic2_via_build_kanji
evidence.text: Tree; Wood

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Humanum)
evidence.text: The entry identifies 《合集》5749, 埶(藝)木, as an oracle-bone use for planting trees and interprets it as ‘plant trees’. It presents this as use in the graph’s original sense. The reading and interpretation are the entry’s report; the underlying rubbing was not inspected in this research.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 木

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum; Fudan Center article by 蕭旭; 中國大百科全書
evidence.text: Evidence supports CUHK’s interpretation of the oracle-bone phrase as tree-related, but the exact inscribed form was not checked against a rubbing here. The Mawangdui witness independently supports a specific phonetic loan use 木(沐); the burial date dates the witness only. Component wording should describe trunk, branches, and roots as parts of one pictorial form. Graphic captions should avoid claiming that every pictured stroke visibly resolves into branches or roots.
evidence.title: Research synthesis based on inspected sources

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Humanum)
evidence.text: The entry describes 木 in oracle-bone and bronze forms as a tree, with upper parts interpreted as branches and lower parts as roots. It quotes the received Shuowen analysis as 屮 above roots, then cites Wang Yun’s objection that 木 is a complete-body pictograph, not a graph composed of 屮. It reports 《合集》5749「埶(藝)木」 as planting trees, and separately notes place and polity-name uses whose relation to the ordinary tree word is not established. These are the entry’s readings; the underlying inscription rubbing was not independently checked.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》
evidence.field: 木部 entry; PDF p. 503, printed p. 490
evidence.text: The 木 entry calls the graph pictographic, describes its upper part as branches and lower part as roots, and gives ‘tree’ as its original sense. It lists uses for leaves, timber, wooden things, coffins, instruments in the ‘eight sounds’, the ‘wood’ phase of the Five Phases, and ‘plain/simple’. The entry does not date those uses or establish their order. I inspected the supplied page image directly; the entry and these lines are legible. PDF p. 504 (printed p. 491) continues other characters, not 木.
evidence.title: 字源, 李學勤主編, 2012; ISBN 9787552800692

edges.subject: character:木
edges.text: The graph is currently used for ‘wood’ or ‘lumber’. 木枋 in a bronze inscription is interpreted as a wooden writing board, supporting an older wood or timber use; its chronology relative to the tree-planting phrase is unresolved.

evidence.source: 漢典
evidence.text: The dictionary lists ‘tree’ and ‘timber/wood’ separately and cites received-text attestations including 《論語》朽木不可雕也 for wood, 《孟子》與木石居 for tree/wood, and 《左傳》就木 for coffin. Its citation list supplies textual sources but generally not composition dates; it therefore cannot by itself establish when each sense arose or a full chronology of extensions.

This supports a historical wood or timber use. The page gives no exact date for this inscription, so it does not establish when that sense began relative to ‘tree’.

It also reports bronze-inscription uses: 散氏盤「桹木道」, interpreted as a tree or place name, and 曶鼎「木枋」, interpreted as a wooden writing board. These records establish separately interpreted tree-related and wood-related uses in oracle-bone and bronze material, but the page gives no absolute date for either cited inscription and does not establish which sense came first. The distinction in period labels alone does not establish semantic chronology.

edges.subject: character:木
edges.text: In a Mawangdui manuscript passage, 木 is reported as a sound-based spelling for 沐. This borrows the graph for another word rather than extending the meaning ‘tree’ or ‘wood’; the first use of this spelling is unresolved.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Humanum)
evidence.text: The entry notes that oracle-bone 木 forms can be confused with a shortened form of 燎/尞, a graphic resemblance/confusion issue, not evidence that 木 itself arose through corruption. It separately records 木 used as a loan for 沐 in the Mawangdui silk manuscript 《胎產書》, line 5, and compares 木猴 with 沐猴 in 《法言》. This is evidence of later phonetic borrowing, distinct from the graph’s pictographic development.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 木

evidence.source: 蕭旭, Fudan University Center for Excavated Texts and Ancient Chinese Characters
evidence.text: The article reproduces the manuscript reading 毋使朱(侏)儒，不觀木(沐)侯(猴), with 木 and 侯 annotated as phonetic loans for 沐 and 猴. It also notes parallels in transmitted medical texts. This supports treating 木 here as a graph loan for the word 沐, rather than as a semantic extension of ‘tree/wood’. The article’s text does not independently date the manuscript’s composition.
evidence.title: 蕭旭：馬王堆帛書《胎產書》、《養生方》校補

evidence.source: 中國大百科全書
evidence.text: The encyclopedia identifies 《胎產書》 as a silk manuscript excavated in December 1973 from Tomb 3 at Mawangdui, Changsha. This dates the excavated witness, not the date when the text or the 木-for-沐 spelling originated.
evidence.title: 帛书《胎产书》 — 中国大百科全书

evidence.source: 蕭旭, 复旦大学出土文献与古文字研究中心
evidence.text: The article prints the manuscript passage with 「不觀木（沐）侯（猴）」 and compares it with transmitted parallels. This supports a context-specific phonetic loan reading 木 for 沐 in the Mawangdui text, distinct from a semantic extension of ‘tree/wood’. The article does not date the text’s composition or establish the first occurrence of the loan.
evidence.title: 蕭旭：馬王堆帛書《胎產書》、《養生方》校補

edges.subject: component:一
edges.text: In one transmitted analysis, 一 marks the lower part of 木; another analysis reads the mark as 丅.

evidence.text: 木下曰本。从木，一在其下。

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說文釋形; 字樣說明
evidence.text: The entry distinguishes two transmitted Shuowen readings: the Daxu text analyzes 木 plus 一 below it; Duan Yucai's annotated text instead reads 木 plus 丅. It also notes that 夲 has an independent sense/pronunciation (tāo, rapid advance) although it has also served as a popular written variant of 本. This establishes competing textual/form analyses and variant use, not a chronological ancestor relationship between 本 and 夲.
evidence.title: Ministry of Education 《Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants》 — 本

evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 形義通解; 字形資料; 說文 and 廣韻 records
evidence.text: The entry interprets 本 as 木 plus 一, with 一 marking the lower part, and gives the original sense as plant root. It quotes Shuowen 木下曰本 and Lüshi Chunqiu with Gao You's root gloss. It displays one small-seal example, seven manuscript forms and one other form, with no examples displayed in its bronze or oracle slots. It gives Guangyun fanqie 布忖. The senses it lists include the base of a long object, trunk, foundation, source/cause, basis, draft and classifier; their order is not a chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.field: 本 entry; formation, glyph sequence and semantic examples; PDF p. 516, printed p. 503; scan /home/catalin/hanzi-etymology-books/research-ocr/ziyuan-full/page-0516/source.png (file SHA-256 f732cc6b3e3988c9455fe2aa8c420cafa0adbc24c01aa76fb742a9f67a1df5b4)
evidence.text: The scanned 本 headword describes the graph as 指事. It says Western Zhou forms add a dot at the part of 木 representing the tree root, and Warring States forms change the dot to a short horizontal stroke. It describes the Shuowen ancient form as 木 above three root-like marks; some Warring States variants use 白 to represent a tree pit. It gives the original meaning as tree root, quotes 《国语·晋语一》 “伐木不自其本，必复生,” and records further uses for plant stem/trunk and figurative fundamental or important matters, including contrast with 末 and an agriculture sense. This is one source’s account; the early graph sequence and the cited works’ composition dates are not independently established here.

edges.subject: character:条
edges.text: In a transmitted 詩經 example, 條 refers to a branch, distinguished in the accompanying gloss from a trunk. This is an attested use, not necessarily the character’s original meaning.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The entry cites 詩經·周南·汝墳「遵彼汝墳，伐其條枚」 for branch usage and quotes Mao’s gloss「枝曰條，榦曰枚」. It reports a bronze-inscription example from the Cai Hou tomb remnant bell,「鳴陽(揚)條虡」, but says the inscription is incomplete and its meaning uncertain; suggestions include reading 條 as 悠 (‘distant’) or taking it as open/sonorous. It reports a Warring States Chu bamboo-slip use of 條 read as 悠 in Guodian 性自命出 slip 31, meaning sorrowful thought, and later transmitted examples for classifier use, 通貫 (‘throughgoing’), and orderly structure. The source does not establish the chronology or semantic bridges among these later uses.

edges.subject: character:来
edges.text: The graph is traditionally explained as a picture of wheat, and lexicographic and transmitted literary evidence records it in grain terminology. The earliest securely dated use of 來 alone for wheat is unresolved.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 周所受瑞麥來麰。一來二縫，象芒朿之形。天所來也，故爲行來之來。《詩》曰：“詒我來麰。”凡來之屬皆从來。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形) of wheat – original character of 麥 (OC *mrɯːɡ, “wheat”) or 麳 (OC *rɯː, “wheat”). The line in the middle represents the ear, the two lines pointing upwards represent leaves, and the lines pointing downwards represent the stem and roots. An additional horizontal line was often added at the top end of the character, possibly used to emphasize the ear of the wheat. Compare 禾; both are unrelated to 釆.
This character has been borrowed for “to come” since the oracle bone script. During the Western Zhou and Warring States periods, additional semantic components, such as 止 (“foot”) or 辵 (“to walk”), were added to differentiate the original sense from the borrowed sense. However, these additions were not inherited in later scripts.
Some consider the derivative 麥 from the addition of 夊 (“to walk slowly”) to be the original form for the meaning “to come”. If so, their meanings have interchanged due to frequent use of 來 for “to come”.
Shuowen connects “wheat” and “to come” from a mythological standpoint: 天所來也 (“it comes from the heavens”). This may be supported by archaeological evidence, which suggests that wheat is not native to China, but originated in the Fertile Crescent.
來 and 麥 have both been reconstructed to begin with *mr- in Old Chinese. The former retains the liquid as /l/, while the latter retains the nasal /m/.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *la-j ~ ra (“to come”) (STEDT). Cognate with 迨 (OC *l'ɯːʔ, “to reach; until”), 賚 (OC *rɯːs, “to bestow”), Burmese လာ (la, “to come”). Also cognate with 蒞 (OC *rɯbs, “to arrive”) according to Schuessler (2007). Unclear if connected to Vietnamese lại (“come; again”).

evidence.text: The article describes late Shang oracle-bone and bronze 來 as a plant-shaped graph, with a stem, paired slanting leaves, and an upper ear-like part; it notes the upper extra mark may be an ear detail or ornamental stroke. It reports oracle-bone contexts using 來 predominantly for ‘come/go’, tribute, future year, and a place name, and argues the added foot graph 麥 was intended to mark the wheat word. It cites oracle-bone examples including 合集33260 for a proposed wheat reading and 合集1027正 and 12872 for motion senses. evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003)
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 杯 as a phono-semantic compound, 木 semantic and 不 phonetic, and places it in the 不 phonetic series. In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction system it gives 杯 *plɯː and 不 *pɯ, *pɯʔ, *pɯ'. The reconstructed forms share an initial and rhyme nucleus but differ in the reconstructed lateral and vowel length; this is compatible with a phonetic-series relationship, not proof of exact identity. The entry also mentions 否 as a variant phonetic analysis with a speculative semantic association (‘block’), for which the inspected page gives no primary paleographic support.
evidence.title: 杯 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: 裘錫圭, 釋「尌」, Fudan University Center for the Study of Excavated Texts and Paleography
evidence.field: discussion of 樹 and 尌 graph history
evidence.text: Qiu argues that 樹 and 尌 were originally one graph/word for ‘plant/set upright’; on his account a form with 木 underwent graphic changes, including corruption toward 壴 and 寸, and 木 was later added to distinguish 樹. He discusses competing explanations and rejects an alternative ‘candle’ interpretation as insufficiently supported. This conflicts in detail with accounts that treat the components as a straightforward semantic 木 plus phonetic 尌 from the outset.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 木 represents the meaning and 卓 represents the sound.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意) and phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *rteːwɢ): phonetic 卓 (OC *rteːwɢ, “high”) + semantic 木 (“tree; wood”) – table. The bottom 十 of 卓 has merged with or been replaced by 木. An obsolete variant that distinguishes the two components is 棹.
From 卓 (OC *rteːwɢ, “high”), as tables are relatively tall (compared to other pieces of furniture like 几 (OC *krilʔ, “stool”)).
Similar descriptive derivations for pieces of furniture include:
* 登 (OC *tɯːŋ, “to climb”) > 凳 (OC *tɯːŋs, “stool”)
* 倚 (OC *qralʔ, *qrals, “to lean”) > 椅 (OC *qral, *qralʔ, “chair”).

evidence.source: 漢典
evidence.text: The entry classifies 桌 as a phonosemantic graph, 从木、卓声. This supports 木 as the semantic component and 卓 as the sound component in the conventional analysis. It does not establish the historical date or sequence of the graph’s formation.

edges.subject: character:桌
edges.text: 桌 names furniture such as a table, desk, or stand. Historical reports cite earlier furniture spellings, but do not show that 桌 itself was used in those early passages.

evidence.source: merged_record
evidence.text: table, desk, stand

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese University of Hong Kong）
evidence.text: Analyzes 桌 as 木 semantic plus 卓 phonetic, meaning a stand/table. Cites 正字通: “桌，呼几案曰桌.” Also cites an example from 兒女英雄傳, chapter 21, including 桌椅 and 一桌葷菜. The database describes 卓-derived “tall” as a possible motivation for the furniture name, but this is an account of the word’s naming, not proof that 桌 was first created by a semantic combination.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：桌

evidence.source: 漢典
evidence.field: 桌—康熙字典 quotation of 正字通
evidence.text: The entry quotes 正字通: “俗呼几案曰桌” (“tables/stands are colloquially called 桌”). Its cited wording documents a lexicographic characterization of the furniture sense; no publication date for the quoted 正字通 passage is supplied on this page.
evidence.title: 桌 zhuō - 漢典

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》
evidence.text: The Ministry dictionary reports historical furniture spellings 倚卓 and 倚棹, cites 楊億《談苑》 for 檀香倚卓 in the 咸平、景德 reign periods (998–1007), and treats 棹 as a variant for the furniture sense. This is a report of textual evidence, not proof that the graph 桌 itself occurs in that early passage; it distinguishes 棹/櫂 in its oar sense as another history.
evidence.title: 教育部《異體字字典》：A01921 桌

evidence.source: 澎湃新闻 / 雅昌艺术网, 张辉
evidence.text: The author reports the name 卓子 in 楊億《談苑》 for the 998–1007 period, cites Southern Song 棹 examples in 朱子語類 and 建炎以来系年要录, and says 卓 and 棹 were both used in Song, Yuan, and Ming. The article reports 明末《正字通》 as an early dictionary recording of 桌, with “俗呼几案曰桌.” These are secondary reports of textual attestations, not a comprehensive search proving first use.
evidence.title: 雅昌专栏 | 张辉：唐宋时期局脚桌流变——《中国家具史》

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, R.O.C., Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A01921 桌: 說文釋形; 釋義; 形體資料表
evidence.text: The dictionary says 桌 is not recorded in Shuowen. It gives furniture and classifier senses, illustrating the furniture sense with a Three Kingdoms novel passage and the classifier sense with Ming-era novels. These are cited textual examples, not proof that the pictured spelling is the earliest form of the furniture word.
evidence.title: [A01921] 桌 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: 澎湃新闻 / 雅昌艺术网, 张辉
evidence.text: The author reports the furniture name 倚卓 in 楊億《談苑》 for 998–1007, Southern Song 棹 spellings in works including 朱子語類, and 明末《正字通》’s 桌 gloss 俗呼几案曰桌. This is secondary historical reporting; it does not establish a complete first-attestation chronology.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.field: 樓 字形、說文、形義通解
evidence.text: The entry records 樓 as 木 + 婁, shows a seal-script example and three manuscript examples, and quotes 說文:「樓，重屋也。从木，婁聲。」It explains the basic sense as a building with two or more stories. The visible evidence does not establish an oracle-bone or bronze form.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 樓

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.field: 樓 字形、說文、形義通解
evidence.text: The inspected entry labels the displayed archaic form as 小篆 (Small Seal), reports no 金文 (bronze) or 甲骨 (oracle-bone) forms, and shows three 簡帛文字 (manuscript) examples. It quotes 說文:「樓，重屋也。从木，婁聲。」and explains the basic sense as a building with two or more stories. Its cited literary examples include an elevated vehicle, a ship structure, a building storey, and premises such as teahouses or taverns. The examples establish uses cited by the entry, not the date of the graph or a chronological chain among senses.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 樓

edges.text: Qin- and Han-period manuscript citations attest 次 for ordered transmission and successive rank. These uses are established by that period, but do not show that they were the graph’s original meaning.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: dated textual attestations and semantic development
evidence.text: The entry cites Warring States bamboo slips and Han silk manuscripts for ‘inferior/next in rank’ or ‘in sequence’: Shuihudi Qin slips, 語書 slip 8, give 以次傳; Mawangdui Laozi A, line 124 (Han manuscript), repeats 其次 for successive ranks. It separately reports a Han silk use written 次 for 恣 (‘indulge’) and a Mawangdui Xici use written 次 where the transmitted Zhouyi has 濟, presenting these as graphic loans/usages, not stages of the graph’s formation. It cites Zuozhuan 僖公元年 for troops lodging at 聶北 and Zhouli 掌次 for temporary tents, but gives no date for those transmitted textual witnesses in the entry. It traces ordered/serial senses with later literary examples (Liu Yuxi and Bai Juyi) without establishing a precise first occurrence.

evidence.field: discussion of 公功肅將祗歡 and alternative readings
evidence.text: The scholarly commentary documents disagreement over how to parse and understand the 洛誥 phrase: older interpreters take 歡 with a joy-related sense, while other proposals read it as 灌 or 勸 and assign different syntax and meanings. Accordingly, this early textual token is evidence for a transmitted graph in the passage, but its precise sense is disputed and should not be treated as an unambiguous early attestation of ordinary ‘joy’ without qualification.

edges.subject: component:丁
edges.text: Some analyses identify the upper strokes as 丁 and propose a phonetic role. In Old Chinese, 丁 *tˤeŋ resembles 正 *teŋ-s (“correct”) and *C.teŋ (first-month reading); in Middle Chinese, 丁 teng resembles 正 tsyengH and tsyeng for those respective readings. These comparisons do not resolve the graphic identity or prove the phonetic analysis.

sound_comparisons.text: 丁 *tˤeŋ resembles 正 *teŋ-s, the separate “correct” reading; the resemblance supports a proposed phonetic association, not the graphic parse by itself.

evidence.source: Dong Chinese
evidence.field: component analysis, historical forms and reading comparison
evidence.text: Dong Chinese presents 丁 as a sound/iconic component and 止 as the foot component, gives 正 Old Chinese *C.teŋ and *teŋ-s, and gives 丁 *tˤeŋ (with additional forms). It dates displayed forms to oracle script about 1250–1000 BCE, late Shang bronze about 1100 BCE, Shuowen seal script about 100 CE and Eastern Han clerical script 25–220 CE. This account independently supports a phonetic proposal but also treats 丁 iconically as a city wall. evidence.text: 董莲池 proposes an ideographic construction from two 匕, described as ancient shallow, long-handled food ladles with pointed ends. edges.subject: character:比
edges.text: In the early Shang phrase 王比望乘, 比 has been read as “follow” or “lead,” “form a close alliance,” or “assist” and “support.” Its precise sense is disputed.

evidence.source: Li Zongkun, Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica
evidence.text: In a 2007 article abstract on the Shang divination phrase 王比望乘, Li reports competing readings: earlier scholars took 比 as follow or lead, others understood it as close alliance, while Li argues it means assist or support—potentially supplying personnel and materials for a campaign. The example is an early Shang use, but its exact sense remains disputed.

edges.subject: character:气
edges.text: Traditional lexicography assigns 气 the meaning “cloud vapor” and calls it pictographic. Specialist discussions caution that this meaning is not secure for the reported oracle-bone occurrences.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 雲气也。象形。凡气之屬皆从气。

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, specialist paleography discussion
evidence.text: The article reports oracle-bone forms of 气 as three strokes, distinguishes the graph 气 from the later small-seal 氣, and reviews competing readings. It cites instances such as 合12532 and 粹771 as proposed cloud/rain uses, but argues that no known oracle-bone context securely uses 气 as a noun meaning cloud vapor. Other proposed interpretations include a “cut/sever” graph, and readings connected with 迄 or 訖; the article records disagreement over how to segment 气至 in 合6057. It concludes that the oracle-bone referent remains unresolved. No glyph image was visually inspected for this report.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「云」與「气」

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, National Taiwan University
evidence.text: The article reviews proposals that oracle-bone 气 in 合12532 and 粹771 refers to cloud/rain, and competing analyses involving a sign for cutting or readings related to 迄/訖. It notes disagreement about the syntax of 合6057 气至 and concludes that no known oracle-bone occurrence securely uses 气 as the noun ‘cloud vapor.’ Thus the oracle-bone referent and earliest sense remain disputed.

edges.subject: character:水
edges.text: One analysis proposes ‘river’ as 水’s original meaning, while another gives the broader meaning ‘water’; which meaning was original remains unresolved.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Humanum)
evidence.field: 形義通解; 字形; 甲骨文用例; 金文用例
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 水 as a picture of flowing water: oracle forms vary in detail, with a central stroke for the current and side dots for droplets; component forms may reduce the current to drops. Bronze forms retain the flowing-water picture, and the entry says Warring States forms continue the bronze tradition. It reports Shang oracle use for water/flooding in 合集 10150, “其㞢(有)大水,” and another oracle use as a sacrificial name in 合集 14407. It also reports a disputed verbal use in 合集 23532 (“今日王其水𡨦(寢)”), with interpretations involving leveling ground with water or washing a temple. Bronze 水 is reported borrowed for 乞 ‘request’ in 沈子簋. These are the database’s reported readings and analyses; the record does not establish the disputed verb’s semantic connection to the noun.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 水

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義通解; 《說文》; 甲骨文用例; 金文用例
evidence.text: The entry describes oracle forms of 水 as picturing flowing water, with a central stroke for the current and side dots for droplets; form and dot count vary. It says bronze forms also depict flowing water and Warring States forms continue the bronze tradition. It reports Shang oracle usage for flood/disaster in 合集 10150, for a sacrificial name in 合集 14407, and a disputed verbal use in 合集 23532, interpreted either as leveling ground with water or washing a temple. The ordinary-noun connection for that verbal use remains unresolved. It separately reports 水 borrowed in a bronze inscription to write 乞 ‘request’. The page quotes the Shuowen account and characterizes its cosmological statements as Han yin-yang theory; it treats 水，準也 as a sound gloss, then describes 水準 as a later compound for a leveling instrument and an abstract level or standard, without dating those stages.

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》, 天津古籍出版社／遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692
evidence.field: 水 entry; PDF p. 970; printed p. 955; graphic history and meaning history
evidence.text: The scan-checked 水 entry calls the graph pictographic and says it first appears in Shang oracle-bone script. It describes varying forms, with a winding stroke for flowing water and side dots for droplets; Zhou-to-Qin forms broadly retain this picture, while Han forms move toward a straighter stroke and connected droplet marks. Separately, it proposes 河流 ‘river’ as the original meaning, then describes extension to rivers generally, water as a transparent liquid, and other liquids. It reports oracle-bone examples used for flooding or flood disaster. Thus the book’s claim about first graphic appearance is distinct from its proposed original sense; the reported flood examples are not stated to establish that sense’s priority.

edges.subject: character:汉
edges.text: 漢 became an ethnic or cultural label associated with the prestige of the Han dynasty. The timing and stabilization are debated, and the earliest securely dated example is unresolved.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Earliest attested in early Western Zhou bronze inscriptions; the 京師畯尊 preserves the form ⿰氵⿱𦰩火. Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *hnaːns): semantic 水 (“water”) + phonetic 𦰩 — name of the Han River. 𦰩 (phonetic; a bound person crying out, probable original form of 嘆 /叹 (tàn)) became confused with 黃 /黄 (huáng) as early as the 伯△鼎 (銘續 0213), and by the Spring and Autumn period the corruption was nearly complete. ⿱𦰩火 (transcribable as 堇 (qín) or 熯) may relate to the oracle bone sacrificial practice of burning disabled people (尪 (wāng)) to pray for rain (⿱黃火).
The usage for the Chinese ethnicity first appeared during the Northern and Southern Dynasties, claiming the Han dynasty as one of the golden ages of Chinese history. Before the Han dynasty, the Chinese referred their land as 華夏 ("Huaxia"), and themselves as 諸華 ("various Hua people") or 諸夏 ("various people/descendants of the Xias"). "Xia" ("Summer; great, splendid") also gave the name to the first semi-legendary Chinese dynasty, the Xia Dinasty (夏朝).

evidence.source: Mark C. Elliott, Hushuo: The Northern Other and the Naming of the Han Chinese
evidence.text: The abstract dates the beginning of the process by which Han came to name the Central Plains people as early as the sixth century CE and argues the meaning stabilized only much later, after the Ming began. This cautions against treating Han as a timeless ethnic label. The abstract does not supply the earliest dated textual example.
evidence.title: Hushuo: The Northern Other and the Naming of the Han Chinese

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

It does not establish a first securely dated ethnonym use or a single continuous semantic chain.

edges.text: 没 is identified as the standardized simplified form of 沒. A separate account describes corruption of the right side in a common variant but does not establish a complete graphic sequence for standardized 没.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Simplified form of 沒.  Pictograph of a hand reaching in the water to grab something. Later the meaning shifted to "drown". This meaning is only used when the character is pronouned "mò". When pronounced "méi" (which is much more common), it means "not have". This meaning is a phonetic loan, unrelated to the original meaning.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary classifies 没 as a variant of 沒 and says its right side was commonly corrupted from the older right side into 殳. It quotes 《類篇》 for several readings of 没, including 莫勃切 and 莫佩切. This supports a graphic-corruption analysis for 没; it does not establish that simplified 没 originated as a planned phonetic substitution.

edges.text: In the common reading méi, 沒 is used for “not have” and “none.” One contested proposal is that the graph used for “sink” or “drown” was borrowed to write this different word because the words may have sounded alike. evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *mɯːd): semantic 水 (“water”) + phonetic 𠬛.
Possibly a colloquial variant of 勿 (MC mjut) or 未 (MC mj+jH), which fused with or was influenced by 有 (MC hjuwX); not derived from 沒 (OC *mɯːd, “to dive; to drown”) (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
According to Schuessler (2007), formed from the convergence of two etyma:
* Proto-Sino-Tibetan *mit (“to extinguish”). The i ~ u alternation is a common phenomenon in Sino-Tibetan.
* An etymon meaning "to dive", whence Burmese မြုပ် (mrup, “to sink; to be submerged”), which is a loan from Proto-Mon-Khmer *(b)ləp (“to immerse”) according to Shorto (1972).
Unrelated to etymology 1.

evidence.text: The entry cites the 《史記·酈生陸賈列傳》 episode “沛公方倨床，洗足” (Liu Bang sitting on a couch while having his feet washed), and 《論衡·譏日》, which distinguishes washing the head, feet, hands, and body. It also cites 《詩經·大雅·行葦》 “或獻或酢，洗爵奠斝” for washing a ritual vessel, and 《儀禮·士冠禮》 for 洗 as a vessel receiving wash water. These citations document foot-washing and vessel-related uses separately; they do not by themselves establish the exact first occurrence or a linear semantic chronology. evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 《說文》; 金文; historical uses
evidence.text: The entry says the bronze form is composed of 水 plus phonetic 曷 and denotes water drying up; it reports 渴 used for 竭 in the Warring States Zhongshan King Fanghu inscription, and quotes the Shuowen gloss 盡也 (“exhausted”). It separately records dryness/parching, thirst in 詩·王風·君子于役, and urgent in 公羊傳·隱公三年. Its Mawangdui Laozi example is a Han manuscript reading 渴 for 竭. The source displays bronze, seal, and manuscript examples; its page shows no oracle-bone example. These are the database’s paleographic and lexicographic assertions, not visual inspection of the glyph images.

Its readings table gives 渴 *Nə-[k]ʰˤat (Old Chinese, Baxter–Sagart notation) and 曷 *[g]ˤat (Old Chinese, Baxter–Sagart notation). edges.subject: character:渴
edges.text: A bronze use is interpreted as “drying up” or “exhausted,” with the graph reported as writing 竭. The Fanghu transcription itself prints 竭 and does not independently confirm the graph identification.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 《說文》; 金文; historical uses
evidence.text: The entry says the bronze form is composed of 水 plus phonetic 曷 and denotes water drying up; it reports 渴 used for 竭 in the Warring States Zhongshan King Fanghu inscription, and quotes the Shuowen gloss 盡也 (“exhausted”). It separately records dryness/parching, thirst in 詩·王風·君子于役, and urgent in 公羊傳·隱公三年. Its Mawangdui Laozi example is a Han manuscript reading 渴 for 竭. The source displays bronze, seal, and manuscript examples; its page shows no oracle-bone example. These are the database’s paleographic and lexicographic assertions, not visual inspection of the glyph images.

evidence.source: Wikisource, 中山王器銘文
evidence.text: The transcribed Fanghu text includes 賙竭志盡忠, where the CUHK entry identifies the bronze graph 渴 as a writing of 竭. The page dates the Zhongshan King vessels to the king’s fourteenth year, approximately 314 BCE. The current transcription prints 竭 and does not itself reproduce or photographically establish the precise graph shape in the inscription.

The page does not establish the exact date of the earliest physical witness of the Shijing line or dated intermediate stages linking ‘exhausted’ to ‘thirsty’. evidence.text: The account presents 渴 as an old graph used for the word later written 竭 in the sense ‘exhausted/dried up’; it does not describe 曷 as a whole graph borrowed to write 渴. edges.subject: character:火
edges.text: Oracle-bone examples include 火 in a literal fire context. The whole graph is analyzed as depicting light and flames from a burning object. Fire remains a current noun sense.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: oracle-bone formation, graphic development, and dated-by-corpus uses
evidence.text: The entry analyzes oracle-bone 火 as a picture of rising flames, with original meaning ‘fire.’ It notes that 火 can be confused with 山: dots are often absent, so inscriptional context and stroke shape matter. The entry reports no bronze form in its collection and says Warring States forms linearize the graph, reversing an upturned stroke and adding a horizontal stroke. It cites 合集30774 火不延 in the literal fire sense; 合集11503 for 火 as the star 大火; and 合集34797 旬亡火, which Chen Weizhan interprets as a loan for 禍 ‘calamity’ based on sound proximity and context. The entry also quotes the Han lexicographic Shuowen explanation, which is a later account rather than direct evidence for the Shang graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component 火

evidence.source: 李學勤主編《字源》, 天津古籍出版社／遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692; supplied original scan directly inspected
evidence.field: 火 entry, graph analysis and graphic development; PDF pp. 900–901, printed pp. 885–886
evidence.text: The 火 headword begins on printed p. 885 and continues onto p. 886. It describes the graph as depicting light and flames from a burning object, with ‘fire/flame’ as its original meaning. Page 886 describes oracle forms as showing light and flames, Warring States forms as linearized into four strokes while retaining a suggestion of rising flame, and later forms as continuing that graphic development. The passage supports an account of 火 as a whole graph, not an analysis into smaller sound or meaning components. I inspected the attached original page pixels and checked the headword, passage, and continuation boundary.

evidence.text: For 點, the entry gives Guangyun 多忝切 and Middle Chinese initials/final/tone categories 端母, 添/忝 rhyme, rising tone, Division IV. 占 has 職廉切 in level tone and 章豔切 in departing tone, with Middle Chinese 章母, 鹽 rhyme, Division III. evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ŋjed): phonetic 埶 (OC *ŋeds) + semantic 灬 (“fire”).
Schuessler (2024) considers this a *-t derivation of Proto-Sino-Tibetan *nwe (“warm”), whence also Burmese နွေး (nwe:, “warm; lukewarm”), နွှေး (hnwe:, “to warm something; to revise”).
Often considered to be related to 爇 (OC *ŋʷjed, “to burn; to toast”) and 焫 (OC *njod, “hot”).

evidence.field: Chinese / Glyph origin / Old Chinese readings
evidence.text: The entry classifies 熱 as a phonosemantic compound: phonetic 埶 and semantic 灬/fire. In Zhengzhang (2003), it gives 熱 *ŋjed and 埶 *ŋeds; in Baxter–Sagart (2014), it gives 熱 *C.nat (or *C.ŋet?). These are different reconstruction systems and should not be blended. edges.subject: character:热
edges.text: 熱 is defined as warm, and cited examples use it for something hot or for heat. Some examples come from transmitted pre-imperial works, but surviving witness dates and a secure earliest attestation are unresolved.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 溫也。从火埶聲。

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 形義通解; 《說文》; cited classical examples
evidence.text: The database analyzes 熱 as 火 semantic plus 埶 phonetic, with a core sense of high temperature. It cites pre-imperial transmitted uses: Mencius 梁惠王下 “如火益熱” for hot; Book of Poetry 大雅·桑柔 “誰能執熱” for a hot object; Mencius 萬章上 “熱中” in an emotional/urgent sense. It also cites Zuo Tradition 昭公元年 “陽淫熱疾” (fever/disease) and a Mawangdui manuscript, 五十二病方 line 50, “身熱” (body fever). These are attestations as represented by the database; they do not by themselves establish a precise semantic chronology among extensions.

evidence.text: The database describes early bronze 愛 as 㤅, formed with 心 as the semantic element and 兂 as the phonetic element, with a core sense of benevolence. evidence.source: Wiktionary, 爸 (reporting Zhengzhang Shangfang 2003)
evidence.text: Reports a phono-semantic analysis: semantic 父 ‘father’ plus phonetic 巴. In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction system it gives 巴 *praː and 爸 readings *praːs and *baʔ. This supports a proposed sound-component relationship within 爸, not whole-character borrowing. The entry does not establish 巴’s original depicted object or independently recover its name.

edges.subject: component:巴
edges.text: 巴 is proposed as a sound component, compared with 爸 as *praː and *praːs respectively in Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system. The identity and original referent of early 巴 remain unsettled.

sound_comparisons.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, 巴 *praː is compared with 爸 *praːs. In Modern Mandarin, 巴 bā and 爸 bà are also a current reading pair; neither comparison identifies 巴’s original name or referent.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Character Database
evidence.text: The database provides an oracle-bone record and a small-seal form and summarizes the Shuowen interpretation of 巴 as an elephant-swallowing giant snake with a very large mouth. The inspected page gives no sequence of readable intermediate forms in its text. The Shuowen interpretation is a historical account, not conclusive proof of the graph’s original referent.
evidence.title: 漢字「巴」：字形演變

evidence.source: CASE 報科學, National Taiwan University
evidence.text: The article reviews disagreements over oracle-bone forms traditionally read 巴. It argues their shapes differ from the oracle-bone snake graph 它 and notes that early textual occurrences of 巴 are chiefly place, polity or group names; it disputes taking 巴蛇 in Shanhaijing as proof that 巴 itself meant snake. It presents a kneeling-person-with-arms interpretation as a proposal, while acknowledging that identification of the graph and its development into later forms remain debated and that a Western Zhou link is missing. This is a modern argument, not a settled paleographic consensus.
evidence.title: 曾被釋為「巴」的甲骨文字與《說文解字》裡的「巴蛇食象」

edges.subject: character:爸
edges.text: A Guangya entry is dated to the Three Kingdoms era and glosses 爸 as “father.” This records use of the word, though it does not provide a dated physical witness for the graph.

evidence.source: 廣雅 via 識典古籍
evidence.text: The entry groups 爸 with 爹 and 㸙 and glosses them as father. The modern research article consulted below identifies this as an early record in the Three Kingdoms era. This is lexical evidence for the father term, not an account of how the graph was formed.
evidence.title: 釋親-廣雅全文原文-識典古籍

evidence.source: Deng Li and Huang Renxuan, Language Research (2026)
evidence.text: The article reports 爸 as a later graph, absent from Shuowen, and cites Guangya (dated by the article to the Three Kingdoms period) 爸，父也; Yu Pian 蒲可切，父也; Guangyun 捕可切，父也; and Ji Yun readings 部可切 ‘爸、爹，父也’ and 必駕切 ‘Wu speakers call father 爸’. It separately dates the colloquial reduplicated form 爸爸 and 阿爸 to Qing texts, while noting the Tang form 郎爸/郎罷 in 顧況’s poem 囝. Its authors argue the father word is phonologically from 父; that is a scholarly interpretation, distinct from the graph’s component analysis.
evidence.title: 现代汉语“父亲”称谓系统音义关系研究

edges.subject: character:牛
edges.text: The graph is interpreted as depicting the animal, and 牛 is reported in an inscription referring to cattle. The earliest securely dated occurrence is unresolved; this is the earliest supported sense, not a dated first use.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry displays 牛 under oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen headings. It describes the form as emphasizing the ox’s head and horns and says its original meaning was the animal 牛. The page does not date individual specimens.
evidence.title: 漢字「牛」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database says oracle-bone and bronze forms depict a frontal ox head with two curved horns; its account notes that Shang bronze forms also show ears, eyes, and nose. It gives the inscriptional phrase 友簋「易（賜）牛三」 as an example of 牛 referring to cattle, and notes personal-name use in bronze inscriptions. These statements report the database’s analyses and examples; they do not independently date the cited inscription here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析「牛」

edges.subject: character:牛
edges.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry glosses 牛 as a large sacrificial animal. This dictionary gloss does not establish a separate earlier sense or the graph’s original meaning.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 大牲也。牛，件也；件，事理也。象角頭三、封㞑之形。凡牛之屬皆从牛。

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, Shuowen Jiezi entry and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The entry transmits Xu Shen’s account: “大牲也” and describes the graph as depicting horns, head, and a raised back/tail feature. Duan Yucai disputes the transmitted gloss and proposes “事也。理也,” explaining 牛 through its work and the dissectible patterns of the animal. This is a historical lexicographic interpretation and later commentary, not independent confirmation of the graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「牛」

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi, 牛 entry, as transcribed by Shuowen.org
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry calls 牛 a large sacrificial animal and describes the graph in terms of horns, head, and tail. Duan Yucai offers a different gloss in his commentary. These are historical lexicographic interpretations, not independent proof of the graph’s formation.

edges.subject: component:元
edges.text: The received analysis identifies 元 as the sound element. In the Baxter–Sagart table, their reconstructed forms share a nasal onset and similar rhyme material, with an added suffix in 玩; this fits the analysis but does not independently prove it. Their modern Mandarin readings, yuán and wán, do not establish the ancient relationship.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry reports the received Shuowen explanation as ‘弄也。从玉，元聲’ and records an alternate graph written with 貝. It cites the Warring States poet Qu Yuan’s ‘惜吾不及古人兮，吾誰與玩此芳草’ for an appreciative/handling sense, and quotes the Yijing tradition for 玩 meaning to study or become familiar with. These citations evidence old literary uses but the entry does not date the first attestation of 玩 or establish a stepwise semantic chronology.

edges.subject: component:玉
edges.text: In traditional 現, 玉 is conventionally analyzed as the semantic element and contributes a jade association.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɡeːns): semantic 玉 (“jade”) + phonetic 見 (OC *keːns, *ɡeːns) — to appear.
Stativized form of the transitive verb 見 (OC *keːns, “to see”), formed by a nasal prefix and expressing the sense "to be visible; to appear" (Mei, 2012).

evidence.source: Japanese Wiktionary, 現
evidence.text: This page analyzes 現 as a phono-semantic graph with 玉 as semantic element and 見 as sound element, and gives the Old Chinese forms Zhengzhang *ɡeːns and Baxter–Sagart *N-[k]ˤen-s. It separately reports a proposal, attributed to Mei (2012), that the “be visible; appear” verb is a nasal-prefix stativized form of transitive 見 ‘see.’ The page also reports the competing account that 現 first wrote a word meaning ‘jade luster’ and was later borrowed for the word ‘appear.’ These are source-reported analyses; this page alone does not establish the relative chronology of those lexical uses.
evidence.title: 現 - ウィクショナリー日本語版

evidence.source: 《教育部國字標準字體筆順學習網》, Taiwan Ministry of Education

This supports the semantic component’s jade association generally, but it does not identify the specific semantic contribution of 玉 in 現.

evidence.field: 現: basic and detailed explanation, cited lexicographic entries
evidence.text: The entry gives 現 as a phono-semantic graph, with 玉 as semantic element and 見 as sound element, and glosses the verb as ‘appear; become visible.’ It separately records noun senses ‘jade luster’ and ‘stone inferior to jade,’ citing 集韻, and cites 廣韻 for “現，俗見字.” It also supplies later examples for ‘appear,’ ‘current,’ and ‘on hand,’ including a Southern Liang quotation for a ‘current/present’ use. These are dictionary-reported senses and examples, not a demonstrated chronology of semantic change.
evidence.title: 現 xiàn - 汉典

evidence.source: 汉典
evidence.field: 《康熙字典》 citations; 《說文》 cross-reference; phonology
evidence.text: The entry reports 《集韻》’s glosses 玉光 (‘jade luster’) and 石之次玉者 (‘stone inferior to jade’), 《正韻》’s 顯也、露也 (‘manifest; reveal’), and cites 抱朴子 for 形現往來. It explicitly says 現 is not a headword in 《說文》 and points instead to 見, whose gloss is 視也 (‘to look/see’). It reports Middle Chinese 匣母 霰韻 去聲, 見小韻, 胡甸切 for 現. These citations document dictionary traditions and reported usage; this page does not provide dated early attestations or settle whether the jade gloss preceded the ‘appear’ word.

edges.text: The earliest cited bronze contexts use 班 in a personal name, including 毛班 on 班簋. These attest name use, not the proposed meaning ‘divide jade’.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: dated bronze evidence and early lexical use
evidence.text: The entry reports 班 as a personal name in the inscription on 弭叔盨, and in the Western Zhou 班簋; it also cites the Chu bamboo-slip text 清華簡一《祭公》, slip 12, with 毛班. These instances attest the graph as a personal name, not the sense ‘divide jade’. The page dates the vessels by period labels but does not supply a precise year.

evidence.source: 故宫博物院 (Palace Museum)
evidence.text: The museum identifies 班簋 as an early Western Zhou bronze vessel with a 198-character inscription. This supports an early personal-name occurrence, not the sense ‘divide jade’.

edges.text: Historical records include 班 meaning ‘separate’, as in 班馬之聲. The cited examples do not show that this sense developed from ‘divide’ or ‘distribute’.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: historical senses and cited textual examples
evidence.text: The entry’s historical dictionary examples include 班瑞 (‘distribute the jade tokens’) under 《尚書·舜典》, separation in 《左傳·襄公十八年》’s ‘班馬之聲’, distribution under 《漢書·王莽傳中》, equality in 《孟子·公孫丑上》, and rank/order in 《文選·東京賦》. It also records later scheduled transport and work-shift senses. These dictionary citations document examples from texts and their traditional attributions; they do not by themselves establish composition dates or a single linear semantic chronology.

edges.subject: component:求
edges.text: 求 is identified as the phonetic element in the traditional dictionary analysis. In Baxter–Sagart’s system, 求 and 球 share Middle Chinese gjuw, while their Old Chinese reconstructions differ slightly; both have modern Mandarin qiú. These comparisons fit the analysis but do not independently establish the exact ancient relation.

edges.subject: character:球
edges.text: Historical dictionary accounts gloss 球 as jade. The reported Qin-period writing does not securely establish the earliest attested sense.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi

evidence.source: 許慎《說文解字》, quoted in the character-specific entry by 中央纪委国家监委网站
evidence.text: The article reports that 球 is first seen in Qin-period writing, formed from 玉 as meaning element and 求 as phonetic element; it quotes the Shuowen gloss as “jade.” It describes 球 used for a round ball as a later borrowing of 毬. This is a modern secondary account of the historical dictionary and graphic record, not an inspected Qin manuscript witness.

It lists senses including fine jade, jade chime, geometric sphere, round or sphere-like objects, sports balls, and a classifier for ball-shaped objects. This establishes historical dictionary accounts and a later sense inventory, not a dated chronology for each extension.

edges.subject: character:球
edges.text: 球 means a ball or spherical object. Its use for the ball word associated with 毬 is explained as borrowing, not as an established semantic extension from jade; the earliest dated use remains unresolved.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɡu): semantic 玉 (“jade”) + phonetic 求 (OC *ɡu).
"Ball", earlier some "kind of jade". Bodman (1980) relates this to Wuming Zhuang klauᴬ² (“ball”), and relates 俅 (qiú, “gem-adorned”) to Tibetan གྲུ (gru, “lustre of gems”). This character had a softened initial in Proto-Min.
Originally written as 毬 (since Tang dynasty) when referring to a ball. The form 球 (since Qing dynasty) is now more common.

evidence.text: The account separates the old jade sense of 球 from use for round objects, which it treats as a borrowing from 毬. It describes 毛-filled balls and later usage of 毬 for round objects more generally. It cites Tang records of 打毬 and later Song usage, but those examples establish historical use of 毬 rather than the precise date when 球 began replacing it.

edges.subject: component:屮
edges.text: Within 生, 屮 depicts the sprout in the sprout-emerging-from-ground image.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.field: 形義通解: graphic formation and evolution
evidence.text: The entry analyzes oracle-bone 生 as 屮 (a sprout) above 一 representing ground, expressing a plant growing out of earth. It says early bronze forms continue the oracle-bone structure; a dot was later added beneath 屮 as a decorative stroke and then became a horizontal stroke, making it resemble 土. Seal script retains the sprout-emerging-from-ground idea. The entry treats Shuowen’s gloss 進也 as an extended sense, rather than the graphic core.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：生

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.field: oracle-bone graph formation and graphic development
evidence.text: The entry analyzes oracle-bone 生 as 屮 over 一, with 一 representing ground: a plant growing from the soil. It says early bronze forms retain this structure; a dot was later added below 屮 as a decorative stroke and became a horizontal stroke, making the lower part resemble 土. Small seal retains the sprout-emerging-from-ground idea. This is a modern paleographic analysis, not a claim that every early variant is visually identical.

edges.subject: character:生
edges.text: 生 is reported in an oracle-bone prayer for childbirth. Other early uses are also reported, so this does not establish childbirth as the character’s first meaning.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.text: The entry cites oracle-bone examples: 合集34078 uses 生 in a prayer for childbirth; 合集8648正 生月 is interpreted as the following month; 合集116正 uses 生 adjectivally of fresh/live birds; 合集10270 refers to a live deer. These show early uses, but the entry’s proposed semantic connection between the following-month sense and life/growth is an interpretation, not a demonstrated chronological derivation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：生

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)

These cited examples establish reported usages, not a chronology among them; the 生月 interpretation remains disputed.

edges.text: One interpretation reads 生月 as “following month,” but other readings are contested. This phrase does not establish a semantic development from plant growth.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.text: The entry cites oracle-bone examples: 合集34078 uses 生 in a prayer for childbirth; 合集8648正 生月 is interpreted as the following month; 合集116正 uses 生 adjectivally of fresh/live birds; 合集10270 refers to a live deer. These show early uses, but the entry’s proposed semantic connection between the following-month sense and life/growth is an interpretation, not a demonstrated chronological derivation.

evidence.text: Tsai’s 1993 article record identifies the study as 卜辭生字再探, published in Bulletin of the Institute of History and Philology 64.8, pp. 1047–1076. The accessible page discusses disagreement over 生月: it presents the established ‘following month’ analysis and argues from lunar waxing/waning, while other readings have taken 生月 as ‘this month’ or questioned the reading. This is a disputed lexical interpretation; it does not establish the character’s graphic origin.

evidence.source: Che-mao Tsai, Fudan University Center for Unearthed Documents and Paleography
evidence.text: Tsai argues that oracle-bone 生月 means the next month, relating it to the moon beginning to grow again, and rejects an alternative reading of the month graph as 夕 in the cited context. The argument concerns interpretation of an oracle-bone phrase; it is not proof that ‘next month’ was the earliest meaning of 生.

edges.text: A historical dictionary glosses 生 as “advance”; a later interpretation treats this as an extended sense. The evidence does not date this sense or show its development.

Shuowen is a historical source and does not independently prove every detail of the earlier oracle-bone structure.

edges.subject: character:用
edges.text: 用/不用 is reported after divination statements to indicate whether a proposed action was carried out. This attested use does not establish the graph’s original meaning.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The database describes the oracle-bone graph as shaped like a bucket, with the left side as the body and the right as a handle. It reports the original sense as ‘bucket’ and says the graph was later borrowed for ‘put into effect; use.’ Its cited examples include oracle-bone inscriptions 合集19762 and 21405 for the form, and 合集1616 and 花東459 for 用/不用 after divination statements, indicating whether the proposed action was carried out.

edges.subject: character:用
edges.text: One Qin-slip context is read 桶, “container” or “measure.” It preserves a container-related use but does not establish the graph’s original meaning or when this use arose.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: For bronze inscriptions, the database records 用 as a verb ‘use’, as a preposition equivalent to 以, and as a conjunction with sequential or causal senses, citing examples including 召仲鬲, 虢季子白盤, 守宮盤 and 禹鼎. It also cites a Qin-slip example in 睡虎地秦簡《秦律十八種》簡100 where 用 is read 桶, ‘measure/container’; this supports continued use of the older noun sense in that context, though it does not by itself establish the relative chronology of every sense.

edges.text: 电 is identified as the simplified form of traditional 電; the date and graphic steps of simplification remain unresolved.

evidence.source: makemeahanzi
evidence.text: Simplified form of 電; lightning 申 from a storm cloud 雨

edges.subject: component:雨
edges.text: In traditional 電, 雨 marks the weather category; when it was added and its original intention remain unresolved.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 陰陽激燿也。从雨从申。

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *l'iːns): semantic 雨 (“rain”) + phonetic 申 (OC *hlin); also ideogrammic (會意 /会意): 雨 + 申 (“lightning”).
Sino-Tibetan or area word; compare Proto-Mienic *liŋ (“lightning”), Chepang प्लीङ्हसा (pliŋh‑, “to flash; to shine brightly”) (Benedict, 1976; Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC)
evidence.field: 說文解字 and 說文解字注
evidence.text: Xu Shen’s entry defines 電 as a brilliant flash from the interaction of yin and yang and analyzes it as 从雨从申. The later commentary says 申 also functions as a phonetic element (亦聲), while explaining its graph as indicating extension. This supports reporting the traditional analysis as 雨 semantic plus 申 phonetic, while recognizing the account is historical lexicography rather than automatic proof of the character’s earliest formation.
evidence.title: 電 diàn - 漢典

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 申 component analysis; graphic history and borrowing
evidence.text: CUHK interprets 申 in oracle and bronze writing as the flickering, bent path of lightning and calls it an early graph for 電. Its account says the branch name was written with 申 by borrowing, then 雨 was added as a semantic marker to create 電. The same entry reports later Warring States changes to side branches, including forms resembling two 口 in Chu writing or 𦥑 in Qin writing. These are the source’s analyses, not an independent inspection of the early inscriptions.

edges.subject: component:申
edges.text: 申 is interpreted as a lightning image in 電; this interpretation has not been independently confirmed by inspection of early forms.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The database interprets early bronze and oracle forms of 申 as depicting lightning’s bent, flickering path, calls it the initial graph for 電, and says 雨 was added as a semantic marker because lightning commonly accompanies rain. It reports later Warring States variants in which branches were altered into paired 口-like forms in Chu writing or 𦥑-like forms in Qin writing. The entry also reports 申 used for the earthly branch in oracle and bronze inscriptions. These are the database’s paleographic interpretations; the early images were not independently inspected here.

edges.subject: component:申
edges.text: 申 is proposed as a sound component in 電, supported by a plausible but nonidentical reconstructed sound comparison.

sound_comparisons.text: These Old Chinese reconstructions have a plausible shared sound relationship, though their details differ.

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Zhengzhang Shangfang data cited on page
evidence.field: 申 and 電 phonology; component role
evidence.text: The page lists, in Zhengzhang Shangfang’s 2003 Old Chinese reconstruction, 申 *hlin and 電 *l'iːns, groups 電 among graphs with 申 as phonetic, and also presents a phono-semantic analysis 雨 + 申 alongside an ideogrammic interpretation. The reconstructed forms are not identical but have a historically plausible shared rhyme/onset relationship within that system; this is supporting comparative phonological evidence, not direct evidence of the component’s original graphic intention. Modern readings listed on the page include Mandarin diàn and Cantonese Jyutping din6 for 電, and the entry for 申 gives Mandarin shēn; these modern forms should not be mistaken for Old Chinese values.

evidence.text: Liu reads 疾加 as a dynamic worsening of illness, distinguishing that gloss from a static “serious illness” interpretation. He analyzes pre-Qin uses of 病 as verbal or adjectival meanings such as trouble, hardship, harm, worry and distress, and argues that noun “illness/serious illness” arose later. This is an attributed scholarly proposal based on transmitted texts, not direct evidence for the earliest physical graph.
evidence.title: 「疾」與「病」

evidence.source: 中国辞书学报第三辑, article on 病 word history, PDF pp. 4–7
evidence.text: The article argues that in seven transmitted pre-Qin works 病 appears with verbal and adjectival uses but not as a noun meaning disease or serious illness; it places noun disease uses after the Warring States period. It also says 病 is absent from oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions and proposes “困苦” (hardship) as its original word meaning. These are the author's claims and deductions; the inspected passage does not establish an artifact-level first graph attestation. This differs from 字源's proposal “本义是重病” and from Liu's interpretation of Shuowen's gloss, so the accounts should remain attributed rather than harmonized.
evidence.title: 中国辞书学报第三辑

edges.subject: character:病
edges.text: Transmitted examples use 病 for being troubled or affected by burdens, and for being concerned about one’s shortcomings. They attest these uses but do not show that they developed from the illness sense.

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, 病 dictionary entry
evidence.text: The entry cites the Shuowen gloss and classical uses: Zuozhuan 襄公二十四年 has 鄭人病之 in the sense of being troubled/affected by the heavy dues; Analects 衛靈公 has 君子病無能焉 in the sense of being concerned about one’s own lack of ability. Kangxi’s collected glosses include worry, hardship, resentment, difficulty, and other extensions. These attest uses in transmitted texts, but the page does not independently date the wording or demonstrate the historical semantic links.

evidence.text: I inspected both supplied scans. The headword is 旳(的), with readings dī and dí; its entry continues on the next page. The text classifies it as a phonosemantic graph and quotes Shuowen: “的，明也。从日，勺声.” It reports the “的然” example from Liji Zhongyong, interprets 的颡 as a horse with a white forehead, and says 的 is used for white while 卢 denotes black in 的卢. edges.subject: character:的
edges.text: In Mandarin, de marks possession or links a modifier to a noun. Historical accounts report 底 as an earlier spelling before 的 replaced it; the spoken word’s origin remains disputed.

evidence.source: merged_record
evidence.text: possessive, adjectival suffix

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Tsu-lin Mei
evidence.field: Abstract: competing origins and chronology of 底/的 particle
evidence.text: Mei (1988) argues that the particle 底 derives from colloquial 之 rather than 者, describing a sound split in which literary 之 preserves a medial lost in the colloquial form. He rejects a 者 > 底 derivation on phonological grounds and proposes grammatical pathways for the phrase-final nominalizer. He dates the particle 底 to Late Middle Chinese, around the 8th–9th centuries, and reports 的 replacing 底 in a 1238 stele. These are Mei’s arguments, while other published analyses disagree.
evidence.title: The Origin of the Particle ‘.te’ 的 and ‘ti’ 底 — Bulletin of the Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica

evidence.source: Qihongtao, Longdong University Journal portal article record and abstract
evidence.field: Abstract and bibliography: early uses of 底 and later spelling substitution
evidence.text: The abstract reports 底 as pronoun and particle in Wei–Jin period literature, widespread in Tang and Five Dynasties texts and still common in Song-period writing; after Yuan, its pronoun use became rare and the particle was replaced by 的. The article is a secondary survey and says its full text must be obtained through CNKI, so the underlying dated examples could not be checked here.
evidence.title: 近代汉语中“底”字的来源及其演变 — 陇东学院学报

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry 的; section on Etymology 2
evidence.text: The page reports three proposals for the particle’s development: lenition from literary 之, lenition from 者, and grammaticalization of Middle Chinese demonstrative 底 (reconstructed tejX). It states that the proposed 之/者 paths face phonological problems, while Shi’s 底 account treats it as a gradual Tang-period grammaticalization and distinguishes the grammatical functions. It lists Standard Mandarin particle de and dì, Cantonese dik1, plus multiple readings for regional equivalents. This is a secondary compilation rather than direct corpus evidence.

edges.subject: character:眞
edges.text: The received seal-script form is 眞 and the modern standard graph is 真. The cited accounts describe their graphic difference but do not specify every step between them.

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 online text and 段玉裁《說文解字注》
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry glosses 眞 as an immortal transforming shape and ascending to heaven, analyzing it through 𠤎, 目, 乚 and 八. Duan Yucai's later annotation treats this as the original meaning and says the classics use the graph for ‘sincere’; he further explains later senses and sound-series characters. These are historical philological interpretations, not direct evidence for the Western Zhou graph's original referent. The Shuowen entry's graph is 眞, while the modern standard graph is 真.

edges.subject: component:艹
edges.text: In the traditional analysis of 著, 艹 contributes a grass or plant category. This component claim is scoped to 著, not asserted as an independent component of 着.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *taʔ, *tas, *da, *taɡ, *daɡ): semantic 艸 (“grass; plant”) + phonetic 者 (OC *tjaːʔ).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-ta-t (“to put; to place”). Cognate with Tibetan སྟད (stad, “to put on; to lay on”), སྟ་གོན (sta gon, “preparation; arrangement”), Burmese ထား (hta:, “to put; to place”). See also 署 (OC *djas, “to put, place”) (STEDT).

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC)
evidence.text: The dictionary analyzes 著 as a phonosemantic graph from 艹 and 者, with 者 functioning as sound. It lists no ancient graphic sequence beyond later clerical forms, so this supports a traditional component analysis but does not independently establish its earliest paleographic shape. The functional reading is not identical to a claim that 艹 specifically means a particular plant in the compound.
evidence.title: 著 zhù、zhuó、zhe — 漢典

edges.subject: character:着
edges.text: 着 is treated as an orthographic variant of 著 in a historical spelling analysis. This does not mean every use of 着 was merely a copying error.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A03506-003 research note and cited historical authorities
evidence.text: The dictionary treats 着 as an orthographic variant of 著. Its note cites a Tang inscription, the 《俗書刊誤》, 《字學三正》, and 《正字通》; the latter sources describe 着 as a俗訛 or copying error of 著. Its editors reason that 著 derives from 艸 plus 者 and that the transmitted form 着 reflects a corrupted writing of 著. This is an explicit historical orthographic analysis, not proof that every modern use of 着 is merely a copying error.
evidence.title: [A03506-003] 着 (著) — Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A03506-003 research note and form table
evidence.text: The entry records 着 in the Tang-period inscription 《唐大泉室三門記》 and cites 《俗書刊誤》, 《字學三正》, and 《正字通》, which label 着 a vulgar or erroneous writing of 著. The editors explain the transmitted shape through the writing of 著/者 and conclude that 着 is an orthographic variant of 著. This is an explicit historical spelling analysis; it does not show that every later use of 着 was only a copying error. The entry lists image records for 《干祿字書》 and other works, but those cited images were not inspected here.

edges.subject: character:着
edges.text: 着 is used as a particle marking ongoing or persistent action. The evidence does not establish when this use arose or how it relates to other uses of 著.

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC)
evidence.text: The dictionary distinguishes readings and senses: zhuó includes ‘put on’ and ‘attach/contact’; zhù includes ‘make manifest’ and ‘write/compose’; zhe is a grammatical particle for ongoing or persistent action. It cites the poem 《焦仲卿妻》 for 著我繡裌裙, and Tang Li Bai for 身著赤霜袍, as wear/put-on uses; it cites early-classical works for manifest/write senses. These are dictionary-attributed textual examples, not independently dated manuscript witnesses, and they do not establish a chronological semantic chain among the senses.

edges.subject: character:𤐫
edges.text: 𤐫 is identified as an older written form of 票. Its upper element was reduced, and its lower 火 was changed to 示 in clerical writing.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說文釋形; 字樣說明; 異體字研訂說明
evidence.text: The dictionary reports that Shuowen’s headform for 票 was 𤐫, glossed “fire flying,” and analyzes it as fire plus a second graphic element. It says the lower 火 changed to 示 through clerical transformation, and that the modern form was later written 票. Its variant note calls 𤐫 the original form of 票. This supports an older graphic form and a clerical change, not the dossier’s altar/offering interpretation.
evidence.title: [A02895] 票 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The linked 𤐫 entry reports Shuowen’s analysis as 火 plus a form represented in the dictionary’s glyph font, quotes Guangyun’s statement that the old graph means “fire flying” and that it is now written 票, and cites Zhengzitong on 票 being written originally as that old form. This is evidence for a documented graphic succession; it does not independently confirm a two-pair-of-hands interpretation or “sparks” narrative.
evidence.title: [A02895-002] 𤐫 (票) - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義通解; 字形資料
evidence.text: The account, citing He Linyi, describes the older form as 𤐫 with an upper [𦥑囟] element and lower 火; it says the upper part was reduced to 覀 and 火 was confused with 示, yielding the clerical form behind modern 票. It gives fire rising as the basic meaning, followed by light rising/wafting and rapid movement. Its displayed graph inventory has a seal form and bamboo-slip examples, but no oracle-bone or bronze examples; this is not evidence that no earlier forms existed.

evidence.text: The entry cites the Shijing, Shao Nan, Xing Lu line “誰謂鼠無牙，何以穿我墉？” for the sense “pierce through.” It separately cites Huainanzi for threading or passing through, Han shu for digging a canal, Tang poetry and later texts for wearing clothes, and Gongyang zhuan for worn or broken. edges.subject: character:站
edges.text: 站 is used for stations in modern contexts, including transport. Proposed borrowing accounts disagree about whether Chinese or Mongolian and Turkic forms came first; neither direction is established here.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Generally considered to be a Mongolian influence in the Yuan Dynasty – an abbreviation of 站赤 (zhànchì, “post stations during the Yuan Dynasty”), from Middle Mongol ᠵᠠᠮᠴᠢ (ǰamči, “post station”) (> Mongolian замч (zamč, “guide; cicerone”)), a derivative of Middle Mongol ᠵᠠᠮ (ǰam, “way, path”) (> Mongolian зам (zam)).
Mongolian ǰam is undoubtedly cognate with Proto-Turkic *jam (“post station”) (> Turkish yam; ~ Russian ям (jam)) with the same meaning; see Yam (route). Also compare Turkish yamçı (“post rider”), Russian ямщи́к (jamščík, “drive, coachman”).
There is no scholarly consensus regarding the direction of borrowing. Generally it is believed that Turkic jam and Chinese zhàn are loanwords from Mongolian ǰam, however some (e.g. Tuymebayev in Казахско-монгольские лексические параллели) believe the directionality is reversed (i.e. Chinese "to stand > stand > station" → Middle Mongol → Turkic → Russian). Whatever the etymology, what is apparent is that the word jam has been around for a long time and was used by Central Asians to designate a key postal relay station or official.
In Chinese, this word has been competing with the native equivalent 驛／驿 (yì, “post station”) since its introduction. Mongol-ruled Yuan Dynasty saw a profusion of usages of zhàn, which was deliberately suppressed in the succeeding Ming Dynasty in favour of yì. Both were used in the subsequent Qing Dynasty, with zhàn eventually predominating in the modern times, being used to render the sense of "station" in modern concepts, such as "train station". Other Sinosphere countries show preference variations too: Vietnamese uses 站 (trạm), whereas Japanese and Korean still use 驛 for "station" (Japanese 駅 (えき, eki), Korean 역 (驛, yeok)).

evidence.source: Wiktionary
evidence.text: The page reports the common proposal that the post-station word relates to Yuan-era 站赤 and Middle Mongol ǰamči, from ǰam “way, path,” while also reporting disagreement about borrowing direction and a contrary proposal in which Chinese 站 (standing → station) precedes Mongol and Turkic forms. The inspected page does not independently establish early attestations and pronunciations for the Mongolian and Turkic forms or prove the sound correspondence. Treat the borrowing etymology as disputed; a Yuan-era institutional association alone cannot demonstrate the direction or source of borrowing.

edges.subject: character:笑
edges.text: 笑 is reported in a Mawangdui manuscript in a laugh-related context; the exact passage’s physical graph has not been verified. Quotations in received classical texts attest the word but do not date surviving graph material.

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry (summarizing cited paleographic scholarship)
evidence.field: 字源; graph forms and analyses
evidence.text: The entry reports that excavated Warring States through Han manuscript forms are written with components interpreted as 艸 and 犬, contrasting these with received dictionary forms in the 竹 section and forms analyzed as 竹+犬 or 竹+夭. It presents a proposed history in which 艸 was confused with 竹 and 犬 with 夭, and also lists alternative proposals involving 芺 or a pictorial form. These are competing hypotheses summarized by the entry, not settled conclusions. It reports a Zhengzhang series assigning 笑 *sqʰows and 夭 *qoːwʔ, *qrow, *qrowʔ, and a separate Baxter–Sagart row for 笑.

These are textual attestations of the laugh/smile word in received classical texts; the cited page does not date the physical manuscripts of those passages, so they should not be treated as dated material graph attestations.

Its cited Mawangdui manuscript example uses 笑 in its laugh sense; this supports lexical use in that manuscript tradition but does not establish the component analysis.

evidence.source: Chinese Wiktionary

evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. ⺮ represents the meaning and 弟 represents the sound.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *diːls): semantic 𥫗 (“bamboo”) + phonetic 弟 (OC *diːlʔ, *diːls). 竹 here refers to the bamboo strips used for writing (e.g. accounting, classification) in ancient times. See also 等.
Alternatively, may have originally been written 弟.
Karlgren (1956: 14) connects this word with → tī 梯 ‘ladder’.

evidence.text: The entry reports the Shuowen form and gloss as “次也。从竹、弟” (sequence; from bamboo and 弟), and cites Duan Yucai's note that the popular form shortened 弟 in writing. It records senses including order/rank, ordinal use before numerals, examination rank, evaluation, passing an examination, and an elite residence. These are dictionary reports, not independent dated first attestations.
evidence.title: A02993 第 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

The Kangxi entry gives Guangyun fanqie 特計切, glosses sequence, and separately records ‘only/just’ and residences; it also says 第 was originally written 弟. ZDIC reports modern Mandarin dì, Cantonese dai6, Tang-period *dhèi, and Middle Chinese 定母霽韻去聲 特計切. edges.subject: character:米
edges.text: 米 is reported in oracle-bone use for rice or grain. Scholarly discussion identifies its early referent as probably dehusked grain broadly, rather than a single crop; the precise first-use date and inscription context are unresolved.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析 / 形義通解
evidence.text: The account treats 米 as depicting grains, and describes the original sense as grains with their husks removed, including grains from several crops rather than rice alone. It reports oracle-bone uses for rice/grain, for the word 敉 ‘pacify’, and as a sacrificial name; bronze inscriptions often use the graph as a clan name. These are reports in the database, not independently dated lexical attestations in this response.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：米

evidence.source: NTNU Chinese Academic Annual, article on Wang Yu's Shuowen commentary
evidence.text: The article cites oracle-bone forms (Heji 71 and 32541) and Chu manuscript forms (Xin 2.029 and Bao 2.95). It reports that the dots were joined into strokes before the small-seal form, noting that the Chu forms show the change predates small seal. It reviews differing interpretations: Li Xiaoding's central sieve proposal, Cai Xinfa's scattered-grains pictograph, and Xu Jinxiong's interpretation as shelled grain kernels rather than a particular crop. The article concludes that 米 originally referred broadly to dehusked grain, not one specific grain, and that modern usage often specializes it to rice. It also cautions against a proposed reconstructed preform based only on writing convenience.
evidence.title: 中國學術年刊第四十七期（春季號）
