evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *rul, *ruls): phonetic 畾 (OC *ruːl) + semantic 糸 (“fine silk”). The original meaning is "rope; to bind", hence any reference to being tired after hard work in the fields or after sewing is a folk etymology based on modern meaning.
; “to bind; rope”
: Related to 虆 (OC *roːl, *rul, “creeper; rambler”), 藟 (OC *rulʔ, “to wind; creeper”) (Wang, 1982).
: Proto-Tai *roːjꟲ (“to string together”) (whence Thai ร้อย (rɔ́ɔi)) may be a loan from Chinese (Manomaivibool, 1975).
Also see 累 (OC *ruːls, *rolʔ, *rols).

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcribing Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai’s commentary
evidence.field: 纍 entry; graphic analysis and glosses
evidence.text: Shuowen defines 纍 as “綴得理也” and alternatively “大索也,” and analyzes it as 糸 with 畾 as phonetic. Duan’s commentary distinguishes 纍 from 絫: he says 纍 is “大索,” while 絫 means “增也” and extends to “延及也”; he reports 累 as a vulgar form for 絫 and says it was not the original clerical transformation of 纍. The received dictionary entry therefore supports a phonetic-semantic analysis of 纍, but also cautions against treating every later 累 use as a simple graphic continuation of 纍.
evidence.title: 說文解字「纍」 - Shuowen.org

evidence.source: CUHK 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 纍 graphic analysis, pronunciations, and cited uses
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 纍 as 糸 semantic plus 畾 phonetic, glosses it as rope, and cites Han text in 《漢書·李廣傳》 using 纍 for a rope, with Yan Shigu’s note 索也. It also gives 《詩·周南·樛木》 for winding/climbing, and 《左傳·襄公二十五年》 for restraint or confinement. It reports Guangyun fanqie 力追 and 力遂, with Middle Chinese categories lai, level and departing tone, hekou, third division. The page displays small-seal examples but no oracle-bone or bronze examples for this graph; it does not establish the date of the earliest attestation of the rope sense.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
According to Shuowen Jiezi, Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *krub): semantic 糸 + phonetic 合 (OC *kuːb, *ɡuːb) – "rich, abundant", perhaps with a reference to precious silk; today it also means "to give". The phonetic component means "to join, to unite", however it is likely unrelated to the original meaning.
Starostin reconstructs Proto-Sino-Tibetan *qǝ̆p (“to give; to supply”), comparing it to Burmese အပ် (ap, “to commit; to deliver; to hand over”), Jingpho ap (“to hand over”), Lepcha ᰀᰤᰬᰱ (kjep, “to add to; to multiply”), ᰃᰤᰱ (gjap, “many”).
In Mandarin, Jin and Xiang, pronunciations 1 and 2 are generally thought of as colloquial and literary readings respectively, from the same Middle Chinese etymon (Zhengzhang, 2002; Liu, 2021; among others). Pronunciation 2, the literary reading, is a regular reflex from Middle Chinese. However, since pronunciation 1 is highly irregular, others have proposed alternative etymologies for it:
* From the contraction of 過與 (MC kwaH yoX, “to pass to”) (Ikeda, 1962; Hirayama, 2000, 2010; Wang, 2022);
* From 乞 (MC khj+t|khj+jH, “to give”) (Zhang, 1989); and
* From 饋 (MC gwijH, “to gift”) (Shimura, 1995).

evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析 / 网; form, structure, and oracle-bone usage
evidence.text: The account says oracle-bone and bronze forms depict a spread net with crossing mesh lines; 网 is the early graph for 網. It describes later graphic development by joining the net’s upper lines into a horizontal stroke, then adding 亡 to form 罔 and 糸 to form 網. evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The entry favors an account in which early Western Zhou inscriptions used 老 for both ‘old’ and ‘father’; adding 丂 as a phonetic marker distinguished 考, with the lower 匕 of 老 usually omitted. It also records a competing account: 丂 was an original graph, proposed to depict an axe handle, borrowed for ‘father’, then given 老 as a classifier. The entry says early bronze 丂 used for ‘father’ lends that account support, but judges the 老-based account better able to explain early Western Zhou usage. These are attributed analyses, not settled formation history.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 考

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 考; formation analyses and examples, lines 171–179
evidence.text: The dictionary presents a 老-based account: early Western Zhou bronze writing used 老 for both ‘old’ and ‘father’; adding 丂 as a phonetic marker distinguished 考, and the 考 form commonly omits the lower 匕 of 老. It also reports a competing account in which 丂 was an original graph, borrowed for ‘father’, and 老 was added as a semantic classifier; the dictionary says early bronze use of 丂 for ‘father’ gives this account some support, but considers the 老-based account a better explanation of early Western Zhou evidence. It reports bronze 考 for ‘father’ in 兮仲鐘 and for ‘consider/estimate’ in 中山王鼎, alongside separate phonetic uses for 孝 and 巧 in named bronze and Warring States texts. The entry supplies no dates for those particular examples and does not establish a semantic bridge from ‘father’ to ‘examine/test’.

evidence.source: CASE報科學 (National Taiwan University Center for Science Education)
evidence.text: The author identifies rare, damaged Shang oracle-bone forms as 能 and describes a bear-like pictograph: the head is reduced to an eye-shaped form, the limbs become more linear, and the short tail remains. The author says the few oracle-bone occurrences are too damaged to establish their use. From oracle bone to Western Zhou bronze, the head changes from an eye-like shape to 㠯, the body is simplified to 月 (肉), and the feet are rearranged side by side; the later bronze, Warring States, Chu-slip, Qin-slip, seal, and clerical forms are described as easier to relate. This conflicts with another paleographic account that considers securely identified 能 earliest in Western Zhou bronze; the Shang identification is therefore disputed, not settled.

evidence.source: 劉雲, Fudan University Center for Unearthed Documents and Ancient Chinese Characters

The article's discussion establishes a material disagreement over whether a Shang form is 能; the identification remains contested. It supplies images of Western Zhou examples including 能匋尊, 鬲比簋, 毛公厝鼎, and 番生簋, but the web text does not provide a dated first inscription.

evidence.text: The entry reports an early Western Zhou bronze use in which 能 functions as a verb meaning ‘be able to’ (citing 周初金文), and a use in 詩經·大雅·民勞 glossed ‘soften the harsh and govern the near’; it says the ‘talent/ability’ sense appears in later Warring States-era texts such as 左傳. edges.subject: character:茶
edges.text: 茶 is described as a later graphic form related to 荼, though medieval variation and uncertainty about early readings leave the precise relationship and timing unresolved.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes 茶 as a later graph, written earlier with 艸 and phonetic 余 as 荼. It gives 茶 as tea plant and tea drink, and cites Lu Yu’s Tang-period 茶經, which calls tea a fine southern tree. It also records later uses for other brewed drinks and, in Ming usage, as a verb ‘drink’. These glosses do not by themselves date each semantic extension.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：茶

evidence.source: Zhang Yongmei, Essays on Linguistics (Peking University Journals)
evidence.text: The 2025 abstract argues that in the Shijing period only 荼 occurred and it did not mean tea; it assigns 荼 a tea sense and reading *deɑ by the Western Han at the latest, with 茶 appearing as a graphic derivative used alongside 荼 for tea. It argues the distinction developed gradually: Tang Buddhist texts show the tea reading of 荼 fading, 茶 increasingly replaced 荼 after mid-Tang, and later Ming dictionaries completed the separation. This is a recent scholarly account, not settled primary evidence; the page provides only an abstract.
evidence.title: “荼”与“茶”表茗茶的形音义源流试探

evidence.source: Victor Mair, Language Log
evidence.text: Mair argues medieval manuscript forms vary in their lower strokes and that 茶 was not necessarily an independent replacement of 荼 at first. In his account, surviving Qieyun manuscript evidence around 700 CE generally writes the tea plant with a graph transcribed as 荼; a 706 CE manuscript gives no 茶 form in its cited line, while a reading that mentions 茶 in another manuscript requires image verification. He reports Guangyun (1007 CE) lists 茶 as俗 relative to the regular form. He also cautions that a Han tomb seal often read 茶陵 may instead read 荼陵. This challenges simple claims that 茶 was securely established in Han times or invented by Lu Yu.
evidence.title: Sinographs for “tea”

sound_comparisons.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese reconstruction, 菜 *sʰɯːs and 采 *sʰɯːʔ share an onset and rhyme; 菜 has an added departing-tone suffix. Modern Mandarin cài and cǎi retain a related initial and rhyme but differ in tone.

It proposes a derivation ‘what is gathered or plucked’ from 采 plus nominalizing *-s, citing Sagart (1999) and Schuessler (2007). evidence.source: Multi-function Chinese Character Database, CUHK
evidence.field: 形義通解; graphic history and early spellings
evidence.text: The database analyzes 菜 as 艸 plus phonetic 采, with vegetable as its basic meaning. It reports bronze inscriptions using the graph for a place name and Qin slips writing the vegetable word as 采 in 采羹. It cites the Guoyu phrase 庶人食菜，祀以魚 and notes a later use for prepared food. evidence.text: The paper reports Qin Shuihudi legal slips’ 采羹 as 菜羹, plus Han silk and Zhangjiashan slip spellings of 菜 as 采. edges.text: In the conventional analysis of 蛋, 虫 contributes an animal-related meaning category.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 虫 represents the meaning and 延 represents the sound.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *l'aːns): phonetic 延 (OC *lan, *lans) + semantic 虫 (“snake, insect”) – "egg", with particular reference to snake eggs.
The non-contracted form is 蜑. In the current version, 延 is abbreviated to 疋.
This character was coined at a late stage in Chinese, since it is unattested on oracle bones, bronzes, Shuowen Jiezi and Guangyun.
From 彈 (MC danH, “pellet”) (Zhengzhang, 2003).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 蛋 as formed from 虫 with abbreviated phonetic 延, with animal egg as its basic sense. It says 蛋 is very late and absent from oracle bone and bronze inscriptions, Shuowen, and Guangyun; cites 字彙補 for both “蛋, anciently written 蜑” and the egg usage “俗呼鳥卵為蛋”; and gives egg examples from Journey to the West chapter 32 and Dream of the Red Chamber chapter 40. It describes later egg-shaped-object and abusive uses but supplies no dates for those extensions.

edges.subject: component:延
edges.text: 延 is analyzed as the sound element; Zhengzhang-series comparisons are similar despite differing modern Mandarin readings.

sound_comparisons.text: In the Zhengzhang Old Chinese system, 延 *lan/*lans and 蛋 *l'aːns are similar, although their modern Mandarin readings, yán and dàn, differ. The historical comparison is compatible with a sound cue, not proof of lexical borrowing.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.text: For 蛋 it records Mandarin dàn and Cantonese readings, while its graph entry has Guangyun status absent. For 延 it records Mandarin yán and Guangyun fanqie 以然, with a separate 去聲 reading 予線; it also displays Guangyun classification for 蜑 as 徒旱, 定 initial, 上聲, 寒/旱, open first division. Thus modern Mandarin 延 yán and 蛋 dàn differ, while the Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstructions *lan/*lans and *l'aːns are similar within that system. Similarity is compatible with a sound component but does not by itself establish a particular borrowed lexical item.

edges.subject: character:行
edges.text: Verbal uses for movement are reported in oracle-bone inscriptions. They attest this use by that period but do not show it was the earliest spoken sense.

evidence.source: Chi-hsiung Cheng et al., University of Chicago Center for East Asian Studies archive
evidence.field: §2 graphic analysis and usage, PDF pp. 4–5
evidence.text: The paper reports oracle-bone forms as a four-direction crossroads, with Western Zhou bronze forms continuing the shape and Chu/Qin manuscript variants also recorded. It lists oracle-bone verbal examples (including inscriptions 21901, 24445, and 33033), and later bronze examples: movement in mid-/late-Western Zhou inscriptions and 德行 in Warring States inscriptions and Guodian Chu slips. It notes that the concrete road-shaped graph could represent both road and movement; thus the graph’s pictorial shape does not by itself establish which spoken sense came first.

edges.subject: character:行
edges.text: Later rhyme-book records distinguish a reading glossed ‘row/rank’ from readings associated with walking, order, and conduct; they do not establish when this sense arose.

evidence.source: Chi-hsiung Cheng et al., University of Chicago Center for East Asian Studies archive
evidence.field: §3 sound and meaning analysis, PDF pp. 6–8
evidence.text: The authors survey four later rhyme-book sound/meaning groupings: 胡郎切 for rank/row; 戶庚切 for walking/going; 下浪切 for order; 下更切 for conduct/action. They propose semantic and phonological relationships among these readings but explicitly frame parts of the ordering as inference and acknowledge that readings in the Jingdian Shiwen do not conclusively settle the chronology. Their discussion presents possible Sino-Tibetan comparisons involving 行 and 胻 as a debated proposal, not an established derivation.

evidence.field: 說明; 說文釋形; 釋義
evidence.text: The entry records the received Shuowen wording “瞻也。从見、示” and Duan Yucai’s reading “从見，示聲.” It glosses 視 first as looking, then gives attested extended senses including examining or observing, treating someone as, eyesight, caring for, administering, comparing, imitating, and a use通「示」. It cites classical examples, including Analects 為政 for examining conduct and Mencius 離婁 for treating a ruler or minister as a body part. These are dictionary-attested senses; the entry does not by itself establish the chronology or derivational path among them.

edges.subject: character:视
edges.text: The cited paleographic analysis identifies Shang oracle-bone contexts, including 視師 and 視方, as uses involving observing. The date of any individual token is not specified.

evidence.source: 裘錫圭, “甲骨文中的見與視,” 復旦大學出土文獻與古文字研究中心
evidence.field: analysis of oracle-bone and bronze forms; dated examples
evidence.text: The author argues that two Shang oracle-bone graphs formerly both read as 見 should be distinguished: the form with a seated human below 目 is 見, while the form with a standing human is 視. The Guodian Chu slips’ distinct forms for 視 and 見 support that reading. He identifies the standing-figure form in Western Zhou bronzes as 視 too. In Western Zhou inscriptions, the pictographic form continued alongside a form written with 見 and 氏 as phonetic; later regional evidence shows the older pictographic spelling persisted in Chu longer than in Jin. The article also reviews an earlier proposal to read one oracle-bone form as 望, and rejects it.
evidence.title: 裘錫圭：甲骨文中的見與視

evidence.source: 裘錫圭, 復旦大學出土文獻與古文字研究中心
evidence.text: The article cites oracle-bone contexts such as 視師 and 視方 and argues that the first means observing an enemy force in preparation for battle. It also discusses Western Zhou bronze inscriptions including 墻盤 and 伯簋, interpreting their graph as 視. The article was originally published in 1999; it reports Shang oracle-bone and Western Zhou bronze evidence, but the inspected text does not assign an absolute date to any one oracle-bone token.

edges.subject: character:认
edges.text: The standard list pairs 认 with 認 as its simplified form.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education of the People’s Republic of China; General List of Simplified Chinese Characters (1986 edition)
evidence.text: The list explicitly pairs 认〔認〕 and separately lists 讠〔言〕 as a simplified component. This supports classifying 認 → 认 as a standardized simplified-form relation and 言 → 讠 as simplification. It does not say that 忍 was historically replaced by 人 as an etymological development; that is a graphic consequence of the simplified form and should not be carried over as the traditional sound analysis.
evidence.title: 简化字总表（1986年版）

evidence.source: Wikisource transcription of the State Language Commission's 1986 reissued General List of Simplified Chinese Characters
evidence.field: 第一表; 简化字总表说明
evidence.text: The list explicitly gives 认〔認〕. Its general notes say simplified characters are paired with their original traditional forms, and that the list's simplified components include 讠. This supports 認 → 认 as a standardized simplification, and supports interpreting the left 讠 as the simplified 言 component. It does not establish 认's antiquity or make 人 the original phonetic component.

edges.subject: component:忍
edges.text: In traditional 認, 忍 is analyzed as the sound component. The reported Zhengzhang Old Chinese forms 忍 (*njɯnʔ) and 認 (*njɯns, *njɯŋs) are compatible with this analysis; the supplied Baxter–Sagart data do not provide a component-to-host comparison.

sound_comparisons.text: The reported Zhengzhang Old Chinese forms 忍 *njɯnʔ and 認 *njɯns/*njɯŋs are compatible with a sound relationship in that system, without establishing a specific sound change.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *njɯns, *njɯŋs): semantic 言 (“speech”) + phonetic 忍 (OC *njɯnʔ).
Compare Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-njan (“to hear; to listen”) (STEDT); cognate with Tibetan ཉན (nyan, “to listen”), Mizo en (“to look; to look at”). Schuessler (2007) suggests another cognate Jingpho non⁵⁵ (“to think; to consider”).

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003)
evidence.field: Glyph origin / phonetic series and compound analysis
evidence.text: The entry classifies 認 as a phonosemantic compound: 言 is semantic and 忍 is phonetic. It lists 認 in the 刃 phonetic series and gives Zhengzhang Old Chinese forms 忍 *njɯnʔ and 認 *njɯns, *njɯŋs. These are system-specific reconstructions, not direct evidence for a particular sound change or for the date of the graphic formation.

The Zhengzhang forms are compatible with a phonetic relationship as a source analysis, but neither system's host form alone demonstrates a sound change, nor does the available B-S data provide the component-host comparison.

evidence.source: 《漢語多功能字庫》, character entry 識
evidence.field: formation; Shuowen; dated usage and semantic senses
evidence.text: The entry reports 識 as 从言、戠聲 and reproduces the 《說文》 gloss 常也、一曰知也. It identifies an early sense as “remember/retain,” citing 《周易·大畜》 君子以多識前言往行 and 《論語·述而》 默而識之. It separately gives “know/recognize,” with 《詩·大雅·皇矣》 不識不知 and 《史記·刺客列傳》 妻不識也; further senses include knowledge, consciousness/perception, flags or markers, and an acquaintance. The source’s ordering is an editorial semantic analysis; it is not a chronology established solely by its gloss list.

evidence.field: 訴 entry: Shuowen graphic analysis and form history

evidence.source: Chinese Ministry of Education *Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants*
evidence.text: The entry quotes the *Hanshu* Chengdi annals wording “趨闕告訴者不絕” (people continually went to the palace to report grievances), and records later named examples for accusation/denunciation, complaint, and telling or pouring out feelings. This supports an early imperial attestation of the graphic word 訴 in an accusation/reporting context via the *Hanshu* citation, while the *Shuowen*’s citation of the *Analects* supplies an earlier traditional textual reference whose surviving written witness is not dated by this entry. The semantic relation among reporting, accusation, emotional complaint, and narration remains underdetermined.

evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ŋaʔ, *ŋas): semantic 言 + phonetic 吾 (OC *ŋraː, *ŋaː).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ŋaq (“to speak”). Compare Tibetan ངག (ngag, “speech”).
According to Schuessler (2007), 言 (OC *ŋan, “to speak; speech; talk”) is 語 (OC *ŋaʔ) with a nominal -n suffix.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *hljods, *hljod, *lod): semantic 言 + phonetic 兌 (OC *l'oːds).
All of the pronunciations of this character are in the same word family apparently derived from a root *lo meaning “to loosen; to relax” (Schuessler, 2007); based on this, STEDT compares the word to Proto-Sino-Tibetan *lot (“free; release; slip; dislocate”), whence also 脫 (OC *l̥ʰoːd, *l'oːd, “to peel off, take off (clothes), escape, etc.”). However, STEDT also offers an alternative derivation from a provisional Proto-Sino-Tibetan *b-tsyat (“to speak, say”), comparing Tibetan འཆད ('chad, “to say, explain”), which is semantically more appealing; the association with the words associated with "release" may be a case of phonetic pigeonholing.
According to the "release" theory, Pronunciation 1 is derived by causative devoicing of 悅 (OC *lod, “to relax; to be delighted”) (pronunciation 3).
Pronunciation 2 is probably the exoactive of pronunciation 1.

edges.text: Traditional 讀 is analyzed with 𧶠 as a sound element; reconstructed readings are similar, though accounts differ on its form and do not establish its original referent or spoken name.

This comparison is compatible with a phonetic relationship, but the reconstruction table is a secondary presentation; the component is not required to share the character’s exact reconstructed form.

edges.subject: character:走
edges.text: A clear verbal use is reported in the bronze-inscription phrase 夙夜奔走. The cited oracle-bone examples are reported as names or place names, not secure verbal attestations.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The database analyzes the oracle-bone and early bronze forms as a person running with arms swinging; later bronze forms add 止 to emphasize the feet. It assigns the basic verb sense “run” to the graph. It reports oracle-bone uses in place-name and personal-name contexts, including 合集17230 and 合集27939; its cited clear bronze verb example is 效卣, “夙夜奔走.” It says the upper running-person shape was later misread as 夭 in Shuowen. This is a modern paleographic account, distinct from Xu Shen’s historical analysis.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: The entry transcribes oracle-bone examples 合集17230 as “貞：王往走災” and 合集27939 as “貞：其令(命)亞走馬.” It classifies the first as a place name and the latter as a personal-name use; therefore these attestations do not independently establish the verbal sense “run.” The entry reports “run” as a basic sense and cites clearer verbal contexts in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions. The specific object of 走馬 here is a horse, but the graph is not thereby a horse pictogram.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析

edges.subject: character:走
edges.text: Classical citations use 走 for fleeing or escaping. Their witnesses are not securely dated here, and they do not show when this sense developed in relation to “run.”

evidence.source: 漢典
evidence.text: The dictionary gives the classical verb sense “run” with citations including 《詩·大雅·緜》“來朝走馬,” 《儀禮·士相見禮》“某將走見,” 《孟子·梁惠王上》“棄甲曳兵而走,” and 《韓非子·五蠹》“兔走觸株.” It separately gives fleeing, moving toward, and later walking uses. These are lexicographic citations to texts of varying composition/transmission histories; the page does not date each manuscript witness, so they should not be presented as securely dated first occurrences.
evidence.title: 走 zǒu - 汉典

evidence.source: 漢典
evidence.text: The dictionary separates run, flee, go/tend toward, walk, travel, visit, leak, lose, servant, and other senses, with later textual examples for several. The broad modern sense “walk/go on foot” differs from the classical run sense; the page supplies examples but not a complete dated pathway establishing when each semantic extension arose. Treat the paths from running to fleeing, going toward, and ordinary walking as plausible semantic developments that need sense-specific chronological evidence, not as chronology inferred from the order of a gloss list.

edges.text: The earliest gloss directly reported here describes feet pawing the ground. Cited examples include a horse pawing the ground and a Tang poem about a hungry horse pawing snow, but they do not establish a secure first-use date for the graph.

evidence.text: The dictionary analyzes 跑 as 足 semantic + 包 phonetic. It gives the earliest gloss in Guangyun as ‘足跑地也’ (feet pawing the ground), and cites 西京雜記, where a horse paws the ground, followed by a Tang poem using 跑 of a hungry horse scraping snow. It says the character later commonly means moving quickly or running, then gives examples for fleeing, losing, and going about business. The citations establish examples across periods but do not by themselves prove every semantic transition.

evidence.field: Glyph origin / Zhengzhang 2003 sound series and readings
evidence.text: This entry identifies 跟 as an 艮-series phonetic graph and lists 跟 Old Chinese *kɯːn and 艮 *kɯːns in Zhengzhang (2003). It gives 跟 Middle Chinese fanqie 古痕切 and category 見開一痕平, with Mandarin gēn and Cantonese gan1; it gives 艮 Mandarin readings gèn, gěn (among others) and Cantonese gan3. In the stated reconstruction, the related initial and rhyme support a phonetic role despite the departing tone suffix on 艮. The source also reports 跟 as cognate with 根 (Old Chinese *kɯːn), attributed to Wang (1982), but no primary text supporting that cognacy was inspected here.

edges.subject: character:跟
edges.text: 跟 is also used for the rear or bottom of an object and for a shoe heel. A dated transition from the heel of the foot is not established.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The entry traces object ‘bottom/back’ uses from heel, citing 清稗類鈔·鑒賞類 (“每冊之跟”), and gives shoe heel as a continuing use. It reports follow as a later common sense and quotes 正字通·足部, “俗謂隨行曰跟”; later cited examples include 三国演义 chapter 28 and 红楼梦 chapter 43. It then explains attendant/servant and marriage senses from follow, and later prepositional/object and conjunction uses with examples from 红楼梦, 老残游记, 龙须沟, and 小二黑结婚. These are the database’s reported citations, not independently dated first attestations of each extension.

edges.subject: character:身
edges.text: Pre-Qin documents are reported to use 身 as a sound element in 仁. One reconstruction compares 身 (*n̥i[ŋ], Middle Chinese syin) with 仁 (*niŋ, Middle Chinese nyin); a separate draft gives different Old Chinese notation. This is 身’s role within 仁, not the formation of 身 itself.

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, 2015 draft discussing Old Chinese and excavated texts
evidence.field: section 4.1; 身 and 仁 phonetic use and reconstruction
evidence.text: The authors state that examples in pre-Qin documents write 仁 rén ‘kind’ with 身 shēn as phonetic. They use this evidence to reconstruct 仁 *niŋ and 身 *n̥i[ŋ], with Middle Chinese nyin and syin respectively. This is evidence for a phonetic role in the compound/graph 仁 and a reconstruction argument; it is not a claim that 身 itself is a whole-graph loan for a pronoun. The draft’s prose does not identify a particular manuscript or provide a date for the examples in the inspected passage.

edges.subject: character:身
edges.text: An oracle-bone inscription is cited in a context concerning the king’s abdominal illness. This supports an early abdomen-related use; it does not establish abdomen as the original meaning.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 / Multi-function Chinese Character Database, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義通解; oracle-bone and bronze evidence; dated textual examples
evidence.text: The database analyzes the oracle-bone and bronze graph as 人 with the abdomen marked, possibly with a navel dot; it proposes abdomen as the original meaning. It cites an oracle-bone use in 合集822正 for the king’s abdominal illness. It separately cites bronze uses for person/body, protection of the king’s person, one’s own action, and a person’s lifetime or era. For Warring States manuscript evidence, it cites Guodian Laozi B strip 8 for 身 meaning body and Qinghua manuscript 程寤 strip 9 for the body. It traces “pregnancy” to the phrase 有身 in the Odes, 大雅·大明, and later whole-body and self meanings. These are the database’s semantic analysis and source citations; the page does not provide absolute dates for each inscription or manuscript.

edges.subject: character:车
edges.text: 车 is the modern simplified form derived from cursive 車.

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Chinese Characters Database
evidence.text: The author identifies 车 as a cursive form of 車, attested by the Sui dynasty at the latest and continuing in later cursive writing, but says it did not become generally used as a standard character until adoption in the first simplified-character list. The formal 1956 reform resolution states that the first table of 230 simplified characters was to be used from 1 February 1956; the 1964 table lists 车 as a simplified component corresponding to 車. These records support the relationship, but do not show the calligraphic exemplars themselves on the inspected page.

evidence.text: The transcribed resolution is dated 28 January 1956 and states the first table of 230 simplified characters was to be used in printed and handwritten documents from 1 February 1956. Its appendix lists 车（車） among the simplified components. This dates standardization, not the earlier cursive form’s origin.

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》 (Taiwan Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants)
evidence.field: 說文释形, standard form, pronunciation, senses, cited examples
evidence.text: This dictionary records 邊 as the standard form, quotes Shuowen’s ‘行垂崖也。从辵，𦤝聲’ and gives Mandarin biān. Its senses include a boundary/frontier, beside or bank, side/edge, limit, direction, and ‘while’ in the paired construction 邊…邊…. It supplies examples attributed to classical works and later texts, including a Tang poem for ‘frontier,’ and cites Shuowen, Yupian (‘塞也’), and Guangyun (‘邊陲也’). The page provides a lexicographic sense history, but the examples shown do not establish the first date or a continuous path for each extension.

evidence.text: This dictionary records 邊 as the standard form, quotes Shuowen’s ‘行垂崖也。从辵，𦤝聲’ and gives Mandarin biān. Its senses include a boundary/frontier, beside or bank, side/edge, limit, direction, and ‘while’ in the paired construction 邊…邊…. It supplies examples attributed to classical works and later texts, including a Tang poem for ‘frontier,’ and cites Shuowen, Yupian (‘塞也’), and Guangyun (‘邊陲也’). The page provides a lexicographic sense history, but the examples shown do not establish the first date or a continuous path for each extension.

evidence.source: 說文解字, online transcription with 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.text: The received entry says ‘復也。从辵瞏聲。戶關切’ (‘return/repeat; from 辵, with 瞏 as phonetic’). Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary cites 爾雅’s ‘還，復返也’ and remarks that classical texts used 還 for the circling sense now commonly written 環. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of a component’s ancient sound or the earliest graph shape.

evidence.source: 漢典 (zdic.net)
evidence.text: The entry separates huán ‘return’ from hái adverbial uses including ‘still/remains,’ ‘more,’ ‘again,’ and ‘also.’ Under huán it gives early/classical citations: 詩經《小雅·何人斯》‘還而不入’ for returning; 《漢書·項籍傳》 for turning/look back; 《禮記·內則》 and other texts for circling; later cited uses cover restoration, repayment, and retaliation. It also records hái-type uses in Tang citations, including 柳宗元 ‘世世還復然’ for ‘still/again,’ and later examples for ‘also’ and ‘more.’ These lexicographic citations establish that the senses are attested in the cited works, but their exact composition dates and whether each sense developed directly from ‘return’ are not established by this entry alone.

edges.subject: component:辶
edges.text: In an analysis of traditional 這 for its proposed older verb use “meet/receive,” 辶 contributes a movement-related meaning. This is not established as a construction of the demonstrative.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 辶 represents the meaning and 言 represents the sound. The character is based on the original meaning "to meet", which is unrelated to the modern meaning.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ŋrans): semantic 辶 (“walk”) + phonetic 言 (OC *ŋan).
The character was originally a verb meaning “to meet”, whose modern pronunciation is yàn. It was later borrowed for the proximal demonstrative “this/here”, by a confusion in medieval handwriting with 遮 (zhē, “this”).
First attested in the Tang dynasty; etymology unclear. Proposed etymologies:
* From 者 (OC *tjaːʔ, “one which”) (Lü, 1985). Wang (1990) notes that 者 always occurs after what is referred to, whereas 這 always before.
*: 者 (OC *tjaːʔ, “one which”) > 者 (MC tsyaeX, “this (possessive case)”) > 者 (MC tsyaeX, “this (general demonstrative)”) > Mandarin 這 /这 (zhè).
* From 之 (OC *tjɯ, “this; it”) (Wang, 1990). Norman (1988) notes that this derivation would be phonologically problematic.

edges.subject: component:言
edges.text: An analysis assigns 言 a phonetic role in traditional 這 for the older verb use “meet/receive.” In Modern Mandarin, 言 is yán and 這 is zhè; this present-day comparison does not establish the proposed ancient sound relation. [E5, E6, X-9a8d3fc9d3ca99811fb0, X-8162e2df6f7495ad174d, X-03d3d036bf0a84610ec7]

sound_comparisons.text: Current Mandarin readings are zhè for traditional 這 and yán for 言. This pair records present-day readings, not proof of the proposed ancient phonetic relation.

evidence.text: The entry identifies 這 as the traditional counterpart of 这 and records 魚變切. edges.subject: component:袁
edges.text: 袁 is identified as the sound element in 遠. In Middle Chinese, 袁 hjwon and 遠 hjwonX share the base form, with X marking the host’s departing tone. In the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese system, the readings are 袁 *[ɢ]ʷa[n] and 遠 *C.ɢʷanʔ. Modern Mandarin readings are 袁 yuán and 遠 yuǎn. These comparisons are consistent with the analysis but do not independently prove it. The early 袁 graph’s referent and original pronunciation remain unsettled.

edges.subject: character:远
edges.text: 远 is the standardized simplified form of 遠, adopted after an existing variant replaced 袁 with 元. The sources support earlier variant use but do not date each specimen individually.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声): semantic 辶 (“walk”) + phonetic 元.
Unorthodox variant simplified from 遠 (袁 → 元) found in various moveable type copies of classical novels. First attested in 《宋元以來俗字譜》, a variant forms dictionary compiled in 1930 that records unorthodox forms (俗字 (súzì)) that have existed since the Song dynasty.
Eventually adopted as an official simplified character by the People's Republic of China in the 1956 Chinese Character Simplification Scheme.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Variant Dictionary
evidence.text: The dictionary classifies 远 as a variant of 遠 and says it appears in 《宋元以來俗字譜》 under 辵, citing popular novels. It explains the graphic substitution as changing the phonetic 袁 to 元. This supports treating 远 as a nonstandard variant later adopted as simplified form; the page does not itself date the cited novel examples individually.

evidence.text: The entry analyzes the bronze form of 送 as 辵 plus phonetic 灷. edges.subject: character:送
edges.text: A received poem uses 送 in a context interpreted as accompanying someone to a place. It attests an early accompanying or sending context, without settling the precise distinction between accompanying and seeing someone off.

evidence.source: 中國哲學書電子化計劃 (Chinese Text Project)
evidence.field: 《詩經·鄘風·桑中》 quotation in search result
evidence.text: The retrieved result quotes “期我乎桑中，要我乎上宫，送我乎淇之上矣,” an early received-text attestation of 送 in a farewell/accompanying-someone-to-a-place context. The date of the poem’s composition and the precise semantic distinction between seeing someone off and accompanying them are not resolved by this result.
evidence.title: 送 - 中國哲學書電子化計劃

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, Book of Poetry
evidence.text: The received poem includes 送我乎淇之上矣; its supplied English translation interprets this context as accompanying someone to the Qi river. This is evidence for an early received-text use in an accompanying/sending context, but neither the poem’s precise composition date nor a transition from this use to later senses is established here. Direct opening of this page returned 403; its search result was inspected.

edges.subject: component:辶
edges.text: In 道, 辶 is the side form corresponding to 辵 in the received analysis and contributes a travel-related category.

evidence.source: dong_chinese
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 辶 represents the meaning and 首 represents the sound.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 所行道也。从辵从𩠐。一達謂之道。

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.field: 道 entry; original definition, component account, extended meanings
evidence.text: The entry defines 道 as a way people travel, analyzes it as 辵 plus 𩠐/首, and gives “one-way access” as a definition. Duan Yucai says 首 also supplies sound, identifies the pronunciation as 徒皓切, and reports extensions to 道理 and 引道. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the graphic analysis or the chronology of those extensions.
evidence.title: 說文解字「道」 - Shuowen.org

edges.subject: component:首
edges.text: The received analysis identifies 𩠐, corresponding to 首, as the sound component; historical reconstructions support a comparison but do not independently prove the graph analysis.

sound_comparisons.text: In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese, 首 *l̥uʔ and 道’s “way” reading *[kə.l]ˤuʔ share a similar final sound, unlike their modern Mandarin readings.

evidence.source: Dong Chinese
evidence.field: 道: formation, component readings, historical pronunciation and graphic timeline
evidence.text: The page analyzes 辶 as the meaning component and 首 as the sound component; it reports Mandarin readings chuò and shǒu for those components and dào for 道, and gives Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese forms 道 *lˤuʔ-s / *[kə.l]ˤuʔ and 首 *l̥uʔ / *l̥uʔ-s, followed by Middle Chinese dawH/dawX for 道. It labels its displayed bronze form Early Western Zhou (~1000 BCE), seal form Shuowen (~100 CE), and clerical form Eastern Han (25–220 CE). These are the page's assertions; its seal/bronze image content was not independently visually inspected here.

edges.subject: component:邑
edges.text: In the traditional analysis of 𨙻, 邑 contributes the city or place category.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A04204; 說文釋形; 字樣說明
evidence.text: The dictionary gives the Shuowen headform as 𨙻 and quotes “西夷國。从邑，冄聲。安定有朝𨙻縣。” It explicitly assigns 邑 the semantic role and 冄 the phonetic role, and identifies 冄 as a variant of 冉 in its own character catalog. This supports the traditional component analysis, but does not establish a dated graphic sequence from 𨙻 to 那.
evidence.title: [A04204] 那 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong

evidence.text: The character page records the Shuowen entry under 𨙻 with 邑 and 冄聲; it says modern 那 is absent from oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions and from Shuowen in its current form. It offers two accounts: the original sense was a distal pronoun, with a Tang poem cited, or 那 writes the Shuowen graph 𨙻 meaning a western state. The page supplies no dated inscription establishing either graphic connection or the state-name-to-demonstrative borrowing sequence.

edges.subject: character:那
edges.text: Interrogative 那, especially in rhetorical questions, is attested from the Eastern Han. Its origin and relation to the distal demonstrative remain disputed.

evidence.source: 馮春田, Shandong University Confucian Studies Institute
evidence.text: The study says interrogative 那, used for asking about matters and especially rhetorical questions, is attested from the Eastern Han and that its origin remains unsettled among scholars. It argues that this interrogative is not directly derived from the distal demonstrative; it reviews proposals connecting it with 如何、若何 or 奈何 and favors reduction and sound change from 奈何 via 奈 to 那. It cites classical examples including 左傳 “棄甲則那？” with Du Yu’s gloss “那猶何也,” but distinguishes that example from the later clause-initial rhetorical interrogative. This concerns word history, not the graphic formation of 那.

The sound comparison supports a phonetic role for 者 in the compound, while the reconstructed difference between the two elements shows that “phonetic” need not mean identical reconstructed syllables.

edges.subject: component:田
edges.text: In the reported 田-plus-土 analysis of 里, 田 depicts a field and contributes that pictured element to the habitable-place interpretation.

evidence.source: shuowen_jiezi
evidence.text: 居也。从田从土。凡里之屬皆从里。

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, CUHK
evidence.field: 形義通解; 里字形、讀音與早期用例
evidence.text: This dictionary states 里 first appears in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, formed from 田 and 土 and interpreted as a place where land and fields are habitable. It reports later bronze forms where strokes in 田 and 土 run together, with the stroke in 土 later extended into the seal-script shape. It cites bronze uses for a settlement head (令方彝), a distance measure (中山王鼎), and as a writing for 裏 in a garment-lining phrase (伯䢅鼎). It also cites Warring States Qin slips for settlement and distance-measure uses, and a Guodian slip where 里 writes 理. These are the dictionary's reported readings of cited artifacts; I did not inspect the glyph images or artifact editions independently.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 里

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, CUHK
evidence.field: 形義通解; bronze and manuscript attestations

evidence.text: The Han-dynasty dictionary defines 重 as “thick/deep” (厚), analyzes it as 从壬東聲 (“壬 as semantic element, 東 as phonetic”), and treats characters in its series as written with 重. Duan Yucai says the senses “solemn/respectful” and “repeated/overlapping” are extensions from 厚, and comments that ancient usage had only the level-tone reading, without the departing-tone reading. evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK)
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 錯 as 从金、昔聲 and gives the original meaning as a whetstone used to work jade or stone. It cites 尚書《禹貢》「錫貢磬錯」 with Kong Anguo’s explanation that 錯 is used to work jade/stone. It separately records metal inlay/decorating in 《鹽鐵論》 and 《國語》, file/tool use in 《列女傳》, polishing in 《鶡冠子》, intercrossing in 《詩經》, mixed/disordered use in 《尚書》, alternating in Wang Bo’s Tang verse, and wrong/error in 《墨子》. These are examples attributed to named works; they do not establish a secure continuous semantic chronology.

evidence.text: The database analyzes 門 as an image of two door leaves, sometimes with a lintel in oracle-bone forms. edges.subject: component:門
edges.text: 門 pictures the gate in the traditional interpretation of 閒.

evidence.source: 蔡一峰, “古文字所謂「閒」「外」通諧說辨議”
evidence.text: The article reports 間 as a later variant spelling of 閒 and cites a Warring States bronze inscription (間右戈, 集成 10974) as an attestation. It cites late Western Zhou bronze examples of 閒, including 㝬鐘 (集成 260), whose graph places 月 outside 門. The author presents the traditional semantic interpretation as a gap at a door, with moonlight entering, and discusses a separate graph with an added 卜 as a Warring States differentiation of 閒. The paper also explains that scholars have proposed phonetic relations involving 月/外, but argues that the sound-series evidence is not secure and favors treating the series separately. This is a secondary paleographic study, not direct inspection of the cited bronzes.
evidence.title: 古文字所謂「閒」「外」通諧說辨議

The quoted 段注 expands the sense from a gap or interval between two sides to spaces, intervals in speech, and leisure; it describes 閒 as a semantic compound and repeats the traditional moonlight-through-a-door-gap account. edges.subject: component:隹
edges.text: 隹 contributes the bird category in the proposed bird-name analysis of 難.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解; 說文; 金文例證
evidence.text: The lexicon reports 難’s original use as a bird name and analyzes 隹 as semantic and the remaining element as phonetic; it reports the later “difficult/easy” word as a phonetic loan. It quotes Shuowen’s bird gloss and says late Spring-and-Autumn bronze forms use 黃 plus 隹, while a late Warring States Zhongshan Wang ding has 隹 plus the phonetic element. The same entry gives bronze examples for ‘difficult to do’ and ‘difficult to approach’ and a bronze phrase 難老, interpreted as ‘long-lived’.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：難

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解; 《說文》; 金文例證
evidence.text: The entry analyzes the graph as originally a bird name, with 隹 as semantic classifier and a remaining element as phonetic, and says the graph was later borrowed for the difficult/easy word. It reports bronze forms before the late Spring and Autumn period written with 黃 and 隹, and a late Warring States Zhongshan Wang ding form with 隹 and the phonetic element. The entry cites bronze uses for “difficult to do,” “difficult to approach,” and the phrase 難老, glossed as long-lived. It does not give the earliest dated bird-name occurrence.

Its further discussion gives differing interpretations of the early component’s depiction, and traces a graphic change in which bronze forms’ lower 火 was later miswritten as marks or 土, contributing to seal-script 堇. This is evidence for a contested component history, not proof that the bird-name of 難 is recoverable from the depicted object.

edges.subject: character:雨
edges.text: Cited oracle-bone inscriptions use 雨 as a noun for rainwater. This is an early attested use, not necessarily the graph’s original meaning.

evidence.source: 小學堂文字學資料庫 (Academia Sinica Institute of History and Philology)
evidence.field: 雨: graph evolution and early usage
evidence.text: The entry describes variable oracle-bone forms: often a stroke represents the sky, with two or three drops below; some drops join the upper stroke, and an extra stroke may be decorative. It says Western Zhou forms connect the outer rain shape into a line, resembling small-seal forms, and Warring States forms sometimes render the drops with a water-like shape. It identifies the original sense as rainwater and cites oracle-bone examples: 《合集》8329 往于河，㞢(有)雨; 《合集》20397 壬戌㞢(有)雨; and verbal uses 《合集》9757 今日雨 and 《合集》12598 今日其大雨. This supports a rain pictograph, but not a single invariant early design or the claim that the top stroke was simply added later. The cited inscription numbers are source locators; this page does not supply absolute dates for those individual records.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 漢字甲骨部件分析 雨

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *riːŋ, *reːŋ, *reːŋs): semantic 雨 (“rain”) + phonetic 令 (OC *ren, *reŋ, *reŋs, *reːŋ, *reːŋs). On the oracle bone script, only thick raindrops are depicted falling from the sky.
Unclear. Schuessler (2007) proposes several possibilities:
* From Austroasiatic; compare Khmer ភ្លៀង (phliəng, “rain”), from Proto-Mon-Khmer *(p)liɲ ~ *(p)liəɲ ~ (p)liiɲ (“sky, rain”).
* Possibly related to Jingpho marang (“rain”), for which STEDT sets up Proto-Sino-Tibetan *m/s-raŋ (“rain”). Starostin also relates it to this Jingpho word and sets up Proto-Sino-Tibetan *rēŋ (“to drop”), also comparing Tibetan སྤྲིན (sprin, “cloud”) and Burmese ရည် (rany, “liquid; juice”).
* Possibly related to 隕 (OC *ɢunʔ, “to drop”) and 霣 (OC *ɢunʔ, “to rain; to fall down like rain”) if one assumes Proto-Sino-Tibetan *r/s/g-wa (“water; rain”) (or its variant *rwe-) can be simplified to *re- and *we-.
The character was later repurposed in 1248 by mathematician Li Ye as a placeholder, extending from its a little bit (of rain) meaning to indicate a bit more remaining. In Li Ye's notation, a number like 302 would be represented as 三百零二 (èr), literally three hundred and remaining two, with the 零 character used as a means of skipping the tens place, by indicating zero tens. It would thus implicitly take on the meaning of zero.

edges.subject: character:非
edges.text: Reported oracle-bone examples use 非 as a negative. Oracle-bone script is the earliest script class identified here, though the examples’ absolute dates are unresolved.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, CUHK
evidence.field: 形義通解; character forms; Middle Chinese reading
evidence.text: The database interprets the oracle bone and bronze graph as wings spread to either side; following Xu Shen and Lin Yiguang, it proposes ‘wings’ as the original sense and derives ‘turn against’ from the wings facing away from one another. It records oracle-bone 非 in 《合集》16927, ‘非𡆥(憂)’, as a negative meaning ‘without worry’, and also as a place name. For bronze inscriptions it gives 毛公鼎’s ‘余非’ as ‘my faults’ and 中山王方壺’s ‘寡人非之’ as ‘I judge it wrong’; Warring States bamboo slips use 非 as a negator. The same page records 非母, 微 rhyme, level tone, division III, 甫微切.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 非

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for Studies of Unearthed Documents and Ancient Chinese Characters; Wang Qingju
evidence.text: Wang argues that 非 and 北 were nearly homophonous in Old Chinese and that 非 split from 北 during the oracle-bone period. She reads the early forms as two people back-to-back, with short strokes added to distinguish the negative graph. She reports that extant oracle-bone examples of 非 include negation and a possible place name, and lists examples in 《合集》10977, 33147, 34707–34709, 24156, 33694, 33479, and 16927–16928. This is Wang’s analysis, not an uncontested account.
evidence.title: 王青菊：釋“非”

evidence.source: 雲漢古文字學論叢, vol. 1
evidence.text: The article describes 非 as a negative adverb and notes that oracle-bone positive clauses with 唯 contrast with negative clauses using 非. It gives parallel questions in 《合集》33694 and 28299. This supports an early negative use but does not date the first use absolutely or establish whether that use developed from a sense such as ‘oppose’ or ‘face away’.

edges.subject: character:面
edges.text: In simplified Chinese, 面 is the standardized counterpart of traditional 麵 in the flour and noodle word. This whole-character writing relationship does not make 麵 an internal component of 面 or establish borrowing from the face word.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形), A man’s face, with an eye exaggerated, derived from 𦣻. The horizontal stroke was added later. Unrelated to 自.
Etymology 2: Simplified from 麵 (elimination of 麥) as adopted by the Chinese Character Simplification Scheme (《漢字簡化方案》) in 1956.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *sV-merl (“face”); cognate with Mizo hmêl (“face”), Jingpho man (“face”). 偭 (OC *menʔ, “to turn; to violate”) is probably cognate (Wang, 1982), perhaps its endoactive (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》 (Taiwan Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants)
evidence.field: 說文釋形; 字樣說明; 釋義
evidence.text: The entry says the Shuowen form is 麪, glossed 麥末也 (Duan's text has 麥屑末也), analyzed as 麥 semantic plus 丏 phonetic. It says 麵 later became a common writing, and that 玉篇 and 廣韻 identify 麵 with 麪. The dictionary explains the later 麵 spelling as using 面 in the sound position, and reports examples for flour/powder in 後漢書 and 麵 in 南史 and Tang poems. Thus the record supports the older graphic analysis and later 麵 spelling, but does not date the transition or establish that 面’s face-word supplied the borrowed word itself.

evidence.field: 形義通解; oracle graph analysis
evidence.text: The database analyzes the oracle form as an eye (目) inside an enclosing outline, representing a face; it reports face as the original sense. It says a bronze form of 面 itself is not attested, though 面 occurs as a component in bronze graphs using 𦣻 plus the enclosure. It also reports a Chu-slip form whose enclosure strokes changed toward 臼, and cites 面 ‘face toward’ in 上博楚竹書二《容成氏》簡14. These are source assertions, not direct inspection of the cited artifacts.

evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形), A man’s face, with an eye exaggerated, derived from 𦣻. The horizontal stroke was added later. Unrelated to 自.
Etymology 2: Simplified from 麵 (elimination of 麥) as adopted by the Chinese Character Simplification Scheme (《漢字簡化方案》) in 1956.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *sV-merl (“face”); cognate with Mizo hmêl (“face”), Jingpho man (“face”). 偭 (OC *menʔ, “to turn; to violate”) is probably cognate (Wang, 1982), perhaps its endoactive (Schuessler, 2007).

evidence.text: The database describes 頁 in oracle and bronze forms as 卩 plus 首: a kneeling human figure with the head visually prominent. Its examples include oracle-bone uses meaning ‘pig’s head’ (合集15684) and ‘bowing the head’ (合集22215); it notes a Western Zhou bronze occurrence in 卯簋蓋 and a phrase 頁手 there, possibly abbreviated or erroneous. Its account of shape change says oracle-bone 頁 may show or omit hair; a W. Zhou bronze has hair; Warring States forms often distort the hair as 止; the small-seal form omits it. This is a database’s paleographic analysis, not direct visual inspection in this research.

evidence.text: Simplified form of 頁.  Pictograph of a head (首) on top of a person (卩). Means "head" when pronounced xié. Has unrelated meaning "leaf" when pronounced yè, due to this character being adopted as a shorthand form of 葉.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形): 首 + 卩 – head of a kneeling person, emphasising “head”.
頁 and 首 (OC *hljuʔ, *hljus) were originally the same pictographic character with the same meaning of “head”, and the graphical difference was that 頁 also included the body in addition to the head of the person.
頁 was later used as an alternative popular form of 葉 (“leaf; page”) to mean “sheet; page (of paper)”, which is its main meaning today.
The original sense of “head” is preserved in the radical 頁, which is used in characters such as 頭 (“head”) and 頸 (“neck”).
Alternative form of 葉 /叶 (“leaf; sheet (of paper)”).

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC)
evidence.field: 說文解字；音韻方言；字源字形
evidence.text: The page reproduces the Shuowen entry 頁, ‘head’, analyzed as from 𦣻 and 儿, and gives 胡結切. It also reproduces Duan Yucai’s note disputing the received wording and explaining the entry as an old form associated with 䭬/首; this records a later textual-critical interpretation, not a settled ancient graphic analysis. The page lists oracle-bone examples (including 乙8780 and 合22217), a mid-Western Zhou bronze 卯簋蓋, Chu bamboo-and-silk examples, a Shuowen small-seal form, and Eastern Han clerical evidence. Its dictionary explains the paper/page use as俗用頁 for 葉 and quotes Qing scholar Zhu Junsheng’s statement that 葉 was the proper graph and 頁 was the common form.

evidence.text: The database reports the bronze graph 飯 as 食 plus 反, with 反 functioning as phonetic. It quotes the Shuowen definition 食也，从食反聲 and two Guangyun spellings, 扶晚 and 符万. edges.text: The traditional character 餓 is glossed as 飢, “hungry,” and literary citations show its use for being hungry. These are the earliest supported sense and attestations here, though their dates do not establish when the character was first used.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry for 餓 quotes the Shuowen definition “飢也。从食，我聲” and gives modern Mandarin è. evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 《說文》; 字形分析; 音韻資料
evidence.text: The page transmits the Eastern Han Shuowen account: “雞，知時畜也。从隹，奚聲。鷄，籒文雞，从鳥。” Its account says Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥, while Qin forms and later use 隹, citing Ji Xusheng. This variation complicates a simple story that 鳥 was only a later substitute for 隹. It gives Guangyun fanqie 古奚 and Middle Chinese categories 見母, 平聲, 齊韻, 開口四等.

edges.text: 鳮 is recorded as a simplified-style variant associated with 雞 and appears as 鳮（雞） in the simplification scheme; its precise route to standardized 鸡 is not established.

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》, Taiwan Ministry of Education
evidence.text: The dictionary treats 鷄 as a graphic variant of 雞, citing Shuowen’s statement that it is the Zhou-script form written with 鳥, and records later dictionaries treating 鷄 and 雞 as equivalent in sound and meaning. It also records 鳮 as a variant and cites a cross-strait simplification comparison associating 鷄 with that form. This supports 鳮 as an attested simplified-style variant; the inspected page does not establish that modern simplified 鸡 arose by a single direct historical replacement of 奚 with 又.

evidence.source: 中华人民共和国国务院, 《汉字简化方案》 digital transcription at Wikisource
evidence.field: 国务院决议; 汉字简化第二表; 汉字偏旁简化表
evidence.text: The 1956-01-28 resolution says the first table was to be used from 1956-02-01 and lists 230 simplified characters; the second table lists 鳮（雞）. The component table lists 鸟（鳥）. This documents the officially published simplified spelling’s relation to 鳮 and the simplified bird component. It does not independently explain the pre-1956 history of 鳮, nor warrant saying that 鸡 formed historically as a semantic compound 又 + 鸟.

edges.subject: character:鸡
edges.text: A Qin bamboo-slip passage is reported to use 雞 for chicken. The oracle-bone place-name use does not show whether this was the graph’s earliest animal meaning.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義通解; 早期用例
evidence.text: The database analyzes early oracle forms as chicken pictures, often emphasizing the comb and open beak; it says 奚 was later added as a phonetic marker because the picture could be confused with other birds. It reports an oracle-bone use as a place name in 《合集》37363 and cites Qin bamboo slips from the Shuihudi annals (簡45), “十二月甲午雞鳴時，喜產,” as a use referring to chickens. It separately reports Chicken as the ordinary sense in Warring States/Qin slips and a Mawangdui silk text. In Mawangdui 《老子乙本》 line 65, 雞 is used as a phonetic loan for 谿 “valley/stream,” with the A copy reading 溪 and the Fu Yi text 谿. The page distinguishes these written uses rather than presenting a gloss list as a chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：雞

edges.text: In a Mawangdui text, 雞 is reported as a phonetic loan for 谿, “valley” or “stream”; another manuscript copy has 溪.
